ABRAHAM SCULTETUS
Greetings.

units.la: MEMINISTI, Frater & affinis honorande, petivisse te à me ante biennium: ut, quæ ego in Anglia collegissem scripta lectu digna, & Germanis nondum visa, vel per Chalcographorum manum tibi communicarem. Nondum satisfeci promissis, idq; ideo, quia redeuntem ex Marchia alia atq; alia nunc itinera, nunc negotia fatigâ-runt. Nuper vero aliquid otii cum nactus essem, excussi supellectilem meam librariam, & non pauca inueni Anglorum scripta, quæ in vulgus Germanorum hodieque ignota, lectu tamen iucunda, addo & proficua nostris, si iis innotescerent, essent futura. Interalia occurrit & hic, quem modo ad te mitto, libellus, cui vtrum plus dignitatis author, an gratiæ materies, eiusque tractatio conciliet, equidem addubito. Auctor est is, cuius pietas, doctrina, integritas, prudentiaque iudicio maximi Regis ante annos non ita multos digna habita fuit, quæ Archiepiscopatus Cantuariensis gloria coronaretur, GEORGIVS ABBATTVS.
units.tr: You will remember, my honoured brother and kinsman, that about two years ago you asked me to pass on to you, either by hand of the printers or otherwise, some of the writings I had gathered in England that are worth reading and not yet seen by the Germans. I have not yet kept my promise, and the reason is that on my return from the March, one journey and then another, now business, have worn me out. But recently, having at last some leisure, I went through my library and found not a few English writings which, though still unknown to the common run of Germans, are pleasant to read and would prove useful to our people if they became known. Among them this little book, which I now send you, has turned up, and I doubt whether the dignity of its author or the subject matter and its treatment will recommend it more. The author is the one whose piety, learning, integrity and prudence, in the judgment of the most excellent King, were not many years ago thought worthy to be crowned with the glory of the Archbishopric of Canterbury: George Abbot.

units.la: Materies sunt sex nobilissimæ Quæstiones, eæque ita pertractatæ, vt in neruosa breuitate grauissimarum rerum copiam inuenias. Atque eminent hic inter reliquas duæ, de Mendacio vna, de auctore peccati altera. Nosti, quod nouum doctrinæ genus nuper inuexerint in scholas suas (vtinam non eius praxin in Respublicas!) qui proditores fidei pariter Ecclesiasticæ & politicæ audiunt, IESVITÆ; nempe à meta, vero Christiano propositâ, minime aberrare, qui vel jurati verum dicere renuunt, aut am-biguis responsis interrogantem eludunt. Huius doctrinæ turpitudinem tam dextrè retegit, & quæ ab adversariis pro mendaciis & æquivocationibus diabolicis dicuntur, tam fortiter convellit Reverendissimus Abbattus: ut fieri non posse statuam, quin, qui hæc diligenter pellegerit, totam Æquivocorum cohortem, perinde ac ipsum Erebi principem sit execraturus.
units.tr: The subject matter is six most noble questions, treated in such a way that in sinewy brevity you will find a wealth of very weighty matter. Two stand out among the rest: one on lying, the other on the author of sin. You know that the Jesuits, who are heard as betrayers of the faith both ecclesiastical and political, have recently introduced into their schools a new kind of doctrine (would that they had not introduced its practice into commonwealths!), namely that those who refuse to tell the truth even under oath, or who mock the questioner with ambiguous answers, do not stray at all from the goal proposed by a true Christian. The most reverend Abbot exposes the shamefulness of this doctrine so skilfully, and so forcefully overturns what our adversaries call the diabolical lies and equivocations, that I would venture that whoever reads these pages carefully will execrate the whole band of Equivocators just as he would the prince of Erebus himself.

units.la: Jam quod crimen atrocius Ecclesiis Re-formatis infertur hodie, quàm quod DEUM iniquitatis non dico patronum, sed autorem ipsum facere dicuntur? At clarissimus ABBATTUS ita hoc diluit: ut una eademque opera & maledicorum accusatorum ora comprimat, & Ecclesiarum magnæ Britanniæ cum Gallicis, Germanicis, aliisque reformatis consensum luculenter commonstret.
units.tr: Now, what more atrocious charge is brought today against the Reformed Churches than that they make God not, I say, the defender, but the very author of iniquity? Yet the most illustrious Abbot refutes this charge in such a way that, by one and the same work, he both silences the mouths of the slanderous accusers and clearly shows the agreement of the Churches of Great Britain with the French, German and other Reformed Churches.

units.la: Mihi quidem vel eo nomine iterata huius libelli lectio perquam fuit grata, quod memoriam mihi renovaret beatæ illius hiemis, quam secutus Serenissimum Principe meum, ante quadriennium in Anglia transegi. Fateor enim, me mirifice recreatum fuisse effusa Reuerendissimi Archiepiscopi in me beniuolentia, candido D. D. Ioannis Kingi, Episcopi Londinensis meritissimi, in me affectu, insigni denique D. D. Iacobi Montacvti, Episcopi tum Bathoniovvallensis, nunc VVintoniēsis, humanitate, qui quasi manu sua ad Regis ter maximi alloquium me ducere non dubitauit.
units.tr: For my part, on this account alone, the repeated reading of this little book was exceedingly pleasing to me, since it renewed the memory of that blessed winter which I spent in England some four years ago, following my most serene Prince. For I confess that I was wonderfully refreshed by the abundant kindness of the most reverend Archbishop towards me, by the sincere affection of the most worthy Dr John King, Bishop of London, and finally by the courtesy of the distinguished Dr James Montagu, then Bishop of Bath and Wells, now of Winchester, who did not hesitate to lead me, as it were by his own hand, to an audience with the most great King.

units.la: Neq; vero obliuione conterere possum dies illos, quos mihi exoptata cum viris clarissimis iuxta & doctissimis conuersatio amabiles pariter & desiderabiles reddidit, cum Matthæo, inquam, Sudliuio, cum Thoma Mortono, EpiscopoCestrensi,cumD.OueralloDecano Paulino,cumGeorgioHaqueuillo,Serenissimo PrincipiCarolo à sacris,cū innumeris aliis, quorum sermones etiamnum animæ meæ iucundum sunt pabulum. Nam quid ego tibi Oxonienses Theologos memorem? Singletonum,qui cum beatis nunc agit, Robertum Abbattum, Professorem tum Regium, nunc alterum ab Iuello Episcopatus Sarisburiensis lumen,
units.tr: Nor can I wear away by forgetfulness those days which my conversation with those most famous and most learned men made both pleasant and desirable: with Matthew Sutcliffe, I mean, with Thomas Morton, Bishop of Chester, with Dr Overall, Dean of St Paul's, with George Hakewill, with Charles, the most serene Prince's chaplain, and with countless others, whose words are still a pleasant food for my soul. For what need I tell you of the Oxford theologians? Singleton, who now lives with the blessed; Robert Abbot, then Regius Professor, now the other light of the see of Salisbury after Jewel;
DEDICATORY.

units.la: Sed quo delabor? Aperietur nobis alius de his dicendi campus. Tu nunc, mi frater, li-bellum hunc, veteris & indubitati mei in te amoris tesseram cape, & prosperein Do-mino age. Heidelbergæ II. Se-ptembr. 1616.
units.tr: But whither do I drift? Another field for discussion will open to us on these matters. Now you, my brother, take this little book, a token of my long-standing and unquestioned love for you, and may you prosper in the Lord. Heidelberg, 2 September 1616.
To the Christian Reader
S.

units.la: CVM superiori anno, ex Academiæ no-stræ prudentissimis institutis, & officij mei ratione, aut Paulina mihi aliqua pu-blice legenda esset Epistola, aut habendæ aliæ prælectiones sex; utilius ego multo & fructuosius judicavi, vel pauca copiosè & dilucide explicare, quam multa summatim tetigisse, aut rapidius festinantiusque transcurrisse. Quamuis etenim breuiuscula illa explanatio scripturarum, antiquioribus Ecclesiæ temporibus satis familiaris fuerit, ut ex Scholiis Basilij Magni in Psalmos Dauidicos facillimum est videre; & eius etiam usus, fructusque non mediocris apud nos hodie esse possit, dum universæ alicuius Epistolæ scopus & materia in arctum, methodo tamen & divisione accurata, compingantur, & ipsi rerum uberiorum fontes lin-gua potius quam digito signentur, è quibus tanquam viva cum scaturigine emergentibus, eæ exhauriri queant aquæ, quibus omnis Dei hortus & irrigetur, & recreetur: tamen, cum procelloso nostro turbidoq; seculo, convenire rectius existimavi, vacillantia hominum judicia confirmare, & in rebus vel ad fidem, vel ad mores pertinentibus, controversis apud aliquos, definite & aperte aliquid pronunciare. Cui quidem sententiæ jam abhinc diu apud me receptæ, illud etiam pondus roburque addidit, quod salutaribus Euange-lij principiis, & elemētis fidei ad populum explicandis, fuggesta, pulpitaque subseruire soleant, cum concertationes & digladiationes, circa res diuinas, exortas, Theologorum scho-læ & Academiæ multo potius, suo quasi iure sibi vendicent. Seligebam igitur, partim impulsu meo, aliorum partim hor-tatu, quæstiones sex (in quibus tanquam in curriculo me ex-ercerem) quas neque mea opera indignas, nec ætati in qua degimus ineptas & importunas autumaui. Vere etenim profiteri licet, in illis arenam offerri, in qua lectionis & iudi-cij non dico mei, sed cuiuspiam Theologi periculum fiat, cum causa sit multiplex, & non paucis difficultatibus inuo-luta: immo vndiq; sit præiudicium, vndiq; præcipitium. Et vt intempestiua non sit nostra disputatio, facit orbis vndi-quaq; deflenda iniquitas & [?]ἀκαταστασία tam varia latèque nunc diffusa, vt nullus fere terrarum locus sit, in quo medela, aut opinionibus & conscientiis, aut consuetudinibus hominum afferenda nō sit. Et non minima malorum aut scrupulorum hodiernorum pars in istis quæ nostro Sermone expediun-tur, hæret, dum hinc mendaciorum frequens & infamis vsus veraces perturbet; illinc de Baptismo conceptæ superstitio-nes conscientias affligant: alicubi ab Astrologorum decre-tis, velut ab Oraculis pendeatur; alibi quid in idolorum tem-plis adeundis vel non adeundis agendum sit, nesciatur: hic, num grassante vel persecutione vel peste fugiendum sit, aut operiendum, dubitetur; illic, quo pacto Deus in malis ope-retur, vt ne agat mala, ambigatur. Quæ quidem omnia vt diuersa sunt, neque vlla serie inter se cohærentia, ita minus audienti aut legenti fastidium parient, cum è maxima va-rietate, minima soleat nausea suboriri: & rari, meo iudicio, futuri sint, quibus in vna aut altera quæstione expendenda, horulam impendisse dolebit. Et alicui fortassis accendetur animus, dum nostra audiat, in simili argumento progredi, aut ea fusius explicare, quæ angustius & contractius pertra-ctandi, scholarum nostrarum consuetudo necessitatem im-posuit. posuit. Pauca etenim sunt, quæ distincte; & ut decet unica, quouis die, expediri poterunt hora. Vbi tamen prout potui, & conatibus meis benedixit Iehoua misericors pater, hæc omnia absoluissem, nihil amplius facitandum existimaui, quam vt in reliquo & consueto studiorum meorum curriculo progrederer, istis penitus missis factis, quæ polito limatoque nostri seculi iudicio non responderent. Verum cum importuna nonnullorum vota sæpius accederent, qui satis pertinaciter precibus contenderunt, vt sui instruendi & satisfaciendi gratia, mearum obseruationum exemplar, ad minus vellem porrigere, & communicando impertire, post longam deliberationem, è consilio etiam eorum, qui autoritate plurimum apud me pollere debent, consultius iudicaui, & petentibus & non petentibus morem gerere, in apertum hominum conspectu qualiacunq; sint emittendo. Prout igitur anno nouissimo, astantium auribus oblata peruenerunt, ita nunc oculis repræsento, mutatis adiectiue vel nullis vel paucissimis, præt[?]erquam eo vnico, de Romanensium novo dogmate cuius primo capite iam mentio facta est. Et illud, quoniam cum argumento tam optime quadret meo, non duxi omittendum, licet eius magna pars intra annum acta gestaq; sit. Reliqua integra prodeunt, de quibus tamen omnibus ista præmittenda atque præmonenda censui.
units.tr: When last year, by the very prudent regulations of our Academy and the duties of my office, I was due to lecture publicly either on some Pauline Epistle or on six other lectures, I judged it far more useful and fruitful to explain a few things fully and clearly than to touch on many things briefly or to pass over them too hastily and superficially. For although that short sort of explanation of the Scriptures was quite familiar to the earlier times of the Church, as may easily be seen from the Scholia of Basil the Great on the Psalms of David, and although its use and no small benefit may be found among us today, provided the aim and matter of some whole Epistle are compressed into a small space, yet arranged with method and careful division, and the very sources of richer matters are indicated by the tongue rather than by the finger, so that waters may be drawn from them as from a living spring welling up, by which the whole garden of God may be watered and refreshed: nevertheless, in our stormy and turbulent age, I thought it more proper to strengthen the wavering judgments of men and to pronounce something clearly and definitely on matters pertaining either to faith or to morals that are disputed among some. This opinion, which I have held for a long time, was given further weight and strength by the fact that pulpits and platforms are wont to serve the salutary principles of the Gospel and the elements of faith to be explained to the people, whereas the schools and universities of the theologians much more rightfully claim for themselves the disputes and contests that have arisen concerning divine matters. I therefore chose, partly at my own impulse and partly at the urging of others, six questions (in which I might exercise myself as on a racecourse), which I judged neither unworthy of my labour nor foolish and out of place for the age in which we live. For it may truly be declared that in them a field is offered in which the risk of reading and judgment, not of mine alone but of any theologian, is tested, since the matter is manifold and entangled with not a few difficulties: indeed on every side there is prejudice, on every side a precipice. And so that our disputation may not be untimely, the iniquity of the world, to be lamented on every side, and the disorder so varied and now so widely spread, make it so that there is scarcely any place on earth where a remedy must not be applied either to men's opinions and consciences or to their customs. And a not inconsiderable part of the evils and scruples of our day sticks in those matters which are treated in our discourse: on the one hand the frequent and infamous practice of lying disturbs truthful people; on the other, superstitions conceived about Baptism afflict consciences; somewhere people depend on the decrees of astrologers as if on oracles; elsewhere it is unknown what ought to be done in going or not going to the temples of idols; here it is doubted whether one should flee or remain when plague or persecution is raging; there it is uncertain in what way God works in evils, so that He does not do evil. All these matters, since they are diverse and not connected with one another in any sequence, will therefore cause less weariness to the listener or reader, since from the greatest variety a least nausea is usually produced; and, in my judgment, there will be few who will regret having spent a little hour on one or another question to weigh. And perhaps some will be stirred in spirit, as they hear our words, to proceed on a similar subject, or to explain more fully those things which the custom of our schools has compelled us to treat more narrowly and briefly. For there are few things which can be distinctly settled, and as befits a single one, in any given hour of the day. When, however, merciful Father Jehovah blessed my efforts as far as I was able and I had finished all these things, I judged that nothing further was to be done than to proceed in the rest of my accustomed course of studies, having entirely set aside those things which would not answer to the polished and refined judgment of our age. But since the importunate prayers of some people often came to me, who quite persistently urged that for the sake of instructing and satisfying themselves I should at least offer and impart a copy of my observations by communicating them, after long deliberation, and also on the advice of those who ought to have the greatest authority with me, I judged it more prudent to comply with both those who asked and those who did not, by sending them out into the open view of men, whatever their quality. Accordingly, just as they reached the ears of those present last year, so now I present them to the eyes, with additions and changes either none or very few, except for the one concerning the new dogma of the Romanists, of which mention has already been made in the first chapter. And since this fits so well with my subject, I did not think it should be omitted, although a large part of it was done and carried out within the year. The rest is published whole, but I thought all these things should be prefaced and forewarned.

units.la: Apud hominum genus, nihil facilius, nihil crebrius reperitur, quâ fingendo & comminiscendo veritati contraire. Insinuat sese puerulo iam balbutienti, mendaciorum pater Dæmon, & semen noxium in tenero spargit animo, quod per omnem vitam cum reliquis peccati zizaniis coalescit. Et vbi data est occasio, inolita iâ & à cunis inueterata, mentiendi in minutiis consuetudo, in fraudes, imposturas, dolos, technas ita tandem prorumpit, vt fides fere penitus ex orbe exulet, & in fœderibus, induciis, pactis, promissis, nihil pene integrum sanctumque permaneat. Hic si vellent vafri homines delicta fateri sua, & ingenue errata agnoscere, multo mi-nor facesseretur Theologo molestia; sed econtra fit, vt non desint qui commenta fraudesque in nonnullis tueri acriter non erubescant, quin potius exemplis è diuina historia peti-tis suos lapsus commendare, aut excusare saltem satagant. Et mirum est quoufq; caro & sanguis in his sibi applaudant, dum nequitiæ & malitiæ apud animum destinatæ & decre-tæ suum, speciosum velum possint obducere. Huic ego næ-uo vehementer cupio remedium afferre, (prout olim Augu-stinus, de Mendacio, & contra Mendacium doctissime dif-ferens) vt qui veritatem apud omnes inuiolatam desidero & exopto. Quo longe odiosior visa est duorum nostratium Southwelli & Gerardi assertio, quippe qua non modo men-dacio, sed & periurio porta aperitur; cui viam dare, vti arbi-tror, extremæ & deploratæ impietatis est. Exurgent Gentes & Ethnici, in die iudicij, & Christianos talia sequentes & docentes condemnabunt. At ne dum alios mendacij coar-guam, ipse tam certum crimen cōsinxisse videar, (quod ego insigniter detestandum semper censui) non pigebit affir-mare, rei gestæ veritatem è testimonio plurium fide dignif-simorum testium apparere. Affuerunt etenim & adstiterunt Gerardo, adeoq; rem omnem scriptis postea consignarunt, D. Richardus Barckleius, Eques Auratus, Custos summus tunc temporis Arcis Londinensis, vir piissimus & doctissi-mus, Gulielmus Wadus Regio Consilio Sanctiori ab Epi-stolis, Edouardus Cookus Attornatus (vt appellant) Gene-ralis, Thomas Flemingus, Regius in negotiis forensibus Pro-curator, omnes fidei inuiolatæ & multis nominibus apud Principem sapientissimam, & Senatum Anglicanum lau-dati & accepti. Vivunt isti omnes, & cuiquam interroganti testimonium reddere parati sunt. Sed & superstes est Gerar-dus, uti omnes credimus, è custodia, non ante ita multos menses, astu elapsus, cui pro se iam tandem respondendi potestas est, si ipsius verba vel in minimo apice scrupulose male capiamus. Quæ ad Southvvellum autem spectant, in aperta Curia acta sunt & transacta. Credo tamen adversa-rios vi ipsa veritatis victos, rem non inficiaturos (utcunque divulgatio ipsis cordi fortassis non sit futura) cum a-liqua, sobrie serioque cogitantibus, huius dogmatis vestigia ante annos aliquot pressa, appareant, licet paucis nostro-rum tunc temporis obseruata. Non grauabor verbo tange-re, quod ante quinquennium non longe ab Oxonio conti-git. Cum potestas extraordinaria illo tempore, sub Regio diplomate viris aliquibus doctissimis & spectatæ integrita-tis facta fuisset, ut quotquot iuxta illos morantes templa ad-ire recusarent, ad se aduocarent, & super quibusdam articu-lis virtute iuramenti præstandi, interrogarent, adductus est unus inter reliquos, qui iuratus etiam ea confidentissime respondit, quæ maxima adstantium pars, indubitatè secus se habere, firmiter crediderunt. Ille tamen post seriam & lo-cupletem monitionem, perrexit dicere quod dixisset, neq; aliam voluit cantilenā canere. Quod cum satis mirati essent omnes, obstinatam eius pertinaciam damnantes tacite, tan-dem unus, aut perspecta aut suspecta saltem fraude, ita infit: Veremur sane plurimū, ne dum ista affirmes, fraudulenter facias, tu autem aliud sermone spondes. Verum num iura-bis, te isthæc quæ dixisti omnia sincere dicere, & cum nulla reservatione? (Eo Reservationis nomine, quod illorum est, secretam tacitamque aut materiæ aut alicuius circumstan-tiæ celationem aut suppressionem innuebat.) Hæc cum se-mel iterumque inculcasset, renuebat planè alter, id ex iure-iurando pronunciare, neque ullo voluit assentire modo. Ita iuvenis illius astutia nonnihil est detecta, & non mediocris iniecta suspicio, aliquid latitare tale, quale in Southvvello & Gerardo nuper magis eminuit. Cum ego isthæc scriberem, præter illos è quorum sermone hæc omnia ad aures peruenerunt meas, virum ipsum ornatissimum & doctissimum, qui talia tunc temporis coram submonuerat, consulendum censui, vt quod compertæ veritatis esset, neque aliud quidquam, scripto mandarem. Is autem non modo hæc omnia agnouit & recognouit, verum pro singulari suo veritatis expiscandæ & enucleate eruendæ desiderio, & pro egregia in meipsum humanitate, aliud etiam communicauit; quod, vt è tenebris iam tandem eruatur, dignissimum iudicaui. Consilij etenim fere vniuersi rationem complectitur, quo instructi Jesuitæ, & è Seminariis emissi sacrifici, in Angliam redeunt. Nihil autem quicquam apud illos magis in arcanis haberi, ex eo manifestum est, quod chartis hæc tantum, non typis, commendentur: quod detegere nolint ipsi, cum in quæstionem venerint: quod nostrorum vix quisquam aut viderit, aut audierit, nisi eminus & à longinquo stans. Quo autore consilia aut præcepta hæc prodierint, ex rei de-{†}prehensæ circumstantiis, non immerito dubitari potest; vt etiam de tempore, perspicuum non est; &, num vnius sint congesta, & conclusa opera, vel potius plurium. In fine petitiones quasdam comperio, quibus Papa Pius Quintus ante annos viginti septem, censuram immiscuisse suam diserte proditur. Postquam etenim petitioni fere cuilibet, aut Annuit aut Abnuit adiungitur, in fine ad verbum subiicitur: Ista petitiones in forma superius scripta exhibita Sanctissimo Patri Pio Quinto, per illustrem Cardinalem D. Francisc. Alciatum Vice protectorem Anglorum, in absentia Cardinalis Morioni, quas omnes & singulas approbauit, vel improbauit dictus Sanctissimus Pater, vt annotatum est, festo Sancti Michaelis Archangeli, viua voce. Anno Domini 1571. In tractatu tamen superiori, vbi quæstiones ad Schisma, ad Tribunal Judicis, ad Missam, ad Baptismum, &c. spectantes discutiuntur, non est simplex solutio, cum negatione aut affirmatione pura, sed rationes decretorum, è Nauarro, Thom, Aquinate, Bonauentura, Patre Roberto, & aliis subiiciuntur: è quarum aliqui-bus coniecturam licet capere, post Annum 1571. & Pij V. tempora, prodiisse. Quamuis enim Martinus ab Azpilcueta Doctor Navarrus, Hispanicè & Lusitanicè Enchiridion siue Manuale Confessariorum & Poenitentium, etiam Pauli Tertij tempore ediderit, non tamen Latinè usquead Annum 1573. quum primum Romæ excusum est, præmissa Epistola Dedicatoria ad Pontificem Maximum Gregorium XIII. Posteaautem in Belgio Antuerpiæ rursus typis mandatum est. Anno 1579. per Christophorum Plantinum; ubi ex Privilegiis, Epistolis & Censuris in fine & principio appositis, de certis priorum editionum temporibus, expresse edocetur. Cum autem Autor operis tunc octogenarius, (quod de se profitetur) in Latina editione plura addiderit, immutaverit, limatius correxerit, verisimillimum iudicetur, è Latino exemplari Autorem Responsionum & Conclusionum istarum omnia desumpsisse, quod tum demum fieri oportuit post Annum 1573. Papalem Cathedram obtinente Gregorio Decimotertio. Et citata è Navarro testimonia, quotquot ego contuli, cum Latino Manuali capitibus numerisque omnino consentiunt. Utcunque tamen isthæc ad Pij Quinti fortassis non pertingant tempora; sub Gregorio XIII. emissa fuisse ex eo constat, quod ante annos duodecim ad illius manus hæc scripta pervenerint, cuius ex humanitate, mihi facta est legendi & transcribendi copia. Et tu certe inter libros unius aut alterius Pontificij, in Romanam sedem devotissimi, & non indocti[?], in agro Southantoniensi deprehensa fuere, cum illic subito venisset explo-ratum, è Iusticiariis Regiis quoad pacem unus, doctis a-liis probisque comitantibus. Et ab illo tempore retinuit a-pud se vir ornatissimus ibi tum præsens, satis habens illorum placita sibi ipsi detexisse; donec intellecto, in nostram De Mendacio materiam hæc aptissime incidisse, sua sponte mihi communicauit. Quod autem apud nostros sacrificu-los, Anglosque Transmarinos, hæc sanctissimæ sint autho-ritatis, neque à nostris conficta, sed ab illis accepta serio: in-de cuiuis non cæcutienti patet, quod perannos iam viginti ultimo elapsos, eorum omnes actiones, gestus, praxes cum istis convenire ad amussim reperiamus. Testes sunt tot fraudes, & evasiones perversæ, quas [?]xaminis[?] tempore, magistratibus ad id munus deputatis, huiusmodi homines toties obtruserunt. Quæ autem de Gerardo & Southvvello retulimus,ita omni ex parte cum Thesibus[?] istis quadrant,ut non ex alio,quam isto hausta fuisse fonte, sit meridiana luce clarius. Operæ precium igitur iudicaui post recentiorum illorum duorum assertiones utcunque disquisitas, ulterius adhuc pergere, & abstrusas rationes,adeoque reconditas ventilare,quibus freti duo illi, reliquique socij talia ausi sint. In quibus, si ea solum, quæ ad Mendacium, Mendacijq; genus summum Periurium, attinent, explicuerim; neque (ut de Schismate, de Baptismo, de Missa aliisque multis, quæ habentur multa, omnino præteream) de reliquis, quæ simul cum iis involuuntur,de Regimine,& autoritate Reginæ Serenissimæ & Invictissimæ, sed & Judicum illius; ut & Papæ etiam ea in re insolentia, verba fecerim: partim illud fuit, quod deMendacio solo redarguendo,mihi scopus erat præfixus,& extra illos cancellos expatiari non oportebat; partim, quod iustis voluminibus, illius postulati (de principe è solio deturbanda) arrogantia & iactantia Antichristiana, à nostratibus discussa demonstrataque fuerit. Quia tamen Christianus intelliget orbis, quæ sint illa,quæ murmure auriculari, suis sectatoribus insulurrant Anglo-Romanenses, proponam verbatim ea, quæ in præsenti negotio ex chartis deprehensis occurrunt, ut, quam misere turpiterque à ge-nuina Euangelij doctrina, & recepta apud omnes Christi martyres sententia, hi Antichristi testes deflexerint, quili-bet libet hominum intelligat. In Quæstionibus ergo pertinen-tibus ad Tribunal Judicis, hæc est secunda: Quomodo sit re-spondendum in Tribunali hæreticorum? Responsio. Optime re-spondet is, qui non erubescit non solum ea, quæ sunt fidei, sed etiam ea, quæ sunt facti; quia in illis est exaltatio fidei, & in his gloria Dei: qui igitur propter hanc suam confessionem occisus est, vere est martyr. Nazar. cap. 11, nu. 40. Subditur immediate: Iuramentum exactum à Iudice non competente, non obligat, nisi secundum intentionem iuran-tis. Nau. cap. 12. num. 8. qui les sunt omnes nunc in Anglia (incompetentes scilicet iudices) in iurisdictione Ecclesiastica, quia currunt, & non mittuntur, Filij sine patre vel matre. Potest igitur Catholicus tractus coram hæreticis, vel recusare iuramentum (quod est prudentius) vel sophistice iurare, & sophistice respondere, singulis suis interrogationibus, nisi inquantum interrogatur de fide. Ibidem. Nam tyrannice interrogatus de fide debet respondere. D. Thom. 2.2. quæst. 3. art. 2. Qui iurat aliquid illicitum facere, cum animo faciendi, bis peccat. Nau. cap. 12, num. 12. Interrogatus ergo de Catholicis indicandis, & iuratus, si prætextu sui iuramenti nominat aliquos, bis peccat; quinetiam, si absq; eo indicat aliquos, peccat mortaliter, quia auxilium fert in mortali peccato. Idem cap. 11. num. 13. Quæstio nona hæc est: Quomodo licitum est æquivocare vel nomina mutare? Responsio. Interrogati à summis Commissariis Regiis, veloerum[?] apparitoribus, An sint sacerdotes, cum sint; vel alias, An sint Catholici; peccant mortaliter, si vel tacent, vel æquivocant; quia ab his interrogantur in odium religionis, in quo casu quilibet tenetur confiteri fidem suam, Marc. 8. Qui me, &c. Et Luc 8. Qui me erubuerit, &c. Apparitores appello non solum eos, qui illo officio funguntur, sed etiam quos paratos video, illos apprehendere ol[?] odium religionis, quemadmodum ancillæ interrogantes D. Petrum, Luc. 22. An tales sint illi, qui sedent ad telonium in oppidis maritimis, d[?] bito[?], qui non tam quærunt promoueri fidem hæreticam per suas apprehensiones Catholicorum, quam impleri suas crumenas: qui igitur illis interrogantibus de eorum statu vel religione, ex simplicitate cordis vel tacent, vel æquiuocant, non peccant, quia non tenentur confiteri, si ob aliud interrogentur, quam ob odium religionis. Pater Rupertus. I. 2. quæst. 5. art. 1. dub. 2. vel ob odium religionis eos interrogare, non est magis probabile in illis, quam ob aliam causam, nimirum quod quæ[?]erunt eorum pecunias. Interrogati in via ab itinerantibus simul, aut in mensa, à simul discumbentibus, vel de statu, vel de religione, possunt vel tacere, vel æquiuocare, quia ipsi ex curiositate interrogât, & conf. si fidei est affirmatiuum præceptum, quod non obligat, nisi pro tempore & loco. Et hic nulla exit, vel vtilitas proximi, vel honor Dei, aut saltem nullum detrimentum proximi, aut Dei, & sic non obligat præceptum. D. Tho prædicto loco. Sequuntur aliæ quæstiones tâ quam Extrauagantes, quæ num eiusdem sint temporis, aut eiusdem personæ determinationes, cuius sunt superiores, non intelligo. Suspicor tamen eiusdem non esse; quia nude proponuntur solutiones, sine aliqua cōfirmatione è Nauarro aut aliis. Istis tamen in fine subiunguntur ea, de quibus Pontifex Pius V. Annuit, vel Abnuit, (vt supra) suum, pronunciauit. Quæstionum tamen vna est: An sacerdos possit, sicut vestes & habitum mutat, ita & comam nutrire, & mutare nomen, & si interrogaretur in portu, vel alibi aliquo nomine ab aliquibus, qui eū habent suspectum, an possit illud negare, scilicet, non esse suum nomen? simile est dubiū de patria, parentibus, amicis, &c. Cum interrogatus fuerit extra iudicium in itinere. Responsio: Potest: nec videtur in hoc casu dubium: potest enim quis veritatem tacere, vel dissimulare, modo directe eam non neget. Et postea: An sacerdos interrogatus in via de locis, à quibus venerit, item de religione sua, An faueat fidei Romanæ necne: posset aliquo responso indirecto, effugere & deludere interrogationem, vel, an teneatur consiteri veritatem? Responsio. Potest aliquis deludere. Tum post multa, quatuor coniunctim sequuntur quæstiones: An liceat Catholico recusare iuramentum, à magistratibus hæreticis ad damnum sui ipsius, & aliorum Catholicorum propositum? Responsio: Imo tenetur recusare, & subterfugere, quantum potest. Sed, An teneatur iuramentum huiusmodi recusare. cusare vsque ad torturam? Responsio: Sic ex iuramento huiusmodi damnum notabile fidei, aut religionis sequeretur, tortura potius subeunda esset. Tum: Quantum iis revelare tenetur per iuramentum requisitum? Respondeo, quia iniuria extortum est iuramentum, & hi magistratus incompetentes sunt Iudices, nil revelare tenetur, quatenus absque mendacio & falsitate subterfugere potest. At, Si temere & inconsiderate haereticis iuramentum dederit, se velle ad omnia interrogata sincere respondere; illi vero interrogant postea, de multis, quae, si revelentur, tenduntin gravissimum Catholicorum damnum, & praeiudicium: Quid in hac causa faciendum? Respondeo: peccavit ita iurando, & iuramentum non debet esse vinculum iniquitatis, & propterea non tenetur ita respondere, sicut superius dictum est. Post unam & alteram interrogationem, de Regina (post Bullam Pij Quinti editam) obedienda, vel non obedienda, sequitur ista quaestio: Orthodoxus Catholica Ecclesiae sacerdos, ab haereticis comprehensus, ad Tribunal Iudicis sistitur, qui ab eo iusiurandum exigit, quo astringitur ad respondendum bona & vera fide, omnibus, quae illi proponuntur, quaestionibus: interrogatur forte quoties Missam celebravit, quo in loco, & quibus praesentibus, &c. Hic si vere, & ut feres [?] habet, responderit, non est dubium, quin, propter grave, quod inde oritur, scandalum, ipse & alii maximis afficientur damnis. Quaritur, an rebus ita stantibus, teneatur sacerdos, cum se, tum alios prodere? Respondeo: non tenetur, quia non est legitimum iudicium. Neque iurantis intentio debet esse, nisi ad ea dicenda, quae tencatur. Quod si esset, dicendi omnia, esset iniqua intentio, quae non obligat, quia esset in praeiudicium aliorum, qui damnum patientur. Non debet tamen mendacium dicere, sed id quod in aliquo sensu est verum, etiam si non fit in sensu interrogantis, quia ad eius intentionem non tenetur respondere. Haec autem quae dixi intelligo, si absit scandalum pusillis; id enim vitare debet, nec ulla danda occasio infirmis peccandi, praesertim in re fidei: potius ponenda vita, si necessarium fuerit ad illius salutem. Tum postea: Hoc tempus & occasio aptissima videtur, ad confitendum Deum coram hominibus, ne Christus Christus ipsum erubescat confiteri coram Patre: sed non tenetur sei-psum, neque alios prodere, non requisitus: sed requisitus de se, consilium esset dicere veritatem, & mori pro fide, si opus est: alios autem non potest revelare: sed quia index haereticus vel schismaticus amittit omnem iurisdictionem, non tenetur. Interrogatus veritatem in iudicio, respondere debet, neque de se, neque de aliis, sed potest [?]Am-phibologicè vel Æquivocè respondendo, iniquitatem iudicis declara-re. Hæc Latinè habentur ad verbum omnia. Cessent amplius mirari, qui vel ad clavum, vel ad remum Reipubl. Anglicanæ sedent, quid in causa sit, quamobrem tam fraudulenter & sophisticè & captiosè à Roma Rhemisque redeuntes, post onus iuramenti sese soleant gerere, cum venenatum istud lac à primo in Seminaria introitu imbiberint, suxerintque. Non potest fons amarus emittere aquas dulces, ut nec ex tribulis uvæ, nec à sentibus ficus colliguntur. Utinam aliquando tandem Romanis philtris & incantationibus pellecti Angli nostri sapere inciperent, & venena euomentes, priusquam in immedicabilem sui corruptelam transfierint, intra patriæ suæ spatia, amœna, salutaria, cœlestibus exundantia fluentis, se continerent: aut, si vellent eousque delirare, ut hostilibus vocati sibilis, in obsequium Pontificium, velint nolint omnes boni, iurare consentirent, in Angliam saltem sub specie ovili, cum lupi sint, redire nollent: aut, si sit redeundum, iniquitatem mendacio, perduellionem periurio cumulare non procederent, sed extra impietatis prodigiosæ ripas se longissime custodirent. Satis sit hucusque præter viam cucurrisse. Veritatis, [?]eiusque simplicis & incontaminatæ, Iehoua Deus est. Vehementer autem illum irritant, qui mendaciis & periuriis, quocunque demum colore fucatis, conatus suos stabilire concupiscunt. Si bona sint, quæ aggrediuntur, bonis promoveant mediis. Si fides sit Christiana, quam disseminatam cupiunt, Christiano incedant passu. Rectissime enim Job cap. 13, 7. Nunquid Deus indiget vestro mendacio, ut pro illo loquamini dolos? vel, ut alij habent: An pro Deo forti loqui debetis iniquitatem, aut pro eo loqui debetis fraudem? Et de istis hactenus.
units.tr: Nothing among mankind is easier or more common than to invent and fabricate in opposition to the truth. The father of lies, the Devil, insinuates himself into the little child while he is still babbling, and sows a harmful seed in his tender mind, which grows together with the other tares of sin for the whole of life. And when the opportunity arises, the habit of lying in small matters, already ingrained and long established from the cradle, at last breaks out into frauds, impostures, deceits and tricks, so that faith almost wholly disappears from the world, and in covenants, truces, pacts and promises scarcely anything remains whole and sacred. Here, if crafty men were willing to confess their faults and frankly acknowledge their errors, far less trouble would be caused to the theologian; but on the contrary it happens that there are not wanting those who sharply defend their inventions and frauds in some cases, and who not only are not ashamed to do so, but eagerly try to commend or at least excuse their lapses by examples taken from divine history. And it is strange how far flesh and blood flatter themselves in these matters, while they can throw a fair veil over wickedness and malice fixed and decreed in the mind. Against this blemish I earnestly desire to bring a remedy, as Augustine did long ago, who discoursed most learnedly on lying and against lying, because I desire and long for the truth to be kept inviolate among all. Much more hateful, therefore, seemed the assertion of our two countrymen Southwell and Gerard, for it opens the door not only to lying but also to perjury; and to give access to this, as I think, is the mark of extreme and desperate impiety. The Gentiles and heathen will rise up on the day of judgment and will condemn Christians who follow and teach such things. But lest, while I accuse others of lying, I myself should seem to have fabricated so certain a crime (which I have always judged to be especially detestable), I will not hesitate to affirm that the truth of the matter done appears from the testimony of several most trustworthy witnesses. For indeed, D. Richard Barckley, Knight of the Golden Spur, then chief Keeper of the Tower of London, a most pious and most learned man, William Wade, Secretary of the Privy Council, Edward Cooke, Attorney General (as they call him), and Thomas Fleming, the royal Procurator in legal business, were present with Gerard and stood by him, and afterwards set down the whole matter in writing: all of them men of unbroken faith, and praised and accepted in many respects by the most wise Prince and the English Senate. All of these men are alive and are ready to give testimony to anyone who asks. But Gerard also survives, as we all believe, having escaped from custody by cunning not many months ago, and he now has at last the power to answer for himself, if we take his words carelessly amiss even in the smallest particle. As for what concerns Southwell, the matters were done and transacted in open court. Yet I believe that our opponents, overcome by the very force of truth, will not deny the matter (however much its publication may perhaps not be welcome to them), since to those thinking soberly and seriously, traces of this doctrine, pressed some years ago, appear, although they were observed by few of ours at that time. I will not hesitate to touch upon a thing that happened not long ago, about five years since, near Oxford. When an extraordinary commission had been given under the royal warrant to certain most learned men of tested integrity, so that they might summon to themselves all who, living in their neighbourhood, refused to attend the churches, and might question them about certain articles under the force of an oath to be taken, one man was brought forward among the rest, who, sworn also, answered with great confidence those things which the greatest part of the bystanders firmly believed were certainly otherwise. Yet he, after a serious and copious warning, went on saying what he had said, and would not sing any other tune. When all were rather amazed, silently condemning his obstinate stubbornness, at last one man, either clearly perceiving or at least suspecting a fraud, began thus: "We greatly fear indeed that while you affirm these things you are acting fraudulently, and that in your speech you promise one thing while meaning another. But will you swear that you are saying all these things you have said sincerely, and without any reservation?" (By the name of reservation he meant that secret and tacit concealment or suppression of some matter or circumstance, which is their custom.) When he had pressed this once and again, the other man flatly refused to pronounce this on oath, and would in no way agree to it. Thus the cunning of that young man was somewhat detected, and no small suspicion was raised that something of that kind lay hidden, such as lately stood out more clearly in Southwell and Gerard. When I was writing these things, besides those from whose speech all these things came to my ears, I thought I should consult the very distinguished and learned man himself, who had at that time admonished such a person in his presence, so that I might commit to writing only what was of proven truth and nothing else. He not only acknowledged and confirmed all these things, but, from his singular desire to search out and bring to light the truth, and out of his remarkable kindness towards me, he also communicated another matter, which I judged most worthy to be dragged at last out of darkness. It embraces indeed the plan of nearly the whole design by which the Jesuits, equipped and sent out from the seminaries as priests, return to England. And it is clear from this that nothing is kept more secret among them, since these things are committed only to manuscript, not to print: which they are unwilling to disclose themselves when they are called into question; and which hardly any of ours has either seen or heard, except by standing at a distance and from afar. By whose authority these counsels or precepts were put forth, it cannot undeservedly be doubted from the circumstances of the discovered matter; likewise, the time is not clear; and whether they were composed and concluded by one author or rather by several. In the end I find certain petitions, to which Pope Pius Quintus is clearly recorded to have added his own censure twenty-seven years ago. For after nearly every petition is attached either Annuit or Abnuit, and at the end is added word for word: These petitions, set out in the form written above, were presented to the Most Holy Father Pius V by the illustrious Cardinal D. Francis Alciati, Vice-Protector of the English, in the absence of Cardinal Morone; all and each of which the said Most Holy Father approved or disapproved, as has been noted, on the feast of Saint Michael the Archangel, by living voice. In the year of the Lord 1571. In the earlier treatise, however, where questions concerning schism, the tribunal of the judge, the Mass, baptism, etc. are discussed, the solution is not simple, with a bare negation or affirmation, but the reasons for the decrees are added from Navarre, Thomas Aquinas, Bonaventure, Father Robert and others: from some of which one may conjecture that it was published after the year 1571 and the times of Pius V. For although Martin of Azpilcueta, Doctor Navarrus, had published his Spanish and Portuguese Enchiridion, or Manual of Confessors and Penitents, already in the time of Paul III, nevertheless it was not published in Latin until the year 1573, when it was first printed at Rome, with a dedicatory letter prefixed to the Supreme Pontiff Gregory XIII. Afterwards it was again printed in Belgium at Antwerp, in the year 1579, by Christopher Plantin; where, from the privileges, letters and censures placed at the end and beginning, the times of the earlier editions are expressly taught. Since the author of the work, then eighty years old (as he himself professes), added many things, changed and corrected more polishedly in the Latin edition, it is judged most likely that the author of these answers and conclusions took them all from the Latin copy, which could only be done after the year 1573, when Gregory XIII was occupying the papal chair. And the citations from Navarre which I have compared all agree entirely with the Latin Manual in chapters and numbers. However, although these things perhaps do not reach back to the times of Pius V, that they were put out under Gregory XIII is clear from the fact that twelve years ago these writings came into the hands of one whose kindness gave me the opportunity to read and transcribe them. And you, certainly, were found among the books of one or another Papist, most devoted to the Roman see and not unlearned, in the county of Southampton, when it suddenly came to light that one of the royal justices of the peace was there, accompanied by other learned and upright men. And from that time the most distinguished man, who was then present there, kept them in his possession, being content to have himself exposed their decrees; until, learning that these things had most aptly fallen into our subject of lying, he of his own accord communicated them to me. That these things, however, are of most holy authority among our priests and the English beyond the sea, and are not invented by us but taken seriously from them: from this it is evident, as clear as the noonday sun, to anyone who is not blind, that over the last twenty years we find all their actions, gestures and practices in agreement with these things, to the very letter. So many frauds and perverse evasions are witnesses, which such men have so often thrust upon the magistrates appointed for that office at the time of examination. But the things we have reported about Gerard and Southwell agree in every part with these theses in such a way that it is clearer than the noonday light that they were drawn from no other source than this one. It therefore seemed worth my while, after the assertions of those two more recent men had been examined in whatever way, to go further still, and to bring to light the hidden reasons, and so deeply concealed, on which those two, and the rest of their companions, have dared such things. In these matters, if I had explained only those things which pertain to lying, and to perjury, the greatest kind of lying, and had not wholly passed over the other matters which are involved with them (as concerning schism, baptism, the Mass and many other things, which are held in great number), I would not have spoken of the rest of these things, which are wrapped up together with them, concerning the government and authority of the most serene and most invincible Queen, and also of her judges, nor of the pride of the Pope in this matter: partly because it was my aim, set before me, only to refute lying, and it was not fitting to wander outside those bounds; partly because that claim (that a prince should be cast down from the throne), with its Antichristian arrogance and boasting, has been discussed and demonstrated by our countrymen in large volumes. Yet, since the Christian world will understand what these things are which the Anglo-Romanists whisper in secret murmurs to their followers, I will set forth word for word those things which occur in the present matter from the papers that were seized, so that anyone may understand how wretchedly and shamefully these witnesses of Antichrist have turned aside from the genuine doctrine of the Gospel and the sentiment received among all the martyrs of Christ. Therefore, among the questions pertaining to the tribunal of the judge, this is the second: How ought one to answer before the tribunal of heretics? Answer. He answers well who is not ashamed to confess not only the things that belong to faith, but also the things that belong to fact; for in the former is the exaltation of faith, and in the latter the glory of God: he therefore who is killed on account of this confession is truly a martyr. Nazar. chap. 11, num. 40. Immediately it is added: An oath exacted by a judge who has no competence does not bind, except according to the intention of the one swearing. Nau. chap. 12, num. 8. Who are all now in England (namely incompetent judges) in ecclesiastical jurisdiction, because they run and are not sent, sons without father or mother. A Catholic, therefore, dragged before heretics, may either refuse the oath (which is more prudent) or swear sophistically and answer sophistically each of his questions, except insofar as he is questioned about faith. Ibidem. For one questioned tyrannically about faith ought to answer. D. Thom. 2.2. quest. 3. art. 2. He who swears to do something unlawful, with the intention of doing it, sins twice. Nau. chap. 12, num. 12. Therefore, questioned about the indicating of Catholics, and sworn, if under pretext of his oath he names some, he sins twice; moreover, if without that oath he indicates some, he sins mortally, because he gives help in mortal sin. The same, chap. 11, num. 13. The ninth question is this: How is it lawful to equivocate or to change names? Answer. Those who are questioned by the chief Royal Commissioners, or by their swift officers, whether they are priests, when they are; or otherwise, whether they are Catholics, sin mortally if they either keep silent or equivocate; because they are questioned out of hatred of religion, in which case anyone is bound to confess his faith. Mark 8. Whoever is ashamed of me, etc. And Luke 8. Whoever is ashamed of me, etc. I call officers not only those who perform that office, but also those whom I see to be ready to seize men out of hatred of religion, just as the maidservants questioning St. Peter, Luke 22: Are these the men who sit at the tax-booth in the seaport towns, who seek not so much to advance the heretical faith through their arrests of Catholics as to fill their purses? Therefore, those who, questioned by them about their state or religion, out of simplicity of heart either keep silent or equivocate, do not sin, because they are not bound to confess if they are questioned for any other reason than hatred of religion. Father Rupert. I. 2. quest. 5. art. 1. dub. 2. To question them out of hatred of religion is not more probable in their case than for some other cause, namely because they seek their money. Those questioned on the road by fellow travellers, or at table by those reclining together, whether about their state or their religion, may either keep silent or equivocate, because they ask out of curiosity; and if there is an affirmative precept of faith, it does not bind except for the time and place. And here no advantage to the neighbour or honour to God comes forth, or at least no harm to the neighbour or to God, and so the precept does not bind. D. Thom. in the aforesaid place. There follow other questions, both extravagant, whether they are of the same time or the same person as the determinations of their superiors, I do not understand. I suspect, however, that they are not of the same; because the solutions are proposed bare, without any confirmation from Navarre or others. Yet at the end of these are appended those things about which Pope Pius V has pronounced his judgment, Annuit or Abnuit (as above). One of the questions, however, is this: Whether a priest may, as he changes his clothes and habit, so also let his hair grow and change his name, and if he were asked in a port, or elsewhere, under some name by some who hold him suspect, whether he may deny that it is his name, namely that it is not his own? A similar doubt concerns his country, parents, friends, etc. When he has been questioned outside court on the road. Answer: He may; nor does any doubt seem to arise in this case: for anyone may keep silent about the truth or dissemble it, provided he does not directly deny it. And afterwards: Whether a priest, questioned on the road about the places from which he has come, likewise about his religion, whether he favours the Roman faith or not, could by some indirect answer escape and elude the question, or whether he is bound to confess the truth? Answer. Anyone may elude. Then, after many things, four questions follow together: Whether it is lawful for a Catholic to refuse an oath proposed by heretical magistrates to the damage of himself and other Catholics? Answer: Indeed he is bound to refuse, and to escape as far as he can. But whether he is bound to refuse such an oath even to the point of torture? Answer: If from such an oath a notable harm to the faith or religion would follow, torture rather is to be undergone. Then: How much is he bound to reveal through the oath required? I answer: Because the oath was extorted by injustice, and these magistrates are incompetent judges, he is bound to reveal nothing, insofar as he can escape without lying and falsehood. But: If he rashly and inconsiderately has given an oath to heretics that he will answer all questions sincerely; and they afterwards question him about many things which, if revealed, would tend to the very grave damage and prejudice of Catholics: What must be done in this case? I answer: He has sinned in swearing thus, and an oath ought not to be a bond of iniquity, and therefore he is not bound to answer as has been said above. After one and another question, about obeying or not obeying the Queen (after the Bull of Pius V was issued), there follows this question: An orthodox priest of the Catholic Church, seized by heretics, is brought before the tribunal of the judge, who exacts from him an oath by which he is bound to answer with good and true faith all the questions put to him: he is asked perhaps how often he has celebrated Mass, in what place, and in whose presence, etc. Here, if he answers truly, and as the bearer has it, there is no doubt that, on account of the grave scandal which arises from it, he himself and others will be struck with the greatest harms. It is asked whether, in such circumstances, the priest is bound to betray both himself and others? I answer: He is not bound, because it is not a lawful judgment. Nor ought the intention of the one swearing to be other than to say those things which he is bound to say. But if it were required to say everything, the intention would be unjust, which does not bind, because it would be to the prejudice of others, who would suffer harm. Yet he must not tell a lie, but that which is true in some sense, even if it is not in the sense of the questioner, because he is not bound to answer according to the questioner's intention. But these things I have said I understand if there be no scandal to the weak; for this ought to be avoided, nor should any occasion of sinning be given to the infirm, especially in a matter of faith: rather one should lay down his life, if it be necessary for their salvation. Then afterwards: This time and occasion seems most fitting for confessing God before men, lest Christ be ashamed to confess him before the Father: but he is not bound to betray himself or others, not being questioned: but, questioned about himself, it would be advisable to tell the truth, and to die for the faith if need be; but others he cannot reveal: yet because a heretical or schismatic judge loses all jurisdiction, he is not bound. Questioned about the truth in judgment, he ought to answer, neither about himself nor about others, but he may, by answering amphibologically or equivocally, declare the iniquity of the judge. These things are all had in Latin word for word. Let those who sit at the helm or at the oar of the English commonwealth cease any longer to wonder what the cause is, why men returning from Rome and Rheims are wont so fraudulently, sophistically and captiously to conduct themselves after the burden of an oath, since they drank in and sucked up that poisonous milk from their first entrance into the seminaries. A bitter spring cannot send forth sweet waters, nor are grapes gathered from thistles or figs from brambles. Would that at some time our Englishmen, enticed by Roman philtres and incantations, might begin to be wise, and, vomiting out their poisons before they are changed into their incurable corruption, might keep themselves within the bounds of their country, pleasant, healthful, overflowing with heavenly streams: or, if they were willing to rave so far that, called by hostile hissing, they should consent to swear, whether they wished it or not, all good men, in obedience to the Pope, at least they should not be unwilling to return to England under the appearance of a flock, though they are wolves: or, if they must return, they should not proceed to heap iniquity on lying and treason on perjury, but should keep themselves very far outside the banks of prodigious impiety. Let it suffice so far to have run beside the way. Jehovah God is of truth, of truth simple and undefiled. But they greatly provoke him who desire to establish their attempts by lies and perjuries, whatever colour they may be painted with. If the things they undertake are good, let them promote them by good means. If it is the Christian faith which they desire to spread abroad, let them walk with a Christian step. For Job rightly says, chap. 13, 7: Does God need your lie, that you should speak deceits for him? or, as others have it: Ought you to speak iniquity for God, or ought you to speak fraud for him? And so far concerning these things.

units.la: De Baptismo disputatio, integram sacramento autorita-tem & dignitatem suam (vt quod diuinum est mysterium) custodiendam suadet: sine meticulosa tamen trepida&q; su-perstitione, quæ multis diffidentiis & suspicionibus conscientias replet, distrahitque animos, ex præscripto Dei verbo non credentium. Quod si certa in Christum Deique promissa, fides collocetur, quæ infantulorum salutem e piis parentibus prognatorum creatoris misericordiæ e fœdere sperandæ commendabit; euanescet protinus audaculorum hominum & muliercularum temeraria insolentia, profanas tam sacrato mysterio manus iniicientium. Fabri fabrilia tractent: & in sanctiorem vocationis sacerdotalis selecti or-dinem, quæ ad suum peculiare officium pertinent, dispen-sent. Sin aliquando laici in prima Ecclesia sacramentum dederint, operæ precium est aduertere, num non illud per-miserit antiquitas, vel larga nimis & libera indulgentia, vt cum Eucharistiam infantulis porrexerint; vel saltem non in quibusuis illud laicis tolerando, sed talibus, qui præ excel-lentia donorum Spiritus sancti, verbum, panemq; vitæ fran-gere, prædicando & explanando, digni haberentur. Vbi tamen vel per istos, vel per alios e populo, signaculum serio sobrieque impressum extiterit, non audeo repetendum esse pronunciare: verum antiquæ & receptæ Ecclesiarum con-suetudini multum tribuo, earumque ita variis in locis, orbi-sque plagis dissieminatarum sententiæ adhuc acquiesco, animum tamen humillime libentissimeque mutaturus, si quisquam (cuiuscunque demum ille sortis sit) e sacris eloquiis, rectaque ratione diuersum edocuerit. Et multo maximas alias instituenti & informanti habebo gratias, vt Christi famulum veritatis studiosum decet. Reliqua de Baptismo, quæ mouentur hodie, dubia, in nostram de Tsippora disputationem non cadunt, ideoque sicco pede, vt oportet, prætermitto.
units.tr: The disputation on Baptism urges that the full authority and dignity of the sacrament be preserved, as befits a divine mystery, yet without anxious, trembling superstition, which fills consciences with many distrusts and suspicions and distracts minds, drawn from the word of God by those who do not believe. But if faith is placed in the certain promises of God and of Christ, a faith that will commend the salvation of little infants, born of pious parents, to the mercy of the Creator, as hoped for from the covenant, then at once the reckless insolence of bold men and silly women will vanish, those who lay profane hands on so sacred a mystery. Let smiths handle smithy work, and let those chosen into the more sacred order of the priestly calling dispense what belongs to their own peculiar office. But if at any time laymen in the early Church administered the sacrament, it is worth noting whether antiquity permitted this, either through an excessively broad and free indulgence, when they gave the Eucharist to infants, or at least not by tolerating it in just any laymen, but in those who, by reason of the excellence of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, were thought worthy to break the word and the bread of life by preaching and expounding. Yet where, by such persons or by others from the people, the seal has been seriously and soberly impressed, I do not dare to pronounce that it must be repeated; but I give great weight to the ancient and accepted custom of the Churches, and I still rest content with the judgment of those Churches so widely scattered in various places and regions of the world, yet I shall most humbly and most willingly change my mind, if anyone (of whatever rank he may be) teaches otherwise from the sacred oracles and sound reason. And I shall hold for very great thanks anyone who instructs and informs me otherwise, as becomes a servant of Christ who is eager for the truth. The rest concerning Baptism, which are doubtful questions raised today, do not fall within our disputation about Tsippora, and so, as is proper, I pass them by with dry foot.

units.la: Astrologorum placita conuulsurus, curiosam artem & Chaldaicam, tam insignem veræ Astronomiæ labem maculamq; aspergentem, e Christianis Reipubl. amotam cupio. Sapiendum est in omnibus: sed ad sobrietatem. Illud iuuenibus initio persuasum aueo, quod nimia tandem experientia, seniores iis in studiis exercitatos docet, frustra scilicet in rebus tam inanibus, tempus, quod vere pretiosum sapienti esse debet, teri. At maius, hoc est, & quod illa vehementius fugienda esse docet, si ita inordinata, præposteraq; sit opera, quæ isthic collocatur, vt non modo ciuili politicoque bono aduersetur, sed & pietati cœlestiq; sapientiæ repugnet. Creaturis etenim sine regula salutari, sine authoritate solida, ea tribuere, quæ sibi reseruanda summa Maiestas existimauit, suaque manu disponenda, est humanæ, & profanæ, & vanæ speculationis, non prudentiæ Christianæ. In syderum fabrica, certisque potentiis, quæ extra controuersiam reperiuntur, diuinum, fas est, vt admiremur digitum, creatoris vt mirificam contemplemur gloriam: sed miserum est & perplexum nimis, vt ea solliciti scrutemur, quæ nusquam sunt. Caueamus igitur ab impostoris fraudibusq; eorum, qui sub quouis genere lucrum captant, & sub verbis speciosis simplices inescant, ex aliena credulitate sua cômoda emungentes. Cum Aruspicibus, Ariolis, Chiromanticis, aliisque eius farraginis, euanuit fere hoc nugiuendulum hominum genus; & sperandum est, vndiquaq; fulgente Euangelij lumine in minorem numerum quotidie contractu iri.
units.tr: Intending to overthrow the opinions of the astrologers, I wish the curious art of the Chaldeans, which casts such a notable stain and blemish upon true astronomy, to be removed from the Christian commonwealth. In all things one must be wise, but with sobriety. I am eager to persuade the young at the outset of what excessive experience at last teaches the elders who have been exercised in these studies: that time, which ought to be truly precious to the wise, is in vain wasted on such empty matters. But greater still, and what teaches that these things must be fled all the more vehemently, is that the labour placed in this area is so disordered and perverse that it not only opposes civil and political welfare, but also resists piety and heavenly wisdom. For to attribute to creatures, without a saving rule and without solid authority, those things which the supreme Majesty has judged to be reserved to itself and to be disposed by its own hand, belongs to human, profane and vain speculation, not to Christian prudence. In the fabric of the stars and in certain powers which are found beyond controversy, it is right that we admire the divine finger and contemplate the wondrous glory of the Creator; but it is wretched and far too perplexing to anxiously investigate those things which nowhere exist. Let us therefore beware of the frauds of these impostors, who seek gain under every kind of pretence, and with specious words ensnare the simple, draining their own advantages from the credulity of others. Together with the haruspices, soothsayers, chiromancers and the other hodgepodge of that kind, this trifling tribe of men has almost vanished; and it is to be hoped that, with the light of the Gospel shining on every side, they will daily be reduced to a smaller number.

units.la: In exemplo Naamanis, receptam apud omnes sanioris cerebri & mentis, sententiam confirmo, idololatricos omnes cultus & ritus, sinceram fidem profitenti auersandos esse. Neque metus etenim, nec spes, neque vlla carnalis & mun[?]dana affectio, apud pectus animosum, sobriaque præditum constantia, ita valere debet, vt, vel cum consensu, vel cum consensus specie, turpissimæ liturgiæ, non modo nostra opinione, sed & scripturarum eloquiis damnatæ, interfimus. Si Iehoua Deus sit, post ipsum eamus, sin Baal sit Dominus, eundem sequamur. Vanæ tamen sunt exceptiones Anglo-Romanensium, per quas, ex non concessis, communibus omnium sectarum argumentis, & friuolis petitionibus principij, vt appellant Dialectici, meretriculam Babyloniam depereuntibus persuasum cupiunt, liturgiæ Anglicanæ Ecclesiæ non communicandum. Ipsi etenim idololatricum apud nos comperiunt nihil, verum omnia, pietatem non fictam, confessionem peccatorum, gratiarum actionem, diuinæ iræ deprecationem, institutionem rudiorum, corroborationem infirmorum, ædificationem omnium redolentia, ita vt isthic renuere vel tergiuersari, sit vel peruicaciæ, vel ignorantiæ, vel præcipitis opinionis potius, quam conscientiæ super petra aliqua solidiore fundatæ. Vtinam tandem aliquando populares nostri, ab amatoriis Romanæ synagogæ poculis expergefacti & oculos aperirent iam diu occlusos, & cum ingenua gratia, diuinæ misericordiæ agnitione, in luce Euangelij copiose diffusa ambularent. Dulcis esset gustantibus lex Dei supra mel, & vltra fauum desideranda. Dum tamen, & nobis causam esse, cur à Babylone secedamus, & illis, quam obrem cum insigni & sincera gratulatione ad nos festinantius accederent, demonstrem; omnigenam præsentiam in templo idolorum, interdictam non censeo. Politica vbi solü obeuntur munia, & cum protestatione aut generali, aut tunc temporis, vbi in discrimen res venerit, speciali, ne scandalum erroris in aliis infirmioribus fiat, in crimen læsæ diuinæ Maiestatis non incurritur. Debitæ tamen circumstantiæ sanctissimæ & prudentissimæ retinendæ sunt, vt, dum corpori, & ciuili apud homines dignitati cōsulatur, animæ vel alienæ, vel nostræ periculum spontaneum non creetur. Qui minores loco sunt, superiorum vestigiis insistunt libentissime.
units.tr: In the example of Naaman I confirm the opinion accepted by all of sound mind and judgment, that all idolatrous worships and rites must be shunned by one who professes sincere faith. For neither fear, nor hope, nor any carnal and worldly affection ought to have such power over a courageous heart, endowed with sober constancy, that we should take part, whether with consent or with the appearance of consent, in the most shameful liturgy, condemned not only by our own opinion but also by the words of the Scriptures. If Jehovah is God, let us go after him; but if Baal is the Lord, let us follow him. Yet the exceptions of the Anglo-Romanists are vain, by which, from unconceded premises, with the arguments common to all sects and with what the dialecticians call frivolous petitions of principle, they wish to persuade those who dote on the harlot of Babylon that one must not communicate in the liturgy of the English Church. For they themselves find nothing idolatrous among us, but everything that breathes unfeigned piety, confession of sins, thanksgiving, deprecation of divine wrath, instruction of the ignorant, strengthening of the weak, and edification of all; so that to shrink back or to evade here is a sign either of obstinacy, or of ignorance, or rather of a hasty opinion, not of a conscience founded upon some firmer rock. Would that our fellow countrymen at last, roused from the amorous cups of the Roman synagogue, would open their eyes, long closed, and walk with ingenuous grace, with the acknowledgment of divine mercy, in the light of the Gospel abundantly poured forth! To those who taste it the law of God would be sweeter than honey, and to be desired beyond the honeycomb. Yet, while I demonstrate both that there is cause for us to secede from Babylon and why they should hasten to join us with notable and sincere rejoicing, I do not judge that presence of any kind in the temple of idols is forbidden. Where only political duties are discharged, and with a protestation either general, or, when the matter comes into danger, special, lest a scandal of error be made for other weaker persons, no one incurs the crime of injured divine majesty. Yet the due circumstances must be kept most holy and most prudent, so that, while care is taken for the body and for civil dignity among men, no voluntary danger is created for the soul, either of others or of ourselves. Those who are lesser in rank most willingly tread in the footsteps of their superiors.

units.la: Fugam in persecutione, intra illos constringo cancellos, quos, puto, tanquam limites terminosque posuit & circum‑scripsit saluator Christus. Priuato igitur hominis discedendi licentiam, (vt olim Tertullianus) non eripio, neque etiam ministro gregis vbique, vt nec ei semper concedo. Perso‑narum temporumque & locorum, quæ occurrunt, circum‑stantiæ, vt in aliis Theologorum, sed & medicorum, & Iu‑risperitorum negotiis, ita in præsenti causa, ipsam conclu‑sionis substantiam immutare consueuerunt. De fuga in pe‑ste non dispar est iudicium: tum manendum esse pastori, pro alienis animabus rationem reddituro, cum diuerrendi discedendi q; copia, priuato, cui media suppeditauit Deus, facillime annuatur.
units.tr: In persecution I confine flight within those limits which, I think, the Saviour Christ set and circumscribed as boundaries and landmarks. I do not therefore take away from the private man the liberty of withdrawing (as Tertullian once did), nor do I always grant it to the minister of the flock wherever he may be. As in the affairs of other theologians, and also of physicians and jurists, so in the present question they are accustomed to change the very substance of the conclusion according to the circumstances of persons, times and places that arise. On flight in plague the judgment is not different: the minister must remain, since he will render an account for other men's souls, when the opportunity of turning aside and withdrawing is most easily granted to a private person to whom God has supplied the means.

units.la: Sexto capite calumniam Ecclesiis Reformatis iniectam & intentatam eluendo amouere desidero. Grauis sane est querela, Protestantium doctrinam, supremum illud augu‑stissimumque Numen, sanctissimum, purissimum, inuiola‑tum vndique, blasphema peccati fouendi macula asperge-re. At leuior est ista, & tolerabilior nostra ex parte accusa‑tio, quia virulentiæ malitiosæ plus, quam solidæ veritatis in se complectitur. Nos è contra laude dignum, acutissimum nostrorum hac in re iudicium existimamus, qui in ipsa con‑troversiæ penetralia descenderunt, obscurissimas eius difficultates rimati, neque tamen ab Ariadnæo scripturarum fi‑lo, in Labyrintho tam ambiguo perplexoque discedentes, neque omnium creatori, suam gloriam vel tantillum mi‑nuentes. Quin potius mirum in modum diuinam & sapien‑tiam & innocentiam prædicant, humanoque generi con‑templandam commendant; dum omnibus impiissimorum actionibus & interesse & præsse doceant, ita tamen, vt cum obliqua reproborum malitia nihil habeat commercij, neq; asperasperginem ullam immunditiæ contrahat. Debuisset habere gratias Ecclesiis Reformatis Romana synagoga, quod magna cum industria, & sincero acumine, post offusas hac in rea Scholasticis tenebras, tanquā è postliminio illud revocarint, quod ita aperte sacratæ docentlitere, & præaliis patrum, Augustinus quam sæpissime, non obscure insinuavit. Sin grati saltem esse Iesuitæ recusarent, à calumnia tamen linguas pennasque cohiberent, neque apertos etiam inimicorum sermones, ita perverterent & contorquerent, ut quilibet è quolibet proferre & facere viderentur. Obscuritatis autem si quid fuerat in scriptis aliquorum Christi famulorum, breui explicatione amouere aut aperire studui, ut apud omnes constaret, quam sanctum illud sit & solidum, quod tuemur.
units.tr: In the sixth chapter I wish to remove, by wiping away, the calumny cast upon and levelled at the Reformed Churches. It is indeed a grave complaint that the doctrine of the Protestants stains that supreme and most august Deity, most holy, most pure, everywhere inviolate, with the blasphemous blemish of fostering sin. But this accusation, so far as it concerns us, is lighter and more tolerable, since it contains more of malicious virulence than of solid truth. On the contrary, we judge the judgment of our men in this matter to be worthy of praise and most acute, who have descended into the very inner sanctum of the controversy, searching out its most obscure difficulties, and yet, not departing from the Ariadne's thread of the Scriptures into so ambiguous and perplexing a labyrinth, nor diminishing in the least the glory of the Creator of all. Rather, they wondrously proclaim both the wisdom and the innocence of God, and commend them to be contemplated by the human race, while they teach that he both takes part in and presides over all the actions of the most impious, yet in such a way that he has no fellowship with the crooked malice of the reprobate, nor contracts any stain of uncleanness. The Roman synagogue ought to have been grateful to the Reformed Churches, because, with great diligence and sincere acuteness, after the darkness cast over this matter by the Schoolmen, they have brought back as if by right of return that doctrine which the sacred letters teach so plainly, and which Augustine, among the other Fathers, has very often insinuated not obscurely. But if the Jesuits refused to be grateful, they should at least restrain their tongues and pens from calumny, and not so pervert and twist even the open words of their enemies that anyone may seem to be saying and doing anything from anything. If there was any obscurity in the writings of some servants of Christ, I have endeavoured to remove or clarify it by a brief explanation, so that it might be plain to all how holy and solid is that which we defend.

units.la: Hæc omnia fido cum animo, & Ecclesiæ Christi prodesse desiderante, pro mea tenuitate exaraui. Si alicubi subrepserit error, qui humanam fragilitatem in tabernaculo hoc morantem comitari consueuit; eius omne iudicium spiritibus prophetarum, & Censuræ Ecclesiæ, præsertim Anglicanæ (cuius eximie per quadraginta annos florentis, sub beatissima & invictissima Regina, me membrum pusillum esse, apprime lætor) submitto & subiicio. Sin vel minimis saluatoris Christi famulis, ex tenui hac opella, tantillum boni accreverit, me aliqua ex parte officio meo functum existimabo. Et cum vires addiderit, otiumque suppeditaverit benignissimus cœlestis pater, enitar assidue, ut cum acceptiore aliquo donario ad altare accedam. Animo intentim benevolo hæc rudiore stilo conscripta, & non elaborato (fucus etenim à scholis Theologorum longissime abesse debet) suscipe Christiane lector, & fruere. Vale.
units.tr: I have written all of this with a faithful mind, desiring to be of use to the Church of Christ, as far as my small ability allows. If any error has crept in, as human frailty, which usually accompanies us while we dwell in this tabernacle, is wont to do, I submit and subject all judgment on it to the spirits of the prophets and to the censure of the Church, especially the English Church (whose most distinguished membership, flourishing for forty years under our most blessed and invincible Queen, I rejoice greatly to be a small part of). But if even the least of the servants of our Saviour Christ should gain some small good from this slight work, I shall consider that I have in some measure discharged my duty. And when the most gracious heavenly Father shall have given strength and leisure, I shall strive constantly to approach the altar with some more acceptable offering. Kind reader, receive these things, written in a rougher style and not polished (for rhetorical ornament must stay far away from the schools of the theologians), with a benevolent mind, and enjoy them. Farewell.
CHAPTER ONE. CONCERNING LYING.

units.la: Genes. 27. 6. Rebecca alloquuta est Iacobum filium suum dicendo: ecce audiui patrem tuum, loquentem cum Esauo fratre tuo, dicendo;
units.tr: Gen. 27. 6. Rebecca spoke to Jacob her son, saying: Behold, I heard your father speaking with Esau your brother, saying;

units.la: 7. Affer mihi venationem, & para mihi cupedias quas comedam: post, benedicam tibi coram Iehoua, priusquam moriar.
units.tr: 7. Bring me game, and prepare me dainties which I may eat; afterwards I will bless you before Jehovah, before I die.

units.la: 8. Nunc itaque fili mi, ausculta voci meæ: rei quam ego præcipio tibi: Et quæ sequuntur.
units.tr: 8. Now therefore, my son, obey my voice in the matter which I command you: and what follows.

units.la: 1. Rei propositio. 4. Mendacii Rebeccæ rationes: 5. Euersæ & solutæ: 7. Aliorum mendaciorum examinatio. 8. Mendaciorum diuisio. 10. 11. pro Mendaciis obiectiones & responsiones. 12. 13. Noua euadendi via. 14. Eius firmamenta. 15. 16. discussa. 17. quod ad priorem referri debeant originem. 18. 19. 20. 22. Eorundem refutatio: 23. è Nauarro. 24. 25. 26. 27. pro aliis Mendaciis obiectiones & solutiones.
units.tr: 1. Statement of the matter. 4. The reasons for Rebecca's lie. 5. Refuted and solved. 7. Examination of other lies. 8. Division of lies. 10. 11. Objections to lies in their favour and replies. 12. 13. A new way of escape. 14. Its supports. 15. 16. Discussed. 17. That they ought to be referred to the earlier origin. 18. 19. 20. 22. Refutation of the same: 23. from Navarre. 24. 25. 26. 27. Objections and solutions concerning other lies.

units.la: AETERNA Dei electio, & decretum ante omnia secula, vt in singulis filiorum Adæ, locum habuit & habebit, ita in nullis illustrius & luculentius, quam in gemina Isaaci prole, Esauo & Iacob. De quibus multa sacræ pronunciarunt literæ, vt ad Romanos nono: {a}Iacob dilexi, Esauum vero odio habui, Malachiæ primo: {b}Nonne frater fuit Esau Iacobo: Esauum vero odio habui: ideo di-sposui[?] montes eius desolationi, & possessionem eius draconibus deser-ti:
units.tr: THE eternal election of God, and his decree before all ages, has had and will have its place in each of the sons of Adam; but in none is it more illustrious and clearer than in the twin offspring of Isaac, Esau and Jacob. Of these the sacred letters have declared much, as in Romans 9: {a}"Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated." Malachi 1: {b}"Was not Esau Jacob's brother? Yet I have hated Esau; therefore I have made his mountains a desolation, and his inheritance a dwelling of dragons in the wilderness."

units.la: Sed ti: Sed nullibi expressius aut dilucidius, quam, ubi prima ipsorum mentio facta est, ubi de concertantibus in utero infantulis, cum mater divinum consuluisset oraculum, respo-sum tulit,{c}Duas esse in eius utero nationes, duos intra viscera dividi populos, quorum alter altero robustior futurus esset, & sic, ut maior natu serviret minori.
