Cuius rei veritas ex multorum seculorum experimentis edocta est; dum in {d}E-domitas Israelitae dominium nonnunquā exercerent, dum sterilior Esauitarum esset habitatio & iniucundior, Israelis fertilior & locupletior: multo tamen maxime, dum istis spirituales divitiae per sanctissimum Dei cultum puramque religionem abunde suppeterent; illis vero contaminatae magis, conspurcataeque ceremoniae, per impietatem, ἀνιέρως[?] & superstitionem quotidie increbrescerent.
units.tr: But nowhere more expressly or clearly than where their first mention is made, where, concerning the little children struggling in the womb, when the mother had consulted the divine oracle, she received the answer: {c}"There are two nations in your womb, and two peoples shall be divided from your bowels; the one people shall be stronger than the other, and the elder shall serve the younger." The truth of this matter has been taught by the experience of many centuries: while the Israelites at times exercised dominion over the Edomites, while the habitation of the Edomites was more barren and less pleasant, and Israel's was more fertile and richer; yet most of all, while to the Israelites spiritual riches abundantly came through the most holy worship of God and pure religion, whereas among the Edomites, ceremonies were more and more defiled and polluted, and daily grew in strength through impiety, {d}"unholiness" [ἀνιέρως?] and superstition.

units.la: 2. Hæc ipsa cum suis futura temporibus, pia prudensque satis fœmina Rebecca, fidei oculis prospexisset & prævidisset, feliciorem beatioremq; secuta partem, ut mundus solet, juniori filio, animum affectumq; suum coepit apponere; quibus poterat conata modis, teneriorem corpore, molliorem mente, evehere & promovere. Et cum in ipsis, quæ ad illud facerent, instillandis & suggerendis, non minimam, uti verisimile est, collocasset operam, oleum sane non perdidit, neque lusit inutiliter, sed idoneum satis filium, qui præcepta imbiberet sua, reperit {e}Nam cum fratrem à venatu redeuntem, Jacob deprehendisset, rabida fere, & canina periturum fame, ut nō posset impastus esurie amplius tolerare; ita callide astuteq; pactus est, ut esculentis, imo iusculetis, dignitate inter fratres summam, primogenituram scilicet, commutaret. Sic fraterno quasi iugo collum Esauus subdidit, spōtaneam propemodum amplexus servitutem. Ubi vero, licet suo fortassis, materno tamen adhuc non satisfecisset animo (certissimis etenim & nō fallentibus indiciis, rem omnem cupit fœmina consummare) alia oblata est occasio, quam auide fatis mater arripuit. Isaacus modo præ senectute cæcutiens, ferinam degustare cupit, vt maiori filio, quum eam adduceret, priusquam debitum Deo & naturæ, expirando, persolueret, paternam benedictionem impertiret. Quæ cum eo esset desiderabilior, quo acceptiore apud Deum loco, Isaacus fuisset, vir pius, Patriarcha, Abrahæ soboles, familiæ princeps, in qua feme vnica[?], Ecclesia, & sanctorum synagoga residéret, non omittendum duxit mulier, quin pia vt videbatur, fraude, ab Esauo in Jacobum transferendam curaret. Suppositititum igitur immisit hominem, vestitum fraternis tegumentis, hirsutum, hispidumque arte factum, qui delicatiores afferendo cibos, furto veluti & insidiis, benedictionem præriperet. Neque expectationi eventus defuit, sed, quod animo concupiuit, præmium, honorariumque tulit.
units.tr: 2. When these things were to come to pass in their times, the pious and sufficiently prudent woman Rebecca, having looked forward and foreseen them with the eyes of faith, followed the happier and more blessed part; as the world is wont to do, she began to set her mind and affection upon the younger son, and by whatever means she could attempt, she set about to advance and promote him, the more tender in body and softer in mind. And when she had, as is likely, spent no little effort in instilling and suggesting those things which would further this, she certainly did not waste her oil, nor did she play in vain, but found a son sufficiently fit to imbibe her precepts. {e}For when Jacob had caught his brother returning from the hunt, nearly raging and dying like a dog from hunger, so that he could no longer bear it unfed from hunger, he so cleverly and shrewdly bargained that, for food, or rather for broth, he exchanged the highest dignity among the brothers, namely the birthright. Thus Esau, as it were, submitted his neck to the yoke of his brother, almost embracing a voluntary servitude. But when, though perhaps satisfied in his own mind, he had not yet satisfied his mother's mind (for by most certain and unfailing signs the woman desired to bring the whole matter to completion), another opportunity was offered, which the mother eagerly seized as the fates allowed. Isaac, now going blind with old age, longed to taste game, so that when the elder son brought it, before he paid the debt owed to God and nature by expiring, he might impart the paternal blessing. Since this was all the more desirable because Isaac stood in higher favour with God, a pious man, a patriarch, offspring of Abraham, prince of the family, in whom the one seed, the Church, and the synagogue of the saints resided, the woman thought it not to be neglected, but with what seemed a pious fraud, she arranged that the blessing be transferred from Esau to Jacob. Therefore she sent in a substitute, clothed in the brother's coverings, made hairy and shaggy by art, who, bringing more delicate foods, by theft and as it were by ambush, would snatch away the blessing. Nor was the outcome wanting to her expectation, but she obtained what she had desired in her mind, the prize and the honour.

units.la: 3. Narratio historiæ cuilibet è nobis ita nota est, vt in ipsa explicanda desudare non sit opus. Est mei potius instituti disquirere, num ex norma pietatis, officiique regula, Rebecca fecerit, quæ marituм suo sic consilio deluserit, & medacio insidioso, sui voti compos facta fuerit: eoque indagare nomine, num in causa aliqua, siue sub probitatis & charitatis specie, siue sub religionis prætextu mentiri liceat, vbi danda mihi venia est, si nudam rerum veritatem persequar, & facta eorum, qui in causa isthac celebres extiterint, ad stateram simplicem diuini verbi exigam, nec errorem eleuare, aut extenuare concupiscam. Id quod ea de causa submo-mendum[?] censui, quandoquidem ex Antiquis non infimus, quin potius, mea sententia, longe maximus {f} Augustinus, sub figuris & mysteriis, futurum aliquid prænotantibus, quorundam mendacia aliquatenus excusare conetur. Qui quidem Troporum & Allegoriarum modus, est aliquanto Augustino familiarior; sed in Psalmis {g} Dauidicis explanandis præcipue, vbi saluatori Christo pene omnia in tropo referenda. ferenda existimauit. Sed & in cæteris suis scriptis hanc con-suetudinem liberalius & indulgentius amplectitur licet eo usque non expatietur, quo usque Origenes, qui, cum omnia fere Allegoricos interpretanda credidit, ipsam literam destruere, sensumque simplicem historiæ eneruare, & delumbare ausus est, eo certe conatu, qui tantum alioqui virum non decebat. Ad rem ipsam igitur ut veniamus:
units.tr: 3. The narrative of this history is so well known to each of us that there is no need to labour in explaining it. It is rather my purpose to inquire whether Rebecca acted according to the rule of piety and the standard of duty, she who thus deceived her husband by counsel and, by a treacherous lie, got what she wished; and to inquire on this account whether, in any cause, whether under the appearance of honesty and charity or under the pretext of religion, it is permitted to lie. In this I must be pardoned if I pursue the bare truth of the matter, and weigh the deeds of those who have been famous in this cause by the plain balance of the divine word, nor do I desire to lift up or lessen any error. I have thought this worth mentioning for this reason: since among the ancients Augustine is not the least, but rather, in my judgment, by far the greatest, who, under figures and mysteries foreshadowing something to come, tries in some measure to excuse the lies of certain persons. Indeed this manner of tropes and allegories is somewhat more familiar to Augustine; especially in explaining the Psalms of David, where he thought almost everything must be referred figuratively to the Saviour Christ. But also in his other writings he embraces this habit more freely and indulgently, although he does not extend it to the point where Origen went, who, since he believed almost everything must be interpreted allegorically, dared to destroy the letter itself and to enervate and weaken the simple sense of history, a venture certainly unbecoming to a man otherwise so great. But let us now come to the matter itself:

units.la: 4. Erant certe rationes prætextu speciosæ, quæ Rebeccam impellerent ad hanc pacisc<bl>e</bl>ndam fraudem. Maternæ dilectionis viscera, non mediocriter incitabant: sed diuina promissio speciatim & præcipue iuniori facta, multo confidentiorem poterat animum addere. Quin & maritii in fratrem [illegible, ~6 letters], & naturalis propensio, qua in Esauum longe factus est procliuior, terrere valuisset, ne aperte ageret. Orationem insuper, precesque patriarchæ, ita Deo chari, diuina benedictio prosequeretur: quantum etenim omnipotens Iehova famulorum suorum fidelibus desideriis solet tribuere? Et humano animo incredibile, planeque impossibile videbatur, paternum ab Esauo auocare affectum, quo, delirante fere impetu, & indulgente nimis, in ipsum ferebatur, ita ut ad dolum technasque confugere necesse haberet. Leoninæ exuuiæ vulpinaque pelle commutandæ fuerant. Sed & ab ore Isaaci benedictionem impertientis, vel isti, vel illi, si penderet momenti ponderisque aliquid, ad veram felicitatem, capiendum id erat breui, & aucupanda occasio, ne subita pater præreptus morte, infecto, discederet negotio. Decrepitus namque iam degebat, & moribundus senex. Funiculo tam multiplici, promissionis in Deo, necessitatis in coniuge, amoris in filio, innixa est Rebecca, eoque prudenter & confidenter satis creuit audacia.
units.tr: 4. There were certainly reasons, specious in appearance, which impelled Rebecca to this pretended fraud. The bowels of maternal love stirred her not moderately; but the divine promise made especially and above all to the younger could add much more confident courage to her mind. Moreover, the husband's [illegible, ~6 letters] toward the brother, and the natural inclination by which he had become far more inclined toward Esau, might have deterred her from acting openly. Further, the blessing of God would accompany the prayer and entreaty of the patriarch, so dear to God: for how much does the almighty Jehovah usually grant to the faithful desires of his servants? And it seemed incredible to the human mind, and plainly impossible, to turn away the paternal affection from Esau, toward whom it was carried with an almost frenzied impulse and excessive indulgence, so that she was bound to flee to guile and tricks. The lion's skin had to be exchanged for a fox's pelt. But also, from the mouth of Isaac, as he imparted the blessing, whether to this one or that, if there was any weight or importance for true happiness, it was to be seized shortly, and the opportunity was to be snatched up, lest the father, suddenly taken away by death, depart with the business undone. For he was already decrepit and a dying old man. Rebecca relied upon a rope so manifold: the promise in God, the necessity in her spouse, the love in her son; and with these her boldness grew prudently and confidently enough.

units.la: 5. Sed ut aduersus Solis radios glacies, in tumultuante Borea crassus vapor, præ meridiana luce nocturnus horror, coram arca Dei Philisthæorum Dagon, nequit consistere, ita animalis carnalisque hominis ratio, &, quæ aspectu gloriosa est, cauillantis cerebri imaginatio, si diuini verbi staterę appendatur, inanis futilisque inuenitur. Justa etenim sanctaque habenda sunt, non, quæ corrupto obfuscatoque nostro perplacent judicio, sed quæ sana solidaq; apud Dominum reperiuntur. Aliter enim ab externa apparitione homo, aliter ab interno appetitu discernit Deus. Cuius si velimus indagare sententiam, id primo, oportet, vt sit loco receptissimum, quod ad Romanos recensuit Paulus, {i}Non faciendum esse malu, vt inde aliquid succedat boni, Deus ita seuero persequitur odio malitiam quamcunq;, vt à {k}specie nequitię omni, nos iusserit abstinere. {l}Puras præcepit gestare manus, immaculatum {m}cor. {n}Quid luci cum tenebris est commercij? quid sincero Deo cum sordibus peccatorum? Vt à Babylone abeundum est, ita nil eius immundum est tangendum. Hinc, quæ aduersus præceptum Domini facta sunt, omnia, licet sub intentione bona, vt loquuntur scholastici, vel sub propositio boni, damnantur, & vt {o}ἐθελοθρησκείαν[?] voluntarij cultus, de quibus pronuncietur, quis ista de manibus requiuit vestris, repudiantur. Tale fuerat id Gedeonis, qui {p}Ephod fecerat, vt per ipsum Deus coleretur, sed, quoniam præter Domini institutum hoc factum fuerat, in perniciem illius suæque familiæ cesserat. Tale, illud {q}Saulis, qui Amalecitarum pecora domum duxerat, vt holocausta sacrificiaque Domino offerret: imprudenter tamē non minus, quam impie, cum Jehouæ potius voci auscultandum esset. Tale, illud {r}Vzzæ, qui Arcam tetigit, sollicito satis animo, ne fortassis rueret, sed, quia audacter nimis, repetina interiit mor-te. Qui in {s}[?]Dane & Bethele aras fabricarunt, licet soli Deo sacrificarint, & cum sacrificiis lege præstitutis, inobedientię tamē, scelerisq; tenebantur rei, quia expressum Dei mandatum, quod ad locum attineret, violarunt, qui {t}obsequium vult, non sacrificium. Quod debetur Deo seruitium, intra limites cancellosque certos circumscribitur, ut nec ad {u}dex-tram, nec ad sinistram declinandum sit. Si alicubi, tum in pietate, id poëtæ obtinet:
units.tr: 5. But as ice cannot stand against the rays of the sun, nor thick vapour in a raging north wind, nor nocturnal horror before the midday light, nor Dagon of the Philistines before the ark of God, so the reasoning of the animal and carnal man, and the imagination of a babbling brain, which is glorious in appearance, if weighed on the balance of the divine word, is found empty and futile. For things are to be held just and holy not which please our corrupted and clouded judgment, but which are found sound and solid before the Lord. For God distinguishes otherwise than man does: man judges by outward appearance, God by inward desire. If we wish to inquire into his judgment, it must first be taken as the most accepted principle, which Paul set down to the Romans: {i}"One must not do evil that good may come of it." God so severely pursues wickedness with hatred that he has commanded us to abstain from every {k}appearance of evil. {l}He commanded us to bear clean hands and an {m}undefiled heart. {n}"What fellowship has light with darkness? What has the sincere God to do with the filth of sins?" As one must depart from Babylon, so nothing unclean of it is to be touched. Hence all things done against the precept of the Lord, though under a good intention, as the schoolmen say, or under the appearance of good, are condemned, and, as {o}self-chosen worship of voluntary cult, of which it is pronounced, "Who has required this at your hands?" they are rejected. Such was that of Gideon, who made an {p}ephod so that God might be worshipped through it; but since this had been done outside the institution of the Lord, it turned to the destruction of himself and his family. Such was that of {q}Saul, who brought home the flocks of the Amalekites in order to offer burnt offerings and sacrifices to the Lord; yet he acted imprudently no less than impiously, when he should rather have hearkened to the voice of Jehovah. Such was that of {r}Uzzah, who touched the ark with an anxious mind, lest perhaps it fall; but because he was too bold, he died a sudden death. Those who built altars at {s}Dan and Bethel, although they sacrificed only to God, and with sacrifices prescribed by law, were nonetheless held guilty of disobedience and wickedness, because they violated the express command of God concerning the place. "He desires obedience, not sacrifice." The service owed to God is confined within certain limits and boundaries, so that one must not turn aside either to the {u}right or to the left. If anywhere, that saying of the poet holds true in piety:

units.la: * Est modus in rebus: sunt certi denique fines, Quos ultra, citraque, nequit consistere rectum.
units.tr: *There is a measure in things; there are, finally, certain limits, beyond and short of which what is right cannot stand.

units.la: Quod in Oceano statutum dicit Job, vel potius apud ipsum Deus, {x}Hucusque venies, & ne procedito, & hic opponet se littus, superbiæ fluctuum tuorum, id in nostro Iehouæ præstando officio sanctissimum esse debet: Hucusque fas est tendere, sed non ultra. Verecundiæ limites si transilieris, gnauiter fies impudens: pietatis finibus si excesseris, mire fies improbus. Id igitur inconcussa stabilitate consistat oportet, faciendum esse nil mali, nec quidem, si spes sit & expectatio futuri maioris boni. {y}Ea, quæ constant esse peccata, nullo bona causa obtentu, nullo quasi bono fine, nulla velut bona intentione, facienda sunt.
units.tr: What Job says is fixed in the ocean, or rather what God himself fixes there: "Thus far you shall come, and no further, and here shall your proud waves be stopped" (Job 38). In performing our duty to Jehovah, this must be held most sacred: it is lawful to strive thus far, but not beyond. If you cross the limits of modesty, you will become shamelessly impudent; if you go beyond the bounds of piety, you will become wonderfully wicked. Therefore this must stand with unshaken firmness: nothing evil is to be done, not even if there is hope and expectation of some greater good. Things that are acknowledged to be sins must not be done for any good cause, under any pretext of a good end, or with any supposedly good intention.

units.la: Quod si illibatum & intemeratum non custodiamus, quæ omnigenæ nequitiæ ansa porrigitur? quam lata ad scelus via sternitur, ut sub prætextu boni, homicidium, adulterium, periurium, proditio in patriam, sacrilegium perpetretur? Quis etenim metas transilientibus, quas Deus statuit, modum aut mensuram præfiniet? Cuiuslibet improbi affectus, sola sibi futura est habena, solum retinaculum.
units.tr: For if we do not keep this unbroken and undefiled, what opening is given for every kind of wickedness? How broad a road is laid down to crime, so that murder, adultery, perjury, betrayal of the fatherland, and sacrilege may be committed under the pretext of good! Indeed, who will set a measure or limit for those who overstep the bounds God has set? For any wicked desire, the only bridle that will be left is the rein alone, the only restraint.

units.la: 6. Secundo, extra omnem controuersiam habendum est, interdicta esse Dei famulis mendacia, hocque simpliciter, & sine exceptione aliqua. {z}Ne efferto rumorem mendacij: Et postea: {a}Averbo mendacij procul abesto, Sic: Ne mentimini, nec fallacia utimini, vllus in proximum suum. Et Dauid: {b}Loquens mendacia non stabilietur coram oculis meis. Et Salomon: Deo odiosus est {c}conflans mendacia testis falsus. Sed & Paulus: {d}Deposito mendacio, loquimini veritatem quisque proximo suo. Et rursum: {e}Ne mentimini, alius aduersus alium. Denique, cum Deus sit veritatis, {f}mendacij autem primus author Dæmon; diuino videtur, ad tempus seruitio renuntianuntiare, qui mentitur, & in Satanæ castra transfugere, eius-que cultui se mancipare. Et generalia ista sunt, ita ut non legatur, hic, autillic, per indulgentiam, dispensationem quasi aliquam concedi. Quibus iactis fundamentis, mentiri malum esse; & nolle, per mala, Deum, bona efficere; humano reperitur lapsu delictoque Rebecca aberrasse, quæ filium promissis blanditiisque suis ad fraudem aggrediendam pelle-xerat. Rea sane apud Deum tenetur mulier, facinoris non admittendi. Quod ne durum fortassis videatur, non solo eo unicoque commenti falsitatisque vitio polluta est, sed & infidelitatem, incredulamque mentem sapere deprehen-ditur. Iam etenim in duas velut distracta, discerptaque partes, dubia mentis fertur, num pollicita vellet Deus præstare sua, de Jacobo præferendo. Si fidele credidisset Dominum; & eius beneplacitum expectasset, & mediis non nisi piis usa fuisset. Deus etenim, cum cuiquam se bene velle, præ se fert, & ea efficere poterat, soletque, quæ ad finem destinatum via sunt. Operienda erat, igitur, cum patientia, divina voluntas: non festinanter & inconsiderate; uti isthic, præoccupan-dum creatoris institutum. Cauendum est igitur, ne illius exemplo ducti similia aggrediamur. Quæ etenim seipsam non poterat excusare, multo minus nos tuebitur. Proponitur fugiendum nobis Rebeccæ mendacium, non imitandum. In Prophetis & Patriarchis, luminibusque antiquorum temporum, non omnia, sed quæ decent, sunt ample-ctenda. Vt hirudo putrescenti inhæret sanguini, sic næuis & lapsibus fidelium immorandum non est; nisi & Noaci ebrie-tatem, & Lothi incestum, & Dauidis cum adulterio homi-cidium, & Salomonis idololatriam, & Jeremiæ impatien-tiam, & Petri cum periurio abnegationem, sequenda & imitanda cogitemus. Legibus viuendum est, non exemplis: Diuinis regulis, & normis, non humanis personis, innitendum est. Vel cum Platone errandum non est. Amicissima præ omnibus debet esse veritas. Vbi bene est, vestigia premito: vbi male, cautus auersare.
units.tr: 6. Second, it must be held beyond all controversy that lies are forbidden to the servants of God, and this simply and without any exception. "Do not raise a false report" (Exod. 23). And afterward: "Keep far away from a false word" (Exod. 23). Thus: "Do not lie, nor deal falsely, any man with his neighbour" (Lev. 19). And David: "He who speaks lies shall not stand before my eyes" (Ps. 101). And Solomon: "A false witness who utters lies is hateful to God" (Prov. 14). But Paul also: "Putting away lying, speak truth each one to his neighbour" (Eph. 4). And again: "Do not lie to one another" (Col. 3). Finally, since God is truth, and the Devil is the first author of lying, it seems that he who lies renounces the divine service, even for a time, and deserts to Satan's camp, and surrenders himself to his worship. These are general statements, so that one cannot read here or there that some indulgence or dispensation is granted. Once these foundations are laid, it is evident that lying is evil, and that to be unwilling to bring about good through evil is to accept God's way. It is found that Rebecca erred in human frailty and fault, when she persuaded her son by her promises and flatteries to undertake the fraud. Indeed, the woman is held guilty before God of a deed not to be committed. Lest this perhaps seem harsh, she was stained not only by this single vice of invention and falsehood, but she is also found to savour of unbelief and a doubting mind. For she is said to have been divided and torn, as it were, into two parts, uncertain in mind whether God would really fulfil his promises concerning the preference of Jacob. If she had believed the Lord faithfully and waited for his good pleasure, and had used only pious means. For God, when he shows that he wishes someone well, can and usually does bring about the means that lead to the appointed end. The divine will had to be awaited with patience, and not hastily and rashly, as she did there, anticipating the Creator's purpose. Care must therefore be taken that we do not, led by her example, undertake similar things. For she who could not excuse herself will much less protect us. Rebecca's lie is set before us to be shunned, not imitated. In the Prophets and Patriarchs, and the lights of ancient times, not everything but what is fitting is to be embraced. As the leech clings to putrid blood, so one must not linger on the stains and falls of the faithful, unless we also think of following and imitating Noah's drunkenness, Lot's incest, David's murder together with adultery, Solomon's idolatry, Jeremiah's impatience, and Peter's denial with perjury. We must live by laws, not by examples; we must rest on divine rules and norms, not on human persons. Nor is one to err with Plato. Truth ought to be the dearest of all things. Where it is well, tread in its footsteps; where it is ill, be wary and turn away.

units.la: 7. De reliquis Sanctorum mendaciis, simile ferendum est iudicium. Cum Abrahamus{g} Saram, sororem suam esse dixerat, æquiuocatio vocis, ne mentiretur, effecit, vt exististimare licet. Sub sororis etenim appellatione, vt & etiam sub fratris nomine, consanguinei Hebræis designabantur; quo sensu, aliqui, Domini fratres, hoc est, Christi dicti sunt,{b} vt{h} copiose disputat Hieronymus. Et apertum est è scriptura, propinqua fuisse ei cognatione coniunctam Saram, cum quodam modo sororem extitisse,{i} rursus & secundo asseuc- raret. Quæ si vera sint, nihil in sermone eius falsi cōpertum est, adeoque non peccauit. Sin mentiendi animo Abimelecho imponere per fraudem cuperet, infirmitatem humanam, nimiamque res redolet timiditatem, neq; poterit excusari. Obstetrices Israelitæ Ægyptiorum regi responso non vero circumuenerunt. Ita filij puerperarum Hebræorum, in ipsa natiuitatis hora nō sunt interempti,{l} Hebraeæ, inquiunt, non sunt, sicut mulieres Ægyptiæ: sunt enim viuidæ, quum nondum venit ad ipsas vlla obstetrix, tam pepererunt. Idcirco (addit Moses) benefecit Deus obstetricibus illis. Ecce pij misericordisque doli præmium, quem non remunerasset Deus, nisi approbassēt. At occurrit doctissime Augustinus: Retributionem à Domino, obstetrices acceptauerunt, non{m} quia mentitæ sunt, sed quia in homines Dei misericordes fuerunt. Et de Rahab meretrice, eadem ferenda est censura, cui bene fuerat, quod{n} exploratores Israelitas texerit, diuinæque vo- ci crediderit, de tradenda Iosuæ Hierichunte, & terra Canaan, non quod falsa pronunciarit. Misereri solet Deus eratis suorum, cum leuiter deliquerint, & in rebus tamen momenti grandioris, sani solidique perstiterint. Sed hoc ex diuina contingit misericordia, non ex qualitate rei, quæ cum ἀνομία sit, & ἀδικία, & ἁμαρτία sit oportet. Ignouit igitur Deus Rahab, & in gratiam accepit, ex eo docturus, se inter-nationes perditas, aliquibus misericordiam impertire, non, vt mentiendi libidine ferremur, animum daturus. Atrcue-ra[?] quid est, quod in ea fœmina tunc amplectendum cogitaremus, cum ad mediocrem Dei notitiam adhuc non peruenisset, sed elementis tantum cultus Dei, & vix ipsis, initiata esset.
units.tr: 7. Concerning the other lies of the saints, a similar judgement must be passed. When Abraham said that Sarah was his sister, an equivocation of the word, so that he might not lie, brought it about, as one may suppose. For under the name of sister, as also under the name of brother, relatives were designated among the Hebrews; in this sense some are called brothers of the Lord, that is, of Christ, as Jerome discusses at length. And it is clear from Scripture that Sarah was joined to him by close kinship, since in a certain way she was a sister, and again he asserted this a second time. If these things are true, nothing false was found in his speech, and so he did not sin. But if he wished by fraud to impose upon Abimelech with an intention to deceive, the matter smells of human weakness and excessive timidity, and it will not be excusable. The Hebrew midwives deceived the king of Egypt with an untrue answer. Likewise the sons of the Hebrew women in childbirth were not slain in the very hour of their birth: "The Hebrew women," they say, "are not like the Egyptian women; for they are lively, and before any midwife comes to them, they have already given birth." Therefore (Moses adds) God dealt well with those midwives. Behold the reward of pious and merciful deceit, which God would not have rewarded unless he had approved it. But the most learned Augustine meets this: the midwives received their recompense from the Lord, "not because they lied, but because they were merciful to the men of God." And the same judgement is to be passed on Rahab the harlot, who was well treated because she hid the Israelite spies and believed the divine voice concerning the handing over of Jericho and the land of Canaan to Joshua, not because she spoke falsely. God is accustomed to show mercy to his people when they have sinned lightly, and yet have stood sound and firm in matters of greater weight. But this happens from divine mercy, not from the nature of the deed, which, since it is lawlessness, injustice, and sin, must be such. God therefore pardoned Rahab and received her into favour, intending to teach from this that he grants mercy to some among the lost nations, not that he would give us a mind carried away by the lust of lying. Moreover, what is there in that woman that we should think worth embracing at that time, when she had not yet come to a moderate knowledge of God, but had only been initiated into the rudiments of the worship of God, and hardly even into those?

units.la: Non erat mirum barbarae, Canaanitidi, meretrici, in mendacium prorumpere: sed de homine Christiano quaerimus, in Christo instituto, robustiore cibo pasto, edocto vt oportet, nō de homine ad Ægyptum, aut Hierichuntem, aut Babylonem pertinente. Et hanc igitur, & obstetrices missas faciamus, cum Augustino testantes; {o}Bonum in iis Deus memorabiliter honorauit, malum autem clementer ignorauit.
units.tr: It was no wonder that a barbarian, a Canaanite, a harlot, broke out into a lie; but we seek this of a Christian man, instructed in Christ, nourished with stronger food, taught as he ought to be, not of a man belonging to Egypt, or Jericho, or Babylon. Let us therefore set aside both the midwives, bearing witness with Augustine: "God memorably honoured the good in them, but mercifully overlooked the evil."

units.la: 8. Sed quoniam in humana vita vsum hæc doctrina habet non mediocrem, (nihil etenim mendacio est facilius, nihil promptius, aut quod magis præsto sit) cumq; non defuerint ætate omni, aut desint, qui mendacia aliqua propugnarint, vt {p}Priscilliani, qui satis esse duxerunt, si corde quis verum retinuerit, cum labiis dolum proferat; & si peregrino, licet non proximo, mentitus fuerit; in interiora adhuc huius controuersiæ penetralia irrumpendum est, vt veritas fartatecta[?] conseruetur, adeoque omnis falsitatis species amoueatur. Mendacium ergo, omnes, {q}falsam esse significationem, cum voluntate fallendi, consentiunt. Falsa esse debet significatio; & cum voluntate fallendi. Vnde, aliud reperitur mentiri, aliud mendacium dicere. Dicit etenim mendacium, verax, cum fabulæ, aut narrationi fictæ ipse fidem adhibens, aliis etiam serio recensét: vbi nulla est decipiendi intentio. Fallendi est voluntas, quæ mentiri facit: ex qua, cū insidiator, incautus verum loquitur, quod tamen falsum esse arbitratur, mentiri non immerito dicatur, animi mali causa. Quoties igitur occurrunt ista, est mendacium. Sed {r}Scho{r}Scholastici, varia esse docent horum genera: Est etenim mendacium, perniciosum, est iocosum, est officiosum. Per-niciosum tum definiunt, cum mala mente cuipiam conatur inferre detrimentum, & falso ad id sermone, tanquam instrumento utimur. In calumniis & conviciis, in detractio-ne, discordiam seminando, in periurio exercendo, testimo-nio, ficto ferendo, istud, locum habet. Tale erat {f}Zibæ com-mentum contra Miphibosethum, {t}Hamanis adversus Iudæos, {u}populi & Seniorum contra Christum. Etin com-muni, ista non desunt, vita. Neq; quisquam Theologorum diffitetur, ista apud Dominum intoleranda esse. De his, inquiunt, id est, præceptum: {x}Adversus proximum tuum, ne pro-ferto testimonium falsum. Et quæ supra, contra mendacia, asse-runtur loca, hæc indubitanter percellunt.
units.tr: 8. But since this doctrine has no small use in human life (for nothing is easier than a lie, nothing more ready, or more at hand), and since there have not been lacking in every age, nor are there now lacking, those who have defended some lies, as the followers of Priscillian, who thought it enough if one kept the truth in the heart while uttering deceit with the lips, and if he lied to a stranger, though not to a neighbour; we must break into the still inner recesses of this controversy, so that the truth may be preserved unconcealed, and thus every kind of falsehood may be removed. All therefore agree that a lie is a false signification with the will to deceive. The signification must be false, and with the will to deceive. Hence it is one thing to lie, and another to tell a lie. For a truthful man tells a lie when, giving credence himself to a fable or a fictitious narrative, he relates it seriously to others, where there is no intention to deceive. It is the will to deceive that makes one lie; and when a treacherous man speaks the truth while the unwary one thinks it false, he may not unjustly be said to lie, for the sake of an evil mind. Whenever such things occur, there is a lie. But the Schoolmen teach that there are various kinds of these: for there is a harmful lie, a jesting lie, and a dutiful lie. They define the harmful lie as that in which, with an evil mind, one seeks to bring harm upon someone, and uses false speech as the instrument for this. This has its place in calumnies and reproaches, in slander, in sowing discord, in exercising perjury, and in bearing false witness. Such was Ziba's invention against Mephibosheth, Haman's against the Jews, and that of the people and the elders against Christ. Nor are such things lacking in common life. Nor does any theologian deny that these are intolerable before the Lord. Concerning these, they say, there is the precept: "Do not bear false witness against your neighbour" (Exod. 20). And the passages cited above against lies strike these down without doubt.

units.la: 9. Ex secundo genere sunt, quæ iocosa appellantur: è quorum numero, ea inprimis secludenda censeo, quibus aliquanto remissiores, & indulgentiores sunt Theologi; talia scilicet, quæ sic pronunciantur, ut quivis intelligat, non serio, sed dioco tantum dicta esse. Ista, inquit Aug. per {y}proferendi mo-dum, lusu quasi, & cum sale aliquo, apparent dicta, ideoq; fallendi ani-mum non habent. Horum ego numero fabulas Æsopicas accenseré, quas, cuiuis homini prudenti mediocriter, & intelligenti, primo oculi ictu satis apparet, de industria excogitari, ut doceant, non ut retibus illaqueent. Quibus eos, quos Apologos viri docti appellitant, adiiciendos existimo, quorum in factis etiam literis usus est. Cuiusmodi illud est {z}Iothami, qui exiisse refert arbores ad creandum regem, ubi olea, vitis, ficus, regium repuerunt officium, admisit cynosbatus, & quæ sequuntur. Ubi, si adnuda velimus verba, rem omnem exige-re, quid subesse poterit veritatis? Sin & proferendi rationem, & loquentis propositum, & manifestā deniq; causam ipsam placebit perpendere, quæ non alio, quam [illegible, ~9 letters], expósita est, modo, in integro res omnis futura est. Apertæ Ironiæ sub {a}subisto cadunt genere, ut illa {a}Eliæ, Baalis Prophetas ludificantis. Nathanis illa parabola, qua {b}Dauidem alloquitur, adeoq; ille {c}Christi tam variæ, ut e vbi agricolam seminatum exiisse testatur, semenq; quadrifariam cecidisse, huic attexedæ sunt Catalogo: quæ, cum afferantur, ut docerēt, demonstrarent, redarguerent, consolarentur, cæteraq; pietatis præstarent munia, neq; vllo alio proposito, non mentiendi, non circumueniendi, nō fallendi voluntate, pro malis aut mendaciis habenda non sunt. Et absit, ut blasphemo cuiusquam ore mendacia nominentur. Nudis etenim vocibus & simplicibus tribuenda non est appellatio, sed sensui, & significato, & scopo apud mentē præfixo. Neq; tamen (ut ad rem redeamus) sub horum bonorum tegmine, iocosa excusamus mendacia, ea nempe leuiculorum hominum commēta, quæ inepte, aut scurriliter, aut ex vsu solo, & consuetudine quadam mentiendi pronunciantur. Ut si quis suam prædicaturus fortitudinem, pugnas cum latronibus ignotis in via, referat, aut huiusmodi alia, quibus enarrandis mirum in modum aliqui delectantur. Et horum sermonum consuetudo non est bona. Licet etenim malitiose non efferantur proposito, ut cuiquam noceant, licet cum ioco etiam, & subsannante ludibrio audiantur, quia tamen fallendi recensentur animo, ut in credulitatem impellant: quia veritati aduersantur, qua nihil Deo potest esse acceptius, quia {d}perditurus est Deus loquentes mendacium, etiam omnes perdet, qui loquuntur mendacium; ex vsu Christianorum ista etiā sunt exterminanda.
units.tr: 9. Of the second kind are those called jocular. Of these, I think the first to be set aside are those which theologians treat rather leniently and indulgently: namely, statements made in such a way that anyone can see they are said not in earnest but only in jest. Augustine says that such things, by their manner of utterance, appear to be said in play, as it were, and with some wit, and therefore they do not have the intention of deceiving. To this class I would assign Aesop's fables, which any prudent and reasonably intelligent person sees at first glance were deliberately devised to teach, not to ensnare with nets. To these I think should be added those which learned men call apologues, of which the use is also found in the sacred writings. Such is that of Jotham, who reports that the trees went out to create a king, where the olive, the vine and the fig refused the royal office, and the bramble admitted it, and what follows. Here, if we wish to strip away the words and examine the matter entirely, what truth could lie beneath? But if it pleases us to weigh the manner of presentation, the speaker's purpose, and finally the plain cause itself, which is set forth in no other way than [illegible, about nine letters], then the whole matter will be seen in its proper light. Cases of plain irony fall under the same heading, such as that of Elijah mocking the prophets of Baal. Nathan's parable, by which he addresses David, and that of Christ so varied, in which he tells of a farmer who went out to sow and the seed fell in four ways, are to be added to this catalogue. Since these were offered in order to teach, to demonstrate, to refute, to comfort, and to perform the other duties of piety, and with no other purpose than that of not lying, not circumventing, not deceiving, they are not to be held as lies or falsehoods. And far be it that lies should be named from the mouth of any blasphemer. For the name is to be assigned not to bare and simple words, but to the sense, the meaning, and the aim fixed in the mind. Yet, to return to our matter, under the cover of these good things we do not excuse jocular lies, namely those inventions of light-minded people which are uttered foolishly, or in a buffoonish way, or from mere habit and a certain custom of lying. Such as when someone, about to boast of his bravery, recounts battles with unknown robbers on the road, or other things of this kind, in the telling of which some people take a wonderful delight. And the custom of such talk is not good. For even if they are not put forward with malicious intent to harm anyone, even if they are heard with jesting and mocking derision, yet because they are recounted with the intention of deceiving, so as to drive people into credulity, they oppose the truth, than which nothing can be more acceptable to God; because God will destroy those who speak a lie, he will destroy all who speak falsehood. Therefore, by the practice of Christians, such things too must be banished.

units.la: 10. Tertium genus, multo difficilius, ut quibusdam videtur, requirit iudicium, hoc est, officiosum: quo significatum id volunt, cum amicitiæ, aut charitatis, aut vtilitatis aliquod officium præstandum sit, idq; vel sibi, vel alij: quod nonnunquam sic contingit, ut nulli damnum inferendum sit, bonum tamen nonnullis exinde oriatur. Istud etiam & misericors nuncupetur, quoniam ex eo misericordia, aut vitæ, aut incolumnitati suæ, vel alienæ exhibetur. Huiusmodi, cum in communi vita, sub infinitis soleant occurrere speciebus proponam aliquot, diluciditatis gratia, in quibus tamen singulis concludendum est, ab eis omnibus fugiendum esse: aut cum Siracida {e}Ne velis mentiri, vllo mendacio, nam af-fi duitas eius non est, futura bono. Rationem ex Joanne assigna-mus: omnis fidelis Deo coniunctus esse debet, sed menda-cium omne à Deo est disiunctissimum; {f}nullum enim men-dacium ex veritate est. Et in Apocalypsi: {g}Omnibus mendacibus portio assignata est, in stagno ardente igne, & sulphure, quod est mors secunda. Et postea: {h}Non intrabit in novam civitatem, quic-quam, quod mendacia loquitur. Sed instantias adhibemus: Pium erat obstetricum factum, de quo supra: pium satis illud Ra-hab quo speculatores abscondit. Utraque interrogatę, si ve-rum fasse fuissent, certa occidione interiissent. Quanto igi-tur facilius, fingendo, & comminiscendo aliquid, e periculo elabendum fuerat, quam certæ occumbendum morti? At respondet {i}Augustinus, quo nemo exactius, aut exquisitius ista explicauit. Si vitam pro Deo, & iustitia, & sanctitate, tem-poralem amisissent; at æternam in cœlis possedissent. Felix est commutatio, ubi vallis hæc miseriarum deseritur; & cœ-lestis perpetuaq; gloria acquiritur. Abnegandi sunt {k}paren-tes, fortunæ, patria, vita denique ipsa derelinquenda est pro Christo. Si pro Christo, & pro veritatis defensione, & propagatione pietatis. Quibus equidem vestigiis omnes sacri martyres instituere, quorum plurimi leuissima abnegatione, aut declinatione, aut extenuatione, à morte euasissent, si mendacio vitam redimendam credidissent.
units.tr: 10. The third kind, which seems to some much more difficult to judge, is the officious lie: by which they mean that which is told when some service of friendship, charity, or usefulness is to be rendered, either to oneself or to another. This sometimes happens in such a way that no harm is done to anyone, yet some good nonetheless arises from it. It may also be called merciful, since by it mercy is shown, either to one's own life or safety, or to another's. Although in common life such lies are wont to occur in countless kinds, I will set out a few for the sake of clarity; yet in each of them it must be concluded that all of them are to be avoided. Hence with Ben Sira: "Do not wish to lie in any way, for habituation to it will not be for good." We assign the reason from John: every believer ought to be joined to God, but every lie is most remote from God; for "no lie is of the truth." And in the Apocalypse: "For all liars a portion is assigned in the burning lake of fire and brimstone, which is the second death." And afterwards: "There shall not enter into the new city anything that speaks lies." But let us raise objections: the deed of the midwives was pious, as mentioned above; that pious deed of Rahab, by which she hid the spies, is also quite pious. Both, if they had been questioned and had told the truth, would have perished by certain slaughter. How much more easily, then, by feigning and inventing something, might they have escaped from danger than submitted to certain death? But Augustine answers, than whom no one has explained these matters more exactly or more carefully. If they had lost temporal life for God, and for righteousness, and for holiness, yet they would have possessed eternal life in heaven. It is a happy exchange, when this valley of miseries is left behind and heavenly and perpetual glory is acquired. Parents must be renounced, fortune, country, and life itself must be abandoned for Christ. If for Christ, and for the defence and propagation of truth and piety. Indeed, all the holy martyrs have followed these footsteps, many of whom would have escaped death by a very slight denial, or evasion, or minimizing, had they believed that life should be redeemed by a lie.

units.la: II. / At qui in meo fortassis sanguine, satis sim futurus pro-digus, in alieno non item. Transfugit ad me frater Chri-stianus, & ut à persequentis abscederem gladio, flagitat. Consanguinitas, Christiana sympathia, periculum immi-nens, misericordia, expetunt, ut tyranno supplicem hunc meum non proderè. Quid si idcirco, me non vidisse, affirma-rem, vt ficquàrentem, & inuestigantè alio transmitterè. Ita fratrè ab interitu vindicabo, & malitiosum hominè à scelere retinebo, & coercebo; qui homicidij, quod nō poterat per-petrare, non erit reus. {m}Quin vide, ne dū alium tuebere, teipsum perdas. Vrget charitas, vt primo te loco respiceres, tui curam ageres. Charitas etenim incipit à seipsa. Et, quæ per-fectissimam exigit obedientiam, lex, iubet, {n}proximum non alias, quam vt teipsum, diligere, cur igitur te destrues, vt aliū extruas? Imo, cur animam pessundas tuam, vt alienā carnem custodias? {o}Os etenim, quod mentitur, occidit animam. Et pperuer-fissime ergo dicitur, vt alter corporaliter viuat, debere alterum spiritualiter mori. Eius potius exemplum imitare, quem nominat idem Augustin. cuius in re isthac toties sermones vsurpo. {q}Erat, inquit, quidam Episcopus, Firmus nomine, firmior voluntate, qui cum ab ipso quæreretur, vbi esset quidam, quem ipse à persecutoribus occultauit, apparitoribus Imperatoriis respondit, se neq; mentiri posse, nec hominem prodere. Et nec è duobus alterum faceret, tormenta multa perpessus est. Quid hoc dici potest fortius, aut honestius? quid cum Christiana constantia coniunctius? Hic patientiam, & amorem exercę tuū, non trepide fingendo, aut veteratorie mentiendo. Vbi etenim falsa loquendo, metas honesti transcenderis, eccepatet ad deliĉta maiora, porta: quid ni etenim, qui vt diceres impulit, vt iurares etiā, moueret? Si, vt falsa dices, consensisti, vt & falsa iures, itidē facile consentias. Nam vt argute Tullius, pro Roscio Comoedo: Quē, vt mētiatur, inducere possum, vt peueret, exorare facile potero. Vere quidem, nam instat tyrānus, vt, quod dixeris, iuramento confirmes. Si annuas, periurus euadis: si renuas, te suspectum vehementer facis. Principiis ergo obsta, à mendacio penitus resiliendo.
units.tr: II. But someone may perhaps say that I may be rather prodigal with my own blood, but not so with another's. A Christian brother has fled to me and begs that I save him from the sword of his pursuer. Kinship, Christian sympathy, imminent danger and mercy urge that I not betray this suppliant to the tyrant. What if, for that reason, I were to affirm that I had not seen him, so that when he was sought and investigated I might send him elsewhere? Thus I would rescue the brother from death, and I would restrain and check the malicious man from crime; he who could not perpetrate murder will not be guilty of it. But see, lest while you protect another, you destroy yourself. Charity urges that you first look to yourself and take care of yourself. For charity begins with itself. And the law, which demands the most perfect obedience, commands that you love your neighbour no otherwise than yourself; why then would you destroy yourself in order to build up another? Nay, why would you ruin your own soul in order to guard another's flesh? For "the mouth that lies kills the soul." And so it is most rightly said that in order for one to live bodily, the other ought to die spiritually. Rather imitate the example of him whom the same Augustine names, whose example I repeatedly use on this matter. There was, he says, a certain bishop named Firmus, firmer in will, who, when he was asked by the imperial officers where a certain man was whom he had hidden from the persecutors, answered that he could neither lie nor betray a man. And, since he would not do either of the two, he endured many tortures. What can be said that is stronger or more honourable? What is more closely joined to Christian constancy? Here you exercise patience and love, not timidly feigning, nor lying craftily. For when by speaking falsely you have crossed the boundaries of what is honourable, the gate opens to greater crimes; for why not, he who has moved you to say what is false might also move you to swear? If you have consented to say false things, so that you may also swear falsely, you will consent just as easily. For as Tullius shrewdly says, in defence of Roscius the comedian: "The man whom I can lead to lie, I can easily persuade to perjure himself." Truly indeed, for the tyrant presses that you confirm by oath what you have said. If you nod assent, you escape as a perjurer; if you refuse, you make yourself greatly suspect. Therefore resist the beginnings, withdrawing entirely from lying.

units.la: 12. Quo miseriora & deflenda magis, sunt illa tempora, in quæ incidimus; dum hodie tanquam in arcanis Romanæ synagogæ habeatur illud, imo clandestinis insusurrationi-bus doceatur, fas esse, non modo homini simpliciter dicenti, sed & iurato, in aliquibus negotiis, à veritate deflectere & deuiare. Ut Africa, sic Italia, semper aliquid apportat noui, & monstri. Dico monstrum, quod à natiua, & genuina Christianæ professionis sinceritate, tam stupendum in modum degenerauit. Dico nouum, quod prioribus est inauditum seculis, apud viros Orthodoxos. Et merito nouitatis (si quid aliud apud illos) taxari poterit, quod emersit nuperrime, & in apricum vix prodiuit, usq; dum in herba delitescens. Nemo etenim illorum tam profano & polluto, aut animo, aut ore repertus est, qui scribendo illud ausus est, in apertum Solis cõspectum emittere, quod secreto tamen murmure prodiderunt, Unctorum Pontificiorum unus & alter. Cum daturos tamen posthac [?]perandum fit, non incommodè iudicaui, ex factis dictisq; submonere, quod futurum augurari licet; quandoquidē opportunitas ita tempestiua, Mendaciorum species indaganti, impresentiarum offeratur. A temporibus Gregorij XIII. Romani Pontificis, quæ Romæ Rhemisq; eriguntur Anglicana Seminaria, noftrates (cum è Britannia discederent) aut fraude illectos, aut vana spe irretitos, aut infamia notatos, aut suo male cõtentos statu, apud illos in Sacrificorũ cooptatos numerum, in Angliam fere quotannis remittunt, ut sub specie docendi, instituendi, cõsolandi, absoluendi, recõciliandi, aliaq;, ut appellant, religionis munia exercendi, incautos, insciosq; homines, præsertim fœminas, & adolescentes, à vera in sanctissimam Principem obedientia diuerterent, & in Pontificium, aut si opus est, Hispanicum obsequium allicerent & aduocarent. Huic veneno remedium, & Antidotum afferre, cum pro officij secundum Deum ratione cuperent, illustrissima Regina, Senatus, regniq; Ordines, seuero interdicendum / Edicto censuerunt, ut, qui Seminaria locaq; vetita adeundo, patriæ non modo desertores, vt transfugæ, verum proditores, vt hostes conspirati, facti fuissent, in transmarinis ad libitum considèrent partibus, sed in ditionem Anglicanam pedem ne efferrent, nisi vellent, vt perduelles, & læsæ Maiestatis rei, vltimum subire supplicium. Sua plurimum interesse Magistratus crediderunt, a grege vulpes, ab ouili lupos abigere, & deterrere; cum pastoribus apud summum Deum & ἀρχιποίμενα Christum, sueq fidei commissorum ratio tam accurata reddenda sit. Sed &, quo salutari quacunq; via perniciosis istorum conatibus obviam iretur, sub capitis periculo prohibuerunt, ne quisquam huic pesti subrepenti auxilium afferret, aut suppetias ullo modo, pascendo, excipiendo, pecuniam impertiendo: imo, neq; tegeret aut celaret, sub carceris discrimine, multæque pecuniariæ, prout Principi visum foret. Quo sagaci consilio, & iustitiæ executione, postquam ipsorum nonnulli, quas satis meruerunt, luissent pœnas: qui secuti sunt, antecessoribus prudentiores facti, (vt semper est deterior posterior dies) salutiferû, vti censent, excogitârunt remedium, cuius feriem libet subdere, vt, cum quali hominum genere nobis sit negotium, & præsens ætas & posteritas sciat.
units.tr: 12. The more wretched and the more to be lamented are those times into which we have fallen; while today it is held, indeed taught by secret whisperings, as among the mysteries of the Roman synagogue, that "it is lawful, not only for a man speaking simply but also for one under oath, in certain business, to turn aside and depart from the truth." As Africa, so Italy always brings forth something new and monstrous. I say monstrous, because it has degenerated in so astonishing a way from the native and genuine sincerity of the Christian profession. I say new, because it was unheard of in earlier centuries among orthodox men. And by the merit of novelty (if anything else) this may rightly be censured, which has emerged most recently and has scarcely come into the light, lurking until now as in the grass. For none of them has been found, with a mind or mouth so profane and polluted, as to dare to put it in writing and bring it into the open view of the sun; yet they have divulged it in secret murmurs, one or two of the anointed Papists. Since, however, they are about to put it into practice hereafter, I have judged it not inappropriate to warn, from their deeds and words, what can be foreseen as likely to happen, since so timely an opportunity is offered for one investigating the species of lies at present. From the time of Gregory XIII, Roman Pontiff, when the English seminaries were set up at Rome and Rheims, our countrymen (when they departed from Britain), either enticed by fraud, or ensnared by vain hope, or branded with infamy, or dissatisfied with their own condition, were enrolled by them in the number of priests, and almost every year they send them back into England, so that under the appearance of teaching, instructing, comforting, absolving, reconciling, and exercising other offices of religion, as they call them, they might turn incautious and unsuspecting people, especially women and young men, away from true obedience to the most holy Prince, and draw and summon them into Papal, or if need be Spanish, allegiance. To bring a remedy and antidote to this poison, since they desired to discharge the duty of their office according to God, the most illustrious Queen, the Senate, and the orders of the realm, by a severe edict decreed that those who, by going to the forbidden seminaries and places, had become deserters of their country, like runaways, and indeed traitors, like conspiring enemies, might remain at their pleasure in the foreign parts beyond the sea, but that they should not set foot in the English dominion, unless they wished, as traitors and guilty of high treason, to undergo the final punishment. The magistrates believed it very much their concern to drive away and deter the foxes from the flock and the wolves from the fold, since an account of their trust must be rendered with the utmost care before almighty God and Christ, the chief shepherd. But also, so that by whatever salutary way the pernicious attempts of these men might be met, they forbade under peril of life that anyone should give aid to this creeping plague, or any support in any way, by feeding, receiving, or lending money; indeed, not even to shelter or conceal them, under danger of prison and fines of money, as it pleased the Prince. After some of them had paid, by this wise plan and execution of justice, the penalties they had richly deserved, those who followed, having become wiser than their predecessors (since the later day is always worse), devised, as they think, a saving remedy, the course of which I am pleased to set out below, so that the present age and posterity may know with what kind of men we have to deal.

units.la: 13. Cum non ita pridem in Anglicana appulisset littora, Southwellus Sacerdos, nihil sibi fore tutius existimauit (vt ex effectu constat) quâ omnes, quibus apud suę factionis homines lateret, indagare vias. Occurrebat nulla facilior, aut expeditior, quam illorû, apud quos degebat, animis suggerendo instillare; vt, si coram Magistratibus in quæstionem vocarentur, ibique peteretur, num Southwellum conspexissent, negarent se vidisse, etiam licet iuramento prius præstito se vera dicturos contestarentur, & præter vera, nihil. Hoc, (quod, vt veri est simillimum, pluribus persuasum extitit) in aperto iudicio, frequentiq; curia, quædam fœmina fassa est; quæ ab vno Judicum post adhibitum iuramentum interrogata, nû in domo Bellamæi Southwellus fuisset, responrespondit; se ab eodem Southwello, longiore sermone inductam fuisse; ut iurata affirmaret, se illum in iisdem, ædibus non conspexisse: licet, reuera ifthac illum vidisset multoties; quod tamen tanquam abditum, aut abstrusum aliquod, apud suum celaret animum. Hoc cum ægre crederent auditores; tam latam & mendacio, & periurio viam muniri, à quopiam mortalium, pietatem vel specie tenus præ se ferente; cum ratione & officio nihil tandem coniunctius esse putauerunt, quam ipsum talis dogmatis authorem consulere, vt pro se responderet. Quod, cum palam, & aperte factum fuisset, non erubuit Southwellus, audacter confiteri, se talia docuisse. Et, vt suâ sententiâ testatam magis faceret, vlteriorem sui dogmatis defensionem suscepit, ex celebri illo Ieremiæ loco, {u}Iurabis, viuit Dominus,in veritate,& in iu-dicio,& in iustitia. Unde conclusum voluit, datam fidem a-pud Iudices de Sacrificis detegendis, pro iuramento habendam non esse; quasi tale examen, quæstioque habita, nec iudicii, nec iustitiæ fuisset. Salubre mehercle consilium, præquo in Antiquis Martyribus, prudentiâ non possumus non desiderare, qui tam solerti, acutoque commento, sed diris cruciatibus non subduxerunt. Verum, ne unius unica, & singularis sententia ifthæc videatur, è qua generalius iudicium faciendum non est, secundum audite, cuius fortassis eo celebrius futurum est testimonii, quo altiore & illustriore Iesuitæ titulo insigniatur.
units.tr: 13. Not long ago, when Southwell the priest had landed on English shores, he judged (as the outcome shows) that nothing was safer for him than to search out ways by which all those who might lie hidden among the men of his faction could be secured. No method was easier or more convenient than to instil into the minds of those among whom he lived a plan: if they were called into question before the magistrates, and were asked there whether they had seen Southwell, they should deny that they had seen him, even though they assured them, after first taking an oath, that they would speak the truth and nothing but the truth. This (as is most likely true, and was believed by many) was confessed in an open court, before a crowded assembly, by a certain woman. When one of the judges, after the oath had been administered, asked her whether Southwell had been in the house of Bellamy, she replied that she had been induced by Southwell himself, through a rather long speech, to swear that she had not seen him in that same house, although in fact she had seen him there many times; but she kept this hidden in her own mind as something concealed and obscure. When the hearers could hardly believe that such a broad road to lying and perjury was being paved by any mortal who professed piety, even in appearance, they judged that nothing was more fitting to reason and duty than to consult the author of this doctrine himself, so that he might answer for himself. When this had been done openly and plainly, Southwell did not blush to confess boldly that he had taught such things. And, to make his opinion more firmly attested, he undertook a further defence of his doctrine, drawing on that famous passage of Jeremiah: "You shall swear, As the Lord lives, in truth, in judgement, and in righteousness." From this he wished to conclude that the pledge given before the judges, to reveal the priests, was not to be held as an oath; as if such an examination and interrogation, held in that way, were neither judgement nor righteousness. A wholesome counsel indeed, by Hercules, in which we cannot but miss the wisdom of the ancient martyrs, who did not withdraw from torments, though they lacked such a clever and sharp contrivance. But lest this be thought the single and isolated opinion of one man, from which no general judgement should be made, hear the following, which will perhaps be the more celebrated as a testimony, the higher and more illustrious the title of Jesuit by which it is marked.

units.la: 14. Iohannes Gerardus Iesuita, in Arcis Londinensis tum habitus custodia, {x}cum per viros tum prudentia, tum {w}authoritate conspicuos, de Southwelli placito edocere-tur, rogatus est ferio, quid de illius dicto iudicii ferret. Neq; poterat vir egregius dissimulare, se etiam in eadem opinione constitutum. Et quo robur ac firmamentum Thesi adderet, Saluatoris Christi exemplum adduxerat, qui consanguineis suis hortantibus, ut gloriolæ captandæ gratia ad festum ascenderet, respondit, {y}Vos ascendite ad diem festum hunc, ego enim non ascendam: vbi inquit, secretam animi intentionem apud se celauit: postea siquidem, profectus est. Neque hic Gerardus subsistit, sed secundo mundi Dominum aggressus est. Christus, inquit, aliquando inficiatus est, {z}filium hominis iudicij diem cognouisse. Hic secretum ille suum apud se celauit, neque aliis diuulgauit, cum tamen, quemadmodum filius fuerat hominis, & iudicij horam probe intellexerit, & aliud quicquam ignorare non potuerit. Addi ditinsuper, quod si cuiusipiam testimonium iuridice requiratur, & in causis seculi, cuiusmodi forenses esse solent, cum tali æquiuocatione responderi non debere: verum in negotiis ad religionem, & Catholicos spectantibus, vt hac Homonymia testis vtatur, fas esse. Pie sane de Iesu, sanctissimo Dei filio, pronunciauit Iesuita. Cæterum cum non sine stupore & horrore aliquo, ex ore tanti, quantus videri voluit Gerardus, Theologi, hæc prolata, viri pij & prudentes audiissent, non tacuerunt coram: Quinimo (cum damnabilia, & blasphema hæc primo aspectu visa sunt) enixe requirebant, mouebant, obtestabantur, vt suam vellet sententiam propria manu conscribere, suisque vellet verbis concipere, ne perperam fortassis, & non dextre ab aliis descripta caperetur. Hic tamen tergiuersari cœperat non mediocriter, Iesuita, nec voluerat vllo pacto mandare literis: nō, quod minus vera extitissent, quæ dixisset, sed, quod nolet in propatulum talia diuulgari. Vrgent tamen adhuc Regii (nam sic fuerant) Officiarij, vt sermoni suo, ab aliis tum præsentibus conscripto, vellet saltem subscribere, vt constaret istiusmodi esse illius, sociiq; defensionem: sed & isthic recusauit. Elegantuli sane homines, qui exceptionib. dicamne tam friuolis, imo euasionibus tam fœdis & portentosis, veritati caliginem offundere obnituntur: Non vidi, hoc est, non vidi, cum proposito vobis enunciandi. Filius hominis nō meuit[?] iudicii diem, hoc est, non nouit cum proposito, aut in-tentione illis declarandi, aut patefaciendi.
units.tr: 14. John Gerard the Jesuit, held at that time in custody in the Tower of London, when he was being informed by men both prudent and conspicuous for authority about Southwell's view, was asked at last what he thought of that saying of his. Nor could the distinguished man conceal that he too held the same opinion. And to add strength and firmness to the thesis, he had cited the example of Christ the Saviour, who, when his kinsmen urged him to go up to the feast in order to win a little glory, replied: "You go up to this feast; for I will not go up," where, he says, he kept the secret intention of his mind hidden within himself; for afterwards indeed he went. Nor does Gerard stop here, but attacks the Lord of the world a second time. Christ, he says, at one time denied that the Son of Man knew the day of judgement. Here he kept his secret hidden within himself and did not divulge it to others, although, as the Son of Man, he had surely understood both the day and the hour of judgement, and could not have been ignorant of anything else. He adds moreover that if someone's testimony is required judicially, and in matters of the world, such as are usually of a forensic kind, one ought not to answer with such equivocation; but in affairs touching religion and Catholics, it is lawful for a witness to use this homonymy. Certainly the Jesuit spoke piously about Jesus, the most holy Son of God. But when these statements were heard, not without astonishment and some horror, from the mouth of a theologian of such standing as Gerard wished to appear, the pious and prudent men who heard them did not keep silent in his presence. Indeed (since these things seemed damnable and blasphemous at first sight) they earnestly asked, urged and entreated him to set down his opinion in his own hand and in his own words, lest it be taken in a faulty way, perhaps badly transcribed by others. Here, however, the Jesuit had begun to evade not a little, and by no means wished to commit it to writing: not because what he had said was less true, but because he was unwilling for such things to be spread abroad openly. The royal officers, for such they were, still pressed him to subscribe at least to his statement, written down by others present, so that it might be established that this was his own and his companion's defence; but he refused even there. Truly these are elegant fellows, who strive to cast a fog over the truth with such trifling excuses, or rather with such foul and monstrous evasions: "I did not see," that is, "I did not see, with the intention of declaring it to you. The Son of Man did not know the day of judgement," that is, "he did not know, with the purpose or intention of making it known or revealing it to them."

units.la: 15. Videte, fratres, si peruigili cautela, & prudentia ser-pentina hodie non fit opus, quandoquidem cum tam versa-tili, lubricoque virorum genere agendum fit. Quid etenim posthac sanctum, aut sincerum fiet? Cui tandem, aut qua in causa, non erit omnium suspecta fides? Aperta dehinc pa-tescet porta, qua pietas & iustitia, & quæcunq; ad humanã societatem pertinent, e natura rerum eliminentur penitus. Illud etenim si fixum firmumq; fuerit, violari posse fidê, Ma-gistratui sub iurisiurandi sacramento datam, quid ni multo magis in priuatis cōmerciis? Si in religionis causa, qua nulla est illustrior, quanto tutius in quacunq; negotiatione expe-dienda? Si hæreticum ita hominem circumuenire liceat, tū & Ethnicū: tum & Atheum: tum certe inimicum: profanū demū quēlibet: & deinceps, vllo vitio confpurcatū. Et breui futurū est, vt pro arbitrio, lucroque nostro, nemo sit futurus mortaliū, in quē nostræ suspicionis faba nō cudetur. De cæ-tero, inducia, pacta, cōuentus, fœderaq; omnia (vt quæ per-sonæ solū laruæq; sint, ad fraudes pertexendas fabricatæ) ad Inferos amandent. Honestissima etenim est respōsio, Iuraui me culturū pacē, & uäquillitatē: verū est; sed sub arcana hac cōditione, nisi hostē incautū posse dephedere: nisi ex rupta pace, maius emolumētū assulgeret. Quid hoc aliud est, quā {a}Iura, periura, secretum prodere noli?
units.tr: 15. See, brethren, whether there is not today need of vigilant caution and serpentine prudence, since we have to deal with a kind of men so shifty and slippery. For what then will be holy or sincere henceforth? In what cause, and to whom at last, will faith not be suspect to all? An open door will then stand wide, through which piety and justice, and whatever pertains to human society, will be thoroughly cast out of the order of nature. For if it is fixed and firm that the faith pledged to a magistrate under the sanction of an oath may be violated, why not much more so in private dealings? If in the cause of religion, than which none is more illustrious, how much more safely in any business to be transacted? If it is lawful to thus circumvent a heretic, then also a heathen, then an atheist, then surely an enemy, and finally any profane person whatever, and afterwards anyone stained with any vice. And soon it will come to pass that, at our own pleasure and gain, there will be no mortal on whom the bean of our suspicion will not be struck. For the rest, truces, pacts, agreements and all covenants (as being mere masks and disguises, devised for weaving frauds) may be sent off to the infernal regions. For the most honourable answer is: "I have sworn that I will cultivate peace and tranquillity"; that is true, but under this secret condition: if one could catch an unwary enemy; if, once the peace was broken, a greater advantage might accrue. What is this other than "Swear, forswear, but do not betray the secret"?

units.la: Quid hoc aliud est, quam cum {b}Priscillianistis damnatis hæreticis conspirare? Præistis, vt nouitius, locutus est Da-uid, {c}Qui iuratus est in damnum suum, non tamen mutat: vt Neophytus, Paulus, {d}Homines per eum iurant, qui sit maior, atq; eisdem omnis controuersia finis, est iuramentum ad confirmationem adhibitum. Fiet iam vir bonus, què peccasse dixit {e}Tullius: eo nomine, quod, cum dierum triginta pactæ essent inducia noctu populabatur agros; perinde quasi dierū, non noctiū,
units.tr: What is this other than to conspire with the condemned heretics, the Priscillianists? As the novice David said: "He who has sworn to his own hurt does not change"; as Paul the neophyte said: "Men swear by one who is greater, and for them the end of every controversy is an oath given for confirmation." So the good man will become one who, as Tully said, sinned, on this ground: that when a truce of thirty days had been agreed, he ravaged the fields by night, as if the truce had been made for days and not for nights.

units.la: {a} Augustin. de hæresibus ad Quod vult Deum. factæ essent inducìæ. Deniq; stantibus istis fidei fundamen-tis, non video, quis periurus, fœdifragus, versipellis, aut mendax homuncio, non Catholicus, non Orthodoxus, non probus & honestus sit habendus.
units.tr: {a} Augustine, On Heresies, to Quodvultdeus. Finally, while these foundations of faith stand, I do not see who should be held as a perjurer, a breaker of faith, a shifty fellow, or a lying little man, unless he is not a Catholic, not orthodox, not upright and honest.

units.la: 16. At quid tandem est, quod affers Southwelle? Religio iuramenti integra, & inuiolata custodienda est in iudicio & iustitia. Negas igitur Confessum Regiorum iudicum, de rebus capitalibus sententiam ferentium, si Sacrificuli Rei sint, iudicium & iustitiam exercere. Luculente illud satis, iam ab hinc diu, confirmatum dedit, {f}qui illud ex proposito ventilauit argumentum. Et ubiq; fere gentium clementissimæ Principis, meridiano Sole clarior apparet moderatio, eousque à cæde sanguineque abhorrentis, ut quam plurimos deprehensos, conuictos, damnatos, propositi etiam tenaces sui, solo multauerit exilio, vita donauerit: & reliquis palinodiam canentibus, & misericordiam imploranti-bus, quotidie, ad patibulum, gratiam regalem, veniamque concedat, verumtamen, si foret ambiguum, num bene, male ve meritos supplicio afficiat, adeoq; num æque, vel iniquius dicat: an vafro cum mendacio, vel subdolo periurio, Christi confessor, è periculo se debeat expedire? Num talibus elabendi modis, usi sunt sancti Martyres, in pietatis causa, etiam cum ad tribunalia, tyrannorum indubitatorum statirent? Apud {g}Nabuchodonosorum tres pueri, apud {h}An-tiochum septem fratres, apud Principes Sacerdotum {i}Apostoli flagris cæsi, apud Herodem {k}Iacobus & Petrus, apud Festum Paulum, ita apud præfectos {m}Ignatius, {n}Polycarpus, {o}Laurentius, aliique iam in cœlis fulgentes lampa-des, veritatem simplicem, confessionem apertam, constantiam virilem, patientiam & cõfidentiam Christianam præferebant: non turpibus suffugiis, & diuerticulis inhonestis, mentiendi, peierandi, dicendi partem, supprimendi reliqua præsentis lucis usuram[?] redimebant. Antiquitus indecorum ChristiaChristiano nomini existimauit {p}Eusebius, cum à Gentilibus ad idololatriam vrgentib. quidam, qui ad altare non ap-propinquauerat, neque quidquam impuri tetigerat, sacrifi-casse tamen affirmaretur, ille vero tacitus eorum tulit con-tumeliam, neque re negata, se inde proripuit. Quid hic di-ceret Eusebius, si modo viueret? Sed beatissimi Saluatoris multo potius exemplum afferendum esset, (qui Pilati sub-selliis astans, iniustitiam, & non iudicium causatus non est, vt sic fucata diceret,) nisi hunc ipsum in participationem fraudis, (horresco dicere) trahendum Gerardus censuisset. At quam pie, quam apposite? {q}Ego ad festum non ascendam; cum ascendere tamen in animo habuisset. Sed non ascen-dam cum proposito enunciandi vobis. Vt in fumum istud abit, si velimus Christum ita loquentem capere: Ego non-dum ascendam ad festum? Qui Nondum dicit, non negat: sed tempus protelando, non adhuc venisse horam, venturam tamen postea, manifestum facit. Et additum Nondum hoc, potuisset perspicere, qui Græcum consuluisset fontem, vbi legitur: ἐγὼ οὔπω ἀναβαίνω εἰς τὴν ἑορτὴν ταύτην, vbi Οὔπω Nondum est. Quod ex ipsa vulgata editione potuisset ediscere, vbi cum in textu legitur, Ego non ascendam, in margine pro varia lectione ponitur Nondum. Et in fine eiusdem versus Οὔπω per Nondum simpliciter redditur. ὁ καιρὸς ὁ ἐμὸς οὔπω πάρεστιν [?], meum tempus nondum impletum est. Sed & tale illud est: Nouit Christus omnia, ideoq; iudicij horam: sed nō nouit, vt ipsis osten-deret. Cum expresse Saluator, Nonscit filius, id est, quatenus filius hominis, & ex carne compositus, vel quatenus creatus esset, non habita ad coniunctam, & counitam diuinita-tem relatione. Et humanam hanc naturam, vt Angelos, vt reliquos mortales, simpliciter non nouisse iudicij, & refur-rectionis horam pronunciauit, ({t}Sed de die illo, ac hora, nemo scit, neque Angeli quidem, qui in cœlo sunt, nec ipse filius, sed pater) non solum, vt illis non aperiret: quod si de aliis hominibus,
units.tr: 16. But what then is it that you bring forward, Southwell? Religion requires that an oath be kept whole and inviolate in judgement and in righteousness. You therefore deny that the council of the royal judges, pronouncing sentence in capital cases, exercises judgement and righteousness if the accused are priests. He gave a sufficiently clear confirmation of this long ago, he who discussed the question deliberately. And the moderation of the most merciful prince, clearer than the midday sun, shines almost everywhere among the nations, so far removed from bloodshed and slaughter that he has fined and exiled many whom he has caught, convicted and condemned, even though they were tenacious of their purpose, and has spared their lives; and, while the rest sing a palinode and implore mercy, he grants them daily, from the gallows, royal favour and pardon. But suppose it were doubtful whether he punishes with death those rightly or wrongly deserving it, and so whether he speaks equally or more unjustly: ought a confessor of Christ to rescue himself from danger by a crafty lie or a sly perjury? Did the holy martyrs use such ways of escape in the cause of piety, even when they stood before the tribunals of undoubted tyrants? Before Nebuchadnezzar stood the three boys; before Antiochus the seven brothers; before the chief priests the apostles, scourged with whips; before Herod James and Peter; before Festus Paul; so before the prefects Ignatius, Polycarp, Laurence, and the others now shining in heaven as lamps, they set forward the plain truth, an open confession, manly constancy, and Christian patience and confidence. They did not buy off the rest of the light's use with shameful evasions and dishonourable hiding-places of lying, perjury, speaking part of the truth and suppressing the remainder. Eusebius thought it unbecoming to the Christian name that, when some man who had not approached the altar and had touched nothing unclean was urged by the Gentiles to idolatry and was declared to have sacrificed, he silently bore their insult and, without denying the fact, went away from there. What would Eusebius say here, if he were alive? But rather the example of the most blessed Saviour ought to be brought forward, who, standing before the bench of Pilate, did not plead injustice and not judgement, so as to say such disguised things; unless Gerard had judged that he too should be dragged into participation in the fraud (I shudder to say it). But how piously, how aptly! "I will not go up to the feast," though he had intended to go up. But I will not go up, with the purpose of declaring it to you. How does this vanish like smoke, if we wish to take Christ speaking thus: "I am not yet going up to the feast"? He who says "not yet" does not deny; by putting off the time he makes it plain that the hour has not yet come, though it will come later. And he who had consulted the Greek source, where it is read: "ἐγὼ οὔπω ἀναβαίνω εἰς τὴν ἑορτὴν ταύτην", where "οὔπω" is "not yet", could have perceived that this "not yet" had been added. He could have learned it from the Vulgate edition itself, where, while in the text it is read "I will not go up", in the margin "not yet" is set down as a variant reading. And at the end of the same verse "οὔπω" is simply rendered by "not yet": "ὁ καιρὸς ὁ ἐμὸς οὔπω πάρεστιν", "my time is not yet fulfilled." But that other saying is of the same kind: Christ knew all things, and therefore the hour of judgement; but he did not know it, so as to show it to them. Since the Saviour expressly said: "The Son does not know", that is, insofar as he is the Son of Man and composed of flesh, or insofar as he was created, without regard to his relation to the divinity joined and united with him. And he declared that this human nature, like the angels and the rest of mortals, simply did not know the hour of judgement and resurrection ("But of that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels who are in heaven, nor the Son himself, but the Father"), not only in the sense that he did not reveal it to them; for if this were said of other men, ...

units.la: E angelisque in eadem periodo, & gradatione adiectis, veli-mus intelligere, ridiculum foret. Nemo scit, ne angeli, id est, ita vt velint aliis renunciare. Sed apud homines pios & doctos, nominasse isthaec, & nude propositsse, satis erat con-futasse. Si prodierit posthac quisquam, qui tueri volet ista, quique explicare, & assecuerant (quod nondum Iesuita[?]) sententiam suam prodet, locus dabitur exactius & scrupu-losius ista discutiendi. Interea vnicum hac in re Gregorii Nazianzeni testimonium subiicio, cui cum obiicerent Eu-nomiani, filium Dei patre esse indigniorem, quia aliquid nesciret, dum diei vltimi horam ignorauerit, Respondit sat[?] {a}enim qui potest ignorare quidquam in universitate rerum ipsa Sapientia? Creaturarum opifex? qui consummator & immutator, finem eorum, quae facta sunt? qui sic novit ea, quae Dei sunt, quemadmodum spiritus hominis, quaecunque sunt in ipso? quid hac cognitione perfectius? Qui accurate novit ea, quae horam illam praecedunt, quaeque velut ipsam finis cutem stringunt; horam ipsam ignorat? Id vero aenigmati simile fuerit. Quemadmodum si quis accurate se dicat scire, quae ante murum sunt, murum ipsum non nosse, veldiei finem scire, principium noctis ignorare; in quibus alterius cognitio, necessario alterum quoque secum trahit. Hucusque disputans, discutiensque loquitur. Immediate tamen difficultatem solvit: Num intelligere quivis facile potest, quod norit ut Deus, ignorare se dicat, ut homo, si quis id, quod in oculos incurrit, ab eo, quod intelligitur, separet? Nam quod filii appellatio hic absolute, nulloque respectu ponitur, non adiecto, cuius filius intelligatur: idipsum facit, ut cogitemus, ignorationem illam religiosius accipiendam esse, relatam ad humanam, non divinam naturam. Hic si ulla videatur delitescere obscuritas, quae lectori intelligenti nulla est, aenigmaticum sermonem explicate tradit Elias Cretensis Episcopus, commentario suo in illum Gregorii locum; qui, cum caetera expedierit, {b}t soluit, inquit, Gregorius id, quod in dubium vocabatur. Quia enim Christus duplex erat, idcirco notam ei fuisse ei fuisse dicit horam illam, tanquam Deo: ignotam vero, tanquam homini. Quod posterius rursum declarans subiicit: si quis id, quodin oculos incurrit, abeo, quod intelligitur, separet. Ea verba quid sibi ve- lunt, hoc quodam modo intelligemus.
