Serui forma, quam Dominus adsumpsit, secundum se quidem considerata, vt creatum quiddam; & serua est, (nam hominis natura, Dei mancipium est, qui eam condidit,) & futurorum cognitionem nullam habet; quanquam ex gratia nonnunquam id consequatur. Verum vt propter hypostasin, siue personae identitatem, & indissolubilem vnionem, viuificus audiebat, ita & futurorū cognitione collocupletatus est. Nam quum vnus sit Christus, non potest simul, & seruus esse suiipsius, & dominus scire, pariter, & ignorare: quam quidem diu vnus esse intelligitur, propter vnionem hypostaticam, quae & ineffabilis est, & indissolubilis. Si vero per exiles mentis cogitationes (nam cateroquin res conferri nequit) adsumptum, abeo, qui adsumpsit, separaueris; tum scilicet, & adsumptum mancipium erit, & ignorare dicetur. Atque eatenus nunc quoque dicitur, horam illam & diem Dominus ignorare, nimirum vt homo. Ita quae aduersus Antiquos, & obsoletos haereticos, diuinitati Saluatoris detrahentes, dicta fuerunt; contra nouum hoc hominum genus, calumniam eidem Christo ob-trudentium, tanquam sophisticam imposturam facienti, locum hodie habent.
units.tr: It would be ridiculous to want to understand the words "Of the angels" in this same sequence and gradation, that is, that they "neither know" in the sense that they wish to report it to others. But among pious and learned people, it was enough to mention these things and set them forth bare in order to refute them. If anyone should come forward hereafter who wishes to defend these things, and to explain them, and who will publish his opinion (which the Jesuit has not yet done), an opportunity will be given of discussing these matters more exactly and scrupulously. Meanwhile, I add one testimony of Gregory Nazianzen in this matter. When the Eunomians objected to him that the Son of God is less worthy than the Father, because he is ignorant of something, since he did not know the hour of the last day, he replied: {a}For how can anyone be ignorant of anything in the universe, if Wisdom itself is not? The Maker of creatures, who brings to completion and changes the end of the things that have been made? who knows the things of God as the spirit of man knows whatever is in him? What could be more perfect than this knowledge? He who knows accurately the things that precede that hour, and that closely bind the end, as it were, does not know the hour itself? That would indeed be like a riddle. It is as if someone said he knows accurately what lies before the wall, yet did not know the wall itself, or knew the end of the day but was ignorant of the beginning of the night; in which cases the knowledge of one necessarily draws the other along with it. Having argued and discussed thus far, he speaks; yet he immediately resolves the difficulty: Can anyone easily understand how one who knows as God can say he is ignorant, as a man, if someone separates what falls under the eyes from what is understood? For since the name of Son is here used absolutely, with no respect added, and it is not stated whose son is meant, this very thing makes us think that the ignorance is to be taken more reverently, referred to the human nature and not the divine. If here any obscurity seems to lie hidden, which is none to an intelligent reader, Elias of Crete, bishop, explains this enigmatic discourse clearly in his commentary on that passage of Gregory; who, having dealt with the other points, {b}and resolves, he says, what Gregory had called in doubt. For since Christ was twofold, therefore that hour was known to him as God, but unknown as man. Declaring this latter point again, he adds: if someone separates what falls under the eyes from what is understood. We shall understand what those words mean in this way. The form of a servant, which the Lord assumed, considered in itself, as a created thing, is a servant (for the nature of man is the bondservant of God who made it) and has no knowledge of future things, although by grace it sometimes attains it. But inasmuch as, on account of the hypostasis, or identity of person, and the indissoluble union, he was enlivened by the Word, so he was also enriched with knowledge of future things. For since Christ is one, he cannot at once be the servant of himself and the Lord, know and be ignorant in the same respect; as long as he is understood to be one, on account of the hypostatic union, which is both unspeakable and indissoluble. But if by slender thoughts of the mind (for otherwise the matters cannot be compared) you separate the one assumed from him who assumed, then indeed the assumed will be a bondservant and will be said to be ignorant. And so far it is still said now that the Lord is ignorant of that hour and day, namely as man. Thus what was said against the ancient and obsolete heretics, who detracted from the divinity of the Saviour, has its place today against this new kind of men, who obtrude a calumny against the same Christ, as if he were practising a sophistical imposture.

units.la: 17. Verum, vt, quod res est, in apertam lucem proferam, vereor, ne ex illa radice haec iam tandem pullularit, quae ante annos aliquanto plures alicubi plantata est. Superioribus etenim temporibus, post Bullam Pii Quinti, contra Principe piissimam Romae effulminatâ, è scrinio sui pectoris, aut depromsit Pōtifex, aut eruditione & authoritate celebrior apud illos Pōtificius aliquis, nescio sane quis, cōclusiones aliquot ad Angliā pertinentes, vt Eleusina tamen Sacra, Cererisque mysteria, nullo pacto diuulgandas. Mihi tamen fas fit proloqui, cū obedientiae sacramento in Romanā sedē non distinear. u Sitin[?] tribunali Haereticorum respondendū sit, iuramentum exactum à Iudice non competente, quales nunc omnes sunt in Anglia, in iurisdictione Ecclesiastica, non obligat, nisi secundum intentionem iuranris. Qui iurabetur igitur, cum sit Catholicus, coram Haereticis, vel recuset iuramentum, quod est prudentius, vel sophisticè iuret, & sophisticè respondeat singulis interrogationibus, si de fide non sint. Interrogatus igitur de Catholicis indicandis, & iuratus, si praetextu sui iuramenti, nominat, detegitque aliquos, bispeccat.
units.tr: 17. But, that I may bring the matter into plain light, I fear that from that root these things have at last sprouted, which some years ago was planted somewhere. For in earlier times, after the Bull of Pius V, thundered against the most pious Prince at Rome, either the Pontiff himself drew from the chest of his breast, or some Papist more celebrated for learning and authority among them, I know not who, put forward certain conclusions relating to England, which, however, like the Eleusinian rites and the mysteries of Ceres, must by no means be made public. Yet it is lawful for me to say, since I am not bound by the oath of obedience to the Roman see. If one must answer before a tribunal of heretics, an oath exacted by an incompetent judge, such as all now are in England in ecclesiastical jurisdiction, does not bind, except according to the intention of the one swearing. Therefore, one who is to be sworn, being a Catholic, before heretics, should either refuse the oath, which is more prudent, or swear sophistically and answer each question sophistically, if they are not concerning the faith. Therefore, being questioned about indicating Catholics, and sworn, if under pretext of his oath he names and discloses some, he sins.

units.la: Sic: licitum est sacerdotibus aequivocare, vel nomina mutare, apud eos, qui sedent in portubus ad telonium, aut si in via interrogentur de religione sua, aut unde venerint, responso indirecto licebit effugere, vel deludere interrogationem. Et si temere quis, & inconsiderate Haereticis iuramentum dederit, se velle ad omnia interrogata sincere respondere, cum petuntur aliqua, quae in praeiudicium fient Catholicorum, quia peccavit iurando, iuramento non tenetur illi respondere. Et si Sacerdos ad tribunal iudicis iuratus petatur, quoties Missam celebrauit, vel apud quos, &c. ut aliis periculum creetur, non tenetur respondere, quia non est legitimum iudicium; nec iurantis intentio debet esse, nisi ad ea revelanda, quae tuto potest. Respondeat tamen aliquo sensu verum, etiamsi non sit in intentione interrogantis. Si de se requiratur, consilium esset dicere veritatem, & mori pro fide, si opus est: alios autem non revelet: etenim non tenetur, quia iudex haereticus, vel schismaticus, amittit omnem iurisdictionem. Si vero in iudicio de veritate interrogetur, nec de se, nec de aliis respondere debet, sed Amphibologice, vel aequivoce affirmando, iniquitatem iudicis poterit declarare. Qui ista iam tandem nouimus, vel à Petri successore nostratibus indulta, vel ab aliquo eius partis Antesigna-no, secrete edocta, de hinc mirari amplius sustineamus. Quid aliud in Southwello, quid aliud in Gerardo, reliquisque eius sortis poterimus expectare, cum à coelesti quasi oraculo ista edidicerunt?
units.tr: Thus: it is lawful for priests to equivocate or change names, among those who sit at the toll-booths in the ports, or if on the road they are asked about their religion, or whence they came, they may escape or elude the question by an indirect answer. And if anyone rashly and inconsiderately has given an oath to heretics that he will answer sincerely to all questions, when some things are asked which would be to the prejudice of Catholics, because he sinned in swearing, he is not bound by the oath to answer them. And if a priest sworn is brought before the tribunal of a judge, as often as he has celebrated Mass, or with whom, etc., so that danger may be created for others, he is not bound to answer, because it is not a lawful judgment; nor should the intention of the one swearing be other than to reveal those things which he can do safely. Let him nevertheless answer the truth in some sense, even if it is not in the intention of the questioner. If he is asked about himself, it would be advisable to tell the truth and die for the faith, if need be; but he should not reveal others: for he is not bound, since a heretical or schismatic judge loses all jurisdiction. But if in a trial he is asked about the truth, he must answer neither about himself nor about others, but by affirming amphibologically or equivocally he may declare the injustice of the judge. Since we now know these things, either granted to our countrymen by the successor of Peter, or secretly taught by some standard-bearer of his party, let us no longer marvel at them. What else can we expect in Southwell, what else in Gerard, and the rest of that sort, since they have learned these things from what is, as it were, a heavenly oracle?

units.la: 18. Hic ut dixit aliquando pro Roscio Tullius: x Quid primum quaerat, aut unde potissimum exordiar Auditores? Post Pontificis illas diras superbe iactitatas, neque iudices sunt in Anglia, præsertim si de Sacrificiis agatur, nec tribunalia æquitatis, nec, quæ ad clauum, Regina, sedeat. Immortales summo patri sunt habendæ gratiæ, quod sinceros magistratus integrosq;, & iudices incorruptos, si alicubi, in Europa; spectatissimam autem fœminam, Augustissimam Principem, si in orbe Christiano, aut vnquam, aut vspiam, nostro regno donauerit, {y}Fremuerunt certe Gentes, aduersus vnctam Domini, sed, qui sedet ab alto, ipsarum cõsilia ludibrio habuit. Quo acerbo felleoque magis animo contra nostræ Reip. Sionisque tranquillitatem coniurauerunt, quo venenatis magis linguis Sanctissimam Dominam, vt {z}Dauidem Shimei, perculerunt, eo altiore & illustriore dignitatis eminentia, & istam & illam extulit, euexitq; mundi Dominus, vtramq; conspicuam, & amicis & inimicis, tanquã in medio coelo Solem proponens. Beatum Albioni dedit Deus seculũ vt calamitati eius inhiantib. & oculi defecerint, & ora exaruerint; lectissimæ autem Principi, {a}vitam prolixam, imperium secumcurum, domum tutam, exercitus fortes, Senatum fidelem, populum probum, orbem quietum, & quæcunq; hominis aut Cæsaris vota sunt: vt, cui Italus maledixerit, ei Dominum vberem in modum benedixisse, satis superq; contestatum fiat. Fruatur, precamur, tali {b}Debora, in æternum, patria, matre in Israele: fruatur tali populo Regina beatissima, inuitis quibuscunque, exitium tam preciosæ animæ imprecantibus. Ita erant apud nos, spectatæ probitatis iudices, & iustitiæ tribunalia. Quin vt deliris istorum somniis paulisper geramus morem: Esto, Pontifex hancipsam, subditosq; suos, censura Ecclesiastica legitima perstrinxerit. An maiores hoc fulmen habiturum vires est, quã illud, de quo Christus, Excommunicationis nodos laqueosq; designans, {c}Dic Ecclesiæ: Quod si Ecclesiam audire neglexerit, sit tibi velut quispiam Ethnicus, & quispiam Publicanus. Sitigitur tanquã Ethnica; simus omnes, vt Publicani. Placet etenim ita ludere, animi gratia. An Ethnicis data fides, an Publi-
units.tr: 18. Here, as Tully once said for Roscius: What shall I first ask, or from what point shall I most fitly begin, hearers? After those dreadful curses of the Pontiff proudly boasted, there are neither judges in England, especially if the matter concerns the Sacrifices, nor tribunals of equity, nor, at the helm, a Queen who sits. Thanks must be given to the Highest Father, immortal thanks, that he has granted sincere and upright magistrates and incorruptible judges, if anywhere in Europe; but a most distinguished woman, a most august Princess, if in the Christian world, ever or anywhere, he has given her to our kingdom. {y}The nations indeed raged against the anointed of the Lord, but he who sits on high has held their counsels in derision. The more bitter and gall-filled their spirit with which they conspired against the tranquillity of our Commonwealth and of Sion, the more with venomous tongues they struck the most holy Lady, as Shimei struck David, the higher and more illustrious the eminence of dignity with which the Lord of the world raised up and exalted both her and that one, setting both conspicuously, to friends and enemies alike, as the sun in mid-heaven. God gave Albion a happy age, so that the eyes of those gaping at her calamity have failed, and their mouths have dried up; but to the most chosen Princess, {a}a long life, a secure reign, a safe house, strong armies, a faithful Senate, an upright people, a quiet world, and whatever wishes of man or Caesar there are: so that, to whom the Italian has cursed, to her the Lord has blessed in abundant measure, may be sufficiently attested and more than sufficiently proven. May she enjoy, we pray, such a Deborah, forever, a mother in Israel, a country: may the most blessed Queen enjoy such a people, though whoever are unwilling, who wish destruction upon so precious a soul. So there were among us judges of proven integrity, and tribunals of justice. But, that we may humour these dreams of theirs for a little: grant that the Pontiff has struck her and her subjects with lawful ecclesiastical censure. Will that thunderbolt have greater force than that of which Christ, marking out the knots and snares of excommunication, said: {c}Tell it to the Church; but if he neglects to hear the Church, let him be to you as a Gentile and a publican. Let her then be as a Gentile; let us all be as publicans. For it pleases them to play thus, for the sake of amusement. Or was faith given to Gentiles, or to publicans...
Tertullian, in the Apologeticus, chapter 30.
Judges 5:7.

units.la: {c} Matth. 18. Publicanis iuramentū, Deo inuocato, factū mendacio & periurio cuertetur? Agedum {d}Abrahame, euge {e}Isaac, lice-cia vobis facta est, Abimelechum post solennem sacramenti religionem circumueniendi, quippe incircumcisum. Non Dauidis magis manu, quam voce capieris, Ægyptie famule, qui Deum contestanti fidem adhibebis, Ieconiah versus Babylonium fœdifragus, iam prudens est, {g}& euadet: quod negauit Dominus, ob promissum violatum vehementer excæ-descens. Sed vt olim Pharisæi iuramenta distinguebant, {h}per altare nihil est: tantundem, si per templum; at si per aurum: per donarium, tum reuera peccatur, ita sane in successoribus Pharisaicæ sectæ, distinctionem isthic expectamus.
units.tr: Matthew 18. Shall an oath sworn to the Publicans, with God called upon, be overturned by lying and perjury? Come now: Abraham, well done; Isaac, you were allowed to deceive Abimelech after the solemn bond of an oath, since he was uncircumcised. Not by David's hand, but by his voice, you will be taken, Egyptian servant, who will give faith to the God you call as witness. Jeconiah, the covenant-breaker toward the Babylonian, is already wise, and he will escape; what the Lord denied, he is greatly embittered by, because of the violated promise. But as the Pharisees once distinguished oaths, "by the altar it is nothing; the same if by the temple; but if by the gold, or by the gift, then indeed one sins," so in the successors of the Pharisaic sect we expect that same distinction here.

units.la: 19. In negotiis ergo iuris, & humani commercii, veritatis oportet proloqui; sed in causa religionis, aut Sacerdotum, & Catholicorum, liberiores sumus. Putabā sane in diuinis negotiis, cautissimo, & mundissimo fuisse ambulandum pedo. Veritatis Sol est Christus, & lampas radiantissima Non{i} ad ipsum, nisi per se, id est per veritatem, veniendum est. Sed{k} mendacium nullum ex veritate est. Annon hoc est, Christi nomen apud Principes erubescere, cum secessibus quærendis, & diuerticulis indagandis, inhonestis Christiano nomini, cōfessio, si non rei, at materiæ connexorū, & coniunctissimorū, coelatur? Alias nos Christus in persona sua edocuit; qui vtcunq; in nonnullis interrogatis mutus fuisset quo se sponte vitam depositurus contestaretur, cum adiuraffet eum tamē Sacerdotum Princeps, vt directe responderet, aperte testatus est, {m}Ego sum. Qui in decē primis persecutionib. laniati sunt, & discerpti martyres; ad Ethnicorum Tribunalia tistebantur: neq; tamen in religionis negotio, vel quoad substantiā, vel circumstantias ingruentes, exceptiones dederunt, quib. freti, quæcunq; pro causæ ratione postulabantur, falso pronunciarent. Detur vnus celebriū illorū Christi testiū, tot linguis per tot secula decantatorū, qui sine labe tunc à piis aspersa, sine inusta ignominia, tale aliquid perpetrarit. Detur aliquis sanctissimorum primae Ecclesiae luminarium, qui tale aliquid scripserit, docuerit, defenderit, immurmurauerit. Nihil illi magis execrandum, apud Dominum senserunt[?], quam in iis, quae ad propriam sui gloriam spectant, vel minimam mundanae falsitatis speciem, aut docere, aut praestare. Nec immerito, cū {n}mendacia, & periuria, in iis, ab Apostolo enumerantur, quae sanae doctrinae sunt contraria. Et testis veloxfuturus est Domi-nus, aduersus falso iurantes. Cum cauisset Deus de semine[?] Canaanitico radicitus extirpando, & ad suam illud gloriam immediate spectasset, vt, quod mandasset, custodiretur; iurati seniores {q}Gibeonitis pepercere. Cum iuramentum illud,in aliena persona multo prius prætitu violasset Saulus,{r} trien-nali fame deliƈtum castigandum censebat Iehoua. Qui vniuersæ Israelis terræ, idq; Dauidis tempore, post prætereritos plures annos, acerbâ fame immiserat; quâ insigniter id in Saule detęstatus est: etiamsi diuinæ voluntatis obsequium in persona sua, adeoq; contra iuramentū temerarium ab aliis datum, obtenderet. Quid in genere de his cogitet, apud Zachariam loquitur: Alter malū alterius ne cogitetis cum animo vestro,{s} & iuramentum falsum ne ametis; nam omnia hæc sunt, quæ odi, dicit Iehoua. Indefinite loquitur, & in vniuerso: [?]uramentum falsum ne ametis: Et hæc sunt, quæ odi,
units.tr: 19. In matters of law and human dealings, we ought to speak the truth; but in a matter of religion, or of priests and Catholics, we are freer. I used to think that in divine matters one must walk with the most cautious and clean step. Christ is the Sun of truth and the most radiant lamp; no one comes to him except through himself, that is, through the truth. But a lie is in no way from the truth. Is this not to be ashamed of the name of Christ before princes, when, in seeking hiding-places and searching out by-ways, the confession is concealed, if not of the matter itself, at least of its closely connected and most intimate parts, which are dishonourable to the Christian name? Otherwise Christ taught us in his own person; though he was silent when questioned about some things, by which he bore witness that he would voluntarily lay down his life, yet when the High Priest adjured him that he should answer directly, he openly testified, "I am." Those martyrs who were torn and mangled in the ten first persecutions stood before the tribunals of the heathen; yet in the matter of religion, whether as to its substance or the circumstances that pressed upon them, they never gave occasion for evasions, relying on which they might utter falsehoods, whatever the nature of the case demanded. Let one of those famous witnesses of Christ, sung of in so many tongues through so many ages, be produced who, when the stain had been cast upon them by the pious, and without any disgrace inflicted, perpetrated anything of that kind. Let someone be produced from the most holy luminaries of the first Church who wrote, taught, defended, or muttered such a thing. They judged nothing more execrable before the Lord than either to teach or to practise even the slightest appearance of worldly falsehood in those matters which pertain to their own glory. Nor rightly, since lies and perjuries are enumerated by the Apostle among those things which are contrary to sound doctrine. And "the Lord will be a swift witness against those who swear falsely." When God had decreed the uprooting of the Canaanite seed, and had directly regarded this for his own glory, so that what he had commanded might be kept, the elders who had been sworn to spared the Gibeonites. When Saul, long before, had violated that oath, sworn in another's person, Jehovah judged that the offence must be punished by a three-year famine. He who had sent a bitter famine upon the whole land of Israel, and that in David's time, many years after, by which he signally detested it in Saul, even though Saul pleaded obedience to the divine will in his own person, and against the rash oath given by others. What he thinks of these things in general he speaks through Zechariah: "Let none of you devise evil against another in your heart, and do not love a false oath; for all these are things that I hate, says Jehovah." He speaks indefinitely and in general: "Do not love a false oath." And these are the things that I hate.

units.la: 20 Sed aperto, directo; mendacio, iuramento contrai-re nolumus. Aut nostra, aut aliena vita est, quæ in discrimen coniicitur, cui cum abunde cautum cupimus, sophistice respondebimus, aut astu deludemus, neq; quidquā, nisi æqui-uoce, & Amphibologice proferemus, reseruata nobis secreta animi intentione. Vita sane dulcis est, sed quit[?] non odit{t} præ Christo vitam, non erit eius discipulus. Quid isthic Augustinus? {u}Ne quis arbitretur, perfectum & spiritualem hominem, pro ista temporali vita, in cuius morte non occiditur anima, siue sua, siue alterius, debere mentiri. Ac eximie vos estis spirituales, qui assueto, & mire delectabili Christianorum nomine contenti non estis; nisi & Iesu coniunctiorum, tanquam cumulus accedat. Vitæ igitur periculum àiusto non auocaret. Sed ne solus hac in causa eat Augustinus, se coniungit Gregorius, Romanus aliquando Pontifex, qui, vt senior est hodiernis Papis, ita etiam multo senior. Sic autem loquitur: {x}Quia scriptum est, Os quod mentitur, occidit animam: & perdes omnes, qui loquuntur mendacium; hoc quoque mendacii genus perfecti viri summopere fugiunt, vt nec vita cuiuslibet per eorum fallaciam defendatur: ne suæ animæ noceant, dum præstare vitam carni nituntur alienæ. Videte, quam late patenti vtatur voce per eorum fallaciam; sic sophisticis etiam delusionibus occurrens. Subdit reuera: Quanquam hoc ipsum peccati genus facillime credimus relaxari: Atnum[?] peccatum est Gregori, & animæ nocet, & occidit animam, & perdet mendaces Deus, & perfecti viri summopere fugiunt, & tamen facile relaxatur? Hoc oportet vt fit, a Deo miserante, qui pœnitentibus, maximorum delictorum veniam concedit, non ex natura aut qualitate criminis. Vt de causa igitur impellente dicere supersedeamus, videamus modum. Cupiissem[?] e scripturis, indubitatæ fidei iudicibus, in re tanta confirmationem aliquam: (vt Æquivoce respondeatur, & deluforie[?], & Sophistice:) quin potius ad Nauarrum, Martinum ab Azpilcueta nos transmittunt; qui celebrioribus sepositis, aut Patrum, aut Conciliorum testimoniis (vt de Sacris taceam literis) magnum illum, beatumque Franciscum nobis refert, puta, tanquam Christum alterum, {y}qui rogatus, quaper-rexisset quidam homicida, qui iuxta eum transierat, manus per manicas immittens, respondit, non transisse illac, intelligens, non transisse per illas manicas. Dextre quidè, ac pulcherrime, & vt Franciscum decuit. Homicidā diuino, humanoq; damnandum iure, ille tuendum censuit; sic & eius exemplo, lupos animas hominum devoraturos, insidiose celandos, boni viri arbitrantur, hodie. At num iuratus, ut vere omnia, & to-tam proloquatur veritatem; & quæsitus speciatim, punctimque, de singulis circumstantiis, de loco, de tempore, de modo, de numero, de personis certis, sic poterit effugere? Mitor sane Iesum Christum, quum Apostolis, quid futurum esset, significaret, non ista docuisse. {i}Ad præsides & reges ducemini mea causa, ut hoc sit eis, & Gentibus testimonium, Hic ad Ethnicos, ideoque, quasi ad non-iudices: mea causa, in negotiis igitur religionis: in testimonium illis, ideoque, ut mors patienda foret. Cur hic oblitus non addiderat: Sed æquiuocandi, deludendi, sophistice iurandi, do-vobis potestatem. Si addidisset ista hæc, res integra fuisset. Verum Arrium illi potius, quam Christum imitandum credi-derunt, {z}qui apud Constantinum Imperatorem, iuramen-to tali deliuorio aliquando vsus est: sed diuina postmodum sese exerente vindicta; periurij, hæreticæque vno momento blasphemiæ, poenas luit acerbissimas.. De illo sic Socrates: Cum apud Constantinum Arrius Niceno Concilio subscri-beret, {a}a Imperator hoc admiratus, illum etiam ad iusiurandum adigit. Ille simulate, & fallaciter istud quoque præstitit. Fucata vero ratio, quaad fraudem in subscribendo vsus fit, sicut ipse audiui, eiusmodi fuit. Arrius suam ipsius opinionem in charta, quam habebat, conscribit: eam sub ala gestat. Iurat se vere, & ex animo sentire, quemadmodum scripserat.. Quam cum nostris hæc conueniunt?
units.tr: 20. But we are unwilling to act openly and directly against a lie or an oath. Whether our own life or another's is put in danger, when we wish to provide amply against this, we will answer sophistically, or deceive by cunning, and we will utter nothing except equivocally and amphibologically, keeping in reserve the secret intention of the mind. Life is indeed sweet, but "whoever does not hate his life for Christ's sake, will not be his disciple." What does Augustine say here? "Let no one think that a perfect and spiritual man ought to lie for this temporal life, in whose death the soul is not killed, whether his own or another's." And you are remarkably spiritual, who are not content with the customary and wonderfully pleasant name of Christians, unless the name of Jesus is added as a heap, as it were, to it. So the danger to life would not turn the just man aside. But lest Augustine go alone in this matter, Gregory joins him, once Roman Pontiff, who is as much older than today's Popes as he is older in years. He speaks thus: "Because it is written, 'The mouth that lies kills the soul,' and 'You will destroy all who speak a lie'; perfect men especially flee this kind of lie as well, so that no one's life is defended by their deceit, lest they harm their own soul while striving to secure the life of another for the flesh." Observe how widely he uses the phrase "by their deceit"; thus he also meets sophistical delusions. He adds indeed: "Although we most easily believe that this very kind of sin is relaxed..." But is it not a sin of Gregory's, and harmful to the soul, and it kills the soul, and God will destroy liars, and perfect men flee it especially, and yet it is easily relaxed? This must be so, by the mercy of God, who grants pardon for the greatest offences to the penitent, not according to the nature or quality of the crime. Therefore, leaving aside for the moment the motive that impels us, let us see the manner. I would have wished for some confirmation in so great a matter from the Scriptures, judges of undoubted faith (so that one may answer equivocally, deceptively, and sophistically). Yet rather they send us to Navarrus, Martin of Azpilcueta; who, setting aside the more famous testimonies of the Fathers or the Councils (not to mention the Sacred Letters), presents to us that great and blessed Francis, as it were another Christ, "who, when asked by a murderer who had passed by him whether he had passed that way, thrust his hands through his sleeves and answered that he had not passed that way, meaning that he had not passed through those sleeves." Dexterously indeed, and very prettily, and as became Francis. A murderer, condemned by divine and human law, he thought ought to be protected; and so by his example, good men today think that wolves about to devour the souls of men should be hidden by cunning. But will one who is sworn to tell the whole truth, and who is questioned specifically and point by point about each circumstance, about place, time, manner, number, and certain persons, be able to escape in this way? I am indeed amazed that Jesus Christ, when he signified to the Apostles what would befall them, did not teach them these things. "You will be led before governors and kings for my sake, for a testimony to them and to the Gentiles": here, to the heathen, and therefore as if to non-judges, for my sake; therefore in matters of religion, as a testimony to them, and therefore so that death had to be suffered. Why did he here forget to add: "But I give you the power to equivocate, to deceive, to swear sophistically"? If he had added these, the matter would have been settled. But they believed that Arius was rather to be imitated than Christ, who once used such a deceitful oath before the Emperor Constantine; but afterwards, when divine vengeance showed itself, he paid the most bitter penalties for perjury and for heretical blasphemy in a single moment. Socrates speaks thus of him: When Arius was subscribing to the Council of Nicaea before Constantine, the Emperor, wondering at this, also bound him to an oath. He did it feignedly and deceitfully. But the feigned method by which he practised fraud in subscribing was, as I myself heard, of this kind. Arius wrote his own opinion on a sheet of paper which he had, and carried it under his arm. He swore that he truly and sincerely thought just as he had written. How do these things agree with ours?

units.la: Qui in hæresi illius neutiquam; verum in fraude, & impostura, tam laudati vbique patris, & filii, & hæredes, & successores sunt dignissimi. Stupendum non est; si tremendum; & verendum, è iustitiæ flagello; consequantur nonnunquam exitum, quum grandissimo, quæ comprehenduntur, libro apud {b}Zachariam, Væ, & maledictiones præ-dicantur in domum falso iurantis intraturæ, & in media re-mansuræ, & eam consumpturæ; cum lignis & lapidibus eiusdem. In corporibus, domibusque huiuscemodi hominum,
units.tr: Those who are his heirs and successors, and most worthy of the praise everywhere of the father and the son, are so not in his heresy at all, but in deceit and imposture. It is no wonder, if it is terrible and to be feared, that the scourge of justice sometimes brings about an outcome such as the great book in Zechariah describes: curses and maledictions are announced to enter the house of the one who swears falsely, and to remain in its midst and consume it, together with its timber and stones. This is what we most often find to be true in the bodies and houses of such men.
(a) Socrates, Ecclesiastical History, 1.25.

units.la: {z} Theodor. Histor. Eccl. 1.14. hæc verissima quam sæpissime comperimus. Beaet[?] multo potius æternus pater, si sanctius illud suum animo reconderent; {c}Non iurabis per nomen meum falso, nec pollues nomen Domini Dei tui.
units.tr: (z) Theodoret, Ecclesiastical History, 1.14. Eternal God would much rather, if they kept that most holy command in their hearts: "You shall not swear falsely by my name, nor profane the name of the Lord your God." (c)

units.la: 21. Huiusmodi fidei articulos, vtinam iam tandem Romani dedisserent Patres. Male audiunt apud omnes, hæc in factis exempla, hæc in dictis Axiomata. Fides data Hæreticis, seruanda non est. {d}Cæsar obsignauit, Christianus orbis resignauit maior Cæsare. Durum sane illud fuit {e}Francisco Seniori Gallorum Regi: quum Sionis Cardinalis Helvetiis persuaserat, fidem Francisco datam de suppetiis ferendis, fallendam esse & relinquendam: factum tamen fuit turpiter. Cum in Gallia inter Carolum Nonum, & Condæum sociosque, pacis ictum esset fœdus, exclamant quotidie in concionibus lesuitæ, {f}pacem non debere fieri cum Hæreticis: Fidem haudquaquam debere seruari: rem piamesse atque salutarem, impuris hominibus manus violentas afferri: Christianum populum aduersus Hæreticos istos armari debere. Ad hoc, Concilii Constantiensis decretum afferunt, & exempla Leuitarum fratres occidentium. Videte, num istorum, aliorumque in lesuitis, similium, vindictam exegerit cœlestis pater, cum tanquam Ecclesiæ, & Reipubl. perniciem, è Gallia nuper illos, & Pontificiorum manu, detruserit. Cæterum quam tristi illud vultu aspexit Zelator Deus, quod commisit aliquando {g}Ladislaus Hungariæ & Poloniæ Rex profane & imprudenter, instigante Pontifice Eugenio Quarto, eiusque Cardinale & Legato Iuliano? Hic etenim quando fœdus cum Amurathe Secundo, Turca, percussum, ex proposito rupisset, inauspicata illa Varnensi, pugna dicamne an clade? cum exercitu & periurij suasore Cardinale miserrime interiit. Fœdi consilii & indigni Christiano nomine, turpissimus exitus. Hæc si crebro facta forent, cum perpetuo dedecore religionis nostræ inurendo, Mahumetani & Turcæ, periuri nimiū ipsi & fœdifragi, interrogare poterint in pactis obfirmandis per quemnam Deum posthac iuraturi simus, vt ad{h} Fran-cos aliquando Romani: vel vt iidem potius ad Carthagi-nienses, per quos Deos fœdus icturi[?] essent, cum respondit ipse{i} Asdrubal, Legatus Punicus, Per eosdem, qui tam infesti sunt fœdera violantibus. Denique[?] tum Hannibale, periurii sui amaras soluissent poenas. Vtinam Romanenses nostri, Christi nomen aut profitentes, aut simulantes, antiquos Romanos, Deum verum non agnoscentes, in promissorum, & iurāmentorum sanctitate emularentur; apud quos nihil quidquam fuerat solenius, quam metu omni seposito, vt{k} Regulus, spe contempta, vt Sextus Pompeius, fidem datam conseruare. Celebre illud est eiusdem Pompeij, quod, quum è Triumviris duo, Octauius Cæsar, & Antonius, iuramento illius fidi, apud ipsum in nauigio conuiuarentur, rogarit illū{l} Menas Pirata, aut, vt appellat{m} Appianus, Menedorus, nū discissis funibus anchoralibus, vtrumque abduceret, sicque ipsum, dominum, possessoremque vnicum Romani Imperii faceret: Is paulisper meditatus, in iussu meo, Mena, inquit, id tibi faciendum fuit. Nunc prasenti rerum statu contenti simus, Id peie-rare enim non est meum, Quam honeste iste Ethnicus? Quan-do, si{n} ius violandum sit, regni gratia violandum esset, ille potius memor fidei, id peierare, dixit, non est meum. Nostri autem, cum regnum, & cœleste, & æternum, periurio sita-mittendum, non acquirendum, perdendum, non lucrandū id peierare volunt esse suum.
units.tr: 21. Would that the Roman Fathers had at last given up such articles of faith. Such examples in deeds and such maxims in words are ill spoken of by everyone: "Faith given to heretics need not be kept." Caesar sealed it, and the Christian world, greater than Caesar, has unsealed it. That was indeed a hard thing for Francis the Elder, King of the French, when the Cardinal of Sion persuaded the Swiss that the faith given to Francis about bringing aid was to be broken and abandoned; yet it was done shamefully. When a treaty of peace was concluded in France between Charles IX and Condé and their allies, the Jesuits cried out daily in their sermons that peace must not be made with heretics, that faith ought by no means to be kept, that it was a pious and salutary thing to lay violent hands on impure men, and that the Christian people ought to be armed against those heretics. To this they cite the decree of the Council of Constance, and the example of the Levites who slew their brothers. Consider whether the heavenly Father has exacted vengeance for such deeds, and for similar ones among the Jesuits, when he recently thrust them out of France, as a ruin to the Church and the commonwealth, by the hand of the Papists. Moreover, with what a sad countenance God the zealot looked upon what Ladislaus, King of Hungary and Poland, once did, profanely and imprudently, at the urging of Pope Eugenius IV and his Cardinal and legate Julian! For when he had deliberately broken the treaty struck with Amurath II, the Turk, that ill-omened battle of Varna (shall I call it a battle or a defeat?) ended with the king and the Cardinal, the promoter of perjury, perishing most wretchedly. An outcome most shameful for a plan so foul and unworthy of the Christian name. If such things were done often, they would, with perpetual disgrace branded upon our religion, allow the Mahometans and Turks, themselves far too perjured and treaty-breaking, to ask in sealing pacts by which God we should henceforth swear, as once the Romans were asked by the Franks, or rather as the Carthaginians were asked, by whose gods they would make a treaty, when Hasdrubal, the Punic envoy, answered: "By the same gods who are so hostile to those who violate treaties." Finally, Hannibal then paid the bitter penalties of his perjury. Would that our Romans, who either profess or pretend to profess the name of Christ, would emulate the ancient Romans, who did not acknowledge the true God, in the sanctity of promises and oaths: among whom nothing was more usual than, with all fear set aside, to keep faith once given, as Regulus did, scorning hope, and as Sextus Pompeius did. Famous is that saying of the same Pompey: when two of the triumvirs, Octavius Caesar and Antony, were feasting with him on his ship under his oath of safe conduct, the pirate Menas, or, as Appian calls him, Menodorus, asked him whether, by cutting the anchor cables, he should carry off both of them, and so make him, his master and sole possessor of the Roman Empire. Pompey pondered briefly and said: "You should have done this on my order, Menas. Now let us be content with the present state of affairs. For it is not my part to break my oath." How honorably that heathen spoke! When, if right must be violated, it would have had to be violated for the sake of a kingdom, he, mindful of his faith, said that it was not his to break his oath. Our people, however, when a heavenly and eternal kingdom is not to be sought by perjury, not gained, but lost, want it to be their own to break their oath for the sake of gain.

units.la: 22. At in sensu suo, & secreta intentione mentis, loquun-tur vera. Non iuit hac, i non per manicas. Non vidi, i, cum proposito declarandi vobis: Quis vnquam hominum, aut mendax, aut periurus appellabitur, si sana, solidaque ista sint? Quid hic, quæso, Psaltes Dauid dicturus est? Quis{o} a-scendet in monte Domini? Qui nō iurauit in dolo proximo suo, Istud certe, in dolo est iurare: & nomen proximi, ad{p} omnem, quo cum agimus, ad Samaritanum, ad Iudæum, ad quem-cunque nostra opera indigentem, se extendet. {q}Falsum non feres testimonium aduersus proximum, i. contra nullum. Non erat Babylonius, Mosaica stante lege, leconiæ Regi vicinia, aut habitatione proximus: cum tamen inter eos contractu esset fœdus, & ex leconiæ parte ruptum; quid hic Dominus? {r}an prosperabitur? an eripiet se, qui fecit ista? qui irritum fecit fœdus, etiamne eripiet se: Et postea: Quum spernat execrationem, irritum faciendo fœdus: quia ecce iunxit manu suam, & omnia ista fecit, non eripiet se. Idcirco sic ait Dominus Iehoua, ne viua ego; nisi execratio-nem mea, quam spernit, & fœdus meum, quod irritum fecit; hoc reponam in caput ipsius. En, vt iuramentum Deus appellat suum; fœdus itidem suum; quia illius nomine contractum. Memorabile il-lud est, quod super eo Ezechielis locum habet Hieronymus: {s}Qui dissoluit pactum, nunquid effugiet? Ex quo discimus, etiam inter hostes seruandam fidem, & non considerandum, cui, sed per quæ iuraueris. Multo enim fidelior inuentus est ille, qui propter nomen Domini tibi credidit, & deceptus est, te, qui per occasionem diuinæ maiestatis hosti tuo, imo iam amico molitus es insidias. Sic ille: Non consi-derandum est, cui, sed per quæ iuraueris. Imo falleris Hieronyme: Apud excommunicatum, apud non iudice, si sacramento astrictus loquar, considerabo non per quem, sed cui iuraue-rim: Etiamsi reuera ille, cui iam teneor respondere, non sit reipsa, sed delira mea opinione, à Sanctorum communione seclusus, aut segregatus: & verissime, loco suo, iudex sit iustissi-mus: sub Deo, principeq;, magistratus nominatus: contra su-res, homicidas, proditores & perduelles gladium nō frustra gerens. Annon hoc est, audaci fronte & perfricta, sacrosan-ctum Dei nomen in vanum sumere, quę qua de causa, adhi-beo testē, si decretū sit apud me fraudulenter agere? è Tarta-reo illo puteo hęc Demonologia, nō Theologia deriuata est & è Christiano exterminata orbe, ad spiritus infernales, retro amandāda est. Gregor. Nazianzenū nemo sobrius celeber-rimum rimum negabit Theologum, ea siquidem appellatione, il-lum veneranda Antiquitatis canicies dignata est: Eius igi-tur audite Theologiam: t Solent plerique dicere u Ἡ γλῶσ᾽ ὁμώμοχ᾽, ἡ δὲ φρὴν ἀνώμοτ᾽[?] x Juraui lingua, mentem iniuratam gero. Quiduis potius argute potest excusari, quam iusiurandum. Nemo prorsus fucum sibi fieri patiatur. Nam iuramentum hoc est; & quantum quaso mali accidit ex ipsa fraude? Quam sincere Grogo-rius? Quiduis potius argute potest excusari, quam iusiurandum. Isti tamen nec argute, neque pie excusabunt. Adiiciam unicum Bernardi testimonium, quo nullum est illustrius. a Quacunque arte verborum quis iuret, Deus, qui conscientiae testis est, ita hoc accipit, sicut ille, cui hoc iuratur, intelligit. Qui vero dupliciter iurat, dupliciter reus fit, quia & nomen Domini in vanum assumit, & proximum dolo capit. Sic Ecclesiae patres: sic olim Christiani. Quid Euangelico dico illustratos lumine? Sic homines animales, quibus sacrarum literarum ne auditum nomen est. Proponit M. Tullius ex Accio illud: b fregistine fidem? Neque dedi, neque do infideli cuiquam. At quid tum dein de Tullius? Est iusiurandum affirmatio religiosa. Quod autem affirmate quasi Deo teste promiseris, idtenendum est. Et postea: Si hinc sibi sumunt nullam esse fidem, quae infideli datur est; videant, ne quaeratur latebra periurio. Si vixisses nunc M. Tulli, vix credendas periurio latebras quaeri, & videres, & doleres. Quam miseri nostri sunt Papismum amplectentes, adolescentes, foeminae, seniores, creduli, imperiti rerum, incauti, in fraudem illecti, quibus tales iam tandem magistri contigerunt, qui plus omnibus sapere, id est, desipere, & a via deflectere, in partibus transmarinis didicerunt.
units.tr: 22. But in their own sense and the secret intention of their mind, they speak truly. "It was not by this way, nor by these sleeves; I did not see, I did not say, with the intent of declaring to you..." Who, pray, would ever be called a liar or a perjurer if those evasions were sound and solid? What, I ask, is the psalmist David about to say here? "Who shall ascend into the mountain of the Lord? He who has not sworn to his neighbour with deceit." Surely to swear with deceit is deceit, and the word neighbour extends to everyone with whom we deal, to the Samaritan, to the Jew, to anyone who needs our help. "You shall not bear false witness against your neighbour," that is, against no one. The Babylonian, under the Mosaic law, was not a neighbour of Jeconiah by proximity or residence; yet there was a covenant between them, and it was broken on Jeconiah's side. What does the Lord say here? "Shall he prosper? Shall he who has done these things escape? He who has made the covenant void, shall he escape?" And afterwards: "Since he despised the curse by making the covenant void, because behold he has joined his hand and done all these things, he shall not escape. Therefore thus says the Lord God: As I live, surely my curse, which he has despised, and my covenant, which he has made void, I will bring upon his own head." See, God calls the oath his own, and the covenant likewise his own, because it was contracted in his name. Memorable is what Jerome says about this passage of Ezekiel: "He who breaks a pact, shall he escape? From which we learn that faith must be kept even with enemies, and that one should consider not to whom, but by what things you have sworn. For he is found to be far more faithful who believed you for the sake of the name of the Lord, and was deceived, than you, who through an occasion of the divine majesty have plotted snares against your enemy, indeed against one who is now a friend." Thus he. One should consider not to whom, but by what things you have sworn. Nay, you are mistaken, Jerome: before an excommunicate, before a judge who is not a judge, if I am bound by an oath and speak, I shall consider not by whom, but to whom I have sworn, even if in truth he to whom I am now bound to answer is not really, but in my deluded opinion, cut off or separated from the communion of the saints; and most truly, in his place, he is the most just judge, named magistrate under God and the prince, bearing the sword not in vain against thieves, murderers, traitors and rebels. Is it not with a bold and hardened brow to take up the most holy name of God in vain, when I call it as a witness, if I have decided to act fraudulently? This demonology, not theology, is derived from that Tartarean pit, and having been banished from the Christian world, it must be sent back to the infernal spirits. No sober man will deny that Gregory Nazianzen is the most celebrated theologian, since venerable antiquity has deigned to honour him with that title. Listen therefore to his theology: "Most people are accustomed to say: The tongue has sworn, but the mind has not sworn; I have sworn with my tongue, I keep my mind unsworn." Anything at all can be cleverly excused rather than an oath. Let no one at all allow himself to be deceived. For this is an oath; and how much harm, I ask, comes from the deceit itself? How sincere is Gregory! Anything at all can be cleverly excused rather than an oath. Yet these men will excuse it neither cleverly nor piously. I shall add the single testimony of Bernard, than which none is more illustrious: "By whatever art of words someone swears, God, who is the witness of conscience, takes it in the sense in which he to whom the oath is made understands it. But he who swears with a double meaning becomes doubly guilty, because he both takes the name of the Lord in vain and catches his neighbour by deceit." So the Fathers of the Church: so the Christians of old. Why do I speak of those enlightened by the light of the Gospel? So too do men of the natural sort, who have not even heard the name of the sacred letters. Marcus Tullius cites from Accius that line: "Have you broken faith?" "I have neither given it nor do I give it to any faithless person." But what then does Tully say next? An oath is a religious affirmation. And what you have promised with affirmation, as if God were the witness, that must be kept. And afterwards: If they take from this that there is no faith owed to someone who is faithless, let them see that a hiding place for perjury is not sought. If you had lived now, Marcus Tullius, you would have seen and grieved that hiding places for perjury are scarcely to be believed as being sought. How wretched are our people who embrace Papism: young men, women, the elderly, the credulous, the inexperienced in affairs, the incautious, lured into deceit, to whom at last such teachers have fallen, who learned in transmarine parts to know more than everyone else, that is, to be foolish, and to turn aside from the way.

units.la: 23, Non immerito sibi nomen arripiunt Sophistarum, (id c etenim eorum proprium est, qui Sophistice respondent.) Vt enim iam olim Sophistae d dicebantur, qui σόφοι non fuerunt, sed inflato tantum cum titulo & ventoso, glo-riosi quidam; qui à recta Philosophorum secta distabant longissime, vehementer apud illos redarguti, contempti, ludibrio habiti, ita isti, in rebus seriis & ad Deum spectanti-bus, fraudulenter & sophistice, iurati, respondentes, ex al-bo verorum Christianorum, tanquam mendaces & periuriorum disseminatores sunt expungendi. Quibus unicum illud est, & miserum certe in his angustiis refugium, incompetentes esse in Anglia magistratus, Reginam, & Senatum, esse non-Judices. Alias etenim ex principiis fundamentisque Casistæ & Canonistæ sui grauissime delinquunt, cuius non pigebit verba recensere. De illo disputans mandato Mosaico, Non sumes nomen Domini, Dei tui in vanū, cuiusmodi homines illud præceptum violare soleant, often-dit: {e}Decimo quarto loco, qui Sophistice, & dolose aliquid iurat, aliter intelligens, quam ille, cui iurat, intelligit, nulla intercedente causa, aut iusta ratione utendi tali duplicitate, non solum peccat mortaliter, ut dictum est, verum etiam postea non adimpleus illud, secundum sanum, & communem intellectum illius, cui præstitit iuramentum. Quoniam quando iurans utitur dolo, aliter vero minime, iuramentum adimpleri debet, secundum sanam, & communem intentionem illius, cui iuratum est. Quæ sit causa intercedens, aut iusta (secundum Nauarrum) ratio utendi tali duplicitate, ex illa eius regula, ediscatur, quæ, quandoquidem ex præcedente præcepto generali nobiscum magis facit, ut citetur, digna est: {f}Nono peccat, qui iurat id, quod est verum secundum mentem suam, non autem secundum intentionem illius, cui iurat, cum esset iussus iurare à iudice competente, seruato ordine iuris, vel se offerendo sponte ad iurandum. Hæc regula est: addit tamen per explicationem: Diximus à iudice competente, &c. Quoniam si index iuramentum exigens, talis non fuerit; velesto[?], quod sit competens, interrogat tamen contra iuris ordinem, vel est alius homo priuatus, qui per metum, aut importunitatem, iuramentum mentum extorquet ; tunc iurare poterit id , quod secundum suam mentem est verum, falsum autem, secundum mentem alterius, cui exhibet iuramentum. Hæc profane satis: sed ex istis principiis, scelestæ nostratium Sacrificorum responsiones, & defensiones conuincuntur esse, nisi illud constituerit, Principem, præsidesque suos, omni authoritate, & iurisdictione excidisse; id quod nullis eorum ampullis, cauillis, calumniis, unquam dabitur effectum, sed Papalem ea in re arrogantiam, & Antichristianam insolentiam boni omnes perpetuo explodent: id, quod merito faciendum esse, iam ab hinc diu docuit Marsilius Patauinus, nuper autem ex Anglis viri doctissimi, & de Ecclesia plurimum meriti, Ioannes Iuellus, suo tempore Episcopus Sarisburiensis, Thomas Bilsonus, modernus Episcopus Wintoniensis, & Ioannes Raynoldus, Decanus Lincolnensis, quos, qui volet, Anglice in signi cū fructu legat. Aliæ si obtrudantur exceptiones, multo magis sunt ridiculæ. Siquidé & ipsi iuramento extra controuersiam aliquando onerantur: &, quod ad formam iuris attinet, ex legum Anglicarum ordine, non præcisò magis, quā antiquo, prudentissime, & cautissime transiguntur omnia.
units.tr: 23. Not without reason do they assume the name of Sophists (for this is indeed the mark of those who answer sophistically). For just as in former times those were called Sophists who were not wise (σόφοι) but only puffed up with a title and full of wind, boastful men who stood very far from the sound school of the philosophers, and were sharply refuted, despised and held in mockery by them, so these men, who in serious matters bearing on God answer fraudulently and sophistically while sworn, must be struck off from the roll of true Christians as liars and disseminators of perjuries. Their only refuge, and surely a wretched one in such straits, is that the magistrates in England, the Queen and the Senate, are not competent, that they are not judges. For otherwise, by the principles and foundations of the Casuists and Canonists, they offend most gravely; I will not hesitate to recite their words. Discussing that Mosaic command, "You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain," and how men of this kind are wont to violate that precept, he sets down: {e}In the fourteenth place, he who swears sophistically and deceitfully, understanding something otherwise than the one to whom he swears understands it, with no intervening cause or just reason for using such duplicity, not only sins mortally, as has been said, but also afterwards does not fulfil that oath according to the sound and common sense of the one to whom the oath was given. For when the swearer uses deceit, and otherwise not at all, the oath must be fulfilled according to the sound and common intention of the one to whom it was sworn. What the intervening cause or just reason (according to Navarrus) for using such duplicity may be, is to be learned from that rule of his, which, since it favours our side more, on account of the preceding general precept, is worth quoting: {f}In the ninth place, he sins who swears that which is true according to his own mind, but not according to the intention of the one to whom he swears, when he had been ordered to swear by a competent judge, the order of law being observed, or when he offers himself willingly to swear. This is the rule; he adds, however, by way of explanation: We have said "by a competent judge," etc. For if the examining judge is not such (or, though he is competent, he questions contrary to the order of law), or if it is some private person who extorts the oath by fear or importunity, then he may swear that which is true according to his own mind, though false according to the mind of the other to whom he offers the oath. These are profane enough matters. But from these principles the wicked answers and defences of our own priests are convicted, unless it is established that the Prince and his magistrates have fallen from all authority and jurisdiction; which will never be brought about by all their bombast, quibbles and calumnies, but all good men will forever hiss down the Papal arrogance and Antichristian insolence in this matter. That this ought rightly to be done, Marsilius of Padua taught long ago, and more recently among the English the most learned men, who deserved much of the Church, John Jewel, in his time Bishop of Salisbury, Thomas Bilson, the present Bishop of Winchester, and John Reynolds, Dean of Lincoln; whoever wishes may read them in English with great profit. If other exceptions are thrust forward, they are far more ridiculous. For they too are at times burdened with an oath beyond dispute; and as far as the form of law is concerned, all things are transacted most prudently and cautiously according to the order of English laws, no less than in the ancient manner.

units.la: Et Sacerdotalis functio, quam obtendunt, in transgressione legum, aut diuinarum, aut politicarum, à Principum castigatione non tutatur: cum, omnis anima potestatibus supereminentibus subiecta sit, oporteat. Unde egregie Chrysostomus: in ista imperantur omnibus, & Sacerdotibus, & Monachis, non solum secularibus: id quod in exordio declarat cum dicit omnis anima potestatibus supereminentibus subdita sit: etiamsi Apostolus fis, si Euangelista, sive Propheta, sive quisquis tandem fueris. Neque enim pietatem subuertit ista subiectio. Et super istos æque, atq; super alios magistratus gladium gestat, non frustra. Id quod nouerunt pijorum Principes, ut Salomon, cum Abiathar, e munere Sacerdotali deturbaret, & Zadocum ea dignitate insigniret, ut {o}Iosiah qui sacerdotes idololatricos occidione occidit. imo Iehu apprime memor, & regiæ potestati imperatum esse, cum aliis, {p}Captie vulpes, vulpeculas, quæ perdunt vites, Baalis {q}sacerdotes ad vnum interfecit. Quæ cum ita se habeant; quam temere, isti pericula & animabus, & corporibus accersunt suis? Quantam faciunt iniuriam diuino nomini, fraudulenter contestando? quantam Regiæ Maiestati, sceleus sceleri, proditionem periurio cumulando? quantam iudicibus, quousq; poterint, circumueniendo & deludendo? quantam populo Christiano, ea aperte præstando, secrete docendo, quæ cum mendaciis, & versutiis in summo genere sunt coniunctissima? {r}Abominatio sunt Domino labia mendacia. Pater cœlestis tandem eorum oculos aperito. Iam ad alia redeo mendaciorum genera.
units.tr: Nor is the sacerdotal office, which they put forward, a shield against the chastisement of princes for the transgression of laws, whether divine or civil, since every soul must be subject to the higher powers. Whence Chrysostom excellently: "In that passage commands are laid upon all, both priests and monks, not only the laymen; which he declares at the outset when he says, 'Let every soul be subject to the higher powers': even if you are an apostle, even if an evangelist, or a prophet, or whoever you may be. For this subjection does not overturn piety. And he bears the sword over these no less than over other magistrates, and not in vain." This the godly princes knew, as Solomon did when he thrust Abiathar from the sacerdotal office and honoured Zadok with that dignity. Josiah, who slew the idolatrous priests with slaughter, and indeed Jehu, very mindful that the kingly power had been commanded (with the others), {p}Catch the foxes, the little foxes that spoil the vines, put to death the priests of Baal to a man. Since these things stand so, how rashly do these men bring danger upon both souls and bodies? How great an injury do they do to the divine name by calling it to witness fraudulently? How great a treason to the Royal Majesty do they heap up, crime upon crime, by perjury? How great a wrong do they do to judges, as far as they can, by circumventing and mocking them? How great a harm do they do to the Christian people by openly performing and secretly teaching those things which are most closely joined with lies and cunning? {r}Lying lips are an abomination to the Lord. Heavenly Father, at last open their eyes. Now I return to the other kinds of lies.

units.la: 24 Sed quam paruum est, unam tantum immutasse vocem: pro Non, etiam, pro etiam, non, cum vita hominis, i-maginis Dei, Christiani, amici, tuenda sit, quæ peribit alias? At nouimus vel in minimis à iustitia exorbitari. Unica iudicis vox, Non, aut Etiam, innocentis sanguini, vel parcit, vel {s}effundendo consentit. Unica Christi vox, / ite vel Venite, aut ad cœlestia animam euehit gaudia, aut in gehennam protrudit. Neque aliena conseruanda est vita, cum dispen-dio, aut iacturâ animæ tuæ. Nam quid in aliis peccatis faciendum esset? Ut, velit debeatve quisquam mori, nisi patriam proditione tradideris, nisi peieraueris, nisi furtum feceris: num in ista prorumpendum est? Phyllis aliqua, aut Amaryllis ita te, tuamque ambit pudicitiam, ut nisi cesseris, laqueum collo fit iniectura, aut seipsam mari immersura. Num illius, tuo vitio, amentiam redimes? Non redemisset {t}pudicus ille Iosephi, si & princeps fuisset, quæ pellexerat, & sua domina. Et tibi, & illi prosis, modo possis: sin nequeas utrique, tuam saluato animam: tuam mundato conscientiam. Verum annon minus tolerabo, perpetuarque malum, {u}neaccidat grauius? Id me docuit Patriarcha Lothus, qui suas Sodomæis filias, potius proposuit vitiandas, quam permitteret, ut viris, & hospitibus stuprum inferrent. Recte sanè; sic Lothus fecerat; sed num pie fecerat? Annon ille male, ut bonum succederet? Nihilo ergo magis id in illo iusto imitandum est, quam vel quod{x} ebrietate in monte, velincestu in spelunca, se contaminarit. Tu ab omni fuge turpi, ut à serpente; & reliquum permitte Deo.
units.tr: 24. But how small a thing it is, to change only one word: "No" for "Yes", "Yes" for "No", when the life of a man, the image of God, a Christian, a friend, is to be guarded, which otherwise would perish! Yet we know that even in the smallest things one may stray from justice. The single word of a judge, "No" or "Yes", either spares innocent blood or consents to its being poured out. The single word of Christ, "Come" or "Go", either carries the soul up to heavenly joys or thrusts it down into hell. Nor is another's life to be preserved at the cost, or the loss, of your own soul. For what ought to be done in other sins? Suppose someone wishes, or ought, to die unless you betray your country, unless you commit perjury, unless you commit theft: must you break out into that? Suppose some Phyllis or Amaryllis so courts you and your chastity that, unless you yield, she will place a noose about her neck or throw herself into the sea. Will you redeem her madness at the cost of your own sin? Joseph's chaste master would not have redeemed it, had he been the prince, whom she had enticed, and her mistress. Help both yourself and her, if you can; but if you cannot do so for both, save your soul, keep your conscience clean. But shall I not endure and bear the lesser evil, lest a greater befall? This was taught me by the Patriarch Lot, who preferred to offer his daughters to the Sodomites to be violated, rather than permit them to inflict lewdness on the men and guests. Rightly indeed; so Lot had done. But had he done it piously? Did he not act wrongly, that good might come of it? In no way, therefore, is that just man to be imitated in this, any more than in his being defiled by drunkenness on the mountain or by incest in the cave. Flee from every base thing, as from a serpent; and leave the rest to God.

units.la: 25 Deægris, quæ obiiciuntur, paris sunt rationis. Quia ægrotat, cupit aliquid cognoscere, cuius notitia, morbum, animíq; affectum exasperabit magis. Aut cum ægrotanti credulitas, & imaginatio multum prosit; Medicorum est, sermone blando lactare, eaque quæ secus habent, ingeminare. At ista Medicorum non sunt, sed hominum mentientium. Quomodo pius sperabit Medicus, assuturum suæ operæ Deú? si malis, & illegitimis utatur mediis? Cōmentis irritatur, & provocatur, vitæ necisq; Dominus; nō placatur. Quæ artis suæ sunt, exercēda sunt, & invocandus Deus, ut conatui velit adesse, & assulgere. Imaginationi, factis veris, occurredum est, non sermone ficto. Recte fecerat, qui credenti, per humorē melancholicum, sibi caput defuisse, pileum plumbeum iniecit, ut onere pressus tandem persentisceret: sin fabulas ingerendo, phantasiam avertere cogitasset, ludibrium fortasis Deo, hominiq; factus ipse fuisset. Neque tamen medico negamus tacendi, aut celandi facultatem, si quid obesse velit, cum proferatur. Et hoc ipsum Theologo etiam permittimus, ut pro re nata, (ne acerbis fortasis legis Mosaicæ minis, languentem obruat conscientiam) doctrinam hanc aut illam ad tempus, occultet: sed ne mentiendo occultet, caveat: sic etenim officij limites transiliuit sui. Non enim ut fingat, fabricetve aliquid minister gregis, id Apostoli facit, qui{y} Iudæis factus est Iudæus, Græcis Græ-cus, infirmis infirmus, imo omnibus factus est omnia, quia talis erat Paulus, ut loquitur Augustinus,{z} Compassione misericordiæ, ricordia, non simulatione fallacia, Et, non mentientis astu, sed com-patientis affectu.
units.tr: 25. The objections raised against the sick are of like reasoning. Because a sick man is ill, he desires to know something, the knowledge of which will only aggravate his disease and the disturbance of his mind. Or, since belief and imagination greatly help the one who is ill, it is the physician's part to soothe him with flattering speech and to repeat what is otherwise. But these things are not the physician's but of lying men. How will a pious physician hope that God will lend His help to his work, if he uses wicked and illegitimate means? The Lord of life and death is provoked and stirred up by inventions; He is not appeased. What belongs to his art must be practised, and God must be called upon, that He may be willing to be present with and to favour the effort. The imagination must be met with true deeds, not with false speech. He acted rightly who, when a man believed through melancholic humour that his head was missing, placed a leaden cap upon him, so that, weighed down by the burden, he might at last perceive it; but if he had tried to turn away the fancy by telling fables, he himself would perhaps have become a laughingstock to God and to men. Yet we do not deny that the physician has the power of keeping silent or concealing something, if he wishes that something not to harm, when it is put forward. And this same thing we also permit the theologian, that, as the occasion arises (lest perhaps by the harsh threats of the Mosaic law he overwhelm a languishing conscience), he may for a time conceal this or that doctrine; but let him take care not to conceal it by lying: for thus he would overstep the limits of his office. For it is not that the minister of the flock should feign or invent anything; that is what the Apostle did, who became a Jew to the Jews, a Greek to the Greeks, weak to the weak, indeed all things to all men, because Paul was such, as Augustine says: by compassion of mercy, not by pretence of deceit, and not by the cunning of a lying man, but by the affection of one who suffers with.

units.la: 26. Illud Iehu, non habet excusationem suam, {a}qui se Baali sacrificaturum verbo spospondit, vt Baalis Sacerdotes interficeret. Quod idolis seruientes sustulerit, pium erat: quod per fraudem, & idololatriae simulationem sustulerit, non ita. Illud laudes {b}habet in scriptura suas, istud vitio non caret. Neque eius calcanda semper sunt vestigia, vt hominis sancti, quippe qui ambitione impulsus, de Achabi familia vindictam sumpsit, non Deo simpliciter, & corde integro placiturus: {c}ad idololatriam siquidem, ipse etiam recidit. Fuerunt tamen, primaeua Ecclesia, qui illius secuti exemplum, suam ad tempus celarunt fidem, & in secreta Hæreticorum colloquia se infinuarunt, vt Hæreticos occultos caperent, ipsosque vel magistratibus, vel pastoribus Ecclesiae proderent. De istis pronunciat doctissimus pater: {d}perniciosius, aut, vt mitius loquar, periculosius isti mentiuntur, vt Hæreticos capiant, quam illi, vt Catholicos lateant. Et, tolerabilius in suis foveis delitescerent vulpes, quam propter illas capiendas in blasphemiae foveam caderent venatores. Qui enim sic alios captant, & suam interea fidem inficiantur, meminisse deberet: {e}Qui negat me coram hominibus, & ego ipsum sum negaturus coram patre meo, qui est in coelis. Videant nostri seculi homines, si qui hoc animo, in coetus Hæreticorum, & malorum, se immittant. E cloaca, & Camarina impietatis se reuocare, Christianum est, & e Babylone recedere, sed de industria, & volenter se ingerere, est profanum.
units.tr: 26. Concerning Jehu: his conduct has no excuse. He promised by his word that he would sacrifice to Baal, so that he could kill the priests of Baal. That he removed those who served idols was pious; that he did it by fraud and by pretending to practise idolatry was not. That deed has praise in Scripture, but this one is free of no fault. Nor are his footsteps always to be trodden, as those of a holy man, since he was driven by ambition when he took vengeance on the house of Ahab, not intending simply and with an upright heart to please God; for he himself also later fell back into idolatry. Nevertheless, in the early Church there were some who, following his example, concealed their faith for a time and insinuated themselves into the secret conversations of heretics, so that they might catch the hidden heretics and betray them to the magistrates or the ministers of the Church. Concerning these the most learned father pronounces: they lie more destructively, or, to speak more mildly, more dangerously, in order to catch heretics, than those others do in order to hide as Catholics. And foxes would do better to lurk in their own holes than for hunters to fall into the pit of blasphemy in order to catch them. For those who thus snare others while meanwhile staining their own faith ought to remember: "Whoever denies me before men, I also will deny before my Father who is in heaven." Let the men of our age see, if any with this intention throw themselves into the gatherings of heretics and of evil men. To withdraw from the sewer and the Camarina of impiety is Christian; and to depart from Babylon is right; but to thrust oneself in there deliberately and willingly is profane.

units.la: 27. Stratagemata belli, si sine vocis, sermonisque abusu fiant, sana cum conscientia poterunt exerceri, vbicun-que bellum iustum est. Ita {f}Aitas Iosua ceperat: sic alios per insidias sanctissimi Imperatores deuicerunt. Si etenim hostes liceat occidere, & modis omnibus non interdictis, licebit occidere. {g}Dolus an virtus, quis in hoste requirat? Sin
units.tr: 27. Stratagems of war, provided they are carried out without abuse of the voice and of speech, may be practised with a clear conscience wherever the war is just. Thus Joshua had set an ambush; so the most saintly emperors have overcome others by treachery. For if it is lawful to kill enemies, and by any means not forbidden, it will be lawful to kill them. Who in an enemy asks whether it is trickery or virtue?

units.la: {a} qui se Baali sacrificaturum verbo spospondit pacem spondeas, cum bellum pares secreto, fraudulenter facis; præsertim si aperte sermone, certam pacem præ te feras. Quo prudentius Senatus noster venerandus fecerat, qui, licet Hispano pacem offerenti specie tenus[?], {h}aurem accommodaret, non credidit tamen nimium fraudulento consilio. Ille tamen satis turpiter, qui tunc omni vi, An-gliam invadere destinauerat. Sed de istis satis. Ita menda-cia in nullo hominum excusanda censemus; non officiosa; non iocosa; non perniciosa; non in Medico; non in Theo-logo; non in Rebecca; non in Rahab; non in obstetrici-bus; nedum in {i}Anania & Saphyra, qui Spiritui Sancto mentiti, tremendas luerunt fui sceleris poenas: sed loquendam veritatem, omnibus, & ubique, nec pro æterna alterius salute, malis utendum mediis: quia sic voluit veritatis Deus, cui cum filio, & spiritu, sit gloria in æternum.
units.tr: If you promise peace by word, while secretly preparing war, you act fraudulently; especially if by open speech you display a certain peace. How more prudently our venerable Senate acted, which, although it lent an ear to the Spaniard offering peace, at least in appearance, did not trust too much to his fraudulent plan. Yet he acted quite shamefully, who had then decided to invade England with all his force. But enough of these. Thus we judge that lies are excusable in no one: not officious lies, not jesting lies, not harmful lies; not in a physician, not in a theologian, not in Rebecca, not in Rahab, not in the midwives; much less in Ananias and Sapphira, who lied to the Holy Spirit and paid terrible penalties for their crime; but the truth must be spoken by all, and everywhere, nor must evil means be used even for the eternal salvation of another; because thus God of truth willed it, to whom with the Son and the Spirit be glory forever.

units.la: CAPUT SECUNDUM. DE CIRCUMCISIONE per Tsipporam.
units.tr: CHAPTER 2. CONCERNING CIRCUMCISION, by Zipporah.

units.la: Exod. 4. 24. Euenit autem in illo itinere, in diversorio quodam, ut occurreret Mosi Jehoua, velut quærens morte afficere eum.
units.tr: Exod. 4. 24. It came about on that journey, in a certain lodging place, that the LORD met Moses, as if seeking to put him to death.

units.la: 25. Sed accipiens Tsippora cultrum acutum, amputauit præputium filij sui, & admouit pedibus illius; nam inquit illa, sponsus sanguinum es mihi.
units.tr: 25. But Zipporah took a sharp knife, and cut off the foreskin of her son, and touched his feet with it; for, she said, you are a bridegroom of blood to me.

units.la: 26. Sic destitit Jehouah ab illo: dixerat autem tunc sponsum sanguinum, propter circumcisionem.
units.tr: 26. So the LORD let him alone: she had said then, a bridegroom of blood, because of the circumcision.

units.la: 1. Infantulum circumcidit fœmina. 3. Circumcisionem excipit Baptismus apud Christianos. 4. Num ad salutem absolute fit necessarius baptismus, 8. An per laicum vel fœminam dari debeat.
units.tr: 1. A woman circumcises the little infant. 3. Baptism takes the place of circumcision among Christians. 4. Whether baptism is absolutely necessary for salvation. 8. Whether it ought to be given by a layman or a woman.

units.la: 12. Et num ita datus, per ministrum Euangelii sit repetendus.
units.tr: 12. And whether, when so given, it must be repeated by a minister of the Gospel.

units.la: Ircumcisionis Sacramentum cuique masculo, apud Israelitas, fuisse imprimendum, ita diserte apud {a}Mosen proditur; vt dubitandi, num è diuina fuerit voluntate, necne, nullus cuiquam sobrio relinquatur locus. Ceremoniam retinuit Abrahæ propago, hoc est, Jacob & filij; neque alia magis fraude, {b}Simeon & Leui, Sichemitas in sua pellexerant retia, quam auferendum esse præputium, suis sociis, & confœderatis, proclamando. Et populus Israeliticus, extra omnem controuersiam, seruitute Ægyptiaca iam pressus, & oppressus in eo carnis signaculo admouendo, Maiorum vestigia persecutus est. Mosi igitur sua caro, &, quam in corpore gestabat, notula, testimonio, vel argumento esse poterat, suos, quos genuerat, filios, eo pacto, in fœderis consortium esse admittendos; sic Deo consecrandos; nec Zelotypus Dominus, & acris in iudicio, sibi, suisque admodum succenseret. Et {d}horrendum est, in manus Dei viuentis incidere. Obiecit tamen remoram pietati, & obsequio Mosaico, vxoris dilectio; quæ, cum è semine {e}Madianitico oriunda esset, nec ex sanctorum prognata prosapia; suæ potius morem gerendum voluntati, patriæque suæ consuetudinibus, insistendum censuit; & circumcisionis sigillum, aut vt vile, sordidumque est aspernata, aut vt crudele, & sanguinarium quiddam, in infantuli sui tenelli carne, est detestata. Importunis igitur, vt probabile est, apud maritum agens precibus, eoque aut blandiendo, aut molestiam facessendo obtinuit, vt aduersus expressum, & speciale Dei mandatum circumcidere neglexerit. Malo sane Mosis exemplo: qui & suam indulgentiam {f}Adami facilitati, versus suam Euam adiungendo, reliquis fœminis incitamento, calcarique esse poterat; vt vel lachrymis, chrymis[?], vel blanditiis, vel malis consiliis, viros suos ita fle-cterent, & pellicerent, ut ipsarum votis, pietatem in Deum, probitatem in homines posthaberent. Quod & Jobi etiam uxor, aggredi ausa est: {g}Benedic Deo, & morere; sed repulsam egregiam tulit. {h}Salomonis autem coniuges, & tentarunt, & penitus peruicerunt. Ita, quae data est hominum initio {f}auxiliatrix, foemina, dubium auxilij genus facta est; dum {i}ad bona non modo non impellat, verum & nonnunquam auocet.
units.tr: That the sacrament of circumcision was to be imprinted on every male among the Israelites is so plainly reported in Moses that no room for doubt is left to any sober person, whether it was by divine will or not. Abraham's offspring, that is, Jacob and his sons, kept the ceremony; nor did Simeon and Levi lure the Shechemites into their snare by any other trick than by proclaiming that the foreskin must be removed from their allies and confederates. And the Israelite people, beyond all controversy, already burdened and oppressed by Egyptian servitude, followed the footsteps of their ancestors in receiving this mark of the flesh. Moses, therefore, could use his own flesh, and the little mark he bore in his body, as a witness or argument that his sons, whom he had begotten, should in this way be admitted to the fellowship of the covenant and so consecrated to God; nor would the Lord, jealous and severe in judgment, be angry with him and his own. And it is a dreadful thing to fall into the hands of the living God. Yet the love of his wife stood in the way of his piety and obedience to the law of Moses. She, being born of a Midianite stock and not descended from a holy lineage, judged that she should rather yield to her own will and keep to the customs of her homeland; and she either scorned the seal of circumcision as something cheap and filthy, or detested it as something cruel and bloody, in the tender flesh of her little infant. So, as is likely, she pressed her husband with importunate prayers, and by coaxing him or by causing him trouble she obtained that he neglected to circumcise, against the express and special command of God. Certainly a bad example for Moses, who by joining his own indulgence to the weakness of Adam, toward his own Eve, could be an incitement and spur to other women, so that they might bend and entice their husbands with tears, or with flatteries, or with bad counsels, so as to put their own wishes before piety toward God and integrity toward men. Job's wife also dared to attempt this: Bless God and die; but she received a notable rebuff. The wives of Solomon, however, both tempted and completely prevailed. Thus the woman, who was given at the beginning of mankind as a helper, became a doubtful kind of help; since she not only does not urge men toward good things, but sometimes even draws them away.

units.la: 2. Qui solet suis, tam turpiter cedentibus, irasci, Deus, neglectum Sacramentum, ita Mosi vitio vertit, ut, cum peregre proficisceretur, & in diuersorium quoddam, noctur-nam illic acturus quietem, sereciperet[?]; occurrerit infestus, subitaq; illata vi, ad mortem fere detruserit, non innocuum filiolum, ut quidam volunt, (quid etenim infelix meruisset puer, cuius crimine Sacramentum dilatum non est) sed Mosen quem ferociter, atrociterq;, merito tamen percusserat. Cum languescés iam maritus, & moribundus decumberet, imminente malo edocta Tsippora, festinabunda accurrit, & arrepto (non saxo acutiore, aut petra acutissima, ut vertit Hieronymus, æquiuocatione inductus vocis, cū perɪx[?], & saxum, vel petra, & acutus culter significetur, ut {k}Tremelius obser-vauit, sed) cultro, tum domestico, tum pastorali instrumento, præputium pueruli amputauit, & ad pedes proiiciens, sui facti impatiens, exclamauit: Sponsus sanguinum es mihi: maritus sanguinarius; cuius sanguis, non nisi infantuli sanguine, est redimendus. Jehova tamen hanc feram obedientiam, foemina factam manu, ita bono, placidoque accepit animo, ut ferire desisteret. Sedata est ira Domini, quæ prius est accensus, & muliebri officio intercedente, virile peccatum abrumpitur.
units.tr: 2. God, who is accustomed to be angry at his own when they give way so shamefully, found fault with Moses for the neglected sacrament in this way: when he was travelling abroad and was about to take his night's rest in a certain lodging, he met him hostile, and, inflicting violence suddenly, nearly thrust him to death; not the innocent little son, as some wish (for what had the unhappy boy deserved, through whose crime the sacrament was not delayed?), but Moses, whom he had nevertheless justly struck fiercely and savagely.
