When her husband, already growing weak and lying as if dying, was in danger, Zipporah, warned, hurried to him, and, taking up a knife (not a sharper stone, or a most sharp rock, as Jerome translates, misled by the ambiguity of the word, since both perix and sela, a rock or stone, and a sharp knife are meant, as Tremellius observed, but) a knife, both a household and a pastoral instrument, she cut off the foreskin of the little boy, and throwing it at his feet, impatient of what she had done, she cried out: you are a bridegroom of blood to me: a bloody husband, whose blood can be redeemed only by the blood of the infant. Yet the Lord accepted this wild obedience, made by a woman's hand, with such a good and calm mind that he ceased to strike. The wrath of the Lord, which had been kindled before, was calmed, and through the intercession of a woman's office the male sin was cut off.

units.la: 3. Mulieris huius facinus, & antiquis temporibus, & præsenti nostro seculo, materiam disputandi suppeditauit. Siquidem cum in locum Circumcisionis, noster accesserit Baptismus, eademque utriusq; Sacramenti, Israelitici, & nostri ratio sit; idem scopus etiam, & finis amborum, ad fidelium liberos, sacris initiandos; ad distinguendos, à reliquo orbis grege; ad internam mundationem, & affectuum amputationem, contestandam: cumque & huius, & illius contemptus, simili luendus sit vindicta; ut, qui characterem non acceperit, ex albo populi Dei, sit expungendus; sine cessitas inuincibilis, & irrefragabilis ingruat, ut loquuntur Scholastici, ut non possit accersi sacerdos, qui lauacro regenerationis, infantulum abluat; quid ni licebit obstetricula, aut mulierculae alicui, salutaribus aquis nuper natum lustrare; adiectis, quae Baptismi sunt propria, verbis; Baptizo te in nomine Patris, & Filii, & Spiritus Sancti; ut nouus hic Christianus, isto expiatus modo, & Originalis labis fœditate liberatus, si è viuis excesserit, in cœlos accipiatur? Si Tsipporæ Circumcisio, iram Domini averterit; & avertet Baptismus, per fœminam datus. Quod si mulieri fas sit, aquam iniicere; quanto magis laico, qui tum {m}caput est fœminæ, ut Ecclesiæ Christus, tum ad Saluatoris effigiem, & lacerdotis personam, accedit propius, muneriq; istiusmodi persoluendo, idoneus magis reperitur. Et hæc certe apud Pontificios, tam altas radices egit opinio, ut & fœminæ, sese Sacramento administrando, immiscere audeant; & Theologi ipsorum, {n}antiquiores, & {o}moderni, scriptis tueri non verentur. Nobis autem contraria, multo magis arridet sententia.
units.tr: 3. The deed of this woman has furnished matter for dispute both in ancient times and in our present age. For since our Baptism has come in the place of Circumcision, and the reasoning of both sacraments, Israelite and ours, is the same, and the aim and purpose of both is the same, namely to initiate the children of believers into the sacred rite, to distinguish them from the rest of the flock of the world, and to attest inward cleansing and the cutting away of the affections; and since contempt of either must be punished by a similar vengeance, so that whoever has not received the mark is to be struck out of the roll of the people of God; if an unconquerable and irresistible necessity arises, as the Scholastics say, so that a priest cannot be summoned to wash the infant with the bath of regeneration, why would it not be lawful for a midwife or some woman to purify a newly born child with the saving waters, with the words proper to Baptism added: I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit; so that this new Christian, cleansed in this way and freed from the foulness of original stain, if he departs from the living, may be received into heaven? If Zipporah's circumcision turned away the wrath of the Lord, Baptism given through a woman will also turn it away. But if it is lawful for a woman to pour water, how much more for a layman, who is the head of the woman as Christ is of the Church, and who comes nearer to the image of the Saviour and the person of the priest, and is found more fit to perform a service of this kind. And certainly among the Papists this opinion has taken such deep roots that women too dare to interfere in administering the sacrament, and their theologians, both older and modern, do not hesitate to defend it in writing. For us, however, the contrary opinion pleases far more.

units.la: 4. In cuius quidem controuersiæ medullam, ut penetremus; eamq; ad vivum usq; resecemus; quid inter nos & ipsos, in Baptismi negotio, conveniat & interfit, operæ precium est, aduertamus. Lotionem igitur istam, & tinctionem Sacramentalem, vehementi desiderio ampletendam[?] esse, & ulnis avidissimis excipiendam testamur; neq; aspernandam esse; aut præ negligentia contemnendam, sub periculo æ-ternæ. ternæ damnationis. Quotusquisq; enim est, Christianorum hominū, qui sic audeat ineptire, vt sanctissimum Saluatorē, rem vilifaciendam tam{p} solenniter præcipere, & in{q} suo ipsius corpore, cōsecrare voluisse, autumauerit? Excindetur à populo, imo è libro vitæ, delebitur nomen eius, qui ita flocci, tanti precij mysterium, æstimabit. Hucusq; conuenimus, Sed Baptismi receptionem, ita ἁπλῶς[?] & absolute esse necessariam, vt qui aquis expiatoriis nō sit ablutus; de facto, si expirauerit, & eo ipso à cœlesti excludatur gaudio, negamus cōstantissime. Vbi etenim, aut anima fidelis fuerit, aut firma Christi apprehensio, in homine adulto; aut vbi nuper nato, accesserit parentum fides; eam animam credimus, ex vi fœderis inter Deum, populumq; suum percussi, in cœlestia tabernacula suscipiendæ esse, etiamsi fluuio salutari priuetur; cum non ex hominis vitio, sed ex mera, solaq; diuina voluntate, cui quis potest resistere? id contingat. Licet etenim illud magni faciat; externo tamen symbolo, ita non se astringit aut alligat Deus, vt non possit, aut nolit, sine sigillo isto quospiam saluos reddere. Eadem erat Circumcisionis ratio apud Israelitas, atq; Baptismi apud Christianos, {r}Fœminis tamen nullis, præputium est abscissum: & quis dubitat, Deboram, Hannam, pias reliquas, cœlestia tetigisse domicilia? Id in maribus quandoque potuit fieri, quod in mulieribus quotidie. {f}Cum per annos quadraginta, Israeliticus populus, in eremo degeret, intermissa est Circumcisio, quousque in Canaan iam tandem perueniretur. Et exiistimandum est, multos ipsorum proficiscentes in via interiisse. Qui si gloria cœlesti, eo pacto excidissent (alia etenim inobedientiæ crimina, præsentę non tangunt materiā) duriuscule videatur cum iis egisse, Paterille (spiritu, qui ipsos, dum Circumcisionem non reciperent, perpetuā sibi, quotidie accersere vindictam passus est, neq; verbo saltē, adhibendum esse remediū summonuit, Misericors Deus, in suū populū, {t}quē dilexit vnice; quemque ex orbe universo selegisset, tam immanis esse no-luit. {n}Octavo die, secundum fuerat, omni masculo praeputium. At {x}Dauidis ille puer, in adulterio natus, die septimo expirauit; priusquam tempus suscipiendi foederis, advenisset. Qui post mortem infantuli, se consolatus est, Dauid, multo magis flere, & in lachrymas erumpere, necesse habuisset, si non modo Solis conspectui, sed & visioni Dei, subreptus fuisset, quanto magis, si in gehennam protrusus, in perpetuis tormentis ingemuisset: quod ex immani {y}aliquorum, de Baptismo sententia, colligere non est incongruum. Alias proculdubio, qui surrexit tranquillus, edoctus est Dauid, alias institutus: qui è lege didicisset, Dominum {z}misericordiâ ostensurum, in millesimam usq; generationem, colentium eum. Sin millesimam: in primam, Alias etiam, nos edocti sumus: Non enim a vobis modo, sed & liberis vestris, facta est promissio, & iis qui à longe sunt. Et, b Si radix sancta est, etiam rami. Et cum alter parentum, infidelis sit, propter fidem tamen, alterius credentis, c liberi sancti sunt. Si sancti, & Deo accepti.
units.tr: 4. In order that we may penetrate to the marrow of this controversy, and cut it out to the quick, it is worth our while to note what agreement and what difference there is between us and them in the matter of Baptism. We testify, therefore, that this washing and sacramental dipping is to be embraced with the greatest longing and received with the most eager arms, and is not to be scorned or despised out of negligence, under peril of eternal damnation. For how few of the Christian men are there who would dare to be so foolish as to think that the Saviour, who commanded so solemnly this thing, not to be made cheap, and wished to consecrate it in his own body, would be despised? He who values so lightly a mystery of such worth will be cut off from the people, indeed blotted out of the book of life. So far we agree. But that the reception of Baptism is so absolutely and simply necessary that whoever has not been washed with the purifying waters, if he has died, and for that very reason is excluded from heavenly joy, we most firmly deny. For where there has been a faithful soul in an adult man, or a firm apprehension of Christ, or where, in a newly born child, the faith of the parents has come in, we believe that such a soul, struck by the force of the covenant between God and his people, is to be received into the heavenly tabernacles, even if it is deprived of the saving stream; since this happens not through the fault of man, but through the mere and sole divine will, which who can resist? For although God makes much of it, yet he does not so bind or tie himself to an external symbol that he cannot, or will not, save some people without this seal. The same was the reasoning of circumcision among the Israelites as of Baptism among Christians. Yet for no women was the foreskin cut off; and who doubts that Deborah, Hannah, and the other pious women reached the heavenly dwellings? What could happen to males at some time has happened to women every day. When the Israelite people dwelt in the wilderness for forty years, circumcision was discontinued until they at last came into Canaan. And it must be supposed that many of them died on the way. If they had fallen from heavenly glory in that way (for other crimes of disobedience do not touch the present matter), it would seem rather harsh to have dealt with them thus; the Father of mercies, who suffered them not to be struck with perpetual vengeance daily because they did not receive circumcision, and did not even suggest by a word that a remedy should be applied, did not wish the one he loved alone, and whom he had chosen out of the whole world, to be treated so cruelly. On the eighth day, it was prescribed, every male shall have the foreskin ... But that boy of David, born in adultery, died on the seventh day, before the time of receiving the covenant had come. David, who consoled himself after the death of the infant, would have been compelled to weep much more and to break into tears if he had been snatched away not only from the sight of the Sun but also from the vision of God, how much more if he had been thrust into hell and had groaned in perpetual torments: which it is not incongruous to gather from the monstrous opinion of some people concerning Baptism. Otherwise, without doubt, David, who rose up calm, was taught otherwise, was instructed otherwise: he, who had learned from the law that the Lord would show mercy to a thousandth generation of those who worship him, if not to the thousandth, then at least to the first. We have been taught otherwise as well: for the promise was made not only to you but also to your children, and to those who are far off. And, If the root is holy, so are the branches. And although one parent is unbelieving, yet because of the faith of the other who believes, the children are holy. If holy, then also acceptable to God.

units.la: §. Potuissent ista, apud animum suum, reponere Pontificij aliaq; etiam præcise de Baptismo dicta, non leuioris momenti; ut quod Christus dixerit, d Qui crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, seruabitur; ita ad mysterij perceptionem, omni modo adhortans, & accingens; sed non addiderit, Qui vero non baptizabitur, condemnabitur; sed, qui non crediderit, condemnabitur: ita solam fidem, ex simplici necessitate, salutis subseruire & conferre demonstrans. Itidem, quod Joannis ille locus, e Amen, amen, dico tibi, nisi quis genitus fuerit, ex aqua & spiritu, non potest introire, in regnum Dei, testante Papistarum antiquorum Coryphæo, magistro Sententiarum, f de illis intelligendus est, qui possunt & contemnunt baptizari: vel de interna regeneratione. Eoque etiam loco non per solum aquæ Baptismum, fieri regenerationem, profitetur, sed & per pœnitentiam: (ac si ipsa satis conduceret:) & per sanguinem. guinem. Et id non modo tuetur Lombardus, sed, & {g}A-quinas, & omnes ipsorum assecl̄ae, Baptismum sanguinis, (triplicem etenim {h}faciunt, Fluminis, Flaminis, & Sanguinis, Fluminis per aquam, Flaminis per Spiritum Sanctum, & Sanguinis per Martyrium) immediatam coelo, viam aperire. Etiamsi fluminis non accesserit ablutio, satisfaciet tamen, siquis Martyrium pro Christo, passus fuerit, ut ad dextram Salvatoris admoveatur. Et hoc ipsum Augustinus, durus alioquin instantum pater, affirmat: {i}Quicunque et-iam non percepto, regenerationis lavacro, pro Christi confessione moriuntur, tantum eis valet ad dimittenda peccata, quantum si ab-luerentur sacro fonte Baptismatis. Quid quod idem Augustinus, in ista quaestione, quod ad adultos spectat, tam procul, ab eo abest, ut non baptisato, salutem simpliciter neget, ut, si & Fluminis, & Sanguinis, defit purgatio, non defore tamen aliquibus, vitam aeternam arbitretur. In {k}Quae-stionibus super Leviticum: Deficiente Sacramento, invisibilis saepe sanctificat gratia; neque tamen est contemnendum Sacramentum. Sed apertius & luculentius, de Baptismo contra Donatistas, {l}Etiam atque etiam, considerans, in-uenio, non tantum passionem pro nomine Christi, id quod ex Baptismo decerat, posse supplere; (sed etiam fidem, conversionemque cor-dis, si forte ad celebrandum mysterium Baptismi, in angustiis temporum, succurri non potest. Et in latrone, cum Christo crucifixo, exemplum perhibet. Cui licet ipse multoties, videatur adversari, quod ad infantes attinet, nimis rigido & austero dato iudicio; {m}Eos ipsos non baptisatos, gehennalibus torqueri poenis, (cui etiam opinioni, {n}Magister Sententiarum, calculum apponit suum) molliendum tamen, durius Augustini iudicium, Pontificii censuerunt, & Lombardo, in Margine, Parisienses Theologi ascripse-runt. Hic Magister non tenetur: dum non aeternis, cruciari ipsos flammis, sed coelestibus amoveri gaudiis, arbitrentur: {o}neque poena sensus, sed poena damni plecti. Eaque de cau-sa, inauditum apud sacras literas, {p}infantum Limbum, è suo cerebro condiderunt, in quo iuxta Purgatorium posito, in-fantuli seponantur; non cruciatibus torti, sed beatorum gaudiorum, & visionis Dei expertes. Ita dum à vera pietatis via, homines distrahantur, in sententias, inter se diversas miserè discerpuntur.
units.tr: §. The Papists could have set aside in their own minds those other statements, of no small weight, made about Baptism as such: for instance, that Christ said, "He who believes and is baptized will be saved," urging people in every way toward receiving the mystery, but did not add, "He who is not baptized will be condemned"; instead he said, "He who does not believe will be condemned," thereby showing that faith alone serves and contributes to salvation by simple necessity. Likewise, that passage of John, "Amen, amen, I say to you, unless someone is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God," is, as the chief of the ancient Papists, the master of the Sentences, bears witness, to be understood of those who are able to be baptized and despise it, or else of inward regeneration. And in that same passage he professes that regeneration is effected not only by the baptism of water, but also by repentance (as though that alone were sufficient), and by blood. Not only Lombard maintains this, but also Aquinas and all their followers, who make a baptism of blood (for they make a threefold baptism: of water, of the Spirit, and of blood; of water by the water, of the Spirit by the Holy Spirit, and of blood by martyrdom), which opens an immediate way to heaven. Even if the washing of water has not taken place, yet whoever suffers martyrdom for Christ will be satisfied, so that he is brought near to the right hand of the Saviour. Augustine too, otherwise a harsh father in the extreme, affirms this same thing: "Whoever die for the confession of Christ, even without having received the washing of regeneration, avail as much for the forgiveness of sins as if they had been washed in the sacred font of Baptism." What of the fact that the same Augustine, in this question, as far as it concerns adults, is so far from simply denying salvation to the unbaptized that he thinks eternal life is not lacking to some, even if the cleansing of both water and blood is lacking? In his Questions on Leviticus: "When the sacrament is lacking, the invisible grace often sanctifies; yet the sacrament is not to be despised." But more openly and clearly, concerning Baptism against the Donatists: "Considering again and again, I find that not only suffering for the name of Christ, which takes the place of Baptism, can supply, but also faith and conversion of heart, if perhaps there is no opportunity to celebrate the mystery of Baptism because of the straits of the times." And he offers the example of the thief crucified with Christ. Although he himself often seems to oppose this, as far as infants are concerned, having given a judgment too rigid and severe, that these very unbaptized infants are tormented with the punishments of hell (to which opinion the Master of the Sentences also adds his own vote), the Papists nevertheless thought Augustine's harsher judgment should be softened, and the Parisian theologians have noted in the margin of Lombard: "This Master is not held to..." since they judge that they are not tormented with eternal flames, but are removed to heavenly joys, and that they suffer not the punishment of sense but the punishment of loss. And for this reason they have fabricated, out of their own brain, a limbo of infants, unheard of in the sacred letters, in which, placed next to Purgatory, little infants are set apart, not tortured with pains but deprived of the joys of the blessed and the vision of God. Thus, while men are drawn away from the true way of piety into opinions diverse among themselves, they are miserably torn apart.

units.la: 6. Quod si adhuc penitius velimus introspicere; aut aperte, aut ex consequenti, veneranda omnis fere, Antiquitatis canicies pro nobis confitit. Equidem non laudo, Con-stantini Magni factum; citabo tamen, {q}Illustris ille Impe-rator, & pro Jesu Christo Antesignanus, ad extremos vitae dies, sui Baptismum distulit, in fluuio Jordane, vbi {r}Christus, à Joanne tinctus est, lauari desiderans. Si salutem non posse recipi, sine isto sigillo, sibi in mentem induxisset, quotidianum animae suae discrimen, tam pius, prudensque Princeps, non subiisset; dum morte repentina, aut in bello, aut in lecto, aut alio quovis modo, potuisset occumbe-re. {s}Iovianus Imperator, sanus satis, & incolumis, cum cubitum iret, in lectulo, mane, mortuus est repertus. Quid si istud Constantino, quod pio viro Iovianus, accidisset? {t}Quod contingere cuiquam potest, cuius potest. {t}Valentinianus Imperator, cum aduersus Sarmatas Quadosque Illiricum vastantes; ita vocem distendit suam, ut mor-tuus intercideret; cum adhuc, salutaribus non esset expia-tus aquis. In numero tamen Christianorum Imperatorum, hunc ipsum, ob pietatis officia, & indicia antecedentia, referre solemus. Imo quod amplius est, sanctissimus Ambro-sius {u}de ipsius obitu funebrem habens orationem, non dubitat, quin præ Baptismi desiderio, quo tenebatur, saluus fieret; Deo pij Imperatoris voluntatem accipiente. Si af-sectus ægritudine dissiluisset, tamen non penitus à tua misericordia, esset alienus, Domine, qui celeritate temporis esset, non voluntate fraudafraudatus. Et vt ista de senioribus, sic de infantulis, quæ sequuntur, {x}Thessalonicæ Ecclesiæ, referente Socrate, in anno, semel tantum, id erat, festo Paschatis, baptizabant. Ob quam causam omnes, vt ipse loquitur, paucis admodum exceptis, absque Baptismo, moriebantur. {y}Romana, vti videtur, Ecclesia, antiquitus in Paschate & Pentecoste. Idipsum de Africana, testatur {z}Tertullianus. Et quamlibet ingruente necessitate mortis, cuiquam petenti, alias non denegarent (ita enim Leo Papa: {a}Baptizandi duo tantum tempora, idest, Pascha & Pentecostes, seruabantur. Sed sic ad has duas festiuitates, connexas sibimet, atque cognatas, incolumium, & in pacis securitate degentium, libera vota differimus; vt in mortis periculo, in obsidionis discrimine, in persecutionis angustiis, in timore naufragij, nullo tempore, hoc verae salutis remedium, cuiquam denegemus) quota tamen pars infantum, subito mortis iaculo, intercepta, sine Sacramento adhibito, expira-uit. Quod de iis recentioribus dicendum est, de quibus {b}Osorius, Pontificiorum non minimus, de rebus gestis Emanuelis Lusitani mentionem facit. Christianos, enim ait, nuper repertos esse, in Cranganore Indiæ, quia a Thoma vsque Apostolo, propagatam suam fidem, ad nostra vsque tempora, retinuerunt. Horum, ille aliquot enumerat ceremonias; inter reliquas vero de Baptismo, sic: Infantes nullo modo, ante quadragesimum diem, nisi periculum aliquod impendere ipsorum vitae, perspectum fuerit, sacris aquis expiantur. Imprudenter sane, hæ omnes Ecclesiæ, (& in iis antiquior Romana) imo insigniter impie: si impossibile sit, quenquam mortalium, cœlestem vitam ingredi, sacro fonte non intinctum; cum inopinata morte perierint certe, infantuli sæpenumero. Multo tutius, Ecclesiæ Europææ Reformatæ, quæ Dominico quouis die, sacratam vndam portigunt, ne vel infirmis dare scandalum, vel de Baptismo, negligentius & vilius sentire, videantur. Qui plura velit cernere, in præpræsenti quæstione, {c}Bernardum consulat, qui Epistola septima & septuagesima, egregie disputat, hominem non baptizatum, posse ad salutem æternam peruenire; si non contemnat Sacramentum, sed morte præoccupatus, careat.
units.tr: 6. But if we wish to look even more deeply, the venerable hoary head of almost all Antiquity speaks for us, either openly or by consequence. Indeed, I do not praise the deed of Constantine the Great; yet I will cite it: that illustrious emperor, and standard-bearer for Jesus Christ, deferred his Baptism until the last days of his life, desiring to be washed in the river Jordan, where Christ was dipped by John. If it had come into his mind that salvation could not be received without this seal, such a pious and prudent prince would not have undergone the daily peril of his soul, since he could have died a sudden death, either in war, or in bed, or in some other way. The Emperor Jovian, healthy enough and unharmed, when he went to bed was found dead in his little bed in the morning. What if that had happened to Constantine, as it did to the pious man Jovian? What can happen to anyone, can happen to anyone. The Emperor Valentinian, when fighting against the Sarmatians and Quadi who were laying waste Illyricum, strained his voice so hard that he died in the middle of it, while he had not yet been cleansed by the saving waters. Yet among the number of Christian emperors we are accustomed to reckon him, on account of his acts of piety and previous indications. Moreover, what is more, the most holy Ambrose, delivering a funeral oration on his death, does not doubt that, because of the desire for Baptism by which he was held, he was saved, God accepting the will of the pious emperor. "If he had been struck down by sickness, yet he would not have been wholly alien from your mercy, O Lord, he who was defrauded by the shortness of time, not by his will." And as with the elders, so with the little infants who follow: in the Church of Thessalonica, as Socrates reports, they baptized only once a year, namely on the feast of Easter. For this reason, as he himself says, almost all, with very few exceptions, died without Baptism. The Roman Church, as it seems, in antiquity baptized at Easter and Pentecost. Tertullian testifies that the African Church did the same. And although, when the pressing necessity of death arose, they would not deny it to anyone asking (for thus Pope Leo: "Only two times for baptizing were observed, that is, Easter and Pentecost. But we defer our free vows to these two feasts, connected and akin to each other, while we are sound and living in the security of peace; yet in the danger of death, in the peril of a siege, in the straits of persecution, in the fear of shipwreck, at no time would we deny this remedy of true salvation to anyone"), nevertheless, what a small part of infants, cut off by the sudden dart of death, has expired without the sacrament being administered. This must be said of those more recent ones, of whom Osorius, no small Papist, makes mention in his account of the deeds of Emmanuel of Portugal. He says that Christians have recently been found in Cranganore in India, who, because their faith has been propagated from the Apostle Thomas down to our own times, have kept it. He lists some of their ceremonies, and among the rest, concerning Baptism, he says thus: "Infants are in no way cleansed with the sacred waters before the fortieth day, unless it has been clearly seen that some danger threatens their life." Surely these all churches (and among them the older Roman one) acted imprudently, indeed most impiously in a remarkable way: if it is impossible for any mortal to enter the heavenly life without having been dipped in the sacred font; since little infants have certainly often perished by an unexpected death. Far safer are the Reformed churches of Europe, which offer the consecrated water on every Lord's day, lest they seem either to give offense to the weak or to think of Baptism more carelessly and cheaply. Whoever wishes to see more on this question should consult Bernard, who in his seventh-and-seventieth Epistle argues excellently that a man not baptized can attain eternal salvation, if he does not despise the sacrament but is prevented by death and lacks it.

units.la: 7. Tanta sane nube testium, circumuallati sumus; Scripturarum, Ecclesiarum, Patrum, Scholasticorum, quibus freti, de puerulis sine vita nascentibus, aut sine Sacramento abreptis, in æterna gaudia, per Dei misericordiam recipiendis, non diffidimus; si parentes in Christum credant. Sed vt in multis aliis, ita in reisthac, error nimis inueteratus, Pontificios ita inuasit, & possedit totos, vt nolint fidem adhibere. Ideoque vt miserorum parentum conscientias affligunt, & discruciant: dum & cœlo animas, & Christiana, quam appellant, sepultura, in templo scilicet, aut cœmiterio, corpora secludant: sic abutendi sacramento, aliis ansam præbent, cum ad media illegitima, & illicita fugere permittant, aut potius doceant. Hinc & laici, & quod multo est absurdius, mulierculæ & fœminæ, ac si non sacerdotes essent, sed sacerdotissæ, baptizare præsumunt; se puerulo moribundo, Christianum opus, & charitate plenum, impertire cogitantes. Zelo sane feruido, at {d}eo qui caret scientia. Potentissima est superstitio multum inolita; & ad nefas nonnunquam impellit. Vtinam in florentissima nostra Anglia, ita populus vbique, sermone veritatis viuo institueretur, vt ab actibus huiusmodi, temperaret semper manus. Sed verendum est, ne vt olim, sub crassiore ignorantia, sic & hodie alicubi, hoc contingat: vt si inter pariendum, periculum ingruat, ne moriatur infans: aut obstetrix, aut alia circumstans fœmina, immittat aquam. Quain re, tanta antehac creuit audacia, vt si infantulus, tanquam {e}Zarah ille Tamaris, ex vtero materno solam manum extrusisset, vel manum baptizarent; dum adhuc, num masculus esset infans, aut fœmina, non intelligerent. Idque quo tutius fieret, solebant tale nomen indere, quod utriusque sexus commune esset, vt apud nostrates, Franciscus & Francisca, Philippus & Philippa, quæ Anglice idem sonant. Non est difficile, viris Theologis, prudentibus & oculatis, ex matronis senioribus, & senioribus, istam inter sermocinandū extorquere, & seipsos ita in præsenti negotio erudire.
units.tr: 7. Surely we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses: the Scriptures, the Churches, the Fathers, the Schoolmen; relying on these, we do not doubt that little children who are born lifeless, or snatched away without the sacrament, are received into eternal joys through the mercy of God, provided that the parents believe in Christ. But as in many other matters, so in this one, an error too deeply rooted has so invaded and wholly possessed the Papists that they are unwilling to give credence to it. Therefore, they afflict and torment the consciences of wretched parents, while they exclude the souls from heaven and the bodies from Christian burial, that is, in the church or the cemetery; and so they give others occasion for misusing the sacrament, since they permit, or rather teach, people to flee to illegitimate and unlawful means. Hence laymen, and what is far more absurd, silly women and wives, presume to baptize, as if they were not priests but priestesses, intending to bestow a Christian work full of charity on a dying infant. Surely with a fervent zeal, but a zeal lacking knowledge. Superstition, once deeply rooted, is very powerful and sometimes drives people to wickedness. Would that in our most flourishing England the people were everywhere instructed by the living word of truth, so that their hands would always refrain from acts of this kind. But it must be feared lest, as formerly under a thicker ignorance, so also today somewhere this should happen: that if danger threatens during childbirth, lest the infant die, a midwife or some other woman standing by pours in water. From this practice, such boldness has grown up before now that, if an infant, like that Zarah of Tamar, had thrust out only a hand from the mother's womb, they would baptize the hand, while they did not yet understand whether the infant was male or female. And to make this safer, they used to give such a name as was common to both sexes, as among our own people, Francis and Frances, Philip and Philippa, which in English sound the same. It is not difficult for prudent and observant theologians to extract this from elder matrons and the elderly while conversing, and so to instruct themselves in the present business.

units.la: 8. Facinus sane istud est temerarium, & præsumptuosum vel in laico, vel in fœmina. Neque vxor Mosis, nostra Tsipora, tale factum tanquam legitimum tuetur. Cuius licet exemplum a doctis & indoctis, ad hoc citari soleat, ad rem istam tamen propugnandam satis præfidiū in se non habet. Siquidem si Tsippora, idipsum facere aggrederetur, quod num fas sit, vel nefas, disputari queat, & merito, num & alij, sic deinceps? Cum quod ex fide non est, præsertim in tanto mysterio, peccatum sit: Sanctorum exempla, in omnibus imitari, periculosum est: Dauidem in omnibus non æmulamur, nedum fœminam marito tam incommodam, vt obstrependo & exclamando turbaret, quemadmodum recte Caluinus (quocunque Bellarminus oblatret modo) & tam importunam, vt ad patrem remittere coactus sit maritus, ne in officio impediret (vt probabiliter colligitur) ob-seruamus, ac cum honore suspicimus; & eousque, vt omnia illius vestigia persequamur. Si obiiciatur, vt solet, dilcessisse Deum, sedata ira, & misso facto Mose, cum vxorcula filium circumcideret, ideoque illud facinus, suo iudicio comprobasse, quid ni de eo etiam ambigatur? Imperatum etenim aliquando est Obstetricibus, vt Israelitarum mascu-los, in puerperiis occiderent. Noluerunt imperatis auscultare, sed mendacio Pharaonem circumuenerunt. Benedixit ergo Deus, obstetricibus deinceps: sed num quia mentitæ sunt? Num quis earum exemplo, mentiri edisceret, & malum libens faciet, vt succedat bonum? facit perperam qui sic facit, vt prioriquæstione demonstrauit. {m}Non quia mentita sunt, benedixit Deus, vt inquit Augustinus, sed quia in homines Dei, misericordes fuerunt. Ita manum, poterat Deus (quam [?], sub-ducere Mosi, non quod circumcideret fœmina, sed quia ta-dem [?], vterque, suo malo, diuino ministerio, vtcunque parere didicissent. At si cedere velimus, (quod sub iudice iam est) non peccasse Tsipporam, in Sacramento imprimendo: vnde laico aut mulieri, ex illius exemplo baptizare permittetur? Est etenim alia Circumcisionis ratio; alia Baptismi; in administrandi modo. {n}Annotauit Caluinus, & recte, in antiquo omni fœdere, & veteri Testamento, nō esse expressum cuius manu, [illegible, ~2 letters] daretur: num sacerdotis, aut patrisfamilias, aut viri, aut fœminæ. {o}lubetur Abrahamus Ismaeli, & familiæ suæ, præputium amputare. Si vrgere velit quisquam, Abrahamo, vt Domino domus, & Regis & Sacerdotis, & Prophetæ munera incubuisse: & fuisse adhuc {p}in lumbis eius Leui, cui postea sacerdotium commissum est: ideoque sub Sacrifici nomine, signaculum illud in-didisse, respondetur facile, meram eam esse coniecturam: cum ab illo, tanquam a rege aut laico, æque poterat id negotium administrari. Ipse {q}Iehosua Princeps, Israelitas in Gilgale, circumcidisse dicitur. Num per populum, vel Leuitas, id transegerit opus, diserta non fit mentio. {r}Circum-cisus est Christus: sed cuius manu, non apparet. Ita nus-quam constat e sacris literis, id cuiquam certæ personæ fuisse iniunctum, neque ex Iosepho toto perlecto, nec Philone Iudæo, de Circumcisione, id poteram animadver-tere.
units.tr: 8. This deed is certainly rash and presumptuous, whether in a layman or in a woman. Nor does Moses' wife, our Zipporah, defend such an act as lawful. Although her example is commonly cited by learned and unlearned alike in support of this practice, it does not in itself provide sufficient protection for defending it. For if Zipporah had undertaken to do this very thing, it could be debated whether it is right or wrong, and rightly so: may others also do so henceforth? For whatever is not of faith is sin, especially in so great a mystery. It is dangerous to imitate the saints in everything: we do not imitate David in all things, much less a woman so troublesome to her husband that she disturbed him by shouting and clamouring, as Calvin rightly observes (however Bellarmine may bark), and so intrusive that the husband was compelled to send her back to her father, so that she might not hinder his duty (as is probably gathered). We observe this with respect and admire it, and to such an extent that we follow all its footsteps. If it is objected, as is often done, that God was appeased and his anger ceased, and that Moses having been dismissed, the little wife circumcised the son, and therefore approved that deed by his own judgement, why should it not also be called into doubt? For it was once commanded to the midwives that they should kill the male children of the Israelites at their childbirths. They did not obey the command, but deceived Pharaoh with a lie. God therefore blessed the midwives thereafter: but was it because they lied? Would anyone learn from their example to lie, and gladly do evil so that good may follow? He who does so acts wrongly, as the prior question has shown. {m} God blessed them not because they lied, as Augustine says, but because they were merciful to the men of God. Thus God could have withdrawn his hand from Moses (which [?]), not because a woman circumcised, but because at last both, to their own harm, had learned somehow to obey the divine ministry. But if we are willing to concede (which is already before the judge) that Zipporah did not sin in administering the sacrament, from whose example will it be permitted for a layman or a woman to baptize? For there is one manner of administering circumcision and another of baptism. {n} Calvin observed, and rightly, that in the whole ancient covenant and the Old Testament it is not expressed by whose hand it was to be given: whether by a priest, or a head of the household, or a man, or a woman. {o} Abraham was commanded to cut off the foreskin of Ishmael and of his household. If anyone wishes to press that Abraham had discharged the offices of lord of the house, king, priest and prophet, and that Levi, to whom the priesthood was later committed, was still in his loins, and therefore that he imposed that seal under the name of sacrifice, it is easily answered that this is mere conjecture, since that business could equally have been carried out by him as by a king or a layman. Joshua the Prince himself is said to have circumcised the Israelites at Gilgal. Whether he performed that work through the people or the Levites, no explicit mention is made. {r} Christ was circumcised, but by whose hand does not appear. Thus it nowhere appears from the sacred letters that this was enjoined upon any particular person, nor could I notice it from reading all of Josephus, or Philo the Jew, concerning circumcision.

units.la: 9. Sed ad verbi Concionatores, baptizandi curam spectare, & non ad alios, ipse Christus testis est. A postolis di-xit, {s}[?] profecti docete omnes gentes, baptizantes eos in nomine patris, & filii, & Spiritus Sancti: vt, quibus baptizandi, iis et-iam prædicandi, incumbat officium. Ita apud {t}Marcum cum annunciationis verbi, meminisset prius: de baptizan-do, alia statim subiungit. Per Iohannem Baptistam, prae-conem poenitentiae, cepit primordium hæc ablutio: & per Apostolos Christi, & ministros Euangelij deinceps propa-gata est. Neque quenquam, huic operi appositus ma-nus in Scriptura legimus, nisi prius per Sanctum Spiri-tum, in numerum Præconum, & Concionatorum verbi, cooptatus esset. Talis etenim fuerat, Philippus Diaco-nus, in quo celebrem exceptionem, contra doctrinam hanc, se reperisse, Bellarminus arbitratur. {u}Nihil enim potest esse manifestius, quam quod Euangelii prædican-di, munus acceperit, & præstiterit: priusquam baptizaret. Cum igitur, qui ex populo sint, concionandi prouin-ciam, non debeant arripere, ne cum {x}Pseudoprophe-tis, cum non mittantur, exire, & currere videantur: cum-que fœminæ, ab {y}Apostolo, diserte sit inhibitum, ne do-cere palam audeat: dispar longe est ratio Baptismi apud nos, quam præputium auferendi, apud Tsipporam[?] Mo-sis. Prohibendum igitur est, ne vel sub superstitionis specie: aut charitatis obsequio: aut intentionis piæ, salubrisque prætextu: eousque Dominum, quisquam tentare audeat, vt diuino Sacramento, tam mystico, tam sancto, sacrilegas iniiciat manus suas, cum non oporteat. Qui præter mandatum Domini, alienum ignem {z}thuribulo indiderunt, Abiha, & Nadab: quamlibet ad suffitum, ipsi Deo faciendum: igne à præsentia Domini, egrediente, con-sumpti, disparuerunt. Negligebant sacerdotes, & {a}Leui-tæ, Arcam Domini, humeris gestare suis, cum ipsam, Da-uid domum reduceret: eoque proculdubio Iehouam of-fenderunt: sed cum Vzzah, Arcæ c[?] rheda prolapsurae, ad moueret dextram, ictu oculi, sic percussus est, vt mortuus expirarit. {b}Vetuisset expresse Deus, ne rem vllam sanctam, attingerent Leuitæ, aut contrectarent, (hoc est, aliter quam præscriptum fuerat) nè morerentur. Non erat sanctior apud Israelitas, ea ipsa At ca fœderis; quam Baptis-mus apud Christianos instituto Salvatoris: regeneratio-nis fons: redemptionis sigillum. Cui igitur id officium, è di-uinis literis, non est concreditum: is ne attingito, {c}Vzziah, cum Rex esset, sibi plura, quam par esset; licere arbitratus, ingressus est templum, & Domino suffitum, super altare, adolere paravit. At secutus est Azariah, Sacerdotum Prin-ceps, & cum eo, octoginta Sacerdotes Iehouæ; viri robusti: qui se intermittendo, obstiterunt; ne altare attingeret. Et cū illic, utrinque tumultuatum esset: ipso Domino plectente, exorta est Regi, in fronte lepra, ut non modo è templo, sed ex omni cuiusquam contubernio, ad diem usque suæ mortis exturbaretur. Sic distincta, esse voluit Deus, Sacerdotum, aliorumque priuatorum munia; neque rebus consecratis, profanos quosuis, se arroganter nimis, & audacter im-miscere.
units.tr: 9. But that Christ himself is witness that the care of baptizing belongs to the preachers of the Word, and not to others. He said to the Apostles, {s} [?] having gone forth, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit: so that to whom the duty of baptizing belongs, to them also the duty of preaching is entrusted. Thus in Mark, after he had first mentioned the proclamation of the word, he immediately adds something else about baptizing. This washing began through John the Baptist, the herald of repentance, and was afterwards propagated through the Apostles of Christ and the ministers of the Gospel. Nor do we read in Scripture of anyone whose hand was applied to this work unless he had first been enrolled through the Holy Spirit among the number of heralds and preachers of the Word. For Philip the Deacon was of this kind, and Bellarmine thinks that in him he found a famous exception to this doctrine. {u} For nothing can be more manifest than that he received and performed the office of preaching the Gospel before he baptized. Since therefore those from among the people ought not to seize the province of preaching, lest they seem to run and go out like false prophets, since they are not sent; and since a woman is expressly forbidden by the Apostle to dare to teach publicly: the reason for baptism among us is far different from the removal of the foreskin in the case of Zipporah, the wife of Moses. It must therefore be prevented that anyone, whether under the appearance of superstition, or the obligation of charity, or the pretext of a pious and wholesome intention, should dare so to tempt the Lord as to lay sacrilegious hands upon this divine sacrament, so mystical and so holy, when it is not fitting. Those who, beyond the Lord's command, put strange fire into the censer, Abihu and Nadab, although it was for incense to be offered to God himself, were consumed by fire going out from the presence of the Lord and perished. The priests and {a} Levites neglected to carry the Ark of the Lord on their shoulders when David was bringing it home, and therefore without doubt they offended Jehovah: but when Uzzah put out his right hand as the Ark was about to slip from the cart, he was struck by a blow of the eye, so that he died. God had expressly forbidden the Levites to touch or handle any holy thing (that is, otherwise than had been prescribed), lest they die. Among the Israelites that very covenant sign was no holier than baptism is among Christians, the fountain of regeneration and the seal of redemption, instituted by the Saviour. Therefore, let him not touch it to whom the office has not been entrusted from the divine letters. {c} Uzziah, when he was king, thinking it lawful for himself to do more than was fitting, entered the temple and prepared to burn incense to the Lord upon the altar. But Azariah, the chief of the priests, followed him, and with him eighty priests of Jehovah, strong men, who by withstanding him resisted lest he touch the altar. And when there was an uproar on both sides, the Lord himself striking, leprosy broke out on the king's forehead, so that he was driven out not only from the temple but from all fellowship with anyone, until the day of his death. Thus God willed the offices of priests and of other private persons to be distinguished, and not for anyone whatever, profane and too arrogant and bold, to thrust themselves into consecrated things.

units.la: 10. De mysteriis noui fœderis, eadem est, & similis ratio, quæ per quemuis è plebe infima, contaminati Author no-luit. Quod in alio, Eucharistiæ, sacramento, manifestum sa-tis est; quippe quod è generali consensu Ecclesiæ, sacerdo-tis solius manu, administrandum est. De altero: Quibus, claues regni cœlorum, conseruandas Deus tradidit; iis et-iam, Baptismi dispensationem concredidit. Sed non claues dedit laicis; non porrexit fœminis. {d} Innocentius tertius Papa, cum fœminam quandam, sese actibus Sacerdotali-bus, ingerere cognouisset, à traditione clauium, ratione du-sta, seuere interdixit: Noua quædam, nostris auribus sunt intimata, quod Abbatissæ, Moniales proprias benedicunt, ipsarum quoque confessiones, in criminibus audiunt: & legentes Euangelium, præsumunt publice prædicare. Cum igitur id absonum sit, pariter & absurdum; mandamus, quatenus, ne id de cætero fiat; curetis firmiter inhibere. Quia licet beatissima virgo, dignior, & excellentior fuerit, Apo-stolis. solis vniuersis, non tamen illis, sed istis, Dominus, claues regni cælo-rum commisit. Tantam sane habent Sacramenta, cum istis affinitatem; vt abiis, meo iudicio, similiter oporteat abstinere modo, ex similitudine. Ex mulierculârum parte confidere raruntistæc probe, & abusum amouendum censuerunt (vt apparet) Patres in Concilio Carthaginensi quarto congregati, qui Canone sanxerunt, e Mulier quamuis docta, & sancta viros in conuentu, docere non præsumat: At simpliciter, & sine limitatione, f Mulier baptizare non præsumat. In quo Canone citando, aperta g Lombardi, & h Gratiani fraus; digna est quæ castigetur; qui ex suo addiderunt cerebro, Mulier baptizare non præsumat, nisi cogente necessitate, quæ verba nisi cogente necessitate, in Concilii Editione non reperiuntur, teste ipso i Bellarmino. Maledicta est Glossa, quæ corrumpit textum. De duobus istis, vt & de Magistro Scholasticæ Historiæ, Petro Comestore, referatur & fabula; fuisse germanos, & vterinos fratres, ex eadem fœmina, adulterio conceptos. Num vere, parum refert: ego potius contrarium sentio, propter seculi temporumque diuersitatem, in quibus vixerunt: at dubitare non est opus; quin vt & vt Simeon, & Leui, sic & duo isti, fratres fuerint in malitia, qui sua, antiquis Patrum Orthodoxorum scriptis, assuere non sunt veriti. Noluerunt fœminis, baptizandi libertatem penitus auferri.
units.tr: 10. The same and similar reasoning applies to the mysteries of the New Covenant, which the Author did not want to be contaminated by any man of the lowest rank. This is clear enough in the case of another sacrament, the Eucharist, since by the general consent of the Church it is to be administered by the hand of a priest alone. As for the other: God handed over the keys of the kingdom of heaven to be kept by those to whom he also entrusted the dispensing of baptism. But he did not give the keys to laymen; he did not hand them to women. {d} Pope Innocent III, when he learned that a certain woman was intruding herself into priestly acts, sternly forbade her from the handing over of keys, the matter having been weighed: Some novelties have been announced to our ears, that abbesses bless their own nuns, and also hear their confessions for sins, and, reading the Gospel, presume to preach publicly. Since therefore this is discordant and likewise absurd, we command that you firmly take care to forbid it, so that it be not done from now on. For although the most blessed Virgin was more worthy and more excellent than the Apostles, the Lord committed the keys of the kingdom of heaven not to her, but to them, to all the Apostles. Certainly the sacraments have such affinity with those things that, in my judgement, one ought likewise to abstain from them by the same analogy. Those Fathers gathered at the Fourth Council of Carthage, as is evident, judged that this abuse should be removed, though they were seldom confident about women's part in these matters. They enacted by canon that a woman, however learned and holy, should not presume to teach men in an assembly; but simply and without limitation, that a woman should not presume to baptize. In citing this canon, the open fraud of Lombard and Gratian is worthy of censure, who added from their own brain: a woman should not presume to baptize, unless compelled by necessity. The words unless compelled by necessity are not found in the edition of the council, as Bellarmine himself testifies. The gloss is accursed which corrupts the text. Concerning these two, as also concerning the master of the Scholastic History, Peter Comestor, a fable is also reported: that they were brothers, full brothers from the same mother, conceived in adultery. Whether it is true matters little: I rather think the contrary, because of the diversity of the age and times in which they lived; but there is no need to doubt that these two brothers, like Simeon and Levi, were brothers in wickedness, who were not afraid to attach their own inventions to the ancient writings of the orthodox Fathers. They did not wish the freedom of baptizing to be taken entirely from women.

units.la: II. Tertullianus in suo, quem de Baptismo edidit, tractatu, m laico necessitatis tempore, vt vulgo appellatur; a-quis lustrare sacris permittit: nullo tamen modo mulierem finit baptizare. Id quod alibi etiam habet; n Non permittitur mulieri in Ecclesia loqui, sed nec docere nec tingere, nec offerre, nec ul-lius virilis muneris, ne dum sacerdotalis officii, sortem sibi vendicare, o Vbi tingere, baptizare significat, testibus o Pontificiis. Huic accedit Epiphanius, qui Marcioni tanquam hæreticum quiddam obiicit: p permittit etiam mulieribus, vt dent baptisma; q Et alibi, ipsi Virgini Mariæ; non licuisse baptizare asserit, tum etenim ipsa, Christum, inquit, aquis aspersisset, neque ut, Ioannes Baptista faceret, passa fuisset. Quae omnia, {r}Bel-larminus, intelligenda asserit, ( nisi urgeret necessitas :) at absolute, & sine exceptione, loquuntur Tertullianus, & E-piphanius: & simplicem non esse, Baptismi necessitatem, ad salutem, satis superius demonstratum est. Sicque friuolae illius & praeposterae, sunt exceptiones. Ita interdictum fuisse in Baptismo, ministerium foeminarum, apud antiquam Ecclesiam manifestum est. De eo autem, qui per laicos fiebat, ut dicam, quod sentio: Cupierunt antiqui Patres, ut ad salutarem fontem, omnes accederent, idque eo (ut verisimile est) ingeminarunt magis, quo & persecutionis feruor, & Gentilium, Christianismum deridentium, & subsannantium, copia & authoritas accessuros magis deterreret. Ad id igitur efficiendum, conniuentia quadam tolerarunt laicos, mysteriis infantulos initiare. Et cum semel in persecutionis feruore, ea increbuisset opinio, succedentibus temporibus latius propagata est. Unde etiam Hieron-mus, iunior tamen ut arbitror, & feruidior, contra Lucife-rianos, {f}Baptizare frequenter, si necessitas cogit, sciimus etiam laicis licere. Valuisset consuetudo, eamq; aut Hieronymus, aut alij aliquot antiquorum, accurate ad stateram, aut trutinam non exegerunt, aut perpenderunt; sed cum aliis, a maioribus, receptis, amplexi sunt, sine disquisitione, aut discussione; ut alicubi, de Purgatorio, opinionem, Augustinus, ab antiquioribus deriuatam accipit; licet {u}alibi, non sine dubitatione, & haesitatione fluctuante. Et ut istud potius credam, {x}illud facit Augustini, ubi aliquanto penitius rem discutiens, Baptismum per manum viri laici, a peccato non audet eximere, ut infra demonstrabitur. Aut, ut Moses aliquando, prae duritia cordium; Israelitas passus est, {y}diuortij, repudiiue libellum, in causis leuioribus dare, sic prae infirmitate hominum, aut duritia aliquorum, laicos, mysteriis imbuere
units.tr: II. Tertullian, in his treatise on Baptism, permits laymen to cleanse with the sacred water in a time of necessity, as it is commonly called; but in no way does he allow a woman to baptize. He also has this elsewhere: "A woman is not permitted to speak in the Church, nor to teach, nor to baptize, nor to offer, nor to claim for herself the lot of any male office, much less of the priestly office," where "to baptize" means "to immerse," as the Papists bear witness. To this is added Epiphanius, who objects to Marcion, as to something heretical, that he "permits women also to administer baptism." And elsewhere he asserts that it was not lawful even for the Virgin Mary herself to baptize; for, he says, she sprinkled Christ with water, but she did not suffer herself to do what John the Baptist did. Bellarmine says all these statements are to be understood as applying unless necessity presses; but Tertullian and Epiphanius speak absolutely and without exception. And it has already been sufficiently shown above that the necessity of Baptism for salvation is not absolute. Thus those exceptions are frivolous and absurd. That the ministry of women in Baptism was thus forbidden in the ancient Church is clear. But concerning the baptism that was performed by laymen, I will say what I think. The ancient Fathers desired that all should come to the saving fountain, and they pressed this (as is likely) the more, since the heat of persecution, and the number and authority of the Gentiles who mocked and scorned Christianity, would deter them the more from coming. To bring this about, they therefore tolerated, by a certain connivance, laymen initiating infants into the mysteries. And once this opinion had grown strong in the heat of persecution, it was spread more widely in later times. Hence also Jerome, though younger, as I think, and more fervent, against the Luciferians, says: "We know that laymen too are permitted to baptize often, if necessity compels." The custom prevailed, and neither Jerome nor some others of the ancients examined or weighed it accurately on the scale or balance; but, having received it with the others from their forebears, they embraced it without inquiry or discussion, as Augustine, in one place, accepts an opinion about Purgatory derived from earlier writers, though elsewhere not without doubt and wavering hesitation. And that I would rather believe this, there is that passage of Augustine where, examining the matter somewhat more deeply, he does not dare to exempt from sin Baptism given by the hand of a lay man, as will be shown below. Or, as Moses once, because of the hardness of their hearts, suffered the Israelites to give a bill of divorce in lesser causes, so, because of the weakness of men or the hardness of some, the Fathers suffered laymen to imbue the mysteries.

units.la: {r} Bellarm. de Baptismo c.7. buere passi sunt. Quod pro certo existimo, in causa fuisse, cur in regno olim nostro, qui abolita superstitione, preces nostras, & Liturgiam, in certam formam librumq; redegerunt, Priuati Baptismi mentionem subintulerunt; nō quod Baptismum datum per laicos, potissimum autem per fœminas, legitimum esse, arbitrati fuissent; sed ne primis Euangelij reuocandi auspiciis, indoctam & insciam multitudinem, à vera pietate deterrerent; illud ingerendo, quod imbibitæ per multos annos opinioni, expresse adeo, aduersaretur. Qua in re, fidem mihi faciunt multa, in nostra Ecclesia, ab illo tempore facta, quibus, homini prudenti appareat, Rectores venerandos, eam voluisse opinionem, paulatim, & pedeten-tim, ab hominum animis, amotam, & euulsam. Sed tolera-tio, & permissio, fas & iustum esse, quod ad tempus toleratur non concludit. {z}Verum qui Liturgiæ nostræ circumstan-tias, accuratissime examinauit, ostendit ex verbis ipsis, nihil posse colligi, de Baptismo fœminarum intellecto; & Baptis-mum priuatum, nihil aliud significare arbitratur, quam qui in domo priuata, non in templo publice, administratur, qui per solum scilicet sacerdotem accersitum detur, nō per laicum aut fœminam. Sed iam tandem missa faciamus, cum primo, an mera sit sacri fontis necessitas, ad salutem acquirendam, & secundo, num recte, secusue faciant & laici, & mulieres baptizantes, disputauerimus. Sed ex istis alia suppullulat dubitatio, non minori digna examina-tione.
units.tr: {r} Bellarmine, On Baptism, ch. 7. They suffered it to be imbued. This I hold for certain was the cause why, in our kingdom, those who, once superstition was abolished, reduced our prayers and Liturgy to a fixed form and book, inserted a mention of private Baptism; not because they judged that Baptism given by laymen, and especially by women, was lawful, but so that at the first auspices of restoring the Gospel they would not deter the untaught and unskilled multitude from true piety by insisting on something so expressly opposed to the opinion that had soaked into them through many years. In this matter, many things done in our Church since that time give me assurance, by which it appears to a prudent man that our venerable Rulers wished that opinion to be removed and uprooted from men's minds gradually and step by step. But toleration and permission do not prove that what is tolerated for a time is right and just. But he who has examined the circumstances of our Liturgy most carefully shows from the very words that nothing can be gathered about Baptism understood as performed by women; and he thinks that "private Baptism" signifies nothing other than that which is administered in a private house, not publicly in the church, and which is given by a priest summoned alone, not by a layman or a woman. But now let us dismiss this. Since we have disputed, first, whether the necessity of the sacred font for acquiring salvation is absolute, and second, whether laymen and women baptizing do rightly or wrongly, another doubt springs up from these, not less worthy of examination.

units.la: 12. In Ecclesia nostra, pro concesso, vti arbitror, doctiores omnes, & Theologi[?] nunc habent, profanas, & sacrilegas, illos omnes, huic Sacramento, admouere manus, qui, cum clauium potestatem, non habuerint concreditam, id audeant attrectare. Verum detur, id quod opus est, apud rudem plebeculam, & superstitiosos dari; quod nefario nimis ausu, aut iste, aut illa, infantulum baptizarit; quid ministro EuanEuangelii in re isthac faciendum est? Si superuixerit puer-lus, num pro iam initiato recensendus est? aut regerenda est aqua, & mysterium iterandum? Salebrosa vere quæstio, & quæ suas difficultates insignes habet. Nam persona ministrantis, ad rem ipsam Sacramenti, videtur facere, cum pastoribus Ecclesiæ, iisque solis eam prouinciam imposuerit Dominus. Hincque non {a}defuerunt, qui fœminæ manu datam talem ablutionem, nihil magis ad Baptismum facere asseueratunt, quam ordinariam aliam aliquam, & quotidianam lauationem. Verumtamen qui laboriofius confideraruntt, & perpetuum, ea in re, Christianorum antiquiorum, consensum expenderunt; ministrantis personâ, non de Esse Sacramenti, sed de bene Esse iudicarunt. Baptismi formam, vt loquuntur Scholæ, iniectionem aquæ, in nomine Trinitatis, existimarunt. Pie igitur fit, si minister tangat solus: at fit etiam, si tangat alius. Qua in re, eandem personæ Sacerdotis, rationem esse censent, in Baptismo: quæ est consensus parentum, in matrimonio contrahendo. Pie facit, qui parenti auscultat suo: adeoque impie, qui parentis pii, consensum negligit, & repudiat: sed si filius, ita impie, contraxerit matrimonium, pro coniugio rato habendum est: quando reliquæ matrimonii circumstantiæ, completæ fuerint. Male igitur factum est, si laicus: peius factum, si fœmina, rem sacrosanctam hanc attigerit. Sed factum est, & quod factum est, infectum esse non potest. Habet locum in re isthac, illud Iuris Axioma, Multa fieri non debent, quæ tamen facta valent, Aspersit ergo lympham, & in nomine patris, & filii, & Spiritus Sancti benedixit, qui non debuit. Sufficere certe, ad admissionem in numerum fidelium, opinamur hucusque, nec ingeminandam esse aquam. Christi causa, cuius est quod datur, & non hominis, est efficax hæc admissio. Et dum in ouilis ostium, intromittatur anima, parum refert per quem, num per furem, aut ipsum custodem ianuæ intromittatur. Dedit modo nomen Christo, & pro milite est accensus. Si quis id, quod non oportuit, vsurpauerit, id agenti, & non patienti, vertendum est vitio. Parum scimus, num ad Hippo-ram[?] sui nati Circumcisio, ex instituto diuino, possit spectare; sed cum vel per fas, vel nefas, praeputium abstulisset, non alium accessisse, qui rursus circumcideret, inuenimus. Sicut non secundo {b}circumcisum fuisse, qui à Samaritanis ad Iudaeos transiisset, dicit Augustinus, de Baptismo Haereticorum disputans. Est vna Circumcisio, sicut {c}vnus Dominus, vna fi-des, vnum Baptisma.
units.tr: 12. In our Church, as I think, all the more learned men and theologians now hold, as a settled point, that all those profane and sacrilegious persons who, not having been entrusted with the power of the keys, dare to lay hands on this Sacrament are to be condemned. But grant what is indeed the case, that among a rude common folk and superstitious people someone, either this man or that woman, has rashly baptized an infant. What is to be done in this matter by the minister of the Gospel? If the little boy survives, is he to be counted as already initiated? Or must the water be poured out again and the mystery repeated? It is indeed a rugged question, and one that has notable difficulties. For the person of the one administering seems to matter for the very substance of the Sacrament, since the Lord assigned that office to the ministers of the Church, and to them alone. Hence there were not lacking those who asserted that such a washing given by a woman's hand contributes nothing more to Baptism than some other ordinary, daily washing. Yet those who considered the matter more diligently, and weighed the perpetual consent of the ancient Christians in this matter, judged that the person of the minister concerns not the being (esse) of the Sacrament but its well-being (bene esse). They held that the form of Baptism, as the schools say, is the pouring on of water in the name of the Trinity. Therefore it is done rightly if the minister alone touches it; but it is done also if another touches it. In this matter they judge that the person of the priest has the same standing in Baptism as the consent of parents has in contracting marriage. He acts rightly who obeys his parent; and so he acts wickedly who neglects and rejects the consent of a godly parent. But if a son has contracted marriage wickedly in this way, it must be held as a valid marriage, once the remaining circumstances of marriage are complete. It was therefore wrongly done if a layman touched this most sacred thing, and worse if a woman did. But it was done, and what has been done cannot be undone. In this matter the legal axiom applies: "Many things ought not to be done which, once done, nevertheless stand." So she sprinkled the water, and blessed in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, one who ought not to have been blessed by her. We think, indeed, that up to this point it suffices for admission into the number of the faithful, and that the water must not be repeated. This admission is effective for Christ's sake, whose it is that is given, and not for the man's. And when a soul is brought through the door of the sheepfold, it matters little through whom, whether through a thief or through the very doorkeeper, that it is brought in. He has only given his name to Christ, and has been enrolled as a soldier. If someone has presumed upon what he ought not, the fault is to be laid to the one who acts, and not to the one who suffers. We know little whether the circumcision of her own son could look, by divine institution, to Hippora; but when she had removed the foreskin, by right or wrong, we find that no other came to circumcise him again. Just as, Augustine says, in disputing about the Baptism of heretics, one who had passed from the Samaritans to the Jews was not circumcised a second time. There is one circumcision, just as there is "one Lord, one faith, one Baptism."

units.la: 13. Celeberrima est historia apud {d}Sozomenum, de Alexandro, Alexandriae Episcopo, & Athanasio, qui postea dictus est Magnus. Cum Episcopus ille, conuiuas, qui pran-derent secum, in littore deambulans, expectaret, puerulorum vidit caetum, in arena colludentium; quos ex gestibus i-psorum, diuini cultus, ceremonias aliquot, repraesentare perspexerat, à longe stans. Et quamdiu nihil, vel petulanter satis, vel audacter nimis, conspexisset transfigi, delectatione aliqua capiebatur. Sed cum ad altiora, videret pergere, accersit è Clero aliquos, non procul degentes, quibus etiam iuuenculorum, ostendit lusus. Sed cum tandem isti, pueros aduocassent; ex ipsorum confessione, hoc edidicerunt, Athanasium scilicet, jam puerum, Episcopi personam, inter iocandum, induentem, adolescentes alios, mysteriis Christianis non imbutos, baptizasse. Et cum forma actionis, & rei circumstantias, accurate disquisissent, pro Ecclesiae ritu, transacta ordine esse omnia, intellexerunt. Testante Sozomeno, Alexander iste, tam Sanctus vir, & prudens, Baptismum Athanasii pro rato habuit, nec iterandum credidit; sed in Catalogum fidelium, omnes libentissime asscripsit, qui ab ipso puero, tinctionem accepissent. Quae istis contradicerent, & exprofesse[?] oppugnarent, rationes sanas & solidas, exinde nō reperio. In Augustino peruoluendo, celebria duo obseruaui loca, ad negocium præsens, non mediocriter {a}cientia. Est altere Libro secundo contra Epistolam Parme-niani. Etsi laicus, Baptismum pereunti dederit, necessitate com-pulsus, quod cum ipse acciperet, dandum esse addidicit, nescio an pie quisquam dixerit, repetendum esse. Nulla etenim cogente necessita-te, sifiat, alieni muneris usurpatio est: si autem necessitas urgeat, aut nullum, aut veniale delictum est. Sed etsi nulla necessitate usur-petur, & aquolibet cuilibet detur, quod datum fuerit, non potest dici non datum, quamuis recte dici possit illicite datum. Modeste Augustinus, uti semper, & caute, nescio an pie quisquam dixerit repetendum esse, sed cum postea, dari Baptismum asseueraverit, neq; potest Sacerdos, quicquam dare amplius, & Sacerdotis Baptismus, regerendus non sit: idem est, acsi assereret, repetendum non esse. Sed & obiter, operæ precium est advertere, se Baptismum licitum, illicite posse dari, affirmare; & laicalem asperionem, licet necessitate factam, a delicto, licet veniali, & leuiori, non audere omnino & absolute, excusare. Quod id est, quod supra, ex Augustino, innuebam.
units.tr: 13. Very famous is the story told by Sozomen about Alexander, Bishop of Alexandria, and Athanasius, who was afterwards called the Great. While that bishop was walking on the shore, waiting for guests who were to dine with him, he saw, standing at a distance, a group of little boys playing in the sand, whom he had observed from their gestures to be representing some ceremonies of divine worship. And as long as he saw nothing done too wantonly or too boldly, he was held by a certain delight. But when he saw them proceeding to more serious matters, he summoned some of the clergy, who were not far off, and showed them the play of the youngsters. And when at last these men had called the boys, they learned from their own confession that Athanasius, already a boy, putting on the person of the bishop in jest, had baptized other young men who were not initiated into the Christian mysteries. And when they had carefully inquired into the form of the action and the circumstances of the matter, they understood that everything had been carried out in order, according to the rite of the Church. Sozomen testifies that this Alexander, so holy and prudent a man, held the Baptism of Athanasius as valid and did not believe it should be repeated; but he most willingly enrolled among the faithful all who had received immersion from that boy. I find no sound and solid reasons from this to refute these things or openly oppose them. In leafing through Augustine I have noticed two famous passages, not a little relevant to the present matter. It is in the second book against the Letter of Parmenianus: "Although a layman, compelled by necessity, has given Baptism to one perishing, which he himself had learned must be given when he received it, I do not know whether anyone devoutly would say it must be repeated." For where no necessity compels, the taking up of another's office is wrongful; but if necessity presses, it is either no sin or a venial one. But even if it is taken up without any necessity, and water is given to anyone by anyone, what has been given cannot be said not to have been given, although it can rightly be said to have been given unlawfully. Augustine, as always, is modest and cautious: "I do not know whether anyone devoutly would say it must be repeated"; but since he afterwards asserts that Baptism is given, and a priest's Baptism cannot be given again (nor should it be repeated), it is the same as if he asserted that it need not be repeated. But also in passing, it is worth noticing that he affirms that lawful Baptism can be given unlawfully; and he does not dare to excuse absolutely a lay sprinkling, although made from necessity, from sin, even if venial and slight. This is what I was hinting at above from Augustine.

units.la: 14. At secundum Augustini testimonium, est amplissimum; {f}Si quis forte, me, in eo Concilio constitutum, vbi talium rerum quæstio versaretur, non præcedentibus talibus, quorum sententias sequi mallem, vrgeret, vt dicerem, quid ipse sentirem, sic modo affectus essem, quo eram, cum ista dictarem, nequaquam dubitarem, habere eos Baptismum, qui vbicunque, & a quibusqunque, illud verbis Euangelicis consecratum, sine sua simulatione, & cum aliqua fide accepissent, quanquam eis ad salutem spiritualem, non prodesset si charitate caruissent, qua Catholica, inserenter ur Ecclesia. Si enim habeam, inquit, fidem, vt montes transferam, charitatem autem non habeam, nihil sum. Sicut iam prætieritis Maiorum statutis, non dubito, etiam illos habere Baptismum, qui quamuis fallaciter id accipiunt, in Ecclesia tamen accipiunt, vel vbi putatur esse Ecclesia, ab iis, inquorum societate id accipitur, de quibus dicitur; Ex nobis exierunt. Pergitadhuc: Ubi autem, neque societas ulla esset, ita crederentium, neque ille, qui ibi acciperet, ita crederet, sed totum ludere, & mimice, & ioculariter ageretur, utrum approbandus esset Baptismus, qui sic daretur, divinum judicium, per alicuius revelationis oraculum, con-cordi oratione, & impensis supplici devotione gemitibus, implorandum esse censerem. Hucusque Augustinus. In quibus profitetur se non audere, id pro Baptismo repudiare, quod à quovis sine fide, cuiuis sine fide, idq; ludicre tantum, & mimice, & ioculariter tribueretur. Sed expresse affirmat, eos, ex illius sententia, Baptismum habere, qui ubicunque illud, & à quibuscunque, verbis Evangelicis consecratum, acceperunt. Ex illius igitur opinione sobriissima; nec post foeminam, nec post quemlibet, ablutio mystica seriò data, & verbis debitis, est redintegranda.
units.tr: 14. But according to the testimony of Augustine, which is very ample: "If anyone, perhaps, placed in that council where such questions were debated, were to press me, without previous opinions of such men whose judgements I would rather follow, to say what I myself thought, I would, being in the same disposition in which I was when I dictated these things, by no means doubt that those have baptism who, wherever and from whomsoever they received it, consecrated with the words of the Gospel, received it without their own pretence and with some faith, although it would not profit them towards spiritual salvation if they lacked the charity by which the Catholic Church is joined together. For if, he says, I have faith so as to remove mountains, but do not have charity, I am nothing. Just as, by the decrees of our Elders already set down, I do not doubt that those also have baptism who, although they receive it deceitfully, nevertheless receive it in the Church, or where the Church is thought to be, from those in whose fellowship it is received, of whom it is said: They went out from us." He goes on: "But where there was no fellowship of believers of this kind, nor did he who there received it believe in this way, but the whole thing was played out as a mime and a joke, I would think that the divine judgement should be implored, by the oracle of some revelation, with united prayer and with supplicating devotion and sighs, to determine whether the baptism so given should be approved." Thus far Augustine. In these words he professes that he does not dare to reject as baptism that which is given by anyone without faith, by anyone without faith, and that only in jest, as a mime and a joke. But he expressly affirms that, according to his opinion, those have baptism who have received it wherever and from whomsoever, consecrated with the words of the Gospel. Therefore, according to his most sober opinion, the mystical washing, seriously given and with the due words, is not to be repeated after a woman, nor after anyone whatsoever.

units.la: 15. Succedunt minoris ordinis, succenturiati milites, similia suffragia perhibentes, praesertim è Gratiano. Isidorus primo. {g}Romanus Pontifex non hominem, judicat, qui baptizat, sed spiritum Dei subministrare gratiam Baptismi, licet Paganus sit, qui baptizat. Secundo, Nicolaus Papa, ad consulta Bulgaro-rum respondens: A {h}quodam Judaeo, nescitis, utrum Christiano, an Pagano, multos in patria vestra, baptizatos asseritis, & quid inde sit agendum, consulitis. Hi profecto, si in nomine sancta Trinitatis, vel tantum in nomine Christi baptizati sunt, quia non illorum, sed eius est, rebaptizari non debent. Et Gratianus ipse, {i}Ecce quan-doque ab Haereticis, Baptisma, cum sua virtute accipitur, cuius tam[?]en necessaria administratio est, ut nec etiam à Paganis datum, possit reiterari. Quorum ego recenseo testimonia, nō quod ex eorū judicio, diiudicandam esse lite arbitrer: (tanti enim ipsos non facio) sed ut & antiquorum, & recentiorum, & Pontificiorum consensum, in re isthac, patefaciam. Cui etiam, & calculum, nostra adiicit suum, Ecclesia; quae cum, facilitate larga (ita etenim appellare licet, si ad laicorum & foeminarum Baptismum extendatur, quod negari, supra docui) propter cordis duritiam, aut plebis ignorantiam, priuatam tinctionem, ad tempus tolerasset, tolerasset inquam (puto sane paulisper tantum) quoad populus copiosius instruere-tur: hanc tandem fert sententiam. Nec dubitet quisquam, quin infantulus eo modo baptizatus, & legitime, & sufficienter baptizetur, neque debeat in templo rebaptizari. Haec eorum erat sanctorum virorum determinatio; qui (vt humana passa est infirmitas, & ferebant illa tempora) superstitioni Papisticae amouendae, & diuini cultus officiis propagandis, insudarunt; & quorum aliquot, suo sanguine veritatem Christi postea confignarunt.
units.tr: 15. There follow, as reserve troops of lesser rank, soldiers supporting similar opinions, especially from Gratian. Isidore, in the first book: "The Roman Pontiff does not judge the man who baptizes, but the Spirit of God supplies the grace of baptism, even if the one who baptizes is a pagan." Second, Pope Nicholas, answering the consultations of the Bulgarians: "You state that many in your country have been baptized by a certain Jew, you do not know whether he was a Christian or a pagan, and you ask what ought to be done about it. Those indeed, if they were baptized in the name of the holy Trinity, or only in the name of Christ, ought not to be baptized again, because it is not theirs but His." And Gratian himself: "Behold, baptism is sometimes received from heretics with its power, whose administration is nevertheless so necessary that it cannot be repeated even if given by pagans." I recount these testimonies, not because I think the dispute is to be decided by their judgement (for I do not value them so highly), but in order to lay open the agreement, in this matter, of the ancients, the more recent writers, and the Papists. To this the Church, too, adds her own vote: she, who by a generous indulgence (for so it may be called, if it is extended to the baptism of laymen and women, which I have shown above should be denied), because of hardness of heart or ignorance of the people, had for a time tolerated private immersion, tolerated it, I say (I certainly think only for a little while), until the people might be more fully instructed, at length delivers this judgement: "Let no one doubt that a little child baptized in that way is both lawfully and sufficiently baptized, and ought not to be rebaptized in the church." This was the determination of those holy men who (as human weakness allows, and as those times bore it) laboured to remove Popish superstition and to propagate the duties of divine worship, and some of whom afterwards sealed the truth of Christ with their blood.

units.la: 16. Nostra etiam tempora, quantum ego noui, ab eorum determinatione non discesserunt, sed tanquam depositum apud nos, & traditum, custodiunt. Adiectio etenim elementi, & inuocatio Spiritus Sancti ea est, quam potissimum respiciunt, & non persona dantis: hoc autem, quoad Baptismi substantiam. Qua in re, vti ego existimo, sic se habet negotium, vt in generatione carnali: in regeneratione scilicet, vt in generatione. Baptizari etenim, est quasi in Ecclesiam generari. Et vt nil, sæpius quam semel generatur, ita decenter institutum fuit, vt nemo sæpius, quam semel baptizaretur. At vt in productione infantuli, & emissione in lucem, obstetriculæ opera, censetur necessaria, cuius manu, & consilio, ex vtero materno, incolumis, infantulus extrahatur, sic minister Euangelij, ad manum oportet, & præsto sit, quum ex labe originali, per aquam sanctificatam extrahitur, qui Adami corruptelis inuoluitur & irretitur. Euangelij minister, obstetricis locum, in renouatione & regeneratione sacramentali supplet. Verumtamen vt nonnunquam, id re ipsa contingit, / quod ficte, & simulate obstetrices Israelitiæ, Pharaoni renunciarunt; fœminas nempe aliquot, sic robustas esse, vt priusquam accesserit obstetrix, pepererint: aut çum præsto non fuerat, quæ debebat interesse, matrona alia vices supplet; & vicariam præstat operam: neque tamen non natum quisquam dixerit, qui iam in lucem prodierit: & pro stolido haberetur, qui infantulo, in uterum maternum, reuertendum diceret, quia defuit quæ adesset: Sic si in Ecclesiam generatus quisquam fuerit, per lauacrum regenerationis, licet eius id non fit factum, cuius debuisset, manu, immo licet peccauerit, & Deo displicuerit, qui manus per præsumptionem & ignorantiam iniecit: non redintegrandum tamen esse factum, & pietas, & ratio, & consensus Ecclesiæ, à quo temere recedendum non est, vehementer suadent. Et hoc nisi concedatur, incommoda infinita, per vniuersam fidelium congregationem, exorientur. Si etenim non sit quisquam, Christianis imbutus mysteriis, nisi qui per Sacerdotem, omni via legitimum, & exceptione maiorem, baptizaretur, quota hominum pars, piorum & fidelium, Christianismi signaculo indigerent? aut quis sciret pro certo, sea quis lustralibus, vt debuisset, fuisse expiatum? Sacerdotis etenim personam, induere potest, qui sacros nunquam est adeptus ordines. Sacros etiam ordines is potest recipere, qui necipse baptizatus, vnquam extiterat. Sed & qui baptizatur, & qui ad gradum ministerii promouetur, ab Episcopo poterit consecrari, & ad Presbyteratum admitti, qui nec ipse legitimus fuerat Episcopus, nec imponendi manus potestatem habuerat. Et hæc, huiusmodique, & posse, & solere, contingere dubia, prudentia, & ratio, & experientia, contestantur: vt nominatim, in rescripto {m}Nicolai Papæ ad consulta Bulgarorum: Et Canonici non friuole, aut ex suppositione, sed occasione data, hæc ipsa discutiunt: vt quæstionibus reuera & bona fide exorientibus occurratur.
units.tr: 16. In our own times, so far as I know, they have not departed from their determination, but keep it as a deposit entrusted to us. For they chiefly regard the addition of the element and the invocation of the Holy Spirit, and not the person of the giver; this, that is, as to the substance of baptism. In this matter, as I judge, the situation is as in carnal generation: in regeneration, namely, as in generation. For to be baptized is, as it were, to be born into the Church. And just as nothing is generated more than once, so it was rightly ordained that no one should be baptized more than once.
