But as in the bringing forth of a little child and its emission into the light, the work of a midwife is considered necessary, by whose hand and counsel the infant is drawn safely from the maternal womb, so the minister of the Gospel must be at hand and present when one who is wrapped and entangled in the corruptions of Adam is drawn out of original stain by sanctified water. The minister of the Gospel supplies the place of the midwife in the sacramental renewal and regeneration. Nevertheless, as sometimes happens in fact, what the Hebrew midwives reported to Pharaoh, feigned and pretended, namely that some women were so robust that they gave birth before the midwife arrived; or when the one who ought to be present was not there, another matron takes her place and performs the office in her stead; yet no one would say that the child was not born, since it had already come into the light; and he would be thought foolish who said the infant must be returned to the maternal womb because the one who ought to have been present was absent. So, if anyone has been born into the Church through the washing of regeneration, even though it was not done by the hand of the one whose hand it ought to have been, indeed even though he sinned and displeased God, who laid on hands through presumption and ignorance, nevertheless that it should not be repeated is strongly urged by piety, by reason, and by the consent of the Church, from which one must not rashly depart. And unless this is conceded, infinite inconveniences will arise throughout the whole congregation of the faithful. For if no one were imbued with the Christian mysteries except one who had been baptized by a priest, lawful in every way and beyond all exception, how small a part of men would be pious and faithful, and would need the seal of Christianity? Or who would know for certain whether someone had been purified by the lustral rite as he ought to have been? For a man may assume the person of a priest although he has never received holy orders. And a man may receive holy orders who was never himself baptized. But also, one who is baptized, and one who is promoted to the degree of ministry, may be consecrated by a bishop and admitted to the presbyterate, although he himself was not a lawful bishop and had not the power of laying on hands. And prudence, reason, and experience attest that these and similar doubts both can and do commonly arise; as, namely, in the rescript of Pope Nicholas to the consultations of the Bulgarians: "And the canons do not discuss these matters frivolously or by supposition, but on occasion given, so that questions which truly and in good faith arise may be met."

units.la: 17. Sic habetis doctissimi Academici, meam de facto hoc Tsipporæ, longam licet, apertam tamen sententiam; in qua explananda, vt & in aliis omnibus, quæ in his prælectionibus, aut dixerim, aut deinceps dicturus sim, si iudicium meum ab alieno dissenserit, det veniā, aliter sentiens. Sicuiquam[?] etenim, vel minimo seruorum Dei, reuelauerit aliter, e sacris literis, Spiritus Sanctus, non peruicaciter, aut peruerse renitar, sed gratulabundus, in illius, etiam pedibus ibo sententiam. Errare etenim possum, Hæreticus esse nolo. Quod autem senserim, esse Baptismum per laicum, aut fœminam, datum, facit perpetuata Ecclesiæ consensio, veritati diuinorum eloquiorum, quantum ego reperio, non repugnans. Et illius sum animi, cuius, est, doctissimus {n} Hieronymus Zanchius, in ea quæstione, Num temporalem iurisdictionem, & principatum, Episcopi & Archiepiscopi Ecclesiæ retinere debeant: multum nempe consensui doctorum & piorum, tribuendum esse, neque a recepta ab antiquioribus temporibus sententia recedendum esse; nisi vbi sacræ literæ, aut diserte, aut aperta, & necessaria collectione, contraria docent. Interea tamen ista sunt, quæ hodierna oratione accepistis, externo Sacramento, non sic astringi & alligari Dei gratiam, vt sine ipso saluare, aliquando nolit. Idcoque & diffidenter quoad Deum, & audacter quoad se, fœminas laicosque facere, qui baptizare aggrediuntur. Tertio tamen cum sigillum[?] sit impressum, vel ab istis, non esse iterandum. Det Deus, vt in veritate perpetuo ambulemus, vt ad gloriam cœlestem tandem perducamur, cum Christo regnaturi, cui cum Patre & Spiritu, sit laus, & gloria, in æternum.
units.tr: 17. Thus you have, most learned Academics, my opinion on this matter of Tsipporah, long indeed, yet open. In explaining it, as in all the other things which I have said or shall hereafter say in these lectures, if your judgement differs from mine, let it pardon me for thinking otherwise. For if the Holy Spirit should reveal to anyone, or to the least of God's servants, anything different from the sacred letters, I will not resist perversely or obstinately, but with rejoicing I will go even at his feet into that opinion. For I can err; I do not wish to be a heretic. That I have judged baptism given by a layman or a woman to be valid is supported by the perpetual consent of the Church, and, so far as I find, is not opposed to the truth of the divine oracles. And I am of the mind of that most learned man, Hieronymus Zanchius, in the question whether bishops and archbishops of the Church ought to retain temporal jurisdiction and principality: namely, that much weight must be given to the consent of learned and pious men, and that one must not depart from the opinion received from more ancient times, unless the sacred letters teach the contrary, either expressly or by a clear and necessary inference. Meanwhile, these are the things you have heard in today's discourse: that the grace of God is not so bound and tied to the external sacrament that it will sometimes refuse to save without it. Therefore women and laymen who undertake to baptize do so both diffidently as regards God and boldly as regards themselves. Yet, since the seal has been impressed, it is to be said that it ought not to be repeated by them. May God grant that we walk perpetually in truth, and that we are at last brought to heavenly glory, to reign with Christ, to whom with the Father and the Spirit be praise and glory for ever.

units.la: OBSERVATIO IN PARAGRAPHUM o capitis præcedentis.
units.tr: Observation on the paragraph of the preceding chapter.

units.la: MArtinus {o} Bucerus, vir accuratæ eruditionis, & pietatis singularis, dum distinctas enumerat Species, functionum Ecclesiasticarum, nonnullos dicit, in primæua & puriore riore Ecclesia, ex laicis, fuisse admissos, ad Sacrarum Scri-pturarum interpretationem, quaetiam aliquando, in prae-sentia Episcoporum, perfuncti sunt. {p}Origenem nominat & alios: tales scilicet, in quibus singulares Spiritus Sancti, dotes elucebant: ut manifestum esset, Ecclesiae rectori-bus, ipsorum operam, non mediocriter, populo, in myste-riis fidei ediscendis, profuturam. Cui si quis adiiciat, quod habet in Confessione sua, vir vere doctissimus {q}Hieronymus Zanchius, indefinite loquens: Credimus etiam per illos, administrandum esse sacrum Baptismum: per quos etiam Euangelium praedicatur: & ex eo, talem inferat conclusionem: licere ergo laicis Baptismum dare, etiam ex principiis nostris, & testimonio Christi, {r}profecti docete omnes gentes, baptizantes eos in nomen Patris, & Filii, & Spiritus Sancti: cum ex praxi purioris Ecclesiae, qui sacros non tetigissent ordines, Euangelium annunciarent: Respondemus, aliam habendam esse rationem eorum, qui simpliciter laici sunt, & ex ple-be promiscue sumpti: qualibus potestas, in Ecclesia Pontificia tribuitur, aquam Baptismalem aspergendi: & contra quos ista potissimum a nobis dirigitur controversia: Aliam autem eorum, qui sunt instar ministrorum Euangelii: quique non modo præ sua, in sacris rebus eruditio-ne, vulgus hominum longe excellunt, sed & speciali, aperto, & communi decreto, Episcopi & aliorum, qui congregationi præsunt, ad illud officium, Scripturæ publice interpretandæ, vocantur. Tales autem, & non alios, aperta Buceri verba norant: Alterum iam munus est, doctrinæ dispensandæ interpretatio: id est, verborum & sententiarum, simplicior explicatio. Hoc ministerium Episcopi obibant; & Presbyteri: nonnunquam tamen, ex ordine Diaconorum, atque Subdiaconorum. Aliquando etiam ex laicis, ad hanc adhibebant functionem, quos deprehendissent, per Spiritum Sanctum, ad eam utiliter obeundam, factos idoneos. Sic Origenes etiam laicus, ad hoc. ad hoc munus ascitus fuit, in Ecclesia Caesareae Palaestinae, per Alexandrum Episcopum Hierosolymitanum, & per Theoctistum, eiusdem Caesariensis Ecclesiae Episcopum, & quae sequuntur. Istos ego non audeo, ad ordinariorum, & vulgarium laicorum, conditiones revocare, cum ad Presbyteros tam prope accedant. Tales autem hodie, prae multitudine ministrorum, in templo Dei inseruientium, vix reperiuntur. Annon tamen de istiusmodi laicis, sermo t Tertulliani & Hieronymi, laicis aliquando baptizare permittentium, intelligendus sit, & non de aliis; doctorum sit iudicium.
units.tr: Martin Bucer, a man of accurate learning and singular piety, when he lists the distinct kinds of ecclesiastical functions, says that in the earliest and purest Church some laymen were admitted to the interpretation of the Holy Scriptures, and at times even performed this office in the presence of bishops. He names Origen and others: men, that is, in whom the singular gifts of the Holy Spirit shone forth, so that it was evident that their labour would be of no small benefit to the Church's rulers and to the people in learning the mysteries of the faith. If someone adds to this what the truly most learned Jerome Zanchius says in his Confession, speaking indefinitely: We believe that holy Baptism is also to be administered by those through whom the Gospel is preached; and from this infers the conclusion that laymen may therefore give Baptism, even on our principles and by the testimony of Christ, who sent forth [his disciples saying]: Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, since in the practice of the purer Church those who had not received holy orders proclaimed the Gospel: we reply that there is one reckoning to be made of those who are simply laymen and taken indiscriminately from the common people, to whom the power of sprinkling baptismal water is granted in the Papist Church, and against whom this controversy is chiefly directed by us; and another of those who are like ministers of the Gospel, and who not only far surpass the common sort of men in their learning in sacred matters, but are also called to that office of publicly interpreting Scripture by a special, open and common decree of the bishops and of the others who preside over the congregation. Such men, and no others, were what Bucer's plain words had in view: The interpretation of doctrine, that is, the simpler explanation of words and sentences, is now another office. Bishops performed this ministry, and presbyters; sometimes, however, men of the order of deacons and subdeacons. At times also, from among the laity, they admitted men to this function whom they had found, through the Holy Spirit, fitted to discharge it profitably. Thus Origen, though a layman, was taken up for this office in the Church of Caesarea in Palestine, by Alexander, bishop of Jerusalem, and by Theoctistus, bishop of the same Church of Caesarea, and what follows. I do not dare to reduce these men to the condition of ordinary laymen of the common sort, since they come so close to the presbyters. Yet such men are scarcely to be found today, because of the great number of ministers serving in the temple of God. Whether the words of Tertullian and Jerome, who allowed laymen at times to baptize, are to be understood of men of this kind and not of others, is for the learned to judge.
CHAPTER III. CONCERNING ASTROLOGY.

units.la: Iudic. 5. 20. E coelis pugnarunt: sidera ipsa, è suis aggeribus, pugnauerunt contra Sisaram.
units.tr: Judges 5:20. From heaven they fought: the stars themselves, from their courses, fought against Sisera.

units.la: 2. 5. Astrologi multorum cognitionem, sibi vendicant: 3. 4. Astronomiae dignitas. 7. Natiuitatum vanitas: 10. & Electionum, 12. & Quaesitorum. 14. 15. contra Astrologiam multa. 16. 17. Quae pro ea afferuntur, soluuntur.
units.tr: 2. The astrologers claim for themselves the knowledge of many things. 3. The dignity of astronomy. 7. The vanity of nativities; 10. and of elections; 12. and of questions. 14. 15. Many arguments against astrology. 16. 17. The arguments brought in its favour are answered.

units.la: ASTIGARE solet saepius, Ecclesiam suam, aeternus Deus, à praeceptis, studiisque sacris deuiantem. Flagellis, virgisque suis, pro calcaribus, quae ad bonum incitent, frenisque etiam, quae à peccato retrahant, uti consueuit. Quod, ut crebrum est, apud Deum, omni seculo; stante lege; vigente Euangelio: ita post Mosis, & Iosuae obitum, regentibus in Israele iudicibus, veritatem plus quam communem obtinuit. Cuius rei exemplan non pauca, cum facillimum sit percurrere, in eo potius uno, mea instabit oratio, de quo, Iudicum {a}quarto dicitur; perrexisse scilicet Israelitas, perperam praeque facere, ideo-
units.tr: Almighty God is accustomed to chastise his Church, very often, when it strays from his precepts and sacred pursuits. He uses his scourges and rods in place of spurs to urge it toward good, and also bridles to hold it back from sin. As this is frequent with God in every age, both while the law stands and while the Gospel flourishes, so after the death of Moses and Joshua, when judges governed Israel, it happened more often than usual. There are not a few examples of this, but since it is very easy to run through them, my discourse will dwell on that one alone, which is told in the fourth chapter of Judges: namely, that the Israelites went on doing evil,

units.la: ideoque Iehovam dedisse, vel vendidisse magis, ipsos, in manus Iabin, Regis Canaan, cuius militiae praefectus, erat Sisa-ra; potentiaque eousque tremenda, ut praeter caetera belli instrumenta, nongentos haberet currus ferratos. Hic, cum per annos viginti, Dei populo, omni modo fuisset formida-bilis, incursando, rapiendo, vndiquaque vexando; commo-ta sunt Deo viscera, ut misericordiam ostenderet, & ut, (satis poenarum exactum cogitans) benigniore oculo, ipsos respiceret. Insigni igitur clade, Canaanitas percussit; currus ferreos dissipavit; exercitum cecidit; ducem Sisaram in fugam vertit; qui turpi modo, & illius ex parte, dedecorosa, foeminea manu interiit. Ita erat admirabilis in suis; formidabilis in hostibus, Iehova, Deborah & Barak, quorum auspiciis, proximo post Deum loco, ista parta est victoria; ne peringratitudinem, tanti beneficij, immemores duceren-tur; siqueindigni, qui reciperent; Hymno, Psalmove, ex propositio, edito, datorem victoriae, Dominum collaudarunt; & in perpetuam rei memoriam, Canticum illud suum, posteritati commendarunt. Cuius serie, sicut multas rei gestae circumstantias, describerunt; ita e coelis, contra Sisaram, exercitumque suum, pugnatum fuisse; ipsaque sidera, ex aggeribus suis, adversus eos dimicasse, contestantur. Quo sermone, quid significatum habeamus, non inutile est disquirere.
units.tr: and therefore Jehovah handed them over, or rather sold them, into the hands of Jabin, king of Canaan, whose army was commanded by Sisera. He was so formidable in power that, besides his other instruments of war, he had nine hundred iron chariots. For twenty years he had been a constant terror to the people of God, attacking, plundering and harassing them in every way. Then God's bowels were moved, so that he showed mercy, and, thinking that enough punishment had been exacted, looked upon them with a kinder eye. Therefore he struck the Canaanites with a notable defeat: he shattered the iron chariots, cut down the army, and turned the leader Sisera to flight, who died in a shameful manner and, in part, by a disgraceful hand, that of a woman. Thus Jehovah was wonderful toward his own people and formidable toward his enemies. Deborah and Barak, under whose auspices this victory was won, held second place after God, so that the people, forgetful of the ingratitude owed for so great a benefit, should not be deemed unworthy to receive it, published a hymn or psalm for the occasion and praised the Lord, the giver of the victory, and, for the perpetual memory of the event, they commended that song of theirs to posterity. In its course they described many circumstances of the deed, and they also testify that the battle against Sisera and his army was fought from heaven, and that the stars themselves, from their courses, fought against them. It is not useless to inquire what we are to understand by this expression.

units.la: 2. Astrologi Iudiciarij, ita etenim frequenti vocabulo, libet appellare, quos Chaldaeos antiqui; Mathesim callen-tet, noui nuncupant, infinitam fere, & illimitatam sideribus, planetisque, potentiam tribuunt: ut, quorum virtute, secre-taq; influentia, quae geruntur ferme omnia in terris, disponantur, & dirigantur. Hinc praedici arbitrantur, futura grandia, seditiones, pestes, bella, inundationes aquarum, Regnorum, & Monarchiarum erectiones, translationes, dissolutiones: ex ipsorum instigatione, & impulsione abdita, in pugnas protrudi homines, adeoq;, inter præliandum, his læta, illis infausta contingere. E cœli schemate iudicium faciunt, quibus, quisque nuper natus, moribus futurus sit; qua con-ditione sit victurus; tenui, an beata; num placidis Musarum studiis, aut ferocioribus belli muniis, animum sit adiun&tu-rus. Quousque vitæ stamen, producendum sit: num flo-renti ætate, sit moriendum, an decrepita: & num spiritus, violento interitu, aut naturali obitu, sit emittendus. Hæc ipsa, penes sidera esse, vt aliis docere cupiunt medijs, sic & sanctissimis sacræ Scripturæ testimoniis, sua dogmata suf-fulcire non verentur. E Genesi, {b}sint luminaria, in Firma-mento cœli, & sint in signa, & tempora, & dies, & annos. Et, {c}So-lem, & Lunam, & Sidera, creauit Dominus, Deus tuus, in mini-sterium cunctis gentibus, quæ sub cœlo sunt. Et {d}Magi, ad Christum adorandum venerunt, è stella edocti. Nullo tamen testimonio, difertius edito, quam isto; vbi plenoore, Prophetissa conclamat, contra hostes, cœlos & stellas, pugnam exercuisse; acsi diceretur; maligno aspectu, ipsos Planetas, Sidaram fuisse intuitos; & non modo ei, infortunium prædixisse, sed & effecisse. Et sane {e}Franciscus Valesius, cum Astrologiæ vniuersæ, rationem cribare, & ventilare, in animo habuisset; in suo, quem de sacra Philosophia, libro conscripsit, hunc potissimum contextum seligendum censuit; (in quo, rei totius, faceret periculum) tanquam specie tenus, apertissime pro ipsis facientem. Cuius sane vestigia, vt à longe stans, obseruare non recuso; ita nolo premere, sed aliquanto copiosius, meam sententiam explicare.
units.tr: 2. The judicial astrologers (for so we may call them by a common term), whom the ancients called Chaldeans and the moderns call the practitioners of the mathematical arts, attribute an almost infinite and unlimited power to the stars and planets, so that by their virtue and hidden influence nearly all things that happen on earth are arranged and directed. From this they suppose that great future events can be foretold: seditions, pestilences, wars, floods of waters, the rise, transfer and dissolution of kingdoms and monarchies; that by their secret instigation and impulse men are driven into battles, and that, in the course of fighting, some things turn out fortunately and others unfortunately. From the configuration of the heavens they make a judgment about what character each person born recently will have, under what condition he will live, whether humble or blessed, and whether he will apply his mind to the gentle studies of the Muses or to the fiercer duties of war. They judge how long the thread of life is to be extended, whether one must die in the flower of age or in decrepitude, and whether the spirit is to be sent forth by a violent destruction or by a natural death. These very things, they say, lie in the power of the stars, as they wish to teach others by the same means; and they do not hesitate to support their doctrines by the most holy testimonies of Holy Scripture. From Genesis: let there be lights in the firmament of heaven, and let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and for years. And: the Lord your God created the sun, the moon and the stars to be a ministry for all nations which are under heaven. And: the Magi came to adore Christ, instructed by a star. Yet no testimony is set forth more plainly than this one, where the prophetess cries out that the heavens and stars fought a battle against the enemies: as if it were said that the planets themselves, with a malign aspect, looked upon Sisera, and not only foretold misfortune for him but also brought it about. Indeed Francisco Valesio, when he had intended to sift and examine the whole reasoning of astrology, in the book he wrote on sacred philosophy thought this passage especially worth selecting, as one which would put the whole matter to the test, because it seemed, at first sight, to favour them most openly. I do not refuse to follow his footsteps, standing at a distance; but I do not wish to press the matter, and I will explain my own opinion somewhat more fully.

units.la: 3. Luculentus igitur, proculdubio est Astrorum vsus, tum ad Dei gloriam prædicandam, tum ad communem nostram vitam. {f}Cæli enarrant gloriam Dei; & opera manuum eius, annunciat Firmamentum. Diem, superiora corpora, discriminant, & noctem; Æstatem, & Hyemem; Ver, & Autumnum, Operationum Lunæ, certa sunt experimenta, in sua illam Oppositione, (cum pleno, per Solis adversos ra-dios, imbuatur lumine) humidioribus magis dominari; me-dullam in ossibus; in cranio cerebrum, extenuare, & rarefa-cere; pure, sanieque ampliore, & exuberantiore, vulnera in-ficere; plantis, & latis, humore, pro alimento indigentibus, copiosius nutrimentum praebere: in aestum pleniorem, flu-xum scilicet, & refluxum, accessum, recessumque insignio-rem, & magis notabilem, Oceani undas commouere. Solis radij, virore terram, vigore animantia, exhilarant: aestiuam producunt siccitatem; aerem immutant; humanaque cor-pora, humoribus afficiunt, e quibus etiam animus, magis morosus fit; naturali tamen, & aperta ratione; quando pro-pter commercium, & coniunctionem tam intimam, ani-ma, & caro, se mutuo delectentur; istius laetitia, illi gaudium adferat; tristitia, dolorem. Ista tamen, alia extrinsecus acqui-sita, in humano corpore, possint efficere. Indubitatum est a-pud Medicos, Epilepticos, aut Morbo Comitiali affectos, Luna plena, aut inchoante, citius cadere. Compertum est ni-mio, (uti ipsis videtur) suo malo, apud valetudinarios: quod Canicula apparete, urentes febres, morbiq; acutissimi graf-sentur. Quid quod pestis, si omnino invaluerit, tum potissi-mum, saeviat, atque furat? Quid quod tum canes, in rabiem crebrius impellantur? Omnē igitur virtute, syderibus nega-re, est aperto sensui & rationi refragari; quibus repugnat, ne-mo sobrius. Etiamsi id liceat, in praesenti submonere; doceri ista non posse ἀποδεικτικῶς, & Demonstratione, à priori data, ut probe g Melanthon, & Astrologorum ingenui maxime; con-fitentur, sed ab affectibus, & observatis, quae quotidie occur-runt, & in quibus, Dei honor, non mediocriter elucescit.
units.tr: 3. Clearly, then, the use of the stars is splendid, both for proclaiming the glory of God and for our common life. The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament shows forth the work of his hands. The heavenly bodies distinguish day and night, summer and winter, spring and autumn. As for the operations of the moon, there are certain experiments: that when it is full, and imbued with light through the opposing rays of the sun, it holds greater sway over moist things; that it thins and rarefies the marrow in the bones and the brain in the skull; that it infects wounds with a greater and more abundant pus and ichor; that it supplies more copious nourishment to plants and to such things as need moisture for food; and that it stirs the waves of the ocean into a fuller tide, that is, a more notable flow and ebb, approach and recession. The rays of the sun gladden the earth with greenness and animals with vigour; they produce dry summer heat, alter the air, and affect human bodies with their humours, from which the mind also becomes more peevish; yet this happens in a natural and open way, since body and soul, by their commerce and so intimate a union, delight in each other, so that the joy of the one brings gladness to the other and sadness brings pain. Other things, acquired from outside, can of course produce such effects in the human body. Physicians are agreed that epileptics, or those afflicted with the falling sickness, fall more quickly when the moon is full or waxing. It has been found, to the great harm (as it seems to them) of invalids, that when the Dog Star appears, burning fevers and very sharp diseases rage. And what of the plague, when it has fully taken hold: does it not then rage and rob most of all? And what of the fact that dogs are then more often driven to madness? To deny all virtue to the stars is therefore to resist plain sense and reason, which no sober man opposes. Even if it is permitted, at this point, to remind the reader that these things cannot be taught demonstratively, by a demonstration drawn from a priori causes, as Melanchthon and the most ingenuous of the astrologers themselves freely confess, they are nonetheless taught from experiences and observations which occur daily, and in which the honour of God shines forth not a little.

units.la: 4. Si velimus pergere, de Oppositionibus & Coniunctionibus Planetarum, verissima est scientia. De Eclipsibus, & defectu Orbium lumine, nec iniucunda est cognitio, nec inutilis, & indubitatae, de istis, traduntur regulae. Neq; quid-quam quam potest esse certius, quam quæ de motu cœli habentur; & iis omnibus, quæ prædictiones sunt, circa propriam ipsius materiam. Ipse Firmamenti conspectus, quam pias, de Deo meditationes, & contemplationes suggerit? Qui præ infinita sua sapientia & potentia, tot lampadas, eo ordine, gradu, decore, collocatas, constituere voluerat. Quibus, ut apud Ethnicos, Gentiles, pro similitudine imaginum, nomina confinxerunt, Coronæ, Aræ, & similium, ita non improbat Deus, sed nostræ, sub similibus, Hebraice, appellationibus, considerationi proponit; ut ex quibus, Creatoris maiestatē, æstimare valeamus. Hinc apud Iobum: {h}Qui fa-cit {i} Arcturum, & {k}Oriona, & {l}Pleiadas, & interiora Austri. Et: {m}Spiritu suo, cœlos ornauit, formauit manus eius, serpentem oblon-gum. Et: {n}An constringes delicias Pleiadum, aut lora Orionis dissolues? E ducesne remotiora signa, quod& tempore suo? aut Arcturum cum filiis suis, duces? Ita apud Hamosum: {o}Opificem Pleiadum, & Orionis; qui & mutat in matutinum, densissimam umbram, & diem noctem obtenebrat. In quibus omnibus, primo manifestum est, Deum, tanquam aliquid gloriæ suæ ducere, quod ista, & hoc ordine, creauerit: Secundo, quod signa isthæc, & Aste-rismos, à nobis sciri voluerit, & obseruari; quo fœcundius, eius magnitudinem admiremur: & Tertio, in exortu nonnullorum siderum, suauiora nobis impertiri, quam alias: ut, in ortu Pleiadum, quæ nobis Vergiliæ dictæ sunt, quæque Vere exoriuntur, & usque ad Autumnum durant; quarum, cum mentionem faceret, suauitatem, quam orbi inferiori afferunt, delicias Pleiadum, nuncupauit. Qui ista dicimus, Astrorum cognitionis, omnem usum non tollimus; imo absit, ut tollere conaremur, sed Astronomiæ præcepta isthæc, accipimus, colimus, obseruamus, in honore habemus, ipsamque scientiam, dignam esse, quæ cum cæteris, veris Mathematicis, honoretur artibus, pronunciamus. Neque dubitamus, quin ut {p}Moses aliquando, testante Stephano Pro-tomartomartyre[?], in omni Ægyptiorum eruditione, fuerat in-stitutus, ( vbi, non minima pars, præter Arithmeticam, & Musicam, & Geometriam, & Hieroglyphica, erat A-stronomia,) & vt {q}Daniel in doctrina Chaldæorum, fue-rat educatus; sic & adolescentes nostri, & hominum Chri-stianorum liberi, ad Philosophiæ, Cosmographiæ, Medici-næ, Navigationis vsum, & ad sacrarum literarum, alicubi intellectum, in istis honeste doceantur, & informentur, mo-do semper illis in memoriam reuocetur, Conditorē Deum cogitare, illi omnia adscribere, eum solum adorare, & stul-titiis, ludicrisque aliis, vltra sobrietatem, sese non contami-nare. Est modus in rebus.
units.tr: 4. If we wish to go on, the knowledge of the oppositions and conjunctions of the planets is most true. The knowledge of eclipses, and of the failure of the orbs to give light, is neither unpleasant nor useless, and certain rules are handed down about these things. Nor can anything be more certain than what is held concerning the motion of the heavens, and all those things which are predictions with regard to their own proper matter. What pious meditations and contemplations of God does the very sight of the firmament suggest? He, in his infinite wisdom and power, willed to set up so many lamps, placed in such order, degree and beauty. Just as the Gentiles, by a likeness to images, invented names for them, such as the Crown, the Altar and the like, so God does not disapprove, but sets them before our consideration under similar appellations in Hebrew, so that from them we may be able to estimate the majesty of the Creator. Hence in Job: He who makes Arcturus, and Orion, and the Pleiades, and the inner parts of the south. And: By his Spirit he adorned the heavens; his hand formed the twisting serpent. And: Can you bind the sweet influences of the Pleiades, or loose the bands of Orion? Can you bring forth the remote signs in their season? Or can you guide Arcturus with his sons? Likewise in Amos: the maker of the Pleiades and of Orion, who turns the deepest shadow into the morning and darkens the day into night. In all these passages, first, it is plain that God counts it a part of his glory that he created these things and in this order. Second, that he willed these signs and constellations to be known and observed by us, so that we might admire his greatness the more fruitfully. And third, that at the rising of some stars he bestows on us sweeter gifts than at others: as at the rising of the Pleiades, which are called the Vergiliae by us, which rise in spring and last until autumn, and of whose sweetness, which they bring to the lower world, he made mention when he called them the delights of the Pleiades. In saying these things we do not abolish all use of the knowledge of the stars; far from it, we would not attempt to abolish it. Rather we accept these precepts of astronomy, cultivate them, observe them, hold them in honour, and declare that this science deserves to be honoured together with the other true mathematical arts. Nor do we doubt that, as Moses was once instructed in all the learning of the Egyptians (in which astronomy, along with arithmetic, music, geometry and hieroglyphics, formed no small part), as testified by Stephen, the first martyr, and as Daniel was educated in the teaching of the Chaldeans, so also our young people and the children of Christian men may honestly be taught and trained in these studies for the use of philosophy, cosmography, medicine and navigation, and for some understanding of the sacred letters, provided that it is always brought to their memory to think of God as Creator, to ascribe all things to him, to worship him alone, and not to defile themselves with follies and frivolous pursuits beyond sobriety. There is a measure in all things.

units.la: §. Verum eousq;, in nonnullis, humana processit curiositas, vt intra istos limites, se nequeant continere; siqueque ei, quæ in se est egregia, Astronomiæ, labes, maculasque asper-ferunt: iuxta illud, literati, vt sua ferebant tempora, Sarisburiensis, De nugis Curialium, {r} Est Astronomia, nobilis, & gloriosa scientia, si clientelam suam, intra moderationis metas, cohi-beat, quam si licentiori vanitate, excedat, non tam Philosophiæ spe-cies, quam impietatis decipula est. Ista qui sic abutuntur, ex eo-rum numero sunt, qui vanitatibus attendunt, & inuigilant, vt est apud Jonam: aut {t}qui curiosas exercent artes, vt illi, qui libros suos combusserunt, qui omnem scrutantur motum, & actionem, ex sideribus, qui mores animi inde exquirunt, qui fatali quasi, creaturarum necessitate, res dirigi arbitrantur: qui cœlum serenum, nubilumque, ante annum, & annos, quouis die futurum prædicunt: qui omnium rerum scientiam venditant; vt {u}Chaldæi, Magi, Astrologi, illi, qui Somniorum coniectores, & interpretes, haberi voluerunt. Et mirum sane est, quousque affectus, & desideria, hominum non malorum, sed proborum & ingenuorum, præsertim vero iuniorum (senioribus etenim expertis, ista fordescunt & vilescunt magis) ad talia exardescant; dum non animo prauo, sed curiositate otiosa ducti; & inordinata sciendi cupidine, quę titillat, alleċti, in his, operam non tam ponant, quam ludant. Quibus id, tāquam laboris merces, nonnunquam contingit, vt non aliis, magis quam sibi, præ credulitate animi, imponant. Quod mirandum nō est, cum, qui summi, in hoc genere, impostores sunt, non alios, magis quam seipsos, imaginationibus suis, circumueniant; eo sane miserandi, vtcunque alias, non fouendi. Horum quidem optimi, id est, modestissimi, & temperantissimi, audacter non pronunciant. Non possunt rationibus, aut argumentis concludentibus, nostra patefieri proposita, sed exemplis, & compertis. Inclinant Astra, non necessitant. Sapiens dominabitur Astris. Astrologorum decreta, nō sunt Præto-ria. {x}Magna certe est veritas, & fortissima. Fidem illi, suis thesibus, & dictatis subtrahendo, vel certitudinem minuendo & extenuando, caliginem, tenebras, alienis oculis, excutiūt. Hoc istorum modo, cœlis inhiare, & futura desiderare, neq; cum ratione, neque etiam cum pietate, est coniunctum.
units.tr: Yet in some men human curiosity has advanced so far that they cannot keep themselves within these limits; and they bring stains and blemishes upon Astronomy, which in itself is an excellent science. Hence that saying of the learned men of their own times, from Sarisburiensis, On the Trifles of Courtiers: Astronomy is a noble and glorious science, if it keeps its clientele within the bounds of moderation; but if it exceeds these with a more licentious vanity, it is not so much a species of philosophy as a snare of impiety. Those who abuse it in this way belong to the number of those who attend to vanities and keep watch on them, as is said in Jonah; or of those who practise curious arts, like those who burned their books; who investigate every motion and action from the stars, who seek from them the dispositions of the mind, who think that things are directed by a kind of fatal necessity of creatures; who predict a clear or cloudy sky a year or years ahead, or any day in the future; who peddle knowledge of all things, as the Chaldeans, Magi, and Astrologers did, and those who wished to be regarded as interpreters and interpreters of dreams. And it is truly astonishing how far the desires and longings of men who are not wicked, but upright and well-born, and especially of the young (for the older, who have experience, grow more disgusted and contemptuous of such things), flare up towards such matters; while, led by idle curiosity and enticed by the tickling desire for knowledge without order, they devote themselves to these things not so much with effort as with play. For them, as a kind of reward for their labour, it sometimes happens that, through credulity of mind, they deceive not others more than themselves. This is no matter for wonder, since those who are the greatest impostors in this kind are deceived by their own imaginations no less than others; they are indeed to be pitied in this respect, though not otherwise to be encouraged. Of these, the best, that is, the most moderate and temperate, do not boldly pronounce. They cannot have our propositions made clear by reasons or conclusive arguments, but only by examples and observations. The stars incline, they do not necessitate. The wise man will rule over the stars. The decrees of astrologers are not binding. Truth is certainly great and very strong. By withdrawing faith from their theses and dictates, or by diminishing and weakening their certainty, they shake off the fog and darkness from other people's eyes. In this manner, to gape at the heavens and desire the future is joined neither with reason nor with piety.

units.la: 6. Dei nomine, propheta Jeremias loquitur: {γ} Incidere in viam gentium istarum ne discitote, & à signis cœlorum ne consternemini; nam statuta populorum, sunt vanitas. Annon Chaldaica, Babyloniaque figmenta isthæc, cum taxet Jehoua; veræ illi pietati, detrahere demonstrat? Et licet occurrat ei loco {γ} Philippus Melanēthon, (qui cum siderum spectator esset, vanitate tamen aliorum communi, supersedit) non prohibere Prophetam, eorum signorum obseruationem, sed metum: non quod non piis metuenda, sed quod non piis metuenda, quibus nil contingent, nisi ex diuina prouidentia, & quod patientia leuius fit, iuxta illud, {z}Ne timete vobis, ab iis qui occidunt corpus; non quia, hoc non fit meticulosum, sed quia repend Deus: Sic, ne metuite à signis cœli; non quia nihil sint, sed quia in iis, præseruabit Dominus: Tamē, vt pacerantivirī dixerim, sīgna cœli, nostro sensu, non obseruanda esse, da esse, ostendit Propheta, cum illic dixerat, Incidere in viam gentium istarum, ne discitote. Quarum gentium, nisi Orientalium? Chaldaicarum, Babyloniarum? Quæ statuta sunt vanitas, nisi quæ de Astrorum, & Signorum cœli abusu, tradebantur? Ethnicam igitur, id est, nimiam, & idololatricam, & superstitiosam, cœlestium speculationem interdicit Dominus. Sed quo pacto, apud Isaiam, deludit, & irridet Deus illa Chaldaica, & consequenter, eorundem usum improbat? Ad ipsam Babylonem, verba sunt: {a}Statiam[?], cum incantationi-bus tuis, & cum multitudine præstigiarum tuarum, in quibus labo-rasti à pueritia tua, si forte possis proficere: si forte præbebis te fortem. Defatisceris in multitudine consiliorum tuorum: Stent iam Astrologi, qui contemplantur stellas, qui notas faciunt in mensibus prædictiones suas, & seruent te ab iis, quæ superuenturæ sunt tibi. Quam amara, est hæc irrisio? Quam directè, prædictores istos feriens? Apud Danielem, {b}Astrologi cum Magis, & Diuinatoribus, & Chaldæis, è diametro quasi, Prophetæ, & Dei spiritui, opponuntur. Generale Christi est præceptum: {c}Ne solliciti estote, de crastino: vbi cum cibum, vestitumque nomi-net, comprehendit omnia, ad humanam vitam conducen-tia. Sed scopus exhortationis, is est, ut de futuris, anxiè non perquiramus, quod agunt vehementer, qui Astrologicas prædictiones, in quâ multis consulunt. Cauendum ergo est, ne audacter, in secreta Dei irruamus; idq; nobis, sine scripturæ voce, sine regula, aut ratione arripiamus, quod futuri prævi-sor, & ordinator Deus, abditum esse voluit. Inspirationes Prophetarum, à Domino, ad res præsignificandas, excitato-rum, extenuamus, & leuiores facimus, si ex Astris, magna, multa, omnia, præuideri possint.
units.tr: 6. In the name of God the prophet Jeremiah speaks: Learn not the way of those nations, and be not dismayed at the signs of heaven; for the statutes of the peoples are vanity. Does he not, while rebuking these Chaldean and Babylonian fictions, show that they detract from true piety? And although Philip Melanchthon meets this passage (who, although he was himself an observer of the stars, nevertheless refrained from the vanity common to others) and holds that the Prophet does not forbid the observation of those signs but the fear of them: not because they are not to be feared by the pious, but because they are not to be feared by the pious, to whom nothing happens except by divine providence; and because it becomes lighter by patience, according to that saying, Fear not those who kill the body; not because this is not a cause of fear, but because God restrains it. So, be not afraid of the signs of heaven, not because they are nothing, but because the Lord will preserve you among them. Yet, to speak as honest men do, the Prophet shows that the signs of heaven are not to be observed in our sense, when he had said there, Learn not the way of those nations. Which nations, unless the Eastern ones, the Chaldean, the Babylonian? What statutes are vanity, unless those which were handed down concerning the abuse of the stars and the signs of heaven? Therefore the Lord forbids the heathen, that is, excessive, idolatrous and superstitious, contemplation of the heavenly bodies. But how, in Isaiah, does God mock and deride those Chaldean things, and consequently disapprove of their use? He speaks to Babylon itself: Stand now with your enchantments, and with the multitude of your sorceries, in which you have laboured from your youth, if perhaps you may profit, if perhaps you may prove strong. You are wearied in the multitude of your counsels. Let now the astrologers, who gaze at the stars, who make known their predictions month by month, stand and save you from those things which shall come upon you. How bitter is this mockery? How directly it strikes those predictors? In Daniel, astrologers are set against the Magi, the diviners and the Chaldeans, as if diametrically opposed to the Prophet and the Spirit of God. Christ's general command is: Be not anxious about tomorrow; where, when he names food and clothing, he comprehends all things that pertain to human life. But the aim of the exhortation is that we should not anxiously inquire into the future, which they do eagerly who consult astrological predictions. We must therefore take care not to rush boldly into the secrets of God, and not to seize upon what God, the foreseer and orderer of the future, has willed to be hidden, without the voice of Scripture, without rule or reason. We diminish and make lighter the inspirations of the prophets, which were stirred up by the Lord to foretell things, if great, many and all things can be foreseen from the stars.

units.la: 7: Sed vt supra, quid ex cœlis colligi possit, docuimus, (quibus illud addimus, quod virtutes fortassis, habét plures, & multas, sed quis scit, num has, & has? Et in isto, vel in illo? Et hodie, vel heri?) Sic, vt è fixo quasi loco, Astrologorum placita,oppugnemus; sermonemque nostrum, certis limi-tibus circumscribamus; quid in iis improbamus, & damna-mus;ostendendum est. Tria sunt,quorum indicium,è Sche-mate coelesti,se posse colligere,inspectores isti siderum, prae-se ferunt. Natiuitates,quas γενέσεις[?] appellant; Delectus, siue Electiones; & interrogationes, seu Quæsita[?]. In Natiuitati-bus, futuros mores, & fortunæ, in vita, morteque, conditio-nem, præfari spondent: In Electionibus,quis dies, huic ne-gotio, vt itineri capessendo, prælio conserendo, fundamen-to domicilij, aut ciuitatis, iaciendo, commodus fit, aut in-commodus: In Quæsitis, quis occideritliominem, quisab-lata furto subripuerit,cæteraque similia, se docere posse, ia-ctitant. Hæc tria damnamus, vt non minus Philosophiæ, & rectæ rationi, quam Diuino cultui aduersa. Et vt de γενεθλι-αλογία[?], primo dicatur loco; cur in rebus natis, actiones, quæ sunt voluntariæ, & voluntas ipsa, quæ quouis momento est mutabilis, à figura coeli pendèrent? Vnde super istam, quæ absolute spiritualis est, tam longe dissita, disiunctaque cor-pora, vim exercebunt: Neque omnino, in puncto tempo-ris, (quod oportet fieri) immutato corpore? Edicta princi-pum, multa iubentia, aut vetantia; auxilium opem seren-tium; impensæ, & facultates, quæ in rebus magnis sunt ne-cessariæ; instrumenta, & media operandi, magni sunt, ad quiduis, ponderis; & hæc tam extra nos, quam extra coe-los, sita sunt. Educatio, in vtramque partem, momentum habet: sic & societas, cui iungimur, quarum {d}vtramuis, piam esse, & sanctam præcepit Dominus; sed frustra, si ex Schemate superiorum corporum, sint metienda singula,
units.tr: 7. But, as above, we have taught what can be gathered from the heavens (to which we add that the powers perhaps have many and various effects, but who knows whether these and these? And in this or that? And today or yesterday?), so, from a fixed position as it were, we must now attack the opinions of the astrologers, bound our discourse within certain limits, and show what in them we disapprove and condemn. There are three things by the indication of which those observers of the stars claim that they can gather from the celestial figure: Nativities, which they call genethliacal [γενέσεις]; Choices, or Elections; and Interrogations, or Questions. In Nativities they promise to foretell future morals and fortune, and the condition in life and death; in Elections they boast that they can teach which day is favourable or unfavourable for this business, such as for beginning a journey, joining battle, or laying the foundation of a house or city; in Questions they boast that they can tell who killed a man, who has secretly stolen goods taken by theft, and other similar things. We condemn these three, as opposed no less to philosophy and right reason than to divine worship. And, to speak first of genethlialogy [γενεθλιαλογία], why should the actions that are voluntary, and the will itself, which is changeable at every moment, depend on the figure of the heavens in things that are born? How will they exert power over that which is wholly spiritual, bodies so far apart and disjoined, and that without the body being changed at the very point of time (which must happen)? The edicts of princes, commanding or forbidding many things; the help and aid that bring assistance; the expenses and resources which are necessary in great affairs; the instruments and means of acting, are of great weight for any purpose; and these lie as much outside us as outside the heavens. Education has weight in either direction; so too does the society to which we are joined, both of which the Lord commanded to be pious and holy; but in vain, if each thing is to be measured from the figure of the superior bodies.

units.la: Verum,quantam isti Deo faciunt iniuriam, qui cum ita spe-ciatim, se, nostra omnia, dirigere dixerit, vt nec {e}passer in terram cadat, nec crinis, capillusve vnus decidat, sine certa eius prouidentia; Astrorum motui, ista tamen tribuent, quæ licet ipsius sint creaturæ, talem tamen, tantamque vim, in rebus ad se immediate spectantibus, iis illum impertiuisse, unde constat? {f}Vtrius aquarum, sic animus Regis, est in manuleho-ua, quocunque vult, inclinat eum. Sed quantam blasphemiae occasionem, hominibus impiis tribuunt? qui si adulterio, homicidio, proditione, omnigena impuritate, sese conspurcâ-rint, in coelos, & ipsum Deum, rem omnem reiicient: ac si eorum operatione, & coactione, in vitia impellerentur, neque abstinere a malo potuissent. Nam praeter Originalem labem, cuius vitiositas, Adamo propaganti, referenda esset, instigatio quaedam, & incitatio, ab Astris proveniret.
units.tr: But how great an injury do those men do to God who, when he has said that he so specifically directs all our affairs that not a sparrow falls to the ground, nor a hair or a single lock falls, without his certain providence, nevertheless attribute to the motion of the stars these things, which, although they are creatures of his, yet—from what source is it known?—he has bestowed upon them such and so great a power over things that pertain to him immediately? As the waters are divided, so the heart of the king is in the hand of the Lord; wherever he wills, he turns it. But what an occasion of blasphemy do they give to impious men! For if they have defiled themselves with adultery, murder, treachery, and every kind of impurity, they will throw the whole matter upon the heavens and God himself: as if they were driven into vices by their operation and compulsion, and could not have abstained from evil. For apart from original stain, the vitiosity of which ought to be referred to Adam propagating it, a certain instigation and incitement would come from the stars.

units.la: 8. Quae ex his sequuntur, absurda alia, sunt infinita: quocumque aliquot, non verebor recensere; vt qui dicam, non minus apud homines Philosophos quâ Theologos. Et primo, quo pacto poterit Constellatio, in Nativitate fulgens, effectusper totam vitam, operari? Quid in causa futurû est, quod annus, & dies quilibet, suas non diriget actiones, æque atque ea vna, in ortu fulgens? Secundo, quo pacto vim suam, exercebunt coelestia corpora? an vt causæ; vel vt signa; vel vt aliud quidquam? At quid tandem, est illud aliud? Cur non nominatur? Signa si dixerint; at quid, precor, in causa propriè erit, cuius, ista sunt signa? Et id etiam proferatur. Si hæc, ipsæ causæ sint, at quo modo operantur? Per tactum? aut emissionem virtutis suæ? At quo pacto aer, qui medius est, ita immutatur, vt ad solum istum feratur, nec ad alium hominem? Cedo certam aliquam experientiam: deprome aliquid, cum ratione, & Philosophia, vel specie tenus coniunctum. Sed nulla ratio; nullus syllogismus; nullum argumentum. Tantummodo, nostris credendum est principiis. Tertio, cuius diei, Horoscopus intuendus est? num eius, qui fuerat Conceptionis? aut illius, qui est Nativitatis? In Conceptione, cum paterno, maternoq;, coniuncto semine, primordia geniti coalescunt; & abditæ, ab eo vsque momento, fouentur virtutes; quæ simul cum paterna, maternaque simililisimilitudine,& hæreditariis etiam morbis innatis,in Natiui-tatis hora,non immutantur; nec immutari valent. A Con-ceptione ergo (si alicunde) suffragatur ratio, sumedum[?] esse iudicium: idque fatetur{g} Haly,insignis Astrologus : efficacia scilicet,fati discernendi,esse in hora conceptus:sed quia hæc ignoretur,ad horam Natiuitatis, Astrologos confugi-se. Detrahunt suis Principiis,qui Natiuitatem, pro Conceptione capiunt; cuius Conceptionis, ex oriendi hora, impossibile est,ut ratio teneatur; dū septimestres, octimestres, nouimestres, imo decem mensum , aliqui sint partus, ut loquuntur Medici; nec post certam periodum completā, determinari potest Conceptionis hora, ex nascendi termino; præsertim cum parturientis robur,aut imbecillitas;sic&obstetricis peritia,aut imperitia,aliaq;quamplurima,partū accelerare,aut retardare cognoscantur. Quarto;incredibile est,ut exacta cœli Revolutio,capiatur;propter festinam suā, in mouendo celeritatem,quæ quibusuis momentis,&minutis temporum alterationem patitur, ex iplorum regulis, & irrefragabili veritate. Vel enim Astrolabium,exquisite nō erit perfectum; aut Mathematicus,eo usurus,paratus nō erit, aut nubes,stellas Soleve intercipient;aut fœmine intra conclaue, Astrologo deforis stanti,partum statim non significabunt: Cuius solius rationis si quis neruos,accurate velit considerare, si obstaret nihil aliud, exclamare tamen poterat,{h}Vanitas vanitatum, & omnia vanitas. Liceret ista persequi ulterius, ex Contradictoriis illorum Principiis; in quibus, cum nonnihil parentibus tribuant; dominanti sideri,pluri-ma:quo pacto,omnium,uno tempore nascentium, unum erit iudicium? ut si Mercurius omnes fures faciat, num parentes omnes generantes,similes erunt? Sed ne tædio sim; ad virorum doctissimorum censuram, volentes remitto. In quibus{i} Origenes,super Iosuam sic: Qui de Astrorum cursibus, vitas hominum,& gesta perquirunt; qui volatus avium,& cætera huiusmodi,quæ di,quæ in seculo prius obseruabantur, inquirunt, de Hiericho, anathe-ma inferunt, in Ecclesiam, & pollunt castra Domini, & vincifa-ciunt populum Dei. Alludit ad anathema Achani. Hic præter seueram, de istis censuram, aduertite, quod cum stulto augurio, & volatu auium, disciplinam hanc coniungat. Basilius magnus, qui initio {k}Hexæmeri, Astrologiam, vanitatem occupatissimam, & negotiosissimam appellauit; /postea ex {l}ipsis naturæ, & rationis, viscer-ibus; & ex Theologiæ, Chri-stianæque fidei præceptis, demonstrat, argumentis, eorum non dissimilibus, quæ iampridem recitaui; impossibile esse, ut de Natiuitate cuiusquam, Astrologorum quisquam, ve-ram ferat sententiam. Ambrosius, in suo {m}Hexæmero, ho-rum in Natiuitatibus coniiciendis, vanitatem, describit, examinat, confutat, irridendam proponit. Qui velit, consu-lat. Ego digito fontes designo.
units.tr: 8. What follows from these premises is an endless series of absurdities. I will not hesitate to list some of them, which will occur to philosophers no less than to theologians. And first, how can a constellation shining at birth have its effect through the whole of life? Why should a year or any given day not direct its actions just as much as that one constellation shining at the moment of birth? Second, by what means will the heavenly bodies exercise their power? As causes, or as signs, or as something else? But what, then, is that "something else"? Why is it not named? If they say signs, then what, I ask, will be properly the cause of which these are the signs? Let that also be stated. If they are themselves the causes, how do they operate? By touch, or by emitting their power? And how is the air between them so altered that it is carried to this one person alone and not to another? Give me some certain experience; produce something, either reasoned out with philosophy or at least joined to it in appearance. But there is no reason, no syllogism, no argument; there is only the bare demand that we believe their principles. Third, the horoscope of which day is to be observed: that of the conception, or that of the birth? At conception, when the seed of father and mother has come together, the first beginnings of the offspring coalesce, and the powers hidden in it from that moment on are nourished; these, together with the likeness of father and mother and the hereditary diseases born with the person, are not changed at the hour of birth, nor can they be changed. So if reason lends support to anything, it is to take the judgment from the conception; and the noted astrologer Haly admits this, that the efficacy of discerning fate lies in the hour of conception, but that since this is unknown, the astrologers have fled to the hour of birth. Those who take the birth in place of the conception undermine their own principles; for from the hour of birth it is impossible to fix the conception, since, as physicians say, there are births at seven months, eight months, nine months, and even ten months, and after a certain period has been completed the hour of conception cannot be determined from the moment of delivery, especially since it is known that the strength or weakness of the mother, the skill or unskill of the midwife, and very many other things either hasten or delay the birth. Fourth, it is incredible that the exact revolution of the heavens can be grasped, because of its swift motion, which undergoes alteration at every moment and minute of time, according to their own rules and undeniable truth. For either the astrolabe will not be perfectly exact, or the mathematician who is to use it will not be ready, or clouds will block the stars and the sun, or the women within the chamber will not announce the birth to the astrologer standing outside. If anyone wishes to weigh carefully the strength of this one argument alone, then even if nothing else stood in the way he could still cry out: "Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity." These points could be pursued further from the contradictions within their principles; for while they attribute something to the parents, they attribute very much to the ruling star. How, then, will there be one judgment for all who are born at one time? If Mercury makes all men thieves, will all the parents who beget them be alike? But lest I weary you, I refer those who wish to the judgment of the most learned men. Among them, Origen, on Joshua, says thus: "Those who inquire about the lives and deeds of men from the courses of the stars, who seek out the flight of birds and other such things which were formerly observed in the world, bring a curse upon Jericho and upon the Church, defile the camp of the Lord, and bind the people of God." He alludes to the curse of Achan. Here, besides his severe judgment of these practices, note that he joins this discipline with foolish augury and the flight of birds. Basil the Great, who at the beginning of his Hexaemeron called astrology a most busy and occupied vanity, afterwards demonstrates, from the very vitals of nature and reason, and from the precepts of theology and the Christian faith, by arguments not unlike those I recited a little while ago, that it is impossible for any of the astrologers to pronounce a true opinion about the birth of anyone. Ambrose, in his Hexaemeron, describes, examines and refutes the vanity of those who conjecture about births, and holds it up as worthy of ridicule. Whoever wishes may consult them. I point out the springs with my finger.

units.la: 9. At sicco, non possum pede, præterire, quid habeat in præsenti negotio, judiciosissimus {n}Augustinus; qui ex Ge-minorum partu, Mathematicorum, de Genesibus, pronun-ciationes euertit. Ex Geminis etenim, uterque, cum uno, eodemq; proseminentur tempore; minimumq; inter eorum Nati-uitates, intercedat spacij; dissimilibus fiunt corporibus, vulti-bus, animis, moribus, nec in ullis studiis, aut vitæ conditione consentiunt. In Esauo, & Jacob instantiâ perhibet; quorum ortus, ita cōiunctus fuerat,{o} ut ex utero, prodeunte Esauü calce tenuerit Jacob; ita ut ipsorum Constellationes, si voluisset omnino intueri, debuisset Mathematicus, ad eundem Horoscopum & eandem Lunam. Qui tamen unquam, fuerant dissimiliores? Hic infans hirsutissimus, & plus quam virilis; ille mollis & fœmineus: hic moribus rigidis, & inobsequiosis; ille placidis, & pacatis: ille seruitio, magnam peracturus vitæ partem; hic dominio: ille pastor; hic venator; & quod maximum fuerat, ille Deo dilectus; hic odiosus. Quis unquam hominum, ex eodem utero prodeuntes, è contrariis magis studiis, consunos vidit? Nec dispar est ratio, quoad gradus multos, in Ge-minis aliis aut Trigeminis. Quid obtrudet, in re tali, Astro-logorum chorus? Nigidius Figulus, insignis Mathematicus, {p}uti refert Augustinus, cū simili premeretur argumento, se, è salebris, seipsum, probe potuisse expedire, cogitabat. Ce-leritati Revolutionum, isthæc imputauit omnia, quæ cum tanta esset, & tā velox, ut ictu quasi oculi, diversum in cœlo, Schema proponeret, diversas infantibus qualitates poterat impertire. Licet igitur multocyus, puer puerum, ex utero se-quatur; cum tamen, non possit non modicum, intervenire intervallum, diversum erit, Geminorum fatum. Cum Revolutionum velocitatem, vellet describere, figulinam cepit rotam, quam, citissime cum fecisset circumuolui; penna in manum sumpta, atramēto repleta, quam velocissime pote-rat, circumgyratam rotam, atramento, semel, atq; iterū ne-tauit. Quæ utraq; licet, uno tanquam Nunc, & momento, infigerentur; cum staret tamen rota, distabant à se mutuo, longe puncta. Hinc, si in tantulo, inquit, corpore, motus ce-leritas, ictu oculi, diversitate tantam faciat, quantam pariet, intervallū, quod, inter partum Geminorum, cœlestia corpo-ra habuere. Ratione istius similitudinis, Nigidius ille, Nigi-dius Figulus appellatus est. Verū Augustt. rectè perpensò ar-gumento; suo, Nigidiū iugulat gladio, acutissimè colligens, quod si tanta sphærarū, & Revolutionū, sit celeritas; impos-sibile est homini, Astrorum inspectori, certam cœlorum fa-ciem, à qua petendum est iudicium, distinguere; ideoq; ra-tiones istas Figuli, æque esse fragiles, atque figulina vasa. Ni-hil sane doctius, nihil acutius, nihil verius, excogitari potest.
units.tr: 9. But I cannot pass by this matter without a word, for it bears on the present question: the most judicious Augustine, who from the birth of twins overturns the pronouncements of the mathematicians concerning nativities. For twins are both brought forth at one and the same time, and even if there is very little interval between their births, they turn out with dissimilar bodies, faces, souls and characters, and they agree in no pursuits or condition of life. He points to Esau and Jacob as an instance. Their birth was so closely joined that Jacob held on to Esau's heel as he came forth from the womb; so if the mathematician had wished to examine their constellations at all, he would have had to look at the same horoscope and the same moon. Yet were any men ever more unlike? The one was a most hairy infant, more than manly; the other was soft and womanish. The one had stern and unyielding manners; the other was gentle and peaceable. The one was destined to spend most of his life in servitude; the other in lordship. The one was a shepherd; the other a hunter; and, what mattered most, the one was beloved of God, the other hateful. Who has ever seen men born from the same womb pursue more opposite studies? Nor is the case different with regard to the many degrees of twins or triplets. What will the chorus of astrologers put forward in such a matter? Nigidius Figulus, a distinguished mathematician, as Augustine reports, when he was pressed by a similar argument, thought he could easily extricate himself from the difficulty. He ascribed all these things to the swiftness of the revolutions, which was so great and so rapid that, in the blink of an eye, it could present a different aspect in the heavens and so impart different qualities to the infants. Therefore, although a boy may follow a boy from the womb much more quickly, yet since a not inconsiderable interval must intervene, the fate of the twins will be different. When he wished to describe the speed of the revolutions, he took a potter's wheel, and when he had made it spin as quickly as possible, he took a pen, filled it with ink, and as swiftly as he could, marked the spinning wheel with ink, once and again. Although both marks were made, as it were, in one now and in one moment, yet while the wheel stood still, the points were far apart from each other. Hence, he says, if in so small a body the speed of motion in the blink of an eye makes such a difference as the interval between the birth of twins would produce in the heavenly bodies. By reason of this comparison, that Nigidius was called Nigidius Figulus. But Augustine, weighing the argument rightly, slays Nigidius with his own sword, most acutely concluding that if the speed of the spheres and revolutions is so great, it is impossible for a man who observes the stars to distinguish the certain aspect of the heavens, from which the judgment must be sought; and therefore those reasonings of the potter are just as fragile as potter's vessels. Truly nothing more learned, nothing more penetrating, nothing more true can be devised.

units.la: 10. Ita Genethliacos missos facimus, & ad Electiones tan-dem accedimus, quæ secundo, à nobis, damnantur loco. In istis, scrutanda docent tempora, & opportunitates; in qui-bus aggrediendaea sunt, quæ tanquam precij alicuius, appe-timus. Tali hora aut die, fausus futurus est aspectus: civita-tis,
units.tr: 10. So we have dispatched the casters of nativities, and at last we come to Elections, which we, in the second place, condemn. In these they teach that times and opportunities must be scrutinised, in which the things we desire as of some worth are to be undertaken. At such an hour or on such a day the aspect will be propitious for laying the foundations of a state or of a household, for entering into marriage, for setting out on a journey, or for joining battle under good omens. What is this other than snatching from God his immediate governance (by which he presides over every single act and thought), and handing it over to creatures?

units.la: {p} Aug. lib. 5. de ciuit. Dei. cap.3. tis, aut domicilij, fundamenta iacienda sunt: coniugium in-eundum est: capessendum iter: auspicato praelium cōserendum. Quid hoc aliud est, quam Deo immediatam suam gubernationē praeripere (qua singulis actibus & cogitatis praeest) & creaturis assignare? Miror sane, quod Mosi opportunitatem istam, ex Ægypto exeundi, è sideribus, non ostende-rit; praesertim Mosi, in iis actibus aut similibus versato. Miror quod Salomoni, felicem horam fundamenti Templi ponē-di; aut Nehemiae, muros Hierosolymis fabricādi & extruen-di, non commonstrārit. Atquam friuola isthæc? Quid hoc aliud est, quam dies, & menses, & tempora, superstitiose ob-seruare? Origenes in Exodum: {q}Dies, inquit, observare, & menses, & tempora, signa requirere, stellarum cursibus adhaerere, Ægyptius est langour: id est, malus Ægyptios, ista decere dicit, nō Christianos. Philippus {r}Melanchthon, Megnonen in {f}Deutero-nomio, appellari, vetarique dicit, qui superstitiose, certos dies eligunt, aut vitant. Et frequens, huius vocis, sensus {s}talis est, in sacris literis, aperte contra Electores istos faciens. In super-quam puerile hoc est, quam negotiis humanis aduersum, ei-que repugnans vocationi, in qua, quemque Deus constituit, vt vano tantum timore, ducti homines, aut spe inani pelle-cti, diem de die, otiose & intempestiue, parati alias, proferāt & protelent? {u}Quis observat ventum, non seminabit, in quis Salo-mon, & qui respicit ad densas nubes, non metet. Et Paulus: {x}Obser-vatis dies, & menses, & tempora, & annos. Vereor de vobis. {y}Augu-stinus Electiones istas, salte perstringit, & doctrinae Astrologorum, de Natiuitatibus, repugnare ostendit: sic: O stulti-siam singularem, eligitur dies, in quo ducenda fit vxor. Credo, prae-terea quia potest, in diem non bonum, nisi eligatur, incurri, & infeli-citer duci. Vbi est ergo, quod nascenti, iam sidera decreuerunt? An po-test homo quod ei iam constitutum est, diei electione mutare? Et sic pergit aperta euincens ratione, quod si magni casus, ex con-stitutione, in Natiuitate, fataliter praestituantur; non esse penes hominem, Electione sua, immutare. En quam si-bi subruunt isti, sua fundamenta?
units.tr: ...the foundations of a city or household are to be laid; marriage is to be entered upon; a journey is to be undertaken; a battle is to be joined under favourable auspices. What else is this than to snatch away from God his immediate governance (which presides over every single act and thought) and to assign it to creatures? I am truly surprised that the opportunity of leaving Egypt was not shown to Moses from the stars, especially since Moses was engaged in such acts or similar ones. I am surprised that Solomon was not shown the happy hour for laying the foundation of the Temple, or Nehemiah the hour for building and raising the walls of Jerusalem. And how frivolous these things are! What else is this than to observe days, months and times superstitiously? Origen, on Exodus: "To observe days," he says, "and months and times, to seek signs, to cling to the courses of the stars, is the Egyptian languor"; that is, he says, these things befit Egyptians, not Christians. Philip Melanchthon says that on Deuteronomy those who superstitiously choose or avoid certain days are called and forbidden to be "Megnonen" [μαγνῶν]. And the frequent sense of this word in Holy Scripture is of such a kind as clearly tells against these Electors. Moreover, how childish it is, and how opposed to human affairs and repugnant to the calling in which God has placed each one, that men, led only by vain fear or enticed by empty hope, should put off and postpone from day to day, idly and out of season, though otherwise ready! "He who observes the wind will not sow, and he who regards the dense clouds will not reap," says Solomon. And Paul: "You observe days, and months, and times, and years. I am afraid for you." Augustine at least assails these Elections and shows that they are contrary to the teaching of the astrologers about nativities, saying: "What singular folly: a day is chosen on which a wife is to be taken. I believe, moreover, that if no good day is chosen, one may fall into a bad day and be led unhappily. Where then is that which the stars have already decreed at birth? Can a man change by choosing a day what has already been settled for him?" And so he goes on, clearly proving by reason that if great events are fatally predetermined by the constellation at birth, it is not within man's power to change them by his own choice. See how these men undermine their own foundations!

units.la: II. Joannes {z}Picus de Mirandula, vir nobilissimus & ele-gantissimus, libros plures conscripsit (vti omnes nouimus) ex proposito, Astrologorum placita, cōuulsuros. De iis, {a}Hie-ronymus Sauanarola, Italus superiori seculo, doctissimus, sic testatur: Qui Pici Mirandulani, libros de Astrologia legerit, & intel-lexerit, neq; Astrologiam irrisserit, dignus ipse est, qui ab omnibus irri-deatur. Sed Picus ille, nobilissimus & eruditissimus, vt acerri-mā perhibet censurā de doctrina ista omni; vt exempli cau-sa: {b}Philosophos antiquorum seculorū, contempsisse potius, quam con-futasse Astrologiam (quod explicatius habet Sauanarola, sic, {c}Aristoteles & Plato, omnem tractantes Philosophiam, Astrolo-giam ne tetigerunt, neque mentionem eius fecerunt. Quam sane non omisissent, si secretum fuisset natura) ita de Electionibus lepide, prudenter tamen loquitur. {d}Quomodo Iupiter, si in nona cæli regione aspiciat, felix iter faceret? Num afflat hominem, aut equi ascensum, aut viam? Si hominem; tum etiam si non proficiscatur, loquia equi ascensio, quomodo cælum pluuia purgabit, aut viam furibus? Quid si plurium dierum iter sit? Num nouus quotidie Iupiter: Quo pacto, istis solide occurri possit, mea non percipit ratio. Sic de aliis suscipiendis, proferre liberet. Christiano igitur homini, vt ista stolidiora fugienda sunt, sic curandum est potissimum, vt pia, & honesta, & reipsa sibi salutaria, aggrediatur: tum precibus inuocandus est Deus summus, vt velit opem, auxiliumq; ferre, afflatuque suo benedicere. Si tempora nubila, pluuiaeq; occurrant tempestates, abstinendum in multis negotiis, suadet ratio, & sensus communis; sed ab isto, illoue Planeta pendere, aspectuque siderum, & miserum est, & superstitiosum, & stultum, cum ominosis illis Ethnicorum, ad Inferos amandandum.
units.tr: II. Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, a most noble and elegant man, wrote several books (as we all know) with the deliberate aim of overturning the opinions of the astrologers. Of these, Girolamo Savonarola, an Italian of the last century and a very learned man, bears witness: Whoever has read and understood the books of Pico of Mirandola on astrology, and has not ridiculed astrology, is himself worthy to be ridiculed by everyone. But that Pico, most noble and most learned, as he declares in his very sharp criticism of that whole doctrine, for example: the philosophers of the ancient centuries despised astrology rather than refuted it (which Savonarola states more fully, thus: Aristotle and Plato, in treating all of philosophy, did not touch on astrology, nor made any mention of it. Certainly they would not have passed it over, if it had been a secret of nature), so also speaks wittily, yet prudently, about elections: How would Jupiter, if he looked upon the ninth region of the heavens, make a fortunate journey? Does he inspire the man, or the ascent of the horse, or the road? If the man, then even if he does not set out, what of the ascent of the horse? How will the sky be cleansed of rain, or the road of thieves? What if the journey is of several days? Does Jupiter become new every day? By what method these things can be solidly met, my reason does not perceive. In the same way one may offer more on other matters to be undertaken. Therefore, for the Christian man, just as these more foolish things are to be avoided, so he must take the greatest care to undertake what is pious, honourable, and truly salutary for himself; then the highest God must be invoked with prayers, that he may will to bring help and aid, and bless with his breath. If cloudy weather and rainy storms should come, reason and common sense urge abstention from many undertakings; but to depend upon this or that planet, and upon the aspect of the stars, is both wretched, superstitious and foolish, and is to be consigned to the Underworld along with the ominous practices of the heathen.

units.la: 12. De Quaesitis, loco tertio, similiter censendum est, Si voluerit te Deus castigare, eoque, violentas prædonum manus, nus, aut furtiuos subtrahentis digitos: aut ægritudinem, aut (vt solemus appellare) immiserit: cur ad mala fugis media, vt vel personam suffurantis, aut morbi exitum, aut liberationis tempus agnoscas. Deus est, qui percutit; ad hunc recurre, solatium quæsiturus, Fœdum est, & indignum Christiano
units.tr: 12. Concerning the questions of the third place, the same judgment must be made: if God has willed to chastise you, whether by the violent hands of robbers, or the stealthy fingers of pickpockets, or has sent sickness, or (as we are accustomed to say) misfortune, why do you flee to the means of evil, so that you may learn the identity of the thief, the outcome of the illness, or the time of deliverance? It is God who strikes; have recourse to him, seeking consolation. It is foul and unworthy of a Christian
If I cannot bend the gods above, I will move Acheron.

units.la: {f}Saulis illud factum, altiore peccatorum gradu ponimus, quo Pythonissam consuluit, de prælij exitu aduersus Philistæos, Sic & {g}Ahaziæ illud, cum æger ex lapsu, è fenestra, ad Beelzebub Deum Ekron, consultū misit, de sanitate sua. At responsum Dei, eandem hodie & in istis; rationem habet, quā eo tempore: Annon Deus est in Israele: Idē est, ac si diceret: Quæcunque contingunt aduersa, à Deo contingunt: Nulla igitur refugii, aut incolumitatis media, inuestiganda sunt, quæ nō ipse præscripserit, Et in istis Quæsita, seu interrogationes istæ, annumerari possunt, quæ Deus, nullo modo præscripsit; imo celata voluit. In Rebus pub. quo hinc damna fluxerint, non facile est numerare: cū suggestiones impostorū, de periculis insequentib. nonnullos homines, meticulosos, & timidiores, perpetua vexari fecerit solicitudine, ne revera contingant: ficq; per metum luum, de Deo diffidentes, sibi mala accelerant, iuxta illud: {h}Quod formidat impius, id euenit ei. Dum etenim apud se, desperabundus subsidat iste impius nec mala ingruentia præoccupet; occasionem sibi perniciei accersit; idque nulla re magis, quam inimicos, & proditores excitando, qui vitā auferant: qui id, eo potius conantur, quādoquidē interitum, imminere ipsi, quē vellent occidere ex prædictionib. arbitrentur. Hoc q; multis Principib. necem attulit; in quibus nominatissimus, meretur esse, {i}pauidus Domitianus. Sed & quandoque efficitur, vt cum ex Astrologorum Tripode, Tyrannis aliquid, de successoribus suis, significatum fuerit, innocentes statim homines, sub suspicione
units.tr: We place the deed of Saul at a higher degree of sin, when he consulted the Pythoness about the outcome of the battle against the Philistines. So too with that of Ahaziah, when, sick from a fall through a window, he sent to consult Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron, about his health. But God's answer has the same reasoning today as it did then: Is there not a God in Israel? This is as if he said: whatever adverse things happen, they happen from God; therefore no means of escape or of safety are to be sought which he himself has not prescribed. And among these may be counted the questions or inquiries which God in no way prescribed, indeed wished to be hidden. In public affairs it is not easy to count how many losses have flowed from this: since the suggestions of impostors, concerning dangers that will follow, have caused some timid and fearful men to be perpetually troubled by anxiety, lest these things really come to pass; and thus through their own fear, distrusting God, they hasten evils upon themselves, according to that saying: What the impious man fears, that befalls him. For while this impious man sinks into despair within himself and does not anticipate the evils that are coming, he brings upon himself the occasion of ruin; and he does so chiefly by stirring up enemies and traitors who may take his life, who rather strive to do this, since they think, from the predictions, that destruction is impending upon themselves, whom they would wish to kill. This has brought death to many princes, among whom the most notable is the fearful Domitian. But it also sometimes happens that when something concerning their successors has been signified by the tripod of the astrologers, tyrants at once kill innocent men under suspicion

units.la: {e} Virgil. Æneid 7. cione occidant, vt quondam Valens, Romanus Imperator, cui cum Astrologi (id enim ex Philosophorum nomine, innuunt Sozomeni verba) aliqua prænunciâssent, de hære- de sibi successuro; tum multis nobilibus innocuis, tum sibi- ipsis, exitium procurârunt. Vnde recte meminit idem Au- thor, prædictiones eiusmodi, quas efferre solent hi artifices, à Romanis, interdictas fuisse legibus, etiam tum, cum Gen- tilem superstitionem professi, ad Christianam adhuc fidem, non accessissent.
units.tr: {e} Virgil, Aeneid 7. ...kill them, as once did Valens, the Roman emperor, to whom, when the astrologers (for by the name of philosophers, the words of Sozomen indicate them) had foretold something about the heir who would succeed him, they brought ruin both upon many innocent nobles and upon themselves. Hence the same author rightly recalls that predictions of this kind, which these practitioners are accustomed to publish, were forbidden by Roman laws, even at the time when they professed heathen superstition and had not yet come to the Christian faith.

units.la: 15. Et in causis aliquibus, lege / etiam, apud nos vetatur, talis inquisitio: præsertim vero in negotiis, ad summum Ma- giftratum, Regnum, & Kemp, spectantibus. Pie sane, & pru- denter, & merito. Nec incommodum fuisset, si in his vulga- ribus Interrogatis, de furto, & iactura prohiberetur, cum hic, nugiuendulum hoc hominum genus, ridicula tantum im- postura, homines capiat; reos, notis insignioribus, describe- do, quæ vix vllibi reperiri possint. Vt: sustulit vir, obliquis o- culis, obstipo capite, dentibus prominentioribus, & perperâ diffpositis, diuaricatis cruribus, distortis pedibus, aliisq;, quæ homini non ineptienti, stomachum movere possint. Neq; tamen adhuc, sollicita, & curiosa mortalium dementia, o- mnino, iis fidem derogauit. Sed præualebit tandem pruden- tia, experientia, & suum malum, vt vlterius non consulant; aut si ista non valebunt, præualebit pietas, vti Iperandum est, cui ista aduersantur: idque ex eorum testimonio, qui plus multo, quam eruditiorum hominum magna pars, tri- buunt Astrologiæ. Nam vt contentus sim Melanƈthonis iu- dicio, de Electionibus, supra citato, audite Christoferū Pezel- lium, qui in Locos Communes Melanƈthonis scripta, vti e- go coniicio, digessit; aut in Obiectiones saltem, & Respon- siones: Quos vtrosq; potius nomino, quia honorifice satis, hanc Artem, non nimis se extendentem, prædicarunt. Sed m Pezelius hæc tria, de quibus dixi, ἐκλογὰς[?], id est, Delectus; ἐγκεφαλι[?] γενεθλιολογίαν[?]), Natiuitatum interpretationem; ἐρωτήσεως[?], Inter- rogationes seu Quaesita, vt Chaldaeorum vanitates damnat; & dicit: isthaec esse superstitiosorum, aut impiorum commenta, quae praeter rationem, in Astrologiam sunt inducta, & quae merito impie- tatis, & vanitatis, damnat Christiana religio. Seuerum certe Astronomi, De Astrologia iudicium. Et de his tribus hactenus.
units.tr: 15. And in some cases, also among us, such inquiry is forbidden by law: especially in matters that concern the supreme magistrate, the kingdom, and the realm. Piously indeed, and prudently, and rightly.
