Nor would it have been inconvenient if inquiries of this common kind, about theft and loss, were also forbidden, since this trifling race of men catches people only by ridiculous imposture, describing the accused by remarkable marks which can hardly be found anywhere: as, the man had a squint, a bent head, prominent teeth set awkwardly apart, legs spread wide, distorted feet, and other things which can stir the stomach of any sensible person. Yet the anxious and curious madness of mortals has not at all withdrawn its trust from them. But prudence, experience, and their own harm will at last prevail, so that they no longer consult; or if these will not avail, piety will prevail, as must be hoped for, to which these things are opposed: and this from the testimony of those who ascribe far more to astrology than the greater part of learned men. For, to be content with the judgment of Melanchthon on elections, cited above, hear Christoph Pezel, who, as I conjecture, arranged the writings into the Loci Communes of Melanchthon, or at least into Objections and Responses; both of whom I rather name, because they have praised this art in fairly honourable terms, not extending it too far. But Pezel condemns these three things of which I have spoken: ἐκλογὰς[?], that is, selections (choices); ἐγκεφαλι[?] γενεθλιολογίαν[?], the interpretation of nativities; ἐρωτήσεως[?], inquiries or questions, as the vanities of the Chaldeans; and he says these are the inventions of superstitious or impious men, which have been introduced into astrology beyond reason, and which Christian religion rightly condemns as impiety and vanity. Certainly a severe judgment of the astronomers on astrology. And so far concerning these three.

units.la: 14. Quartum quiddam est, in quo ingenii sui, industriaeque vires, vulgo magis, & aperte exercent: malo sane minori, sed fraude non dissimili; dum acris immutationes, serenas, nubilasque tempestates, siccitatem, pluuiam, niues, aquarum inundationes, famem, pestem; prognosticis suis, praedicant. Quorum omnem rationem, (praesertim vero, quod ad coeli faciem spectat) tollendam, aut abominandam non censeo. Apud Matthaeum etenim, citat Christus, & non improbat, Populi Iudaici obseruationes: {n}Quando serum[?] est diei, dicitis, serenitas erit; rubet enim caelum: Et mane, hodie erit tempestas, rubet enim caelum triste. Ita habent nautae, & agricolae praedictiones suas; usu collectas, de quibus tamen, verissime affirmamus, ex Meteoris potius, quam coelestibus inclinationibus illas pendere. Sed & ab aqueis, & terrestribus censuram faciunt; ut apud {o}Lucanum, est videre, qui nau-tam inducit, Caesari, qui solus in Italiam, nauigare cupiebat, praefantem, ex auium gestu, & similibus, quanta procella iam continuo fremeret. Ex his, & ex aspectu Solis & Lunae, unius diei, aut duorum fortassis, probabilia Prognostica, haberi possunt: sed cum ante mensem, annum, lustrum, pronunciare velint, in scopulos infamiae, se immittunt, suosque libellos ridendos propinant: id quod saepe contingit, cum lepidioris ingenii aliqui, ipsorum plures, omnino inter se pugnantes & diffidentes e diametro, conferre velit. In quibus, illud etiam non indignum est animaduertisse, quod maximas rerum immutationes, non praeuideant, sed in insignissimis euentibus, tanquam muti pisces silent: ut in morbis extraordinariis, aut diluuiis, non raro contingit. Leui-nus {p}Lemnius, in suo, de Astrorum usu libello, profitetur sudoriferam illam Cardiacam, quae Anno 1529. inter tot hominum millia, grassata est: sed & inundationem, super omnem fere Galliam Belgicam, quater ab Anno 1530. ad 1552. factam, à nullo Astrologorum, fuisse pronunciatam. Nonnunquam tamen, ut ea loqui videantur, quae speciem aliquam prae se ferant, astutia callidiore, ea proponunt, ut ex sideribus cognita, quae quiuis è plebe homulus si sensum velit intendere, non poterit non cognoscere. Vt cum messis turbata fuerit, futuram famem: Id quod hodie, nimis verum est, si Diuinae Maiestati, nobis ob peccata succensenti, aliter videretur: vbi cum superiorum, frumentum annorum, consumptum sit, & praecedentes aestates, Autumnique pluuiis vehementioribus obruti fuere, metuendam fuisse famem, panisq; penuriam, difficile non erat, ita pridem afflueuerare. Potest tamen incogitabilis misericordiae Pater, & hanc etiam leuare necessitatem, pro beneplacito suo: quod ut faciat, obsecramus. Sed quid isthaec ad sidera? Eodem plane modo, Monarcharum actiones speculantur, in publico, tanquam in Theatro, propositas: sed & secretiora Principum consilia, venantur, & rimantur, è quibus inimicitias, aut bella exarsura, eloquantur. Egregiam certe laudem. E coelorum tamen motib.se motus istos, in terra, exugere protestantur, cum in iis, nihil tale insit. Occasiones etenim hominum, quas arripiant, & leuitas animorum, proximo post Diuinam voluntatem loco, ista excitant; non leues Planetarum inclinationes, de quibus illi tam stupenda efferunt, ut Seneca non sal-sius quam verius, {q}Videbis quinq; sidera diuersas agentia vias, & in contrarium praecipiti mundo nitentia. Ex horum leuissimis motibus, fortuna populorum dependent, & maxima, ac minima proinde formantur, prout aequum, iniquumue fidus incesserit. Grauissimus
units.tr: 14. There is a fourth thing, in which they exercise the powers of their talent and industry more commonly and openly: with a lesser evil, indeed, but no less deceit; while they foretell by their prognostications sharp changes, clear and cloudy weather, drought, rain, snows, floods of waters, famine, and pestilence. I do not think the whole reasoning behind these (especially as far as it concerns the appearance of the sky) should be removed or abominated. For in Matthew, Christ cites and does not disapprove the observations of the Jewish people: When it is evening, you say, it will be fair weather, for the sky is red; and in the morning, today there will be a storm, for the sky is red and gloomy. Thus sailors and farmers have their predictions, gathered from experience; of which, however, we affirm most truly that they depend rather upon meteors than upon celestial inclinations. But they also make judgments from watery and earthly signs; as may be seen in Lucan, who introduces a sailor warning Caesar, who alone wished to sail into Italy, from the behaviour of birds and similar signs, how great a storm was already about to roar at once. From these, and from the aspect of the sun and moon, probable prognostics of one day, or perhaps two, may be had; but when they wish to pronounce a month, a year, or a five-year period ahead, they throw themselves upon the rocks of infamy and offer their own little books to be laughed at: which often happens when some of them of a more witty disposition wish to compare themselves, all of them mutually contradictory and utterly at odds. In these matters it is also not unworthy to notice that they do not foresee the greatest changes of things, but, in the most remarkable events, fall silent like dumb fish: as often happens in extraordinary diseases or floods. Levinus Lemnius, in his little book on the use of the stars, professes that sweating sickness, the cardiac plague which raged in the year 1529 among so many thousands of people, and also the inundation which, from 1530 to 1552, came four times over almost all of Belgian Gaul, was not foretold by any of the astrologers. Sometimes, however, so that they seem to say things which bear some appearance, with a more cunning cleverness they put forward things as known from the stars, which any common fellow of the people, if he would apply his mind, could not fail to know. For example, when the harvest has been spoiled, they foretell a coming famine. This is indeed only too true today, if the Divine Majesty, kindled against us because of our sins, should see it otherwise; for when the grain of the preceding years has been consumed, and the previous summers and autumns have been overwhelmed by very heavy rains, it was not difficult to foresee that famine and scarcity of bread were to be feared. Yet the Father of unthinkable mercy can also relieve even this necessity, according to his good pleasure; which we beseech him to do. But what has this to do with the stars? In exactly the same way, they watch the actions of monarchs, which are set forth publicly as in a theatre; but they also hunt out and search into the more secret counsels of princes, from which they declare that enmities or wars are about to break out. A remarkable praise, certainly. Yet they profess that they draw these movements on earth from the motions of the heavens, when there is nothing of the kind in them. For the occasions which men seize upon, and the levity of minds, stir these up, next after the divine will; not the slight inclinations of the planets, of which they report such astonishing things, as Seneca, no less truly than wittily, says: You will see five stars pursuing diverse courses, and striving toward the contrary in a headlong world. From these slightest motions the fortunes of peoples depend, and the greatest and least things are accordingly shaped, as the star has moved favourably or unfavourably. The most serious
{p} Leuinus Lemnius de Astrorum vsu.

units.la: {q} Seneca in consolatione ad Marciam 28. Seneca, Ironia mordace & amara, decreta Mathesim prosi-tentium, sic perstringit.
units.tr: {q} Seneca in consolatione ad Marciam 28. Seneca, with biting and bitter irony, thus lashes those who practise astrology.

units.la: 15. Nisi nimio vos taedio afficerem, infinita sane è Theo-logis, Philosophis, Historicis, Legumlatoribus, Politicis, possem adducere, quae communi consensu, fidem, & existi-mationem istis detrahunt: quib. vel eorum aliquot, tantum nominandis, contentus ero, alii cuipiam, in largum prose-quenda, relicturus. Ut sciremus igitur, nō è Sole, aut siderib. terrae fertilitatem dependere, {r}in Genesi edocemur, germi-nasse terram, antequam sol, & luna fabricarentur; quibus tamen, ad id ministerium, dehinc Deus utitur. Hoc {f}/ Philo-nis est Iudaei: Non omisit tamen, etiam {t}Chrysostomus, Nenimium, inquit, sideribus tribueremus; ante solis, stellarum-que creationem, tellus semina protulit. Quam inutile sit, rerum futurarum, scientiam captare, docet {u}Tullius: Non est utilis futurorum scientia, nam quae vita esset Priamo, si miserias suas futuras praesciisset? Diu tamen, feliciter vixit Priamus. Iterum Tullius, {x}Omnesne, qui Cannis ceciderunt, uno Astrofue-runt? Et ibi tertio: Pompeio, Crasso, Caesari multa à Chaldaeis di-ctafunt: neminem eorum, nisi in senectute, nisi domi, nisi cum clarita-te, esse moriturum. E contra observat {y}Seneca, Claudio Im-peratori, quotannis, Astrologos praedixisse mortem, & falso cum adhuc superuiueret. Egregia est {z}Phauorini disputa-tio, apud Gellium, & digna, quae tota legatur: Hic cum lucu-lentis argumentis Mathesim oppugnasset, concludit, inutile esse, futura praescire sic: Aut aduersa, inquit, euentura sunt, aut prospera: Si dicunt prospera, & fallunt, miser fies, frustra expectan-do: si aduersa dicunt, & mentiuntur, miser fies, frustra timendo: Si vera respondent, saepe non prospera sunt, tam inde, ex animo miser fies, antequam è fato fies: si felicia promittunt, eaque euentura sunt, tum plane duo erunt incommoda: & expectatio, te spei suspensum fa-tigabit, & futurum gaudii fructum, spes tibi iam defloruerit. Sequi-tur etiam {a}Taeiti, grauissimi Historici iudicii: Mathematici genus
units.tr: 15. If I did not weary you excessively, I could certainly cite endless testimonies from theologians, philosophers, historians, lawgivers and political writers, which by common consent strip these people of credit and reputation. I shall be content to name only a few of them, leaving the fuller treatment to someone else at leisure. That we may know, then, that the fertility of the earth does not depend on the sun or the stars, we are taught in Genesis that the earth sprouted before the sun and moon were made; yet God afterwards uses these for that ministry. This is the view of the Jew Philo. Chrysostom also did not omit it: Lest we should attribute too much to the stars, he says, the earth brought forth seeds before the creation of the sun and the stars. How useless it is to seek knowledge of future things, Tully teaches: The knowledge of the future is not useful, for what kind of life would Priam have had if he had foreknown his future miseries? Yet Priam lived long and happily. Again Tully: Did all who fell at Cannae perish under one star? And there, a third time: Many things were foretold by the Chaldeans to Pompey, Crassus and Caesar: that none of them would die except in old age, at home, and in glory. On the other side, Seneca notes that astrologers foretold the death of the Emperor Claudius every year, and falsely, while he was still alive. The disputation of Favorinus, in Gellius, is outstanding and worth reading in full: when he had attacked astrology with clear arguments, he concludes that it is useless to foreknow the future, thus: Either the events to come will be adverse or they will be favourable. If they tell of favourable things and are wrong, you will be wretched, having waited in vain; if they tell of adverse things and lie, you will be wretched, having feared in vain. If they answer truly, often the things are not favourable, so you will be wretched in mind before you are wretched by fate; if they promise happy things and these come to pass, then there will plainly be two disadvantages: the expectation will weary you, suspended in hope, and the hope will already have withered before the fruit of joy that is to come. There also follows the judgement of the grave historian Tacitus: The class of mathematicians, faithless to the powerful, deceptive to those who hope, which in our state will always be forbidden and always be kept.
{r} Genesis 1. 14.
{f} Philo the Jew, On the Creation of the World.
{t} Chrysostom, Homily 5 on Genesis.
{u} Tully, book 2 On Divination.
{x} Tully, as above.
{y} Seneca, On the Death of the Emperor Claudius.
{z} Gellius, book 14, chapter 1.

units.la: {a} Tacitus Hist. lib. 1. genus hominum, potentibus infidum, sperantibus fallax; quod inno-stra civitate, & vetabitur semper, & retinebitur. Eodem {b}teste, factum est sub Tiberio, decretum de istis Mathematicis, & magis, Italia pellendis, eorumque unus saxo deiectus est, {c}Suetonius etiam in Tiberio, fatetur id decretum, sed A-strologis deprecantibus, & artem se relicturos profitenti-bus, dicit Imperatorem, veniam dedisse. {d}Iustiniani, extant leges, adversus istos, & {e}Vlpianus, eos Romae, aqua, & igni interdictos dicit, eorumque bona publicata. Neq; legimus, ullum Imperatorum Romanorum, aperte tolerasse, unico excepto Juliano Apostata, qui perhibente {f}Sozomeno, A-strologiam, & Nativitates, exerceri sub se passus est, & non-nunquam procurauit. Et quis fuerit Julianus, probe cognoscimus. Quid quod {g}Juvenalis, Chaldaeos ut ridiculos homines, tacite perstrinxit. Julius Firmicus, qui magnum se Magistrum Matheseos profitetur: largumque ea de re, ante multa secula, conscripsit librum, maximeque nominis A-strologus habetur: præ legum metu, (uti ego existimo) Imperatorum fata, non posse è sideribus, alioqui modo tali, con-cipi profitetur. At reliqui eius farinæ, omnes, in Principum Nauitatibus coniectandis, potissimum operam locare so-lent, quippe ex quibus, plurimum pecuniæ sint emunctuři, & lucraturi. Audite {h}eius verba: Aruspices turbabant exta, de industria, cum de Imperatoribus consulerentur. Sic solius Impera-toris fatum, è stellis non potest conici, quia is terram regens, à solo Deo regitur. Claudet ista {i}Picus Mirandulanus, Si in cœlo plures sphæræ sint, quam octo, fallitur Ptolomæus, è quo plurima sumunt, & tota vetus Astrologia: si non plures, fallūtur noui, qui ut de pluri-bus judicium faciunt. Secundo idem Picus: Ptolomæus, qui in Genethliacis, est optimus malorum, locum septimum in schemate, con-sulto, hoc est, Astrologo tribuit, qui hodie in Quæstionibus, rei quæ-sitæ datur. Et tertio: Astrologia experientia non constat, cui supra omnia innititur, cum experientia, sit sæpe expertorum: sed eadem Constellationes, & Revolutiones nunquam bis revertuntur, nedum sapius, ut oportuit, si certæ inde regulæ colligendæ essent. Ista festinus præterea, sed hora labitur, & ad prudentes, & intelligentes loquor.
units.tr: {a} Tacitus, Histories, book 1. By the same witness, under Tiberius a decree was made concerning these mathematicians, and they were to be expelled from Italy, and one of them was thrown from the rock. {c} Suetonius also, in his life of Tiberius, admits this decree, but says that the Emperor granted pardon when the astrologers pleaded and professed that they would give up the art. There are extant laws of Justinian against them, and Ulpian says that they were banished from Rome by water and fire, and their goods confiscated. Nor do we read that any Roman emperor openly tolerated them, with the single exception of Julian the Apostate, who, according to Sozomen, allowed astrology and the casting of nativities to be practised under him, and sometimes promoted it. And we know well enough what sort of man Julian was. What of the fact that Juvenal lightly satirised the Chaldeans as ridiculous men? Julius Firmicus, who professes himself a great Master of Mathematics and wrote a long book on this subject many centuries ago, is regarded as the most famous of astrologers; yet from fear of the laws (as I think) he professes that the fates of emperors cannot be conjectured from the stars, at least not in such a manner. But all the others of that stripe are wont to devote their efforts especially to casting the horoscopes of princes, since from these they are accustomed to squeeze out and gain the most money. Hear his words: The haruspices were troubling the entrails on purpose, when they were consulted about the emperors. Thus the fate of the emperor alone cannot be conjectured from the stars, because he, ruling the earth, is ruled by God alone. Pico della Mirandola closes these matters: If there are more spheres in heaven than eight, Ptolemy, from whom they take most things and the whole of old astrology, is wrong; if there are not more, the new astrologers are wrong, who make judgement about more. Secondly, Pico again: Ptolemy, who in his genethliacal writings is the best of the bad, assigns the seventh place in the figure to the astrologer, that is, the one who today is given in questions to the thing asked. And thirdly: Astrology does not rest on experience, on which it leans above all, since experience is often the experience of experts; but the same constellations and revolutions never return twice, much less as often as would have to be the case if sure rules were to be gathered from them. Moreover, I speak these things hastily, but the hour slips away, and I speak to the prudent and the intelligent.

units.la: 16. Nunc superest, ut pauca, quæ ex adverso afferuntur, tollantur è medio. Ea, aut Scripturæ sunt, aut experientiæ. E sacris literis, citantid[?] Geneseos: {k}Sint luminaria in cœlo, insigna, & tempora, & dies & annos. Hinc, signa esse futurorum, conantur ostendere. At nil hocaliud est, in signa, & tempora, quam in signa temporum, quod revera sunt: dum diem, & noctem, & æstatem & hyemem, & ver & autumnum: sic serendi, metendique opportunitates, distinguant. Quo nomine, quia tempora significant, Gnomoni in Horologio, transitiones horarum edocenti, comparantur. Et illud asserunt Deuteronomii: {l}Sunt in ministerium gentibus: hoc est, per calorem & lumen. Sed venerunt {m}Magi ex Oriente, ut Christum quærerent, insignes Astrologi. Et gratulamur venisse Magos, ut primitias Gentium. At laudant ista, Magorum disciplinas. Siccine? Venerunt ad Christum meretrices: neque magis ille; meretricias, quam Magicas; revera neutras, approbavit artes. Sed quare venerunt Magi, præceteris? Ut homines eruditi, apud populum valentes, & præstantes, & Euangelio propagando, cum domum rediissent, aptissimi. At quare per stellam ducti sunt? Dicamne ut {n}Origenes? Ut {o}Balaami Prophetia, de Christo, per stellam significato, impleretur. Imo potius, ut relicta antiqua sua, Astrorum disciplina, in novum hunc Salvatorem, Astrorum Dominum, per stellam novam, patefactum, inspectarent. Et singularis fuit hæc stella, nihil cum illis Magorum; commune habens, ut quæ non in Firmamento, apparuerat; sed in aere potius: Qui etenim alias, super domū stare; distincte[?] discerneretur? Meælestioni[?], nihil occurrit aliud, præterquam de Sisara illud, unde depromptæ est; initio orationis meæ, huius controuersiæ discutiendæ occasio: è cœlis pu- gnarunt; & sidera ex aggeribus pugnauerunt. Quo quidem interpretando, candide profiteor, me à p Francisco Valesio opinione discedere, qui ex stellis, significatos putat Angelos: qui in Ordinibus suis Hierarchicis (scilicet (secundum illam nempe q Dionysii adulterini Hierarchiam) pugnauerunt. Nec vt ipsi assentiam, magis ex eo, moueor, quod ex Apocalypsi citat, Draconem videlicet, ex cœlo tertiam partem r stellarum, cauda excussisse, id est, vt inquit Valesius tertiam partem Angelorum. Hoc etenim æque est obscurum, & sua indiget confirmatione. Sed pugnasse è cœ- lis interpretor, res cœlestes, hoc est, desuper demissas, pluuias, uen- tos, grandines, procellas; ita sidera, quia harum rerum, in tractatione sua, sunt instrumenta; ex aggeribus, id est, superioribus regionibus aeris, translata locutione, à militibus ex editiore loco pugnantibus. Et vt ita exponam, multa me mouent: Analogia scripturarum: recta ratio, & vsus Dei: qui sic hostes perdit, vt apud Dauidem, s depluet super imp- obos, prunas, ignem & sulphur, ventusque procellosissimus [?], portio capitis eorum. Sic M. Aurelii t disiecit hostes, post preces legionis Christianorum. Sed & hunc in modum, exponunt scriptores, superiorum seculorum, u Lyra, Glossa ordinaria, Petrus Cantor, Petrus Comestor Magister Historiæ Scholasticæ, Dionysius Carthusianus, Hugo de Vienna, & quos pluris facio, quam illos omnes, x Tremelius & Iunius; qui ipsis verbis prius à me citatis, historiam exponunt. Quibus vt maiorem etiam, adhibeam fidem, facit y Josephus, qui hanc narrans rem ipsam, Sisaram & milites, procella fuisse obrutos, confirmauit. Nihil ergo ista ad Astrologorum sidera, quæ quo modo Israelitas, à Cananæis pugnantibus, distinguerent & inter- noscerent?
units.tr: 16. It remains now that the few things brought against us be removed from the midst. These are either from Scripture or from experience. From the holy letters they cite Genesis: Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven, for signs, and for seasons, and for days and years. From this they try to show that they are signs of things to come. But this is nothing other than "for signs and seasons," that is, signs of seasons, which they truly are, since they distinguish day and night, summer and winter, spring and autumn, and thus the opportunities for sowing and reaping. On this account, because they signify seasons, they are compared to the gnomon on a sundial, which indicates the transitions of the hours. And they also assert that passage of Deuteronomy: They are for ministry to the nations, that is, through heat and light. But the Magi, famous astrologers, came from the East to seek Christ. And we rejoice that the Magi came, as the firstfruits of the Gentiles. Yet they praise those arts on the ground of the Magi's teachings. Is that so? Harlots came to Christ too, and he approved neither the harlot's arts nor the magical ones; indeed neither. But why did the Magi come, rather than others? Because they were learned men, powerful and distinguished among the people, and, once they had returned home, most suited to spreading the Gospel. But why were they led by a star? Shall I say, as Origen does? So that the prophecy of Balaam about Christ, signified by a star, might be fulfilled. Nay rather, so that, having left their ancient astrological discipline, they might look upon this new Saviour, the Lord of the stars, revealed by a new star. And this star was singular and had nothing in common with those of the Magi, in that it had appeared not in the firmament but rather in the air; for otherwise how could it be clearly seen standing over a house? Nothing else occurs to me on this text, except that passage about Sisera, from which the occasion of discussing this controversy was taken at the beginning of my discourse: They fought from the heavens; the stars fought from their courses. In interpreting this, I frankly confess that I depart from the opinion of Francis Vallesius, who thinks the angels are signified by the stars, who fought in their hierarchical orders (namely according to that Hierarchy of the spurious Dionysius). Nor am I moved to agree with him by the fact that he cites from the Apocalypse that the dragon, that is, swept a third part of the stars from heaven with his tail, that is, as Vallesius says, a third part of the angels. For this is equally obscure and needs its own confirmation. But I interpret "they fought from heaven" to mean heavenly things, that is, things sent down from above: rains, winds, hailstones, storms; so too the stars, because they are the instruments in the handling of these things; and "from their courses," that is, from the higher regions of the air, by a figurative expression, as soldiers fighting from higher ground. And to explain it thus, many things move me: the analogy of Scripture, sound reason, and the way of God, who destroys enemies thus, as in David, he will rain upon the wicked snares, fire and brimstone, and a horrible tempest; this shall be the portion of their cup. So too he scattered the enemies of Marcus Aurelius after the prayers of the Christian legion. But writers of earlier ages also explain it in this way: Lyra, the Ordinary Gloss, Peter the Chanter, Peter Comestor, Master of the Scholastic History, Denys the Carthusian, Hugh of Vienne; and those whom I value more than all of them, Tremellius and Junius, who explain the history in the very words cited by me before. To add still more weight to these, Josephus, relating this very event, confirmed that Sisera and his soldiers were overwhelmed by a storm. Nothing, then, has to do with the stars of the astrologers; how could those stars distinguish and recognise the Israelites from the Canaanites who were fighting them?

units.la: 17. Quod proximo obstat loco, est experimentorum collectio, in quibus viri isti, sunt quam fœcundi. z Nascente Alexandro, Magi Persici cecinerunt, suo imperio, exitium impendere. {a}Calanus Alexandro, in Babylone, mortem futuram praedixit. At Nigidius Figulus, {b}teste Suetonio considerato cœli schemate, sub quo ortus est Octauius Augustus: ei orbis imperium portendi pronunciauit. Et certe si quis aurem velit accommodare, hodie suorum Comper-torum[?], & Probatorum multitudine, aures obtundent. Sed respondemus breuiter. Primo, paucis horum, adhibemus fidem, Diffidentia & incredulitas, vt facit Atheos: sic credulitas facit stultos. Secundo, forte fortuna, aliquando vera proferunt, vt qui de Somniis coniectationes faciunt: aliquando, aliunde, quam à sideribus edocti: vt credendum est, illud Nigidii Figuli, ad Christi aduentum, allusisse: qui Augusti tempore, venturus fuerat, spiritualiter orbi imperaturus. Et istud, ex Prophetarum eloquiis depromptum, ad Romanos vsque, per rumores, disseminari poterat. Loquuntur alii, in rebus Politicis, cum secretiora Principum, aut priuatorum, consilia expiscati fuerint. Tertio, non à sideribus, sed à Daemone, suggeruntur, quae vera proclamant, vt egregie {c}Augustinus: Non immerito creditur, cum Astrologi mirabiliter, multa vera respondent occulto instinctu fieri, spiritum non bonorum, quorum cura est, has falsas & noxias opiniones, de Astralibus fatis, inserere humanis mentibus, atque firmare, non Horoscopi notati, & inspecti aliquid arte, quae nulla est. Idipsum est, {d}viri docti, nostro seculo, iudicium de Ascletarione[?] Mathematico, tum Domitiano Imperatori, tum sibi, vio-lentam mortem, mire, vere tamen praedicente: hoc Daemonis astuti fuisse opus. Nemo in istis, Cardano fuerat auda-cior, verum illi {e}hereditaria fuit cum Daemonibus consuetudo, vt loquitur Nicolaus Remigius, & alicubi id habet etiam Iulius Scaliger. Et Diabolus, sane, aliis, permittente Deo, eam praescientiam impertit, sine fiderib[?], vt Germano seruo, qui vt refert {f}Iosephus, Agrippae, tunc temporis, in miseria extrema constituto, regnum pronunciauit, & felicem vitā; sed mortem intra quinq; dies, cum bubonem rursus, quem tunc viderat, conspexisset. Qui huic veritatis prædicendæ materiam suppeditauit, sine Astris: sed ex Augurio: ex instinctu suo, mouet Astrologos nonnunquam: id est, Dæmon. Et de his hactenus, Cum igitur è Scripturis sacris, vanitatem, & impietatem Chaldaicam redarguerim: ex rationis etiam, & Philosophiæ fundamentis, Mathesim hanc euerterim, ex Historicorum, Legumlatorum, Politicorum sententia, Astrologiam damnandam esse, docuerim, Christiani homines, ab ista, vt à vanitate impia, fugiamus: vt artem curiosam amoueamus, & ne audiatur nomen eius, in vicis nostris. In Deum potius, oculos conuertamus, qui sua sponte, bona, plagasque dat, & oremus, vt auertat, belli, famisque formidanda mala, sui nominis gratia, suique Christi causa, cui cum Patre, & Spiritu Sancto, sit decus & gloria, nunc, & in secula seculorum. Amen.
units.tr: 17. What comes next in the text is a collection of experiments, in which these men are remarkably productive. At the birth of Alexander, the Persian Magi foretold that ruin was threatening his rule. Calanus predicted to Alexander, at Babylon, that he would die. And Nigidius Figulus, according to Suetonius, having considered the configuration of the heavens under which Octavius Augustus was born, declared that the rule of the world was portended for him. And indeed, if anyone were willing to lend an ear, today they would deafen us with the multitude of their so-called Comperti and Probati. But we reply briefly. First, we give little credence to a few of them; distrust and disbelief, as the Atheists do, and credulity, which makes fools. Second, by chance, they sometimes utter true things, as those who make conjectures about dreams do; sometimes they have learned them from some source other than the stars. It should be believed that the saying of Nigidius Figulus alluded to the coming of Christ, who, in the time of Augustus, was about to come and rule the world spiritually. And this, drawn from the utterances of the Prophets, could have been spread abroad as far as the Romans through rumours. Others speak of political matters when they have ferreted out the more secret counsels of princes or private persons. Third, what they proclaim as true is not suggested by the stars but by the Demon, as Augustine excellently says: It is not unreasonably believed that when Astrologers answer many true things marvellously, this happens through a secret instinct of a spirit that is not good, whose concern it is to insert and fix these false and harmful opinions about astral fates in human minds, not through anything known by the art, which does not exist, from a horoscope noted and inspected. The same is true of the judgment of the learned men of our own age concerning the mathematician Ascletario, who marvellously but truly predicted a violent death both for the Emperor Domitian and for himself: this was the work of the cunning Demon. No one in these matters was bolder than Cardan, but he had, as Nicolaus Remigius puts it, a hereditary acquaintance with Demons, and Julius Scaliger also says so in places. And the Devil, certainly, with God's permission, imparts this foreknowledge to others without the stars, as he did to the German slave who, as Josephus relates, pronounced that Agrippa, then placed in extreme misery, would reign and live happily, but would die within five days, when he saw again the owl that he had then seen. He who supplied the matter for this prediction of the truth, without the stars, but from augury, by his own impulse, sometimes moves the Astrologers: that is, the Demon. And so far concerning these matters. Therefore, since I have refuted from the sacred Scriptures the Chaldean vanity and impiety, and have also overthrown this science on the foundations of reason and Philosophy, and have taught, from the opinion of Historians, Lawgivers and Politicians, that Astrology is to be condemned, let us Christians flee from it as from impious vanity, so that we may banish this curious art and let its name not be heard in our villages. Rather let us turn our eyes to God, who of his own accord gives good things and blows, and let us pray that he may turn away the dreadful evils of war and famine, for the sake of his own name and for the cause of his Christ, to whom, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be honour and glory, now and for ever and ever. Amen.

units.tr: CHAPTER FOUR. CONCERNING PRESENCE AT IDOLATROUS WORSHIP.

units.la: 2 Reg. 5. 17. Dixit Naaman: saltem detur, quæso seruo tuo, duorum mulorum onus, è terra: non enim est factURUS amplius, seruus tuus, holocaustum, aut sacrificium, Diis alienis, sed Iehoua.
units.tr: 2 Kings 5:17. Naaman said: Let there be given then, I pray, to your servant, a load of two mules' burden of earth; for your servant will no longer offer burnt offering or sacrifice to other gods, but to Jehovah.

units.la: 18 Hac in re, condonet Iehoua, seruo tuo: quum ingreditur dominus meus, ædes Rimmonis, vt incurvet se ibi, (nam is nititur manu mea) si incurvauero me, in æde Rimmonis, Hoc incurvare meum in æde Rimmonis, condonet quæso Iehoua seruo tuo, in hac re.

Presence at idolatrous worship is not simply forbidden. 14. Common opinions about Naaman's act. 15. The state of the question and its resolution.

units.la: ON incommode Ecclesiam, sicut hodie est, aut post Christum natum fuit, Firmamento, sideribus undequaq; vestito, comparare liceat, quum sonus doctrinae Apostolicae, & Euangelicae, per omnes orbis plagas ad Orientem & Occidentem, ad Meridiem & Septentrionem, ut in sphaera octaua, stellae, sit diffusus. Ante Christum tamen, carne indutum, quae erat fidelium congregatio, alicui orbi, sphaerae inferiori, puta Solis, aut Lunae; conferri poterat: ubi in corpore immenso, & fere infinito, una tantum stella, una lampas emicat, cum reliquae eiusdem coeli partes, ita sint translucidae, & transparentes, ut lumen non repercutiant; adeoque sine lumine, & quodam modo, in tenebris, aut caligine, versari affirmentur. Talis fuerat, Ecclesiae ratio, per multa Secula, quae in unico Israele, ut in una stella, elucens, per reliquas Gentium, & Ethnicorum nationes, non tantum delitescere, sed & penitus disparere; visa est. Quibus tamen temporibus, ut suam Deus, potentiam, nullis finibus contentam, nullis limitibus constrictam, & circumscriptam ostenderet, sed pro suo beneplacito, expatiantem; & ut ex Gentilium, quibusdam Primitiis, vocationem Gentium, futuram innueret, certos aliquot selegit, certisque temporibus; qui despectis nationibus, testimonium nomini ipsius ferrent; Iobum in terra Huz, Iethronem, in Madianitis; in Cananaeis, Rahab, & quem potissimum, nostra designatura est oratio, Naamanem in Syris.
units.tr: It is not inappropriate to compare the Church, as it is today or has been since the birth of Christ, to the firmament clothed on every side with stars, since the sound of apostolic and evangelical doctrine has spread through all the regions of the world, to the East and the West, to the South and the North, like stars in the eighth sphere. Before Christ came in the flesh, however, the congregation of the faithful could be compared to some lower sphere of the world, say of the Sun or the Moon, where in a vast and almost infinite body only one star, one lamp, shines forth, while the remaining parts of that same heaven are so translucent and transparent that they do not reflect light, and are therefore said to dwell without light, as it were in darkness or mist. Such was the condition of the Church for many ages, which, shining in the one Israel as in one star, seemed not merely to lie hidden but to have utterly disappeared among the remaining nations of the Gentiles and heathens. Yet in those times God, so that he might show his power, not contained by any bounds nor restricted or confined by any limits, but ranging according to his good pleasure, and so that he might signal from some firstfruits of the Gentiles the future calling of the Gentiles, chose certain persons at certain times, who, despising the nations, would bear witness to his name: Job in the land of Uz, Jethro among the Midianites, Rahab among the Canaanites, and, most especially, the one whom our discourse is concerned with, Naaman among the Syrians.

units.la: 2. Quem cum Pater aeternus, e speciali sua misericordia fidelium Catalogo, inscribere, electorum numero adiunge- re voluisset; lepra prius, inficiendum curauit: ancilla Israe- litica donauit; quae Prophetam Elizaeum, vt tali morbo, in Dei nomine curando, idoneum commendaret: vt in Israe- lem proficisceretur, impulit; vt Prophetae tandem aliquan- do auscultaret, effecit: quibus mediis, ab impetigine, lepra- que sua, immunis, mundusq; euasit. In istis, dum praepollen- tem virtutem, Domini exercituum, famuliq; sui Elizaei san- ctitatem experiretur, mirum est, quam insigni desiderio, ex- ardesceret, Iehouam Israelitarum Deum, colendi, & agno- scendi, Ecce, inquit, iam noui, nullum esse Deum, in tota terra; nisi in Israele. In piam, & fidelem confessionem erumpit. At- que iterum, tanquam fructum fidei, subiungit suae: Non est factiurus amplius, seruus tuus, holocaustum aut sacrificium, Diis alie- nis, sed Iehouae. Veruntamen, vt in nouitiis, recenterque con- uersis ad Dei cognitionem, assueuit fieri: superstitiosam, ha- bet cogitationem, de pulvere Israelitico, terraque, vel Pro- phetae pedibus, conculcata, acsi ipsi quaedam ineesset specia- lis sanctitas; araeque, ex eadem conficiendae; magis fauere Dominus. {a}Pomponius Mela, cuiusdam Insulae meminit, quam a serpentum, & colubrorum copia, Colubrariam ap- pellat: haec cum scateat multo, & malefico genere serpen- tum, ideoque sit inhabitabilis: si quis humum Ebusitanam adducat, pulverem nempe ex alia congestum insula, eumq; circumfundat, tutus erit, qui versatur intus, serpentibus, a- spectum huius pulueris, fugientibus. Non dissimilem, nostet Naaman, credidit inesse virtutem, humo terrae, quam ap- pellamus Sanctæ; dum vel profana omnia, posse abigere exi- stimaret, vel, sacra vi imbuere. Ita humi, adhuc repit, neo- phytus iste, non vt aquila, in altum elatus, sed infirmus scien- tia, aliquanto plus, quam oportuit, incumbit terrae.
units.tr: 2. When the eternal Father, out of his special mercy, had wished to inscribe him in the catalogue of the faithful and to add him to the number of the elect, he first arranged that he should be infected with leprosy; he gave him an Israelite servant girl, who recommended the prophet Elisha as suitable to cure such a disease in the name of God; he urged him to set out for Israel; he brought it about that at last he listened to the prophet; by these means he escaped, free and clean, from his scab and leprosy. In these things, while he experienced the powerful virtue of the Lord of hosts and the holiness of his servant Elisha, it is remarkable with what remarkable desire he burned to worship and acknowledge Jehovah, the God of the Israelites: "Behold," he says, "now I know that there is no God in all the earth, except in Israel." He bursts forth into a pious and faithful confession. And again, as a fruit of faith, he adds of his own: "Your servant will no longer offer burnt offering or sacrifice to other gods, but to Jehovah." Nevertheless, as is wont to happen among novices and those recently converted to the knowledge of God, he entertains a superstitious thought about the dust of Israel and the earth trodden under the prophet's feet, as if some special holiness inhered in it, and that the Lord would therefore be more favourable to altars made from the same. Pomponius Mela mentions a certain island, which he calls Colubraria from the abundance of serpents and snakes; since it teems with many and a harmful kind of serpent, and is therefore uninhabitable, if anyone brings Ebusitan earth, namely dust carried over from another island, and scatters it around, whoever stays within will be safe, since the serpents flee from the sight of this dust. Naaman, not unlike this, believed that there was a power in the earth which we call holy, supposing that it could drive away all profane things, or else imbue them with a sacred power. So this neophyte creeps upon the ground, not lifted up on high like an eagle, but weak in knowledge, leaning on the earth somewhat more than he ought.

units.la: 3. At secundum fuerat[?], quod animo, non arrisit suo, quin- mentem potius, tanquam aculeo pupugit: quod, in patriam reuer-
units.tr: 3. But the second matter, which did not please his mind, pricked him rather like a goad: that, on returning to his homeland,

units.la: a Pomp: Mela lib. 2.[?] reuersus, Idololatrico cultui, Rimmonisque adorationi, interesse, opus haberet; cum in Regio comitatu, templum adeundum esset; ibique pro morefuo, Naamanis dextrae, initeretur Princeps. Cum anxius esset, & sollicitus, quid in re isthac faceret, Diuinam implorat misericordiam, Prophetamque, vt est credibile excitat, vt pro eo, preces fundat: ne crimini apud Deum, id factum vertatur. Cui, cum respondeat Propheta: Abi cum pace, neque vllam adiciat increpationem; quin potius, aut laudare, aut tolerare videatur; dignus sane locus est (me iudice; neque solo me, sed Theologis aliis multis) quid discutiatur; vt quid in causa non dissimili faciendum sit, quantum indagari poterit, cognoscatur. Illud igitur, primo constat; è iudicio Naamanis, Liturgiæ Idololatricæ, vt vulgus superstitiosorum hominum solet interesse, pro nefando, & illicito habendum esse. Is etenim, cui de praesentia sua, scrupulus iniectus est; cum ad Ciuile tantum, & Politicum, praestandum munus, adesset; Idolumque ipsum corde auersaretur; (vt qui prius, pollicitus fuerat, se nulli alii Deo, quam Iehouae, sacrificaturum) sine dubio, incuruationem, & adorationem, damnasset; & participationem, licet simulatam, improbasset. Et cum Diuino instituto, veraque religione, conuenit optime, quadratque, haec opinio. {b}Ore etenim, confitendum est, ad salutem. Qui vero eousque, a confi-tendo, abest, vt praesentia sua, impurum honoret cultum; quid aliud agit, quam re ipsa, abnegat? {c}Qui vero me abnegauerit, coram hominibus; abnegabo, inquit Christus, & ego illum, coram Patre meo, qui est in coelis. Qui non est mecum, contra me est. {d}Dominum, Deum tuum, adorabis, eique foliseruies. Et {e}Exite e Babylone populemi, neparticipes sitis peccatorum eius, & ex plagis eius accipiatis. Denique, Primaeua Ecclesia, cos in Lapsorum, potissimum numero, habendos censuit, qui incensum simulachris adolere aut ipsorum ceremoniis, sua corpora coniungere consensissent. Quorum temporum iudicium, corroborat, Pauli ea sententia, qui cum {f}Idolothytis, abstineri voluerit, comedendis, quale quaeso iudicium, deadora-tione haberet?
units.tr: a Pomp. Mela, book 2. he would need to take part in idolatrous worship and the adoration of Rimmon, since in the royal retinue a temple had to be entered, and there, according to custom, the prince would lean upon Naaman's right hand. Since he was anxious and troubled about what to do in this matter, he implores the divine mercy, and, as is credible, he stirs up the prophet to pour out prayers for him, so that this deed may not be counted against him before God. When the prophet answers him, "Go in peace," and adds no rebuke at all, but rather seems either to praise or to tolerate, the passage is certainly worth examining (in my judgement, and not mine alone, but that of many other theologians) so that what must be done in a similar case may be known, as far as it can be investigated. First, then, this is established: by Naaman's judgement, participation in idolatrous liturgy, as the crowd of superstitious people is accustomed to attend it, is to be held wicked and unlawful. For he, whose scruple concerned his presence, since he was present only to perform a civil and political duty, and since he abhorred the idol itself in his heart (as one who had previously promised that he would sacrifice to no other God than Jehovah), would without doubt have condemned the bowing and the adoration, and would have disapproved even of a feigned participation. And this opinion agrees and accords well with divine institution and the true religion. b "For with the mouth confession must be made unto salvation." But whoever is so far from confessing that by his presence he honours an impure worship, what else does he do than in fact deny? c "But whoever shall deny me before men, him will I deny, says Christ, before my Father who is in heaven." "He who is not with me is against me." d "You shall worship the Lord your God, and serve him alone." And e "Come out of Babylon, my people, that you be not partakers of her sins, and that you receive not of her plagues." Lastly, the primitive Church judged that those who had consented to burn incense before images, or to join their bodies to their ceremonies, were to be counted chiefly among the lapsed. The judgement of those times is confirmed by the saying of Paul, who wished that abstinence be made from eating food offered to idols; what sort of judgement, I ask, would he hold concerning adoration?

units.la: 4. Et communia sint ista argumenta, Religionum, Sectarum, Hæreseων omnium. Nam cum {g}unum tantum, sit Deus, una fides, unum baptisma; cum ad coelum semita, ut arcta est, & angusta, sic simplex etiā, & unica, cum pietas, & Dei cultus, tanquam in indiuisibili, constituatur, neque multiplex distractio placere potest; communicatio, cum orationibus & sacramentis alienis, generali omnium consensu, merito repudiatur. Post {h}unam & alteram admonitionem, Haereticum hominem reiice, vel deuita. Si {i}accesserit quis, ad vos, & doctrinam hanc, non adfert; ne recipite eum domum; nec Aue, et dicite. Et {k}Habes, qui tenent doctrinam Nicolaitarum, quod odi. Celebre illud est {l}Iohannis Euangelistae, apud Eusebium, qui quanto-cyus, à Cerintho se subduxit, ut & {m}discipuli eius, Polycarpi, ad Marcionem. Si tanto uterque Haereticum odio prosecutus est, ut sub eodem versari tecto, aut sermone familiari, imo pacato, versus illum uti, recusauerit: puto, cane peius, & angue odisset cum tali hominum fæce precando, & Deum invocando, sociari. Num cum Orthodoxis Nouatiani, cum Arrianis Catholici; cum Manichaeis aut Pelagianis, Pius Augustinus, quod ad Diuina attinet, participarunt? Unde, Excommunicationis censura, in Ecclesia adversus Haereticos obtinuit, nisi quod, à cætibus fidelium eos amouendos, Christiana suaderet religio, qui non eadem, cum Orthodoxis, de Deo, aut pietate sentirent, & sua adulterina pertinaciter tuerentur, {n}Paulus ille Samosatenus, ab omni, quae sub coelo erat, Ecclesia est excommunicatus. {o}Theodoretus, Antiochi cuiusdam meminit, qui Iovianum (hicali-quando, Arrianus fuisset Episcopus: conversus est tamen pestca[?] ad rectam[?] in Christo fidem:) sibi manus imponere, nullo modo patitur, sed econtra, manum execratur illam, quæ blasphemam Eucharistiam tetigisset. Non desunt hac in re exempla multa, è veneranda Antiquitatis historia, deprompta; sed & nostra tempora copiosa sunt. Anabaptistarum conuenticula, quis nostrum non detestatur? Qui è Familia Amoris, prius fuerant in Anglia, (quorum aliquot ego noui) & qui postea Barhoistæ, à Principe suæ sectæ, meruerunt appellari, nihil minus quam damnabile habuerunt, Ecclesiæ Anglicanæ se adiungere.
units.tr: 4. And these arguments are common to all religions, sects and heresies. For since there is "one God, one faith, one baptism"; since the path to heaven, as it is narrow and strait, is likewise simple and single, and since piety and the worship of God are established as if in something indivisible, and a manifold division cannot be pleasing: communion in prayers and sacraments with others is rightly rejected by the general consensus of all. After "a first and a second admonition," "Reject a heretical man, or avoid him." If "anyone comes to you and does not bring this doctrine, do not receive him into the house, nor say to him, Hail." And "You have those who hold the doctrine of the Nicolaitans, which I hate." That famous story is told of the Apostle John, in Eusebius, who fled at once from Cerinthus, as also the disciples of Polycarp did from Marcion. If each of them pursued heretics with such hatred that they refused to dwell under the same roof, or to use towards them even familiar, or rather peaceable, conversation: I think they would have hated being joined, with such a dregs of men, in prayer and in invoking God, more than a dog or a snake. Did Augustine, with respect to divine matters, share anything with the Novatians among the orthodox, with the Arians among the Catholics, or with the Manichaeans or Pelagians? Hence the censure of excommunication prevailed in the Church against heretics, since the Christian religion urged that they, who did not think the same as the orthodox about God or piety, and who stubbornly defended their adulterated opinions, be removed from the assemblies of the faithful. That Paul of Samosata was excommunicated by the whole Church that is under heaven. Theodoret mentions a certain bishop of Antioch, who (who had once been an Arian bishop, but was nevertheless converted to right faith in Christ) by no means suffered to lay his hands upon him, but on the contrary cursed that hand which had touched the blasphemous Eucharist. Many examples in this matter are not lacking, drawn from the venerable history of antiquity; but our own times are also rich in them. Who among us does not detest the conventicles of the Anabaptists? Those who had previously been of the Family of Love in England (some of whom I myself knew), and who afterwards deserved to be called Barrowists, from the prince of their sect, had nothing less than a damnable intention of joining the Church of England.

units.la: 5. Sed quoniam, inter Pontificios, & Protestantes, maxima hac de re, intercessit controuersia: quid quisque egerint, aut senserint, paucis discutiendum existimo. Non est nouum in hoc Regno, sed à Pij vsque Quinti temporibus, Anno 1569. Bullam excommunicatoriam aduersus Serenissimam Eius Maiestatem, emittentis, assuetum: vt qui, Romani, iurati sint, in verba Magistri, nostris interesse sacris, scelus & piaculum habeant. Cum Principi, celebrique Ordinum Conuentui placuisset, vt lege speciali caueretur, quod adire recusantes, siue pecunia mulctarentur: iuxta illud Christi,{p} Cogite eos ingredi, & illud, vbi, optime{q} Augustinus docet, Principibus ex officio incumbere, quamuis non ad fidem, ad fidei tamen media, id est, Verbi auditionem; & Sacramentorum perceptionem impellere; exortus est è Noftratibus vnus, qui Papistarum renuentium, causam suscipere professus est: & vt Campianus pugil ille, & athleta Romanæ synagogæ, in re non absimili fecerat, proponit rationes (quas nouenario, non denario, vt Campianus ille, complectitur numero) quamobrem congregationibus nostris, sese immiscere non liceret. Istas, Howletus quidam etiam Anglus, (ita etenim aut vero, aut fictitio se appellat nomine) cum conspexisset, quam primum Duaci (illud etenim præfigitur: cum domi potius factum fit) in lucem emittendas curauit: præmissaque Epistola ad Reginam Angliæ Sanctissimam, suorum patrocinium tantæ Principi commendauit. Author tamen, quod monendum est, illud pro concesso, in principio arripit, Pontificiam Religionem esse maxime Orthodoxam, nostramq; Hæreticam, & ei fundamento superstruit omnia. Prudenter sane, quod ex tali Petitione Principii, vt loquuntur Dialectici, auspicatus est oratione suam. Ita etenim sine sanguine & sudore, parta erit victoria: cum opera multo maxima, in eo collocanda esset, vt meretriciam esse nostram, vel schismaticam, Ecclesiam demonstraret. Id quod nulla ipsorum industria effectum iri poterit. Tamen, cū ipsius rationes præferant aliquid, & tam ad nostram, quam ad suam causam faciant fere omnes, non pigebit illas breuissime recitare, vt cuius sint precii, ponderisque, contra nos, intelligatur.
units.tr: 5. But since a very great controversy has arisen between the Papists and the Protestants on this matter, I think it right to examine briefly what each side has done or thought. In this kingdom it is not new, but has been customary since the time of Pius V, in the year 1569, when he issued an excommunicating bull against the most serene Majesty of this realm, that those Romanists who have sworn to the words of the Master should consider it a crime and a sacrilege to attend our sacred services. When it pleased the Prince and the assembled estates of the realm that a special law should provide that those refusing to attend should be punished by fines, appealing to that saying of Christ, Compel them to come in, and to what Augustine teaches most excellently, that it is the duty of princes, by virtue of their office, to urge people, though not to faith itself, yet to the means of faith, that is, the hearing of the Word and the reception of the Sacraments; one of our own people arose who professed to take up the cause of the refusing Papists. Like that champion and athlete of the Roman synagogue, Campian, did in a not dissimilar matter, he sets out reasons (which he arranges in a number of nine, not ten as Campian did) why it is not lawful for them to mingle with our congregations. A certain Englishman, Howlet (for so he calls himself, whether by his true name or a fictitious one), when he had seen these, took care that they should be sent out into the light as soon as possible at Douai (for that is printed at the front, though it was perhaps really done at home); and with a letter prefixed to the most serene Queen of England, he commended the defence of his people to so great a Prince. The author, however, must be warned that he takes for granted at the outset that the Papist religion is the most orthodox, and ours heretical, and builds everything on that foundation. Certainly prudently, since he begins his speech from such a petition of the principle, as the dialecticians say. For in this way the victory would be won without blood or sweat, when the greatest effort ought to be spent on showing that our Church is a harlot, or schismatic. This will never be achieved by any effort of theirs. Nevertheless, since his arguments carry some weight and bear almost all on our cause as well as on theirs, it will not be tedious to recite them very briefly, so that their worth and weight against us may be understood.

units.la: 6. Primo igitur, fana Protestantium, tangenda non sunt, ob periculum infectionis. Quo etenim pacto norimus, quin cum eousque in malorum puteum, nos sponte descenderimus, vt peruersorum Synagogā velimus visitare, in sensum reprobum, pergat nos tradere Dominus, & gratiam subducendo, permittere, vt ruamus in æternum. Si non audiisset serpentem Eua, neque ipsa, nec Adamus periisset. Improbarum actionum, etiam media fugienda sunt. Teipsum occidere cum interdicitur, ne quid facias, quod propensum est, & procliue ad mortem vetatur. Quanto magis cauendū est, ne tali via ambules, qualis ad perpetuam animæ tuæ perniciem ducit. Recte istud, Howlette & appositæ[?]: (vt quæ sequuntur multa, si contaminatos esse Anglorum cætus, & Deo odiosos confirmasses :)( Deo odiosos confirmasses :)( Nam qui tangit picem, inquinabitur ea. Et qui in luto habitat, verendū est, ne cænosus prodeat. Ex consuetudine videndi ea, quæ offensionem in initio peperierunt, frigescere solet, & languescere Christiana constantia. Secundo, abstinendum censet, ne scandalum detur, & offendiculum consçientiis aliorum ponatur. Et qui {t}tanquam[?] istorum parvulorum scandalizaverit, praestat ei, ut mola asi-naria, collo appendatur, & in mare proiiciatur. Ieroboamus, cum aureos proposuisset vitulos, quot milliaanimarũ, in laqueos apertæ Idololatriæ perpulerat? Sed & recte hoc Howlette[?] sensu tuo: cum
units.tr: 6. First, the temples of the Protestants must not be touched, on account of the danger of infection. For how do we know that, having descended so far into the pit of evils, by our own will, so as to wish to visit the synagogue of the perverse, the Lord will not hand us over to a reprobate mind, and by withdrawing grace permit us to fall into eternal ruin? If Eve had not listened to the serpent, neither she nor Adam would have perished. Even the means must be avoided of wicked actions. When you are forbidden to kill yourself, you are told not to do anything that is inclined and prone to death. How much more must care be taken not to walk along a road that leads to the perpetual destruction of your soul. Howlet rightly says this, and appositely [?]: (since many of the things that follow would have confirmed that the assemblies of the English are polluted and hateful to God:) (hateful to God:) (For he who touches pitch will be defiled by it.) And he who dwells in the mire must fear lest he come out covered with filth. From the habit of seeing those things which at first caused offence, Christian constancy is wont to grow cold and languish. Second, he judges that one must abstain, lest a stumbling-block be given and an obstacle be placed before the consciences of others. And whoever shall offend one of these little ones, it were better for him that a millstone be hung about his neck, and that he be cast into the sea. How many souls did Jeroboam, when he set up the golden calves, drive into the snares of open idolatry? But Howlet also rightly says, in your sense: since
Let him who is a greater ox learn to plough with the lesser.

units.la: Et exemplis potius (ea nostra est imbecillitas) vivamus, quā-legibus.
units.tr: And let us live by examples rather than by laws (such is our weakness).
The world is ordered.
According to the example of the king.

units.la: Nobilium vestigiis, ignobiles, doctorum, indocti, patrum fi-lii, dominorum servi, robustiorum infirmi solent insistere: & cum plures peccare coeperint, excusabit multitudo: malum vitio non vertetur. Tertio, religionis signum est, mysteriis fidei communicare, quod qui fecerit ad Deos alienos, suam abnegasse professionem, merito iudicabitur. Nec in isto certe inficias imus, cum Ecclesiam frequentare, pietatis sit testera, neq; Circumcisio, Iudaei magis signum fuerat, aut {y}Fron-tem, signaculo crucis notare, Christiani in primaeua Ecclesia, quam huic, vel illi hominum coetui, se adiungere, est cum ipsis, quib. sociamur, eandem religionem profiteri. Et hucusque convenimus ambo, si in genere, de Haereticis synagogis adeundis, disputetur.
units.tr: The footsteps of the noble are commonly followed by the base, of the learned by the unlearned, of fathers by sons, of masters by slaves, of the stronger by the weaker; and when more have begun to sin, the multitude will excuse it: the evil will not be counted a fault. Third, it is a sign of religion to share in the mysteries of the faith, and whoever does so with the gods of others is rightly judged to have renounced his profession. Certainly in this matter we do not deny that to attend the Church is a token of piety, nor was circumcision more a sign of the Jew, or marking the forehead with the sign of the cross a sign of the Christian in the primitive Church, than joining oneself to this or that assembly of men is professing the same religion as those with whom we associate. And so far we agree, if the dispute is about entering heretical synagogues in general.

units.la: 7. Quarto loco ponit. Schisma esse, & ruptam Catholicæ unitatis: cum in duo diuersa distrahi, unitatis non fit, sed diuisionis. Vbi si e contra obiiciatur, quod si tanti damni & incommodi fuisset, Tridentinum Concilium, aperto Canone interdixisset: Respondet, inclusiue, & ex consequenti Tridentinos damnasse Patres, cum Lutheranos, & Caluinistas, Haereticos pronunciarint: & ex dogmatib. Orthodoxorum omnium, Haereticis communicandum non fit. Hic de schismate consentimus, si modo incorrupta Romana stetisset EccleEcclesia: Una etenim cum sit veritas, ei uni adhærescen-dum est: neque luci {z}convenit cum tenebris, aut Christo cum Beliale, aut templo Dei cum Idolis. De Concilio ta-men, aliquantum dubito. Nam cum, a testibus Pontificiis, Magnates aliquot, Nobilesque Anglicani, per Legatos, in ea quæstione, Concilium interpellarint, præ memoriæ lapsu, aut oblivione Patres non omiserunt. Quin potius credo, per conniventiam quandam, tacitos præteriisse, prospicientes, quam incommodum futurum esset, tot, tantisque suarum partium, aut carceris, aut exilij molestiam facessere. Et nescierunt, an aliquis venturus esset Pontifex, qui iactura suæ partis, deliberate perpensa, ad damnum resarciendum, Liturgiam Anglicanam, posset approbare, & confirmare. Id quod {a}à Papa Gregorio 13. Reginæ oblatum fuisse (modo titulus supremæ Gubernationis, Romanæ sedi redderetur) peruagato hominum, & magnorum sermone, ia-ctitatum aliquando significat Howlettus. Num vere illud an falso, nescio: at solet ex indulgentia sua, Sanctissimus Pa-ter, quæ videntur duriora, nonnunquam concedere, quo facilius, secreta sui cordis desideria, amplissime consequa-tur. In quo genere istud est, quod {b}Campianus, & Personius in Anglia recurrentes Dispensationem, Romæ obtinuerunt, ut ad periculum præsens declinandum, ipsi, aliique ipsis obsequiosi, maiestatem Regiam colerent, & honorarent ad tempus, donec Bulla Pii Quinti in executionem duceretur. Quintum est quod adiicit, verendum esse, ne interpretetur Deus, adstantem, simulue genua flectentem, participare & consentire. Et hic nos etiam, in Idololatricis, timide agendum esse censemus: cum corporis gestus observet, & cordis angulos, qui purissimis est oculis, rimetur Deus: cui nihil potest esse abditum, aut abscónditum: illeque non iudicet, ut homines. Qui {c}Achani commilitones interficiendos destinauit, cum illius peccato, non essent primaprimario contaminati; sed quia apud ipsum simul versantem, repertum est Anathema, subito, & nobis succensere potest, & vehementer excandescere. Ne igitur decipiamur, {d}Deus etenim non irridetur. A perta est sexta ratio, quod dissimulationis est, accedere; quod non est ita Christianum. Apertos namque esse decet, & simplices, Iesu nostri discipulos; necaliud in lingua promptum, aliud in pectore clausum habere: istud prætextu, reipsa illud velle. Quin veniant bona fide, qui infirmi sunt, ut doceantur: ut Ecclesiæ fidelium adiungantur, & in fumum istud abit, quod vrgetur.
units.tr: 7. Fourthly, he sets down that it is a schism, and a breach of Catholic unity, since being divided into two opposed bodies is not unity but division. Where, if on the contrary it is objected that, had it been of such great loss and inconvenience, the Council of Trent would have forbidden it by an express canon, he answers that by implication and by consequence the Tridentine Fathers condemned the Lutherans and the Calvinists, pronouncing them heretics; and that by the doctrines of all the orthodox, nothing is to be shared with heretics. Here we agree about the schism, provided only that the Roman Church had remained uncorrupted: for since truth is one, one must cling to it alone; nor does light agree with darkness, or Christ with Belial, or the temple of God with idols. About the Council, however, I have some doubt. For when, according to Papist witnesses, several magnates and English nobles through their envoys petitioned the Council on that question, the Fathers did not omit to do so through forgetfulness or lapse of memory. Rather I believe they passed over it in silence through a certain connivance, foreseeing how inconvenient it would be to bring trouble of imprisonment or exile upon so many and such great men of their own party. And they did not know whether there would come some future Pontiff who, having deliberately weighed the loss of his own party, could approve and confirm the English Liturgy to make good the damage. Howlet indicates that this was once offered to the Queen by Pope Gregory XIII (provided the title of supreme governor were restored to the Roman see), boasted of in the widely circulated talk of men and great persons. Whether this is true or false I do not know; but the most holy Father is wont, from his indulgence, to grant sometimes what seem the harsher things, so that he more easily attains in the fullest measure the secret desires of his heart. In this category is that which Campian and Persons, running back into England, obtained at Rome by dispensation: that, to avert present danger, they themselves and others obedient to them should for a time honour and reverence the Royal Majesty, until the bull of Pius V was put into execution. The fifth point he adds is that one must fear lest God interpret the standing by, or the kneeling beside, as participation and consent. And here we too judge that we must act cautiously in idolatrous matters, since God, who has the purest eyes, searches the bodily gestures and the corners of the heart; nothing can be hidden or concealed from him, and he does not judge as men do. He who appointed Achan's fellow soldiers to be slain, though they were not primarily contaminated by his sin, but because the accursed thing was found while they were dwelling with him, can suddenly be angry with us and burn vehemently. Lest therefore we be deceived: God is not mocked. The sixth reason is that to draw near is a matter of dissimulation, which is not so Christian. For the disciples of our Jesus ought to be open and sincere, and not to have one thing ready in the tongue and another shut up in the breast, pretending under that pretext to will in fact the other. Rather let those who are weak come in good faith, that they may be taught, and that they may be joined to the congregation of the faithful; and that which is urged will vanish into smoke.

units.la: 8. Argumenti septimi loco, id occurrit, quod solum continuo nos stare videtur, & in quo, aliquid momenti esset, modo verum esset: Liturgiam scilicet nostram, publicamq; orandi formam, esse maculis temeratam, & conspurcatam, imo impiam esse; ita ut ipsi consentire, pessime peccare sit. Neque eam, inquit, calumniam id amouere potest, quod totus fere liber, è Prophetis, & Psalmis desumptus sit; quod Euangelia, ex Euangeliis; Epistolæ, ex Epistolis seligantur, cum scripturas, {e}Dæmon etiam citárit, sed male intellectas & applicatas perperam. Sed, quatuor de causis Liturgia Anglicana, contaminata est: Primo, quia corrupta est, translatio Scripturarum: Secundo, quia per Ministros totum opus peragitur, non per Sacerdotes, & Sacrificos. Tertio, quia multa liber habet, contra Papam; ut cum in Hymno in fine, à Papa, Turcaque, defendi petitur. Quarto, quia tantum non habet boni, quantum oportuit, Ista quidè omnia, doctissime nostrates, Juellus, Fulcus, alij refutárunt, præsertim Wiburnus, qui libro ex proposito edito: Epistolæ præfixæ, & Rationum omnium, velapices persecutus est; & gloriosam iactantiam incongruis consequentiis consarcinatam, sic coarguit: ut non opus sit plus adiicere; præsertim cum Howletti, pura & nuda sit affirmatio, sine adiunctis solidis probationibus. Cum eo tamen, in hoc conspiramus; quod si Idololatricus, impiusve, nostrer versus Deum cultus fuisset, ab eo plane discedendum esset. Cum malis etenim, in malis communicare, excusabile non est. Et s Horrendum est, in manus Dei viuentis incidere. Octauum est, quod Schismaticis copulati, omnia perdunt beneficia, religionis suæ; vt Eucharistiæ, & Missæ, sex Sacramentorum aliorum, clauiũ Ecclesiæ: præmij bonorum operum, communionis Sanctorum. Ista non discutimus, quippe quæ incerta sunt, & inconfessa, sed eousq; assentimur, vt extra veram Ecclesiam salutem non esse, asseueremus: & qui scorto se applicuerit à vera Christi sponsa excidit, neque vllis per eam datis beneficiis fruitur. Nonum est, quod omnes omnium religionum, sese, à diuersis religionibus separant: quod quoniam supra dixi, vlteriore non eget explicatione. Et si obtrudatur, inquit, Imus quidem, sed ad templum materiale, non spirituale, quod est cordis. Respondet, At cum externa professione, multa mala, concomitantur alia, Ista demum sunt firmamenta nouem, quibus nixus ille, Romanum Pontificem admirantes, à conuentibus Anglicanis auocaret.
units.tr: 8. Among the arguments of the seventh kind, there is one which alone seems to stand firm against us and in which there would be some weight, if it were true: namely, that our liturgy, our public form of prayer, is defiled and polluted by stains, indeed impious, so that to agree with it is to sin most grievously. Nor, he says, can this slander be removed by the fact that almost the whole book is taken from the Prophets and the Psalms, that the Gospels are chosen from the Gospels, and the Epistles from the Epistles, since the Devil also quoted Scripture, but misunderstood and wrongly applied. But the English liturgy is contaminated for four reasons: first, because the translation of the Scriptures is corrupt; second, because the whole work is carried out by ministers, not by priests and sacrificers; third, because the book contains many things against the Pope, as when at the end of a hymn it is asked to be defended from the Pope and the Turk; fourth, because it lacks as much good as it ought to have. Our most learned countrymen, Jewel, Fulke and others, have indeed refuted all these points, especially Whitgift, who in a book published for this purpose pursued the prefatory epistle and all the reasons, even the smallest points, and refuted that glorious boast, patched together from incongruous consequences, so thoroughly that there is no need to add more; especially since the assertion of Howlet is a bare and naked statement, without solid proofs attached. Yet with him we agree on this: that if our worship of God were idolatrous or impious, we ought plainly to withdraw from it. For it is not excusable to share in evils with evil men. And, It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God. The eighth point is that by joining schismatics they lose all the benefits of their religion: the Eucharist and the Mass, the other six sacraments, the keys of the Church, the rewards of good works, the communion of the saints. We do not discuss these things, since they are uncertain and unconfessed, but we assent so far that we affirm there is no salvation outside the true Church, and whoever attaches himself to a harlot has fallen away from the true bride of Christ and enjoys none of the benefits given through her. The ninth point is that all men separate themselves from the various religions of others; since I have said this above, it needs no further explanation. And if it is objected, he says, that they go indeed, but to the material temple, not the spiritual, which is of the heart: he replies that with outward profession many evils go along with it. These are finally the nine supports on which that man leaned, to draw those who admire the Roman Pontiff away from the English assemblies.

units.la: 9. Quis autem, aspectu est ita hebeti, vel cerebro obtusso, vt in nostram, hæc conuerti posse parte, non videat, paucissimis exceptis? Commune illud Rhetores appellant Exordium, quod tam in aduersariorum, quam nostram, {f}flecti causam potest. Sic, Communia sunt isthæc Argumenta, {g}Nostri autem Romanam Synagogam, aperte esse Idololatricam, confirmando, quia honorem Deo, Christoq; debitum, imaginibus, aquæ lustrali, pani Eucharistico, multisq; creaturis tribuat, iustissima de causa, diuortium ab ea faciendum esse, & secedendum, demonstrant. Nobis vero illi, ne speciequidem, Idololatriam obiiciunt. Superstitionibus ergo illorum, nos subducimus, neque liecre interesse proclamamus. Vnica etenim cum Religio, possit esse vera, vtrinque claudicandum non est: non in duas opiniones discedendum. {h}Si
units.tr: 9. But who is so dull of sight, or so blunt of mind, that he does not see, with very few exceptions, that these arguments can be turned against our side as well? The rhetoricians call this a common topic (exordium), since it can be bent to the cause of the opponents as well as to ours. Thus these arguments are common, while our people, by confirming that the Roman synagogue is plainly idolatrous, because it gives to images, to holy water, to the Eucharistic bread and to many creatures the honour owed to God and Christ, demonstrate that we must rightly and justly separate and withdraw from it. But as for us, they cannot even bring the charge of idolatry against us. We therefore withdraw from their superstitions, and we proclaim that it is not lawful to take part in them. For since there can be only one true religion, we must not limp on both sides, nor divide ourselves into two opinions. If
{f} Chemnitz, in the Examination of the Council of Trent.

units.la: {h} 1. Reg. 18. 28. Iehoua sit Deus, sequimini ipsum; sin Baal sit Deus, ite post eum. Non animum, mentéq; solam requirit Deus, sed & robur, quod est corporis, & ipsum corpus; multo maxime vero linguam. Si accedat ad ipsum ista, abscedat illa, in cœlo spiritus, in gehenna caro constituetur. Duæ autem cum sint sorores, animus & corpus, idem subibunt, aut gaudij aut doloris iudiciū. Reprehendit aliquando quædam, Origenes in persona sua: Quid mihi prodest, si genua corporis mei, ad orationē veniens, fle-ctam Deo, & genua cordis mei, flectam Diabolo. Nobis vero è conuerso licet dicere, quid mihi prodest, si genua cordis Deo flecto, & genua corporis Diabolo? Vtrumq; malū est, & hypocriticum. Vtinam aut calidus esses, aut frigidus, inquit Christus, Laodiceno Angelo: Cum vero tepidus sis, neq; vel frigidus, vel calidus fiet, vt evomam te, ex ore meo. Dura sententia, aduersus dissimulatores istos.
units.tr: {h} 1 Kings 18:21. If the LORD be God, follow him; but if Baal, then go after him. God does not require the mind and the soul alone, but also the strength, which belongs to the body, and the body itself, and above all the tongue. If that goes to him, and this turns away, the spirit will be set in heaven and the flesh in hell. Since soul and body are two sisters, they will undergo the same judgment, either of joy or of pain. Origen sometimes rebukes certain things in his own person: What does it profit me if the knees of my body, coming to prayer, are bent to God, and the knees of my heart are bent to the Devil? But conversely we may say to ourselves: what does it profit me if the knees of my heart are bent to God, and the knees of my body to the Devil? Both are evil and hypocritical. Would that you were either hot or cold, says Christ to the angel of Laodicea: but because you are lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spew you out of my mouth. A hard sentence against such dissemblers.

units.la: Caueant ergo, qui Idolorum cultui præsentes adstant, cum impius sit ille cultus, & irreligiosus; nam recte Lactantius: Non est dubium, quin religio nulla sit, v-bicunque est simulachrum: Caueant, qui Missam adeunt, quo hominibus morem gerant; cum non minus illa sit, aduersus Deum impia, Christiq; passioni, & sacrificio derogatoria, quam apud homines, theatrica, histrionica, & ridicula, vt probe describit Sleidanus, fumigationes, geniculationes, aliosque gestus proponendo; & quod modo distendantur, modo reducantur brachia; & huiusmodi infinita. Balaamiticos hos ritus fugiendos esse, Reformatores Ecclesiarum transf marinarum, crediderunt; sicq; nostri, Marianis temporibus, Pastores & Episcopi magnusque indoctorum grex, quorum aliquot, natiuæ suæ patriæ, amicisque valedixêre, in exilium profecti; alij dignitatibus, fortunisque renunciarunt, tertij vero, igneam probationem tolerarunt, ne conscientiæ suæ, vim inferrent, aut fratribus scandalum parerent, aut Dei seruitium, humanis fœditatibus permiscere viderentur,
units.tr: Therefore let those beware who stand present at the worship of idols, since that worship is impious and irreligious; for Lactantius rightly says: There is no doubt that there is no religion wherever there is an image. Let those beware who go to the Mass in order to please men, since it is no less impious against God, and derogatory to the passion and sacrifice of Christ, than it is theatrical, histrionic and ridiculous among men, as Sleidan describes well, setting out the fumigations, genuflections and other gestures, and how the arms are now stretched out, now brought back, and countless things of this kind. Our reformers of the churches beyond the sea believed that these Balaamite rites must be fled from; and so our own ministers and bishops in the times of Mary, and a great crowd of unlearned people, some of whom bade farewell to their native country and friends and went into exile, others renounced dignities and fortunes, and others endured the fiery trial, so that they would not do violence to their conscience, nor cause a scandal to their brethren, nor seem to mix the service of God with human filthiness.

units.la: 10. Hi cum fecerint,quod oportuit,& religionis suæ sanctitatem, sanguinis effusione confignarint, non poterant, non omnium seculorum Hypocritis,aut meticulosis hominibus,ignauiam,timoremque suum exprobrare;qui,ut præsenti consulerent vitæ,aut quod minus est,diuitiis,& existimationi temporali; in lupanaria superstitionum,se ingesserunt,& renitente aliquando animo,vel blanditiis aliquorum pellicientibus,vel legum rigiditati cesserunt. Tales semper, Orthodoxi nigriore signarunt nota,& ad quiduis duci posse existimarunt, Helcesaitæ, Hæretici nominantur,& taxantur,qui fidem dissimulare & in corde tegere docuerunt, extra quidlibet proferre. De Priscillianistis, quod habet Augustinus,huc referri potest: isti etenim asseuerant, in corde retinendum esse,quod verū est;ore autem,ad alienos, proferre falsa, peccatum nullum esse; Et hoc esse scriptum, Qui loquitur veritatem,in corde suo; tanquam hoc, satis sit ad iustitiam, etiamsi loquatur quisquam, in ore mendacium,quando non proximus,sed alienus hoc audit. Si in cætero sermone,sic dissimulare liceat;& in religione & fide abneganda: quod si & hanc negare fas sit, & cuiusuis sectæ, hæresisque conuenticula frequentare. Istos autem Priscillianistas,Hæreticos Augustinus pronunciauit. Eis adiungimus,aut si possit fieri,peiori habemus numero,qui usurpare solent illud,de quo dixi{1} supra,
units.tr: 10. When these men had done what they ought, and had sealed the holiness of their religion with the shedding of blood, they could not fail to reproach with cowardice and fear the hypocrites or timid men of every age, who, to protect their present life, or what is less, riches and temporal esteem, thrust themselves into the brothels of superstitions, and, with the mind sometimes resisting, yielded either to the enticements of some who coaxed them or to the rigour of the laws. Such men the Orthodox have always marked with a darker brand, and they have thought that they could be led to anything; the Helcesaites are named heretics and censured, who taught that faith should be dissembled and hidden in the heart, and professed outwardly. What Augustine says of the Priscillianists may be applied here: for they assert that what is true must be retained in the heart, but to utter falsehoods with the mouth before strangers is no sin; and that this is what is written, He who speaks the truth in his heart; as if this alone were enough for righteousness, even if someone speaks a lie with his mouth, when it is heard not by a neighbour but by a stranger. If it is lawful to dissemble in other speech in this way, then also in religion and faith, and to deny them; and if it is right to deny this too, and to frequent the little assemblies of any sect or heresy. Augustine pronounced these Priscillianists heretics. To them we add, or if it can be done, we count as worse, those who are accustomed to use that saying I mentioned above,
