{2} Swear, forswear, but do not reveal the secret.

units.la: Videant Campianus, Personius, & alij nostrates, transfugæ postea Romani & Rhemenses; si, cum sæpius, in ista Academia, in supremum Regiæ Maiestatis Dominium & Iurisdictionem, in causis Ecclesiasticis, tamquam in ciuilibus, sollenniter iurauissent; post discessum suum, in transmarinis, illud Ethnici non usurpauerint, si non voce, & sermone, at reipsa:
units.tr: Let Campion, Persons and the others of our countrymen, later Roman deserters and Rhemists, see whether, when they had so often, in this Academy, solemnly sworn to the supreme dominion and jurisdiction of the Royal Majesty in ecclesiastical causes, as in civil ones, they afterwards, once they had departed beyond the sea, did not use that saying of the heathen, if not with the voice and speech, yet in deed:

units.la: {f}Iuraui lingua, mentemineiuratamgero. Si alicubi, confidenter, constanter, fideliter, sine fraude su-co, aut dolo malo agendum sit, tum certe in Diuinis, iisque, quæ ad immediatam animarum salutem spectant.
units.tr: {f} I have sworn with my tongue, but I carry my mind unsworn. If anywhere one must act confidently, constantly, faithfully, without fraud or evil deceit, then certainly in divine matters, and those which concern the immediate salvation of souls.

units.la: II. Mirum tamen est, quanta fraus in religione simulanda, per omnia secula inualuerit, Constantini tempore, vt refert {t}Eusebius, Hæretici se Catholicos simularunt, cum tempore premerentur; & cæteris Catholicorum, se immiscuerunt. Ne Imperatoris iram prouocaret, quantam visus est {u}Arrius, agere pœnitentiam? quasi fictas effudit lachrymas? quale symbolum fidei suæ cudit: quod tamen, utrinq; exponi poterat: quas ille scribendo & rogando, insumpsit vires, vt in communionem Episcopi sanctissimi Alexandri reciperetur? idq; postridie faciendum fuerat, cum interea, ex Diuinio iudicio, creparet medius. Sed quas ille preces, putamus, quæ adire sacrificia recusasset? Similis erat magistri, discipulus, {x}Leontius Arrianus Episcopus, qui, cum Christi æqualitatem, cum Patre suo, negare aperte non auderet, ne legibus deprehensus, plecteretur; affirmare autem & confiteri nollet: Arrianam suâ sententiam, diu celauit, nō canore eferendo, quod debuerat, Gloria patri, & filio, & Spiritui sancto: Sed aliud fortassis, eius loco submurmurando. Perstringit {y}Euagrius Iustinum Imperatorē, quod ipse, Orthodoxis faueret, vxor vero eius Hæreticis; fortassis, inquit Euagrius, dedita vtérq; opera, vt vtriq; placerent generi. Odiosum sane istud, in priuata persona; in Rege odiosius; cui omnia, bona fide agendafunt; potissimū vero in Religionis negotiis. Quo fœdior erat, {z}Iuliani Apostatæ impostura; qui, vt Christianos milites, Idolis suis, reuerentiam quandā exhibere faceret, pecuniam suâ manu diuisurus, iuxta aram sessitat, cui simulachra adstabant, edicens, vt quicunq; nummos cuperet accipere, thura super altari, prius adoleret, incensumq; offerret. Cuius rei mysterium, sensumq; abditum, cum milites ignorarent, solumq; Imperatori præstandum esse officium crederent, fecerunt quam libentissime. Sed postea, cum in-fidias intellexissent, reversi, pecuniam proiecerunt, neque ea legepossidere voluerunt; ut manifeste ostenderent, quam perfecto odio, Idolomaniam detestarentur. Dignus sane is, qui gehennalibus manciparetur flammis, & digni illi, qui in perpetuam rei memoriam, fama celebrarentur; qui nec per insidias, simulachra colere tolerarent. Quibus ut adiunga-tur, is meretur, qui apud {a}Theodoretum, omnia dura tormenta subit, & misere excarnificatur, potius quam vel obolü, Idololatrico templo extruedo, aut reedificando donaret.
units.tr: II. It is nonetheless remarkable how much fraud in pretending religion has prevailed through all ages. In the time of Constantine, as Eusebius reports, heretics pretended to be Catholics when they were under pressure, and mingled themselves with the rest of the Catholics. Lest he provoke the anger of the Emperor, how much penance did Arius seem to perform? Did he pour out tears as if feigned? What creed did he forge for his faith, which nevertheless could be explained in either sense? With what strength did he, by writing and begging, labour so that he might be received into communion by the most holy bishop Alexander? And this was to be done the next day, when meanwhile, by divine judgment, he burst asunder in the middle. But what prayers, do we think, would he not have made, who refused to approach the sacrifices? Leontius, the Arian bishop, was a disciple like his master: since he did not dare openly to deny the equality of Christ with his Father, lest he be caught by the laws and punished, yet he was unwilling to affirm and confess it; he long concealed his Arian opinion, not by singing out loudly what he ought, Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, but perhaps by murmuring something else in its place. Evagrius censures the Emperor Justin, because he himself favoured the Orthodox, but his wife favoured the heretics; perhaps, says Evagrius, both of them worked at it so as to please each of their kin. That is surely odious in a private person; in a king it is more odious, since all things must be done in good faith by him, and especially in matters of religion. More foul still was the deception of Julian the Apostate, who, in order to make Christian soldiers show some reverence to his idols, sat beside an altar on which the statues stood, to distribute money with his own hand, and ordered that whoever wished to receive coins should first burn incense on the altar and offer it. The soldiers, not knowing the secret meaning of this, and believing that only the duty of paying respect to the Emperor was required, did it most willingly. But afterwards, when they understood the trick, they returned, threw the money away and would not keep it on such terms, so as to show plainly with how perfect a hatred they detested idolatry. Surely he deserved to be given over to the flames of hell, and those men deserve to be celebrated with lasting fame in memory of the event, who would not tolerate, even through trickery, the worship of images. To these may be added the man who, in Theodoret, undergoes all the harsh torments and is wretchedly tortured to pieces rather than give even a penny toward building or rebuilding an idolatrous temple.

units.la: 12. Infinita possem, in re isthac, utrorumque, & recusantium, & amplectentium, proferre exempla: istis tamen supersedens, non possum tacere, ingeniosos semper fuisse homines, & nunc esse, in iis tegendis, faciendis tamen, quibus sua adversaretur Religio; ut fierent tamen, suaderet commoditas, {b}Plutarchus, Ismeniam [?] quendam Thebanum memorat, qui, cum urbis suae nomine, ad Artaxerxem Persarum Regem, Legatus mitteretur; adorare, more Persarum, Graecis tamen invisissimo, iussus; ut & suis, sub praetextu, Regi vero etiam, specie satisfaceret, annulum e digito dimisit, inclinansque se, eum sustulit; sicque speciem adorantis praebuit.
units.tr: 12. In this matter I could bring forward countless examples, of both those who refused and those who embraced it. Yet passing these over, I cannot keep silent that ingenious men have always been, and still are, skilled at concealing things and at doing, while contrary to their own religion, the very things that convenience urged them to do. Plutarch records a certain Ismenias [?] of Thebes who, sent as envoy from his city to Artaxerxes, King of the Persians, was ordered to worship in the Persian manner, a thing most hateful to the Greeks. So that he might satisfy both his own people in appearance and the King in reality, he let a ring fall from his finger, and bending down, picked it up; thus he gave the appearance of one worshipping.

units.la: Non inferiori, quin sublimiori potius, illud gradu collocandum est, quod habet {c}Procopius, hunc in modum: Cum aliquando, magno praelio confliduri essent Hunni, & Persae, Persarumque sub Peroza Duce ita periclitaretur exercitus, ut extremum excidium metuendum esset, transfigere noluit hostis, aut incolumes dimittere, nisi Peroza ipsum Hunnorum Regem adoraret. Hic cum religionis gratia, nullo pacto consentire vellet Peroza, Magi consulunt, ut Soke [?] oriente, qui tum erat Persarum Deus, versus Hunnum tenderet, & ac si Regem veneraretur, Solem more Persico adoraret. Quod & factum est. Verendum est, ne profana nostra aetas, a talibus [?] exemplis non abhorruerit; cum aut qui se Religio-
units.tr: This deed must be placed not lower than the former, but rather on a higher step, as the one recorded by Procopius, in this manner: When the Huns and the Persians were once about to join in a great battle, and the Persian army under their general Peroz was in such danger that total destruction was to be feared, the enemy refused either to spare them or to let them go unharmed, unless Peroz himself worshipped the King of the Huns. When Peroz, for the sake of his religion, was unwilling to agree in any way, the Magi advised that, with the sun rising [?], which was then the god of the Persians, he should turn toward the Hun and, as if he were paying reverence to the King, worship the sun in the Persian manner. This he did. It is to be feared that our profane age has not shrunk from such examples, since either those who wish to be called Religious have entered the Masses, or those who falsely call themselves Catholics attend our prayers in a fraudulent manner, yet safely, as they themselves think.

units.la: fos dici volunt, Missas adierint, aut qui Catholicos, falso ta-men se nominant, nostris intersint precibus fraudulento modo, tuto tamen, vt ipsi cogitant. Cuiusmodi is est: acsi quis auribus cera obturatis templum ingrederetur, vt audire nihil posset, vel loco positus disiuncto, per vnam aut alteram horam, cum assidentibus, sermones conferret, nec lectis, aut edoctis attenderet: aut si domina sub mundo muliebri, ancillam suae personae non dissimilem vestiret, & ornaret, veloque, quod nostris foeminis vsitatum est, vultum obtegeret, vt sic legibus sub fuco occurratur: vel si hymnorum tempore, & Psalmorum, per Paulinam aedem iter quis capesseret, Londini, adhibitis duobus, pluribusve famulis, qui iuramento insidioso contestentur, se in templo dominum suum vidisse, precum tempore. Odiosa ista est apud Deum dissimulatio, qui non ficta, callidaq; ratione coli vult, sed aperta, & simplici. Aut ipsi totus adhaereto, aut totus abscedito. Sed omni caue modo, nec intus aliud, aliud foris, expositio, & de industria retineas. Tantum etenim ab eo abes, vt praemium, & mercedem eius à Deo auferas, vt inuisus potius ipsi reddare. Nam si id Achillis apud Homerum, alicubi locum obtineat: {d}
units.tr: Such is the case of one who entered a church with his ears stopped with wax, so that he could hear nothing, or who, having taken a place apart, spent an hour or two conversing with those sitting near him, and paid no attention to the readings or the teaching; or if a lady, dressed in worldly finery, clothed and adorned a maidservant not unlike her own person, and covered her face with a veil, as is customary for our women, so that she might thus slip past the laws under a disguise; or if, at the time of the hymns and psalms, someone made his way through St. Paul's church in London, with two or more servants present who would swear under a treacherous oath that they had seen their master in the church at the time of the prayers. Such dissimulation is hateful before God, who wishes to be worshipped not by feigned and crafty reasoning, but by open and simple means. Either cleave wholly to him, or wholly withdraw. But by all means beware lest you have one thing within and another outwardly, and keep this as a deliberate policy. For you are so far from gaining his reward and recompense from God that you make yourself rather hateful to him. For if that saying of Achilles in Homer holds anywhere:

units.la: Ἐχθρὸς γάρ μοί κεῖνος ὁμῶς Ἀΐδαο πύλῃσιν Ὅς χ᾽ ἕτερον μὲν κεύθει ἐνὶ φρεσὶν, ἄλλο δὲ βάζει. Inimicus enim ille mihi, aeque ac Inferorum portae: Qui aliud quidem occultat in mentibus, aliud vero dicit.
units.tr: Ἐχθρὸς γάρ μοί κεῖνος ὁμῶς Ἀΐδαο πύλῃσιν Ὅς χ᾽ ἕτερον μὲν κεύθει ἐνὶ φρεσὶν, ἄλλο δὲ βάζει. [Hateful to me as the gates of Hades is that man who hides one thing in his mind and says another.]

units.la: tum apud Deum certe; & in negotiis Religionis maxime: Necigitur palam, nec secreto Idololatrico cultui, vel cum consensu, vel cum consensus specie, praesens adesto. Dicoturfus, nec cum consensu, nec cum consensus specie, praesens adesto.
units.tr: it certainly holds before God, and most of all in matters of religion. Therefore one should be present neither openly nor secretly at idolatrous worship, either with consent or with the appearance of consent. I say, therefore, that one should be present neither with consent nor with the appearance of consent.

units.la: 13. Vbitamen (vtad nostri Naamanis causam, aliquando accedam propius, gradatim licet, & pedetentim, vt in re difficili) dum affirmem adstandum non esse, cum consensus vel specie, praesentiam omnem qualemcunq; interdicta non existimes. existimo. Siquidem vt de violenta coactione nihil dicam, vi quis robore compulsus, aut compedibus astrictus, interesse vrgeatur (vim patiens, vt in corporeo adulterio {e}Lucretia, vbi duo fuerant, vnus tamen adulter) rationes multæ occurrunt aliæ, secundum quas, adstare, & intueri permittitur. Si peregre proficiscens, per liberas Germaniæ, aut Poloniæ ciuitates, transiturus essem; & vt meipsum in circumstantiis particularibus erudirem, per fenestras, aut cancellos sacelli alicuius, vbi Missa priuata celebratur, otiosus spectator starem, quid fieret obseruans; & vt Sacrificio molestiam non exhiberem, sic nullam reuerentiæ, vel per genuflexionem, vel capitis detectionem, signum ederem, non dubito, quin tuta hoc posset facere conscientia. Neque etenim consentiens accedit, aut animus, aut actus meus Sacrificio. Ita, si ex occasione, reprehensurus venirem, in qua re, hominum san-ctissimorum facta, imitanda habemus. Cum {f}Jeroboamus aureis vitulis altaria erexisset, incensumq; obtulisset (qua in re, se insignis Idololatriæ reum constituit) accurrebat Propheta sacrificanti, & ex præcepto Dei accurrebat; sed vt iram Diuinam, in Regem, & in Aram seuere interminaretur, nō vt superstitiosæ impietati se commisceret. Elias Propheta, cum Dei maiestatem, debitamque gloriam, à sacrilego Baalis honore, distincta cuperet, in cōspectu multitudinis, Baalis sacerdotibus, se arbitrū quasi stitit, inspiciendo, alloquendo, obseruando, irridendo. Quis loco poterat esse cōiunctior, licet animo esset disiunctissimus, cum ipsorū circa altare saltationem, aut transcensionem potius, cum exclamationes sonoras egregie, cum fui sectionem, & cum cultris dilacerationes præsens aspiceret. Eliæ tamen pietas, zelus, cædes versus Baalitas, scopus, sermo, finis ad quem collimauit, à vel minima impietatis labecula, aut profanationis suspicione eximunt. Superstitionis nihilo erat magis incusandus, quam Magiæ Moses: cum incantatores Pharaonis, suas exerexercere præstigias, præsens animaduerteret. Sed & istis adiungendus est Paulus Apostolus, qui {h}Athenis, superstitiosa intueri non recusauerat. Apud Danielem vero aliquid est, quod ad causam nostram accedit proxime, licet in omnibus circumstantiis non consentiat. {i}Congregauit Rex Nabuchodonosor, præfectos, Legatos, Præsides, vbium & Proviinciarum suarum, vt coram aureo simulachro adoraturi, prostrati procuberent. Non manserunt domi suæ, tres pueri, Shadrach, Meshach, & Abednego: venire non repugnauerunt, in locum Idololatricum, & vbi actus Idololatrici præstandi essent: sed Regis placitum expectaturi, cum reliquis conuenirent. Vbi vero corpora incuruanda essent sua, & in faciem procidendum fuisset; ecce reliquis deiectis, hi soli stant, & mori potius elegerunt; quam vel minima corporis inclinatione, Idolum honorare. Quis præsentiam istorum, lingua mala, & petulanti, vituperabit, aut insectabitur, & non inflatis potius, vt aiunt, buccis, ipsorum constantiam, fortitudinem, magnanimitatem prædicabit, & vere admirabitur?
units.tr: 13. Yet (so that I may come a little closer, step by step and gradually, as in a difficult matter, to the case of our Naaman) while I affirm that one must not stand by with consent or its appearance, do not think that I forbid every kind of presence whatsoever. I think not. For, to say nothing of violent compulsion, if someone is forced by strength, or bound in fetters, and is compelled to be present (suffering violence, as Lucretia did in the case of bodily adultery, where there were two, yet only one was the adulterer), many other reasons occur, according to which it is permitted to stand by and look on. If, travelling abroad through the free cities of Germany or Poland, I were about to pass through, and in order to instruct myself in particular circumstances, I were to stand idly as an observer at the windows or grille of some chapel where a private Mass is celebrated, watching what is done; and so that I would not cause trouble for the sacrifice, I were to give no sign of reverence, either by genuflection or by uncovering my head, I do not doubt that I could do this with a safe conscience. For neither my mind nor my action joins itself in consent to the sacrifice. Likewise, if I came on the occasion to rebuke, we have in this matter the deeds of most holy men to imitate. When Jeroboam had set up altars with golden calves and offered incense (in which matter he made himself guilty of notorious idolatry), the prophet ran up to the one sacrificing, and ran up by command of God; yet he ran up to threaten the divine wrath severely against the king and the altar, not to mingle himself in superstitious impiety. The prophet Elijah, when he wished the majesty of God and the honour due to Him to be kept distinct from the sacrilegious honour of Baal, stood in the sight of the multitude, as it were a judge, among the priests of Baal, looking on, speaking, observing, and mocking. What place could be more closely joined to them, even though his mind was most distant from them, than where he saw with his own eyes their leaping about the altar, or rather their crossing over it, their loud shouts, their self-laceration, and their tearing with knives? Yet Elijah's piety, zeal, and slaughter of the Baal-worshippers, his aim, his speech, and the end he aimed at, free him from even the slightest stain of impiety or suspicion of profanation. Moses was no more to be accused of superstition than of magic, when he saw the sorcerers of Pharaoh present, performing their tricks. To these must also be joined the Apostle Paul, who at Athens had not refused to look at superstitious things. In Daniel there is something which comes very close to our cause, although it does not agree in all its circumstances. King Nebuchadnezzar gathered together the prefects, legates, governors, and rulers of his provinces, so that they might fall prostrate and worship before a golden image. The three boys, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, did not remain at home: they did not refuse to come into the idolatrous place, where the idolatrous acts were to be performed; but, waiting for the king's pleasure, they met with the rest. But when their bodies were to be bowed and they were to fall on their faces, behold, while the others were cast down, these alone stood, and chose rather to die than to honour the idol by the least bending of the body. Who would revile or assail the presence of these men with a malicious and wanton tongue, and would not rather, as people say, puff out their cheeks and proclaim and truly admire their constancy, courage, and magnanimity?

units.la: 14. Ista igitur aperte docent, Naamanem in eo simpliciter non peccasse, quod Rimmonis limina calcârit, aut simulachrum aspexerit (vt de eo, tanquam facto disputemus, quod futurum Naaman credidit) nisi aliquid adiungeretur aliud. Si animo accessisset Hypocritico, aut obsequio vllo superstitioso, reuerentiam Idolo exhibuisset; excusari tum non poterat. & Profitetur tamen apud Helizæum, se alienum non {k}culturum Deum, sed Iehouam tantum. Mala igitur mente, nihil factum est. Is solus scrupulus animo inhæret, num, vt Ciuile, Politicum, Obsequiosum præstaret officium, non Religiosum, adesse liceret. Ex Ciuili munere, siue Aulico, a Regis latere discedendum ei nō fuerat, vt qui fortassis, summus ei esset Cubicularius, æque atque Militiæ {l}Præfectus, Cum ad superstitiosum exercendum cultum, Rex templum ingrederetur, incubuit Naami, illiusque est innixus manui, siue imbecillitatis causa, quatenus senex esset; siue maiestatis, quatenus Rex. Hic cum commode, non posset Princeps adoraturus Rimmonem, eius manu, manum suam iniicere, nisi genua flectendo, etiam Naaman se in-curuaret, veritus est Naaman, ne illa ipsius incuruatio, quæ Regi facta est, pro adoratione simulachri haberetur. Et ista cogitatio, mordere conscientiā & pungere videtur. Prophe-tæ responsio ambigua est, & quæ materiam huius argumenti ventilandi, nonnullis suppeditauit: Itopace; quod aliqui interpretatū volunt, vt non responsio, vlla ex parte, quæstioni fit, sed mera valedictio, ad rem ipsam non habito respectu. Alij, Itopace, id est, Orabo pro te, ne hoc crimē tibi imputetur, aut vt in via vel posthac, tibi animus immutetur, ne ista facias. Ita & Naamane obsecrante faciunt, vt pro eo Propheta apud Deum intercederet, cui respondet, Itopace, id est, hoc tibi annuo: orabo pro te. Et adiiciunt, quis scit, si Naaman, Elizei precibus apud Dominum intercedentibus, ita conuertere-tur, vt vel officio suo cederet, vel tantum in accessu ad Idolū abstineret, & conscientiam suam, fidemq; in Iehouam, manifesto profiteretur. Itopace, habent aliqui, id est, Deus tibi felix iter, faustumq; impertiat, sed non dicit Elizæus, ito, & sic facito, vel consilium dando, vel approbando. Sed harum interpretationum aliquot, rem in medio relinquunt, dum simpliciter pro se ferant valedictionem, sine responsione aliqua. Alij è coniectura loquuntur: nam si velimus cedere, Prophetam pro eo orauisse, æque illud esse poterat, vt Dominus illi tranquillitatem animi in re licita donaret, atq; in re mala immutationem. Iis, qui nec laudasse, nec iussisse, nec approbasse asserunt, facile occurritur; cum dicetur, Prophetam e-cōtra nullo modo factum prohibuisse, vituperasse, aut refutasse. Ita omnia adhuc sunt incerta, & dubij hic feruntur viri doctissimi. Solum illud superest quod bis geminauerit mihi Dominus sit misericors, vbi veniam videtur petere, vt in causa non legitima. Verum teneram id arguit cofcientiam, non edoctam satis, & informatam, quid reuera nefas esset, & simpliciter non liceret; quæ cum tamen pia esset, & devotionis plenissima, scrupulo cito percellitur, & vel minimâ offensiunculam libenter non dat. Nihil igitur certi, ex contextu elicitur. Quod ad caput ergo quæstionis attinet.
units.tr: 14. These things, therefore, plainly teach that Naaman did not sin simply in this, that he trod on the threshold of Rimmon or looked at the image (let us discuss this as an act which Naaman believed would happen), unless something else were added. If he had come with a hypocritical mind, or with any superstitious compliance, and had shown reverence to the idol, he could not then be excused. And yet he professes before Elisha that he will not worship any other god, but Jehovah only. Therefore nothing was done with an evil mind. This alone troubles his mind: whether, in the course of performing a civil, political, and dutiful service, and not a religious one, he might be allowed to be present. By reason of his civil office, or his court post, he could not have left the king's side, since he was perhaps the chief of his chamberlains, just as he was prefect of the army. When the king entered the temple to perform the superstitious worship, Naaman leaned on him and rested upon his hand, either because of weakness, inasmuch as he was old, or because of majesty, inasmuch as he was king. Here, since the prince, about to worship Rimmon, could not conveniently lay his hand on his hand without bending his knees, Naaman feared that he too would bow himself, and that this bowing of his, made to the king, would be taken for worship of the image. And this thought seems to bite and prick his conscience. The prophet's answer is ambiguous, and has supplied some with material for discussing this question: Itopace; which some wish to be understood as follows: that it is not a reply in any respect to the question, but a mere farewell, with no regard had to the matter itself. Others take Itopace to mean: I will pray for you, so that this crime may not be imputed to you, or so that in the way, or hereafter, your mind may be changed, so that you do not do these things. So they also do when Naaman entreats, that the prophet might intercede for him with God; to which he replies, Itopace, that is: I grant you this, I will pray for you. And they add: who knows whether, with Elisha's prayers interceding with the Lord, Naaman might be so converted that he would either give way in his office, or only abstain from approaching the idol, and openly profess his conscience and his faith in Jehovah. Some have Itopace to mean: may God grant you a happy journey and a prosperous course; but Elisha does not say, go and so do it, either by giving counsel or by approving. But some of these interpretations leave the matter open, while they simply take the words as a farewell, without any answer. Others speak from conjecture: for if we were to grant that the prophet prayed for him, it could equally be that the Lord would grant him tranquillity of mind in a lawful matter, and a change in an evil one. To those who assert that he neither praised, nor commanded, nor approved, it is easily answered that the prophet, on the contrary, in no way forbade, blamed, or refuted what was done. Thus all things are still uncertain here, and learned men are carried in different directions. Only this remains: that he twice repeated The Lord be merciful to me, where he seems to ask pardon, as in a case not lawful. But this indicates a tender conscience, not sufficiently taught and instructed as to what was really wrong and simply not allowed; and since it was nonetheless pious and full of devotion, it is quickly struck by scruple, and does not willingly give even the smallest offence. Nothing certain, therefore, is drawn from the context. Let us now come, then, to the head of the question.

units.la: 15. Ecclesiæ Europæ, quantum ego indagando inuestigare possum, in hoc cardine rem omnem vertunt; vt ob Politica obeunda munia, si quis vocetur; aut si ex onere officij quod sustinet, illud ipsi incumbat onus; Ciuilis obedientiæ gratia, non Religiosæ, possit interesse; ita tamen, vt nec gestu, nec voce, Idololatricis spurcitiis honorem cedat. Vbi primo aduertendū est, oportere ex officio illu[?] accede-re: in qua causa illud est, ac si serenissima Regina nostra, dum facellū Regium cum solenni pompa adeat, viro nobili, alias Pontificio, gladiū Regalem gestare, imperaret. Nam cū sui sit arbitrij, ad illud munus, quemlibet destinare; ad obedientiam experiendam, vel animi sui gratia, & cuipiam tali, pro arbitrio eam prouinciam imponat. In hac causa per 12. Delega-tos suos, Concilium Trident, Nobilibus permisit, vt fine cō- trouersia, id munus exequatur, si {m}Howletti libro supra ci-tato, velimus fide adhibere. Is author, sub quatuor certis cō-ditionibus, quas Qualificationes appellat, licere Orthodoxo, ad Hæreticorum Ecclesiam, tempore Liturgiæ suæ accedere, ex præcepto Principis, demonstrat: vt si quis, cum reliquis Consiliariis, aut Deputatis, Paulinam ædem adire, Londini iuberetur; Primo, inquit, propter merum sit temporale, vel ciuile negotium. Secundo, ob particulare aliquod Politicum negotium, Tertio, ea causa conueniendi, palam cognita sit, ne ignorantibus scandalum pariatur. Quarto, nullum exhibeatur reuerētiæ signum, aut genu flectendo, aut caput detegendo. Quod permisit Concil, Trid, id exercet aula Regia apud nos; neq; Proceres omnium partium rem aliter inter-pretari solent, ut sio opus esset, amplissimis testimoniis, & ex-perientiis, liceret confirmare. Deerat hoc Officium, Ciui-lecq; negotium, Nobilibus multis e numero Protestantium, cum aliquando Carolus Quintus, summiq; Imperij Electo-res, {m}Augustæ congregarentur. Ibi cum Imperator ex zelo suo, ante omnia tetata[?], aut proposita Reip. negotia, Missam audire solennem cuperet, ad templi usq; fores, e reformata Religione, multi Principes, eunte comitati sunt; ulterius autem pergere renuerunt. Si ipsis, ex ciuili aliquo, quod gestassent[?] munere, incubuissent, personæ Principis, inter sacra ad-stare, puto sane non abnuissent. Id quod in Duce Saxonie, eo tempore expertum est: quod cum nobile sit exemplum, nō pigebit breuissime, rem ab initio repetere, & cōmemorare,
units.tr: 15. The churches of Europe, so far as I can discover by investigation, turn the whole matter on this hinge: that for the performance of political duties, if someone is summoned to them, or if the burden of the office he bears falls upon him, he may be present out of civil obedience, not religious; but in such a way that he yields honour neither by gesture nor by voice to the idolatrous filth. Here it must first be noted that he ought to go by virtue of his office. In this case it is as if our most serene Queen, when she goes to the royal chapel with solemn pomp, were to order a noble, otherwise a Papist, to carry the royal sword. For since it is at her discretion to assign anyone to that duty, she may impose that task, at her pleasure, upon whomever she likes, either to test his obedience or for the sake of his own spirit. On this matter, through its twelve delegates, the Council of Trent permitted the nobles to perform that duty without controversy, if we are willing to give credit to Howlett in the book cited above. That author, under four fixed conditions, which he calls qualifications, shows that it is lawful for an Orthodox man, by command of the prince, to attend the church of the heretics at the time of their liturgy: as, for example, if someone, with the other councillors or deputies, were ordered to go to St Paul's in London. First, he says, the reason must be purely temporal or civil business. Second, it must be for some particular political business. Third, the reason for assembling must be openly known, so that it gives no scandal to those who are ignorant. Fourth, no sign of reverence is to be shown, either by kneeling or by uncovering the head. What the Council of Trent permitted, the royal court among us practises; nor do the nobles of all parties usually interpret the matter otherwise, as could be confirmed by the most ample testimonies and experiences if there were need. This duty and civil business was lacking to many nobles of the Protestant party when Charles V and the chief electors of the Empire were at one time gathered at Augsburg. There, when the Emperor, out of his zeal, wished to hear the solemn Mass before all the affairs of the state were taken up or proposed, many princes of the reformed religion accompanied him as far as the doors of the church, but refused to go any further. If they had applied themselves to some civil duty which they had undertaken, I think they would certainly not have refused to stand among the sacred rites in attendance upon the person of the prince. This was experienced in the Duke of Saxony at that time; and since it is a noble example, I will not hesitate to recount the matter briefly from the beginning.

units.la: 16. {o}Carolus ille Quartus, Romanorum Imperator, qui modum, & ordinem, Imperatoris Germaniæ eligendi, & honorandi condidit, in solenni illo Edicto, quod Bulla Aurea nuncupatur, ut septem destinauit Electores, Bohemiæ Regè, Archiepiscopos tres, totidemq; Seculares, uti nominant, Principes, ita certum cuiq; constituit munus, ad uberiorem Cæsareæ Maiestatis dignitatem & amplitudinem: Bohemiæ Regem, Sacratissimi Imperij Archipincernam, Archiepiscopum Coloniensem, per Italiam, Archicancellarium; Archiepiscopum Treuirensem, per Galliam & Regnum Arelatense Archicancellarium; Arohiepiscopū Moguntinum, per Germaniam, Imperij etiam Archicancellarium: Comitem Palatinum Rheni, sacri Imperij Archidapiferum; Ducem Saxoniæ, Archimarescallum; Marchionem Brandeburgensem, Archicamerarium. His omnibus, cum honoris multa tribuat insignia, tum potissimum capite sequenti, cuius Titulus est, De ordine processionis Principum Electorum, & per quos insignia deportentur. Saxoniæ Duci id speciatim donat, ut Regalem ensem deferat, & cum eo, Imperatorem torem, seu Regem Romanorum immediate praecedat. Quod cum facere, Duces Saxoniae soleant, abillo usq; tempore; nominatimque, & expresse praecipiatur, cum processio sit[?] ad res sacras, verissimum est, Caroli Quinti tempore, motam fuisse Quaestionem hanc, ex parte Ducis Saxoniae; num ob Civile obeundum munus, liceret Missae interesse? Cui {p}responsio ea, à Melanethone, caeterisque Theologis data est, licere adesse, quod ad suum officium, esset evocatus, non ad Missam, velut ad cultum Divinum. Cui acquivit Saxo, & cum Georgio Brandenburgico solo, ingressus est, reliquis Protestantium foris stantibus. Ubi, ultra omnem controversiam satis pie, res transacta est, si aperta Protestatione, vel scripto, vel voce edita, non Religionis gratia, se hoc facere contestaretur. Id, quod tanquam Theologus, viris omnibus nobilibus faciendum suaderem, si causa simili teneantur; ut Protestationem nempe, de ratione consilii sui facerent, ut & suae famae, & conscientiae aliorum infirmiorum consulere censeantur. De Duce Saxoniae, parum refert, num verbis specialibus, de facto isto cauerit, cum e generali Protestatione, contra Religionem Romanam (unde & ipse, & alii confoederati, primo Protestantes dicti sunt) animi sui sententiam prius aperuisset.
units.tr: 16. That Charles IV, Emperor of the Romans, who established the manner and order of electing and honouring the Emperor of Germany, in that solemn edict which is called the Golden Bull, appointed seven electors, the King of Bohemia, three archbishops and as many secular princes, as they are called, and assigned to each a fixed office, for the greater dignity and amplitude of the Imperial Majesty: the King of Bohemia as Arch-cupbearer of the most sacred Empire; the Archbishop of Cologne as Arch-chancellor through Italy; the Archbishop of Trier as Arch-chancellor through Gaul and the kingdom of Arles; the Archbishop of Mainz as Arch-chancellor through Germany, also of the Empire; the Count Palatine of the Rhine as Arch-steward of the holy Empire; the Duke of Saxony as Arch-marshal; the Margrave of Brandenburg as Arch-chamberlain. To all of these, while he bestows many marks of honour, he especially gives them in the following chapter, whose title is: On the order of procession of the Electoral Princes, and by whom the insignia are carried. He grants this specifically to the Duke of Saxony, that he should carry the royal sword, and with it immediately precede the Emperor or the King of the Romans. Since the Dukes of Saxony have always done this from that time onward, and it is expressly and by name prescribed, and since the procession was to sacred things, it is very true that in the time of Charles V the question was raised on the part of the Duke of Saxony: whether, for the sake of performing a civil duty, it would be lawful to be present at Mass? To this, the answer was given by Melanchthon and the other theologians: it is lawful to be present, since he was summoned to his office, not to the Mass as to divine worship. The Saxon agreed to this, and entered with George of Brandenburg alone, the rest of the Protestants standing outside. In this case, the matter was settled quite piously beyond all controversy, if he had openly declared, either in writing or by voice, that he was doing this not for the sake of religion. This is what I would advise all noblemen, as a theologian, to do if they are bound in a similar case: namely, that they make a protestation about the reason for their action, so that they may be considered to provide both for their own reputation and for the conscience of weaker brethren. Concerning the Duke of Saxony, it matters little whether he took care to say this in special words about that act, since he had earlier made known the sentiment of his mind in a general protestation against the Roman religion (whence he himself and the other confederates were first called Protestants).

units.la: 17. Secundo observandum est, nullum reverentiae signum mysteriis impiis exhibendum esse. Nam, si quando non postulat executio Civilis officii, cum reliquis genu flectétibus, inter elevationem hostiae, ut appellant, aut ad rem similem, nos velimus incurvare; Religiosum nunc autsuperstitiosum servitium praestitimus, & in apertam offensionem incurrimus. Imo si nolentibus nobis, fiat aliquid, quod honorem Idolo addat, ex nostra parte, aperte reclamandum est, ut ad rem abominandam. {q}Theodoretus insigniter memorabile habet exemplum, Valentiniani, qui postea Imperator designatus est, Is cum militum hastatorum, in Palatio Juliani Apostatę merentium, Tribunus esset, è dignitatis ratione, Imperatorem fuerat præcessurus. Julianus ad Fortunæ fanū profecturus cum esset(id quod inter choreas,& saltationem fecerat)non recusat Valentinianus(vt ex munere Ciuili oportuit)antecedere, adeoque templum ingredi. Sed cum more receptum fuerat, vt Ædituii accedentes, aqua lustrali, quotquot ingrederentur, spargerent, venit vnus, qui & Valentinianum lustraret. Is autem, vbi vidit aquæ guttam, suæ lævæ aspersam, pugnis cædit Ædituum, seq; inde non expiatum, sed turpi labe pollutum clamitat. Quod factum cum tyrannus execrabilis Julianus conspicaretur, in exilium eum relegavit. Homo vere Christianus, qui Ciuilem obedientiā, in re, & loco profanis ostendit, sed à Simulachrorum honore, illibatam conscientiā custodiuit. Vt cæteri pugno feriant, non requirimus, sed detestationem suam manifestam faciant. Quæ de Nobilibus & Officiariis, versus Principem suum dicta sunt, de aliis minoris conditionis, etiam sunt intelligenda. Ancillæ, ad dominæ pedes inuigilanti & ministranti, necessitas ingruit, vt, sicut alibi, dominæ vestes magnificentio-res à tergo ferat, sic in templum, vbi Missa contaminata canitur. Si tanquam heræ, magistræq; pedissequa velit ingredi, non vetatur: sin corporea submissione, genu-flexione, in-curuatione, vel minimum rei deferat obsequium, male factum est. Ea vero excepta reuerentia, vt pergat, non impedimus. Et hæc aperta est {r}PetriMartyris sententia, de pedissequa, quæ & alia de Nobilibus necessario includit.
units.tr: 17. Second, it must be observed that no sign of reverence is to be shown to impious mysteries. For if the execution of a civil office does not require it, and we were to bow ourselves along with the others who kneel during the elevation of the host, as they call it, or at some similar thing, we would have rendered religious or superstitious service and would incur open offence. Indeed, if, against our will, something is done that adds honour to an idol, we must openly protest on our part, as against an abominable thing. Theodoret gives a remarkably memorable example of Valentinian, who was afterwards designated Emperor. He was then tribune of the spearmen serving in the palace of Julian the Apostate, and by reason of his rank he was to walk before the Emperor. When Julian was about to go to the shrine of Fortune (which he had done amid dances and leaping), Valentinian did not refuse, as his civil office required, to go before him, and so to enter the temple. But since it was the custom that the attendants, as those entering came in, sprinkled them with lustral water, one came who sprinkled Valentinian too. He, however, when he saw a drop of water sprinkled on his left side, struck the attendant with his fists, and cried out that he had been not cleansed but polluted by a shameful stain. When the detestable tyrant Julian saw this deed, he banished him into exile. He was a truly Christian man, who showed civil obedience in a profane matter and place, but kept his conscience unharmed from honouring images. We do not require that others strike with their fists, but that they make their detestation plain. What has been said of nobles and officials toward their prince must also be understood of others of lower rank. Should a maidservant, attending and waiting on her mistress's feet, be under the necessity, as elsewhere, of carrying her mistress's finer garments behind her, so in the temple where the defiled Mass is sung: if she wishes to enter as a companion of her mistress and as a mistress's attendant, she is not forbidden; but if by bodily submission, by genuflexion or bowing, she pays even the slightest service, it is wrongly done. Yet, with that reverence excepted, we do not hinder her from going on. And this is the plain opinion of Peter Martyr concerning the attendant, which also necessarily includes other matters concerning nobles.

units.la: 18. Noua ista non sunt, quorum similia, magna ex parte, in tribus pueris apud Danielem, & in Valentiniano comperimus. Aliena non sunt, quæ Germanicis Theologis tanta celebritate congregatis, quæ Regno nostro, & Reip. Anglicanæ, quæ Petro Martyri; ita quæ Howletto, imo Concilio Tridentino, vel eius Delegatis, post deliberationem placuerunt: Quod si cuiquam, vel noua, vel aliena videantur, sciat vnum è veteribus disserte[?] approbasse. Et vt ingenue fa-tear, quod res est, è remota Ecclesiæ antiquitate, vnum so-lum, modica lectione adhuc reperi, qui de istis ex professo, imo obiter disserit. Is est /Tertullianus, libro suo de Idololatria, cuius, quoniam tam apertum est iudicium, sicque cum nostro instituto faciens, non pigebit verba referre. Vtinam quidem, inquit, nec videre possimus, quæ facere nobis nefas est. Sed quoniam ita malis circumdedit seculum Idololatria, licebit adesse in quibusdam, quæ nos homini, non Idolo officiosos habent. Plane ad Sacerdotium, aut Sacrificium vocatus, non ibo; proprium enim Idoli officium est; Sed neque consilio, neque sumptu, aliave opera, in eiusmodi fungar. Si propter Sacrificium vocatus, adsistam, ero particeps Idololatriæ; si me alia causa coniungit sacrificanti, ero tantum spectator sacrificij. Caeterum quid facient servi, vel liberi fideles, item Officiales, sacrificantibus dominis suis, vel Patronis, vel Præsidibus adhærentes. Sed si merum quis sacrificanti tradiderit, imo si verbo quoque aliquo, sacrificio necessario, adiuuerit, minist.er habebitur Idololatriæ. Huius regula memores, etiam Magistratibus, & Potestatibus, officium possumus reddere, secundum Patriarchas, & cateros Maiores, qui Regibus Idolo-lolatris, usque ad finem Idololatriæ apparuerunt. Hæc manifesta est Tertulliani sententia, cum nostra conueniens: hi-cere adesse, in quibusdam, quæ nos homini, non Idolo, officiosos habent. Et secundum ista, de Naamanis facto, (si modo id factum fuerat, quod futurum ipse præ se tulerat) iudicium damus; videlicet, si ob honorem solum, Regi suo domino cedendum, templum ingrederetur, ipsum non peccâsse; præsertim, si de pietate, in Iehouam vnicum, professionem edidisset: sin cum vllo ad Idolum obsequio, aut obsequij specie, accessisset, non potuisse excusari.
units.tr: 18. These things are not new; we find similar things to a great extent in the three boys in Daniel, and in Valentinian. Nor are they foreign to the Germans, who gathered in such great celebrity, nor to our kingdom and the English commonwealth, nor to Peter Martyr; likewise they pleased Howlett, indeed the Council of Trent or its delegates, after deliberation. But if to anyone these things seem either new or foreign, let him know that one of the ancients has clearly approved them. And to confess ingenuously what is the case: from the remote antiquity of the Church I have found only one, after a modest reading, who discusses these matters professedly, or indeed incidentally. This is Tertullian, in his book on Idolatry, whose judgment is so plain and so agrees with our purpose that I will not hesitate to quote his words. Would indeed, he says, that we could not even see what it is unlawful for us to do. But since the age is surrounded by so many evils of idolatry, it will be lawful to be present at certain things which hold us as officials to the man, not to the idol. Plainly, if called to the priesthood or to the sacrifice, I will not go; for it is the proper office of the idol. Nor will I serve in such a capacity by counsel, expense, or any other work. If I should be present because I was called on account of the sacrifice, I shall be a sharer in the idolatry; if another cause joins me to the one sacrificing, I shall be merely a spectator of the sacrifice. Otherwise, what shall servants or free believers do, or officials who attend their masters, patrons or governors while they sacrifice? But if someone hands over a mere thing to the one sacrificing, or even if by some word he assists the sacrifice that is necessarily required, he will be held a minister of idolatry. Mindful of this rule, we can also render service to magistrates and powers, after the example of the patriarchs and other great men who appeared before idolatrous kings right up to the end of idolatry. This is the plain opinion of Tertullian, agreeing with ours: that it is lawful to be present at certain things which hold us as officials to the man, not to the idol. And according to these principles we give judgment on the deed of Naaman (if indeed it was done as he had himself foreshadowed): namely, that if he entered the temple only out of honour, to yield to his lord the king, he did not sin, especially if he had professed, out of piety, that he worshipped Jehovah alone; but if he had approached with any obedience to the idol, or the appearance of obedience, he could not be excused.

units.la: 19. Si obiiciantur alia, non est difficile respondere. Vt si interrogetur, quamobrem potius relicta patria, non accessit Hierosolymam, vbi à tali periculo, scrupuloque omni immunis esse poterat; & quare ipsi Elizæus id non præ-ceperit? occurrit Petrus Martyr, & tres assignat rationes. Prima est, vt doceret, omni loco liberum esse, Deum colere; tam Naamani in Syris, quam Judæis, Hierosolymis. Secunda est, vt fama gloriaq; Dei, tam inter Aramitas, & Gentes, quam apud suos celebraretur, id, quod ex eius reditu in patriam, necesse erat fieri. Et tertia, quia isto tempore, Hierosolyma conspurcata esset, vt, si migraret in locum nihilo melio-rem, se subduceret, Istis igitur de causis, in sua patria voluit Naamanem manere Deus. Quod si vlterius vrgeatur;
units.tr: 19. If other objections are raised, it is not hard to answer them. For example, if someone asks why Naaman, having left his homeland, did not go to Jerusalem, where he could have been free of such danger and every scruple, and why Elisha did not prescribe this to him, Peter Martyr comes forward and assigns three reasons. The first is that he might teach that God may be worshipped in any place, by Naaman among the Syrians just as by the Jews at Jerusalem. The second is that the fame and glory of God might be celebrated, both among the Aramaeans and the Gentiles and among his own people, which had to happen from his return to his homeland. And the third is that at that time Jerusalem was defiled, so that if he had moved to a place no better, he would have withdrawn himself. For these reasons, then, God willed that Naaman remain in his own country. But if the objection is pressed further:

units.la: Cum ergo rediisset, officio suo, munerique Politico, recte poterat cedere, sicque magis, scrupulo isto, animum eximere, & liberare. Negare non possumus, quin, si suæ[?] non potuisset satisfaceret conscientiæ, recte fecisset, si dignitate discef-fisset, id, quod olim {u}Iouianus, qui postea Imperator fuerat, apud Julianum Apostatam, fecerat: Sin ex simplici scientia, & non ficta, aut dissimulata, se à spurcitie immunè inuenisset conseruatum, quid ni libere frueretur dignitate sua, vt apud Pharaonem Joseph, apud Artaxerxe Nehemiah, apud Assuerum Esthera, apud Babylonium Daniel. Pij etenim homines, cum Principibus etiam malis propinqui sint, & bona promouere, & malis remoram obiicere, multoties possint. Et in istis efficiendis, vt malis peragendum non est mediis, quo pij succedat aliquid, sic cauendum est, ne Ecclesiæ desint, vel potius Deo, qui tali eos vt {x}Estheram fortassis, collocauit loco, quo eius gloriam sartam tectam, & incolumē, pro virili sua parte tuerentur. Sicq; cū de Naamane isto, quid senserim, docuerim, orandum puto Deum, vt puro nos spiritu, per omnē vitā dirigat, primoq; innocentiæ, & integritatis donum, deinde de prudentiæ, & cœlestis sapientiæ, velit impertire, vt {y}pie, iuste, sobrie degentes in hoc seculo, & beatā spem expectemus, & apparitionem gloriæ consecutemur, per Christum Iesum, cui cum Patre, & Spiritu Sancto, sit honor, & gloria, nunc, & in secula seculorum, Amen.
units.tr: Since, therefore, he had returned, he could rightly give up his duty and his political office, and so free himself and release his mind from that scruple. We cannot deny that, if he could not satisfy his conscience, he would have acted rightly by leaving his dignity, as Jovian, who afterwards became emperor, once did under Julian the Apostate. But if, from simple and unfeigned knowledge, he found himself preserved free from the defilement, why should he not freely enjoy his dignity, as Joseph did under Pharaoh, Nehemiah under Artaxerxes, Esther under Ahasuerus, and Daniel under the Babylonian king? For godly men, since they are near even evil princes, can very often both advance good things and place a check on evil. And in bringing these things about, just as evil means must not be used so that something good may follow, so care must be taken that the Church is not left without them, or rather, without God, who perhaps placed such people, as Esther, in a position where they could guard his glory intact, safe and sound, as far as lies in their power. And so, having taught what I think about this Naaman, I think we should pray God that he would direct us in every part of life by his pure Spirit, and that he would first grant the gift of innocence and integrity, then of prudence and heavenly wisdom, so that, living piously, justly and soberly in this age, we may await the blessed hope and obtain the appearing of glory, through Christ Jesus, to whom with the Father and the Holy Spirit be honour and glory, now and for ever and ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT QVINTVM. DE FVGA MINISTRI, IN persecutione, aut peste.
units.tr: CHAPTER FIVE. ON THE FLIGHT OF A MINISTER, IN PERSECUTION, OR PLAGUE.

units.la: Act. 9. 23. Expletis autem multis diebus, inierunt simul Iudaei consilium, Saulum interimendi.
units.tr: Acts 9:23. Now when many days were fulfilled, the Jews took counsel together to kill him.

units.la: 24 Sed intellecta sunt Saulo insidiae eorum: adseruabant autem portas, die ac nocte, ut eum interimerent.
units.tr: 24 But their laying in wait was known to Saul. And they watched the gates day and night, that they might kill him.

units.la: 25 Acceptum igitur eum discipuli nocte, per murum demiserunt, su-ne submissum in sporta.
units.tr: 25 Then the disciples took him by night and let him down through the wall, lowering him in a basket.

units.la: 1. 3. Causae Paulum ad fugam impellentes. 4. 5. 6. 7. laico in persecutione licet fugere. 8. Non sic Ministro gregis. 11. Exempla, & rationes, pro fuga pastoris, ducuntur, & soluuntur. 17. Laico pestis tempore licet diuertere. 19. Sed ministro manendum est.
units.tr: 1–3. The causes impelling Paul to flee. 4–7. In persecution a layman may flee. 8. Not so the minister of the flock. 11. Examples and reasons for the flight of a pastor are adduced and resolved. 17. In time of plague a layman may turn aside. 19. But a minister must remain.

units.la: ERISSIMVM illud est, Iohannis Baptistae, a posse Deum ex lapidibus, excitare filios Abrahamo. Qui enim illos, ad fidem in Christum conuerterit, quorum corda silice, & adamante fuerint duriora, ipsisque cautibus (quod ad pietatem spectat) asperiora, recte filios e saxis, credenti Abrahae dicatur excitare. Cuius si in alio quoquam, in Paulo Apostolo, periculum factum est qui cum caedem & sanguinem, aduersus omnes Saluatorem profitentes, spiraret: literisque rogatu suo, a summo Sacerdote acceptis, minabundus Damascum versus proficiscebatur: ut omnes eius vias, arreptos, vinculisque onustos, Hierosolymam abduceret, incarcerandos, accusandos, occidendos, praecellenti de coelo lumine, tanquam fulgure, perstrictus oculis, voceq; coelitus emissa, perculsus corde: lupū exuit subito, induitque agnum: animoque penitus immuta-tus, post colloquium, cum Anania quodam habitum ( cuius manu visum receperat, & sacris Baptismi aquis expiatus fuerat) in Christi praeconizationem, singularemque eius gloriae dilatatione erupit. Ita, per conspicuam Dei misericordiam, deceptus est Satanas, qui cum leonem, tigridemque rapacem, aduersus Christi fideles, se crederet emisse, qui lanienam virorum, foeminarum, omnium faceret, proque virili sua, Ecclesiam sanctorum radicitus extirparet, molisque ipsa fundamenta subrueret, pro Christo pugilem, & Coryphaeum quendam, Antesignanum celeberrimum reuera dedit, cuius, in multis millibus, nescio an orbe toto, vix quisquam similem reperire posset. Maligno siquidem deposito furore, concionari coeperat, publiceque denunciare, Iesum Christum Dei magni esse vnigenitum, idque publice, & priuatim sermone prae se ferre, argumentis veritatem demonstrando, & Iudaeos peruicaces, vi ipsa Scripturarum peruincendo.
units.tr: That saying of John the Baptist is very remarkable, that God is able to raise up children to Abraham from the stones. For he who converts to faith in Christ those whose hearts are harder than flint and adamant, and rougher than the rocks themselves as far as piety is concerned, may rightly be said to raise up children from stones to Abraham who believed. If this was tested in anyone else, in the Apostle Paul it was: he who breathed slaughter and blood against all who professed the Saviour, and, having received letters from the high priest at his request, was setting out threateningly toward Damascus, intending to lead away in chains to Jerusalem all whom he found on the way, men and women, to be imprisoned, accused and put to death. Struck down by a light from heaven surpassing the sun, as if by lightning, with his eyes dazzled, and by a voice sent from heaven, struck to the heart, he suddenly cast off the wolf and put on the lamb; his mind was wholly changed, and after a conversation with a certain Ananias (by whose hand he had recovered his sight and had been cleansed by the holy waters of baptism) he broke out into the proclamation of Christ and the wide spreading of his singular glory. Thus, through the conspicuous mercy of God, Satan was deceived. He had believed he had released a lion and a ravening tigress against the faithful of Christ, one who would make a butchery of men and women of every kind, and who, as far as in him lay, would root out the Church of the saints and undermine its very foundations; yet he gave instead a champion for Christ, a certain leader and most famous standard-bearer, the like of whom, among many thousands, scarcely anyone in the whole world, I think, could find. For, his savage rage laid aside, he began to preach and to proclaim publicly that Jesus Christ is the only-begotten of the great God, and this he displayed openly and privately in speech, demonstrating the truth by arguments and overcoming the obstinate Jews by the very force of the Scriptures.

units.la: 2. Quo successu inopinato, vt prae gaudio exultabant fratres, ita indignari coepit Satanas, militesque sui fremere: Nam cum ipsum, quem in casses, laqueosque suos, infinitas perducturum animas speraret, iam armenta abigere, praedamque locupletem auertere conspiceret, quam indignis putamus, tulit ille modis, qui perniciem humani generis ardenter desiderat? Ministros igitur, famulosque suscitauit suos, tenebrarum, malitiaeque filios, qui ex insidiis illum intercipere, & occidere tentarent. Qui vi alios prius petiit, nunc ipse vi petitur, lacessens lacessitur, occidens occidendus quaeritur. Ita quam primum pietati, & religioni sincerae, quisquam nomen dederit, non deerunt, qui lingua venenata maledicere, qui Theonino mordere dente, qui manu sanguinaria perimere aggredientur. Et Isaacus IsmaeIsmaelem habebit suum, & fratrem Cainum Abel, & Doegum Dauid. {b}Luci cum tenebris, fideli cum infidelibus, sanctissimis Christi famulis, cum deuotis Christi hostibus, quæ erit consensio? Cum igitur & Christi, & suis popularib. & cōpatriotis Iudæis, ἀποδεικνὺς[?] demonstraret, Mariæ filiu, esse ipsum Messiam, Redemptorem Israelis, eumque quem contempsissent, despectui habuissent, imo fœdo turpique crucifixissent modo, futurum iudicem viuorū, & mortuorum; consilium inierunt Iudæi isti in Damasco degentes, vt ipsi os obthurarent, non silentium imponendo, sed è luce illum penitus, & viuis tollendo. Quod vt sine controuersia effectum darent, ad vrbis portas, custodes apposuerunt, qui transeuntem subito adorirentur. Truculentæ illorum iræ exceptâ vita nihil poterat satisfacere.
units.tr: 2. With this unexpected success, as the brothers rejoiced exceedingly, so Satan began to be indignant and his soldiers to rage. For when he saw that the man whom he had hoped would lead infinite souls into his snares and nets was now driving off the herds and turning away a rich prey, in what manner, do we think, did he bear it, he who ardently desires the ruin of the human race? He therefore roused up his own ministers and servants, the sons of darkness and malice, who sought to intercept and kill him by treachery. He who before had assailed others by force is now himself assailed by force; the one who was lashing out is now sought to be struck down. So, as soon as anyone gives his name to piety and sincere religion, there will not be lacking those who will set about to curse him with a venomous tongue, to bite him with a Theonine tooth, to destroy him with a bloody hand. Isaac will have his Ishmael, and Abel his brother Cain, and David his Doeg. What agreement can there be between light and darkness, between the faithful and the unfaithful, between the most holy servants of Christ and the devoted enemies of Christ? Since, therefore, he was demonstrating to both Christ's and his own fellow countrymen and compatriots, the Jews, that the son of Mary is himself the Messiah, the Redeemer of Israel, and that he whom they had despised and held in contempt, indeed had crucified in a foul and shameful manner, will be the judge of the living and the dead, those Jews who lived in Damascus took counsel to stop his mouth, not by imposing silence, but by removing him altogether from the light and from the living. That they might bring this about without dispute, they placed guards at the city gates who would suddenly fall upon him as he passed. The savage fury of these men could be satisfied by nothing short of his life.

units.la: 3. Verum Deus, qui & capillos recensere, & passerculos obseruare, pro insigni sua omniscientia consueuit, rabidissimis leonibus quasi frænum iniecturus, malitiam malignantium clementer compescuit. Coniuratorum hostium consilia, patefecit fratribus Paulum amore complectentibus, qui innocentis sanguinem nolentes effundi, multo maxime vero iuuenis, tanta indole, tam accurata eruditione, tam suaui eloquio, tam celebri in Scripturis peritia, qui eousque posset postea honorem Dei promouere, & fidem Christi propagare: quo poterant adminiculo ferebant opem, & ab acie gladii, vt poterant, tutabantur. Postquam igitur eum non in propatulo degere, sed in locis abditis delitescere passi essent, vt ferebat occasio, nocturnis tandem obducti tenebris, ad vrbis mœnia accesserunt, & vel reperta via, vel muro perforato, fune, in sporta pendentem demiserunt. Ita fugit Paulus, festinando, gradumque accelerando, à morte ereptus. Et seipsum meliorib. Ecclesiæ temporibus referuans, factus postea est instrumentum, organumque illustre Diuinæ laudis, per omnes orbis plagas. Quod ut mislum[?] faciamus, & de ipsius laboribus dicere supersedeamus, inuestigandum est potius, num & aliis hominibus Paulina persequenda sint vestigia? num & ipsis etiam liceat se furori tyrannorum secreto subducere? Discerpitur etenim nonnunquam fidelium congregatio, Domitianorum & Diocletianorum gladio; & fremunt mali homines, ita ut nauis Ecclesiæ, in Oceano mundi, præ turbinibus, & procellis, interitura videatur; cum licet volens sit spiritus, & pröptus, infirma possit esse caro. Quâdo igitur, qui pro Christo, & eius confessione, rubore suffunditur, à iudice mortuorum sit amandandus in gehennam; operæprecium est indagare, num pietatem colenti, in persecutione liceat fugere: præsertim autem Ministro Euangelii, qui gubernatoris agit vices, & non minus pro alienis, quam pro sua, animabus, rationem est redditurus. In eo igitur, & alio non multum dispari, propter rerum similitudinem, fuga scilicet, cum pestifera sæuierit tempestas, hodierna, duce Deo, versabitur disputatio.
units.tr: 3. But God, who is accustomed, by his remarkable omniscience, to count even the hairs of the head and to watch over the sparrows, restrained the malice of the malicious in mercy, as if about to put a bridle upon raging lions. He revealed the plans of the conspiring enemies to the brothers, who embraced Paul with love; they were unwilling that the blood of an innocent man be shed, and most of all of a young man of such character, of such careful learning, of such sweet eloquence, of such celebrated skill in the Scriptures, who could afterward advance the honour of God so far and spread the faith of Christ. With whatever aid they could, they gave help, and, as they were able, they protected him from the edge of the sword. Therefore, since they allowed him not to live openly but to hide in secret places, as the occasion required, at last, with night's darkness drawn over them, they came to the city walls, and either by a way found or by a breach made in the wall, they let him down, hanging in a basket by a rope. Thus Paul fled, hastening and quickening his pace, snatched from death. And, reserving himself for the better times of the Church, he afterward became an instrument and an illustrious organ of the divine praise through all the regions of the world. But, leaving this aside and forbearing to speak of his labours, it is rather to be inquired whether the footsteps of Paul ought also to be followed by other men, and whether it is lawful for them too to withdraw secretly from the fury of tyrants. For the congregation of the faithful is sometimes torn apart by the sword of Domitians and Diocletians, and wicked men rage, so that the ship of the Church, on the ocean of the world, seems about to perish amid whirlwinds and storms, although the spirit may be willing and ready, while the flesh may be weak. Since, therefore, he who blushes for Christ and his confession is to be sent by the judge of the dead into hell, it is worth the effort to inquire whether, in persecution, it is lawful for one who cultivates piety to flee: especially for a minister of the Gospel, who acts as the vicar of the governor and will have to give account no less for other men's souls than for his own. Therefore, in this and another not much different matter, on account of the similarity of the circumstances, namely flight, when a pestilential storm rages, today's disputation, God leading, will be carried on.

units.la: 4. Naturalem quendam vitæ amorem, ingenerauit omni homini Deus, quo ad sui conseruationem perpetuo fertur, neque libens in perniciem incurrit. Et, ut recte est obseruatum, hoc desiderium Deus indidit, ne leui qualibet arrepta occasione, tristitiæ vel inuidiæ, vel metus, violentas sibi quisquam inferret manus, mortemq; consciscerct. Unde, breui id contingeret tempore, ut euersum, & dissipatum humanum genus disperiret. Quod cum noluerit huius fabricæ artifex prudentissimus, desiderium suæ tuendæ, fouendæq; vitæ, cuiuis dedit. Et huius affectus recordatio, homini Christiano, calcar potest addere hæsitanti, ut iniuriam venientem euitet, se è medio subtrahendo. Cum enim Deus æque pedes suppeditarit, quibus discedere valemus, atque manus ad pugnandum, & dorsum ad ferendum, & tolerandum omnia; pedum etiam beneficio aliquando est utendū. Præsertim, cum id nullo Scripturæ sacræ testimonio prohibeatur, Cui id accedit etiam, quod virium suarum nemo ita potest sibi esse conscius, vt non & suam, in cruce perferenda debilitatem agnoscat. Quis etenim è carne, sanguineque constitutus, sibi tantam patientiam spondere præsumat, vt (cum posset prius tuto decedere) ferarum dentibus, igne, gladio, eculeo, exquisitissimis tormentis circumseptus, non contremisset, & lingua titubet, & mente vacillet? {c}Corruptibile corpus aggrauabit animam, & spiritui pere se prompto, appendit debilis, & infirma caro. {d}Qui stare videtur sibi, videat ne cadat. Non e superbiendum vnquam est, sed timendum potius. {f}Qui tantos sibi spiritus gestasse visus est, vt si omnes Christum desererent, ipse non esset desertus: & si moriendum esset, discedere recusaret: cum ad ipsum capitis discrimen peruenisset, in aula Sacerdotum Principis, suum Dominum tremebundus, & meticulosus abnegauit. Annon igitur erit satius, cum obtulerit opportunitatem Dominus, occasionem omnem præscindere, & amputare, in exilium proficiscendo, aut in eremum, aut cauernam, aut syluam abeundo, quam periculo venienti (speciose audacterque se obtrudere) & in ipso conflictu ita tergiuersari, & misere succumbere, vt fidei, professionique Christianæ, apud exteros, & inimicos Dei, labecula aspergatur? Quod si inter fugiendum, quis deprehensus fuerit, tum Diuinum auxilium, est precibus implorandum, vt robur, & confidentiam velit addere, ad nomen ipsius, mortem vsque, confitendum. Sed id post experta omnia.
units.tr: 4. God implanted in every man a certain natural love of life, by which he is perpetually borne toward his own preservation and does not willingly rush into destruction. And, as has been rightly observed, God gave this desire so that no one, on seizing upon any slight occasion of sadness, envy or fear, should lay violent hands upon himself and bring death upon himself; otherwise, in a short time it would come about that the human race, overturned and scattered, would perish. Since the most wise artificer of this fabric did not will this, he gave to each the desire to preserve and cherish his own life. And the recollection of this affection can add a spur to a Christian man who hesitates, so that he may avoid an approaching injury by withdrawing himself from the midst. For since God has equally supplied feet by which we are able to depart, and hands for fighting, and a back for bearing and enduring all things, the benefit of the feet must sometimes also be used: especially since this is forbidden by no testimony of Holy Scripture. To this is added also that no one can be so conscious of his own strength as not to acknowledge his own weakness in bearing the cross. For who, being made of flesh and blood, would presume to promise himself such patience that, when he could have departed safely beforehand, surrounded by the teeth of beasts, by fire, by the sword, by the rack, by the most exquisite torments, he would not tremble, and his tongue would not falter, and his mind would not waver? "The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly tent presses down the mind that is eager to think." "He who seems to himself to stand, let him see that he does not fall." It must never be proud, but rather feared. "He who seemed to himself to have such great spirit that, if all were to desert Christ, he himself would not be deserted; and that if he had to die, he would refuse to depart; yet when he came to the very peril of his life, in the court of the chief priest, trembling and fearful, he denied his Lord." Would it not therefore be better, when the Lord has offered an opportunity, to cut off and remove every occasion, by going into exile, or departing into the wilderness, or a cave, or a wood, than to thrust oneself forward boldly and showily into an approaching danger, and in the very conflict to turn aside and wretchedly succumb, so that a little stain is cast upon the Christian faith and profession among foreigners and enemies of God? But if, in the course of fleeing, someone is caught, then the divine help must be implored with prayers, that he may be willing to add strength and confidence to confess the name of Christ even unto death. But this is to be done after everything has been tried.

units.la: §. Qui vixerunt olim pii, in turbinibus, & procellis, in hunc portum, & nō alium, nauigia sua applicuerunt. {g}Cum Dauidi insidias tetendisset Saul, & per seipsum, & alios quotidie illū quæreret, vt interficeretur: in exteras nationes peregre proficiscendo, in montibus & syluis, & speluncis se abdendo, Dauid vitam tutatus est. {h}Annon etiam per fugam, furori Absfolonis se subduxit? Post Stephani caedem, fideles omnes, {i} Apostolis solis demptis, fugiendo sunt subrepti.
units.tr: §. The pious men of old, when storms and tempests drove them, brought their ships into this harbour and no other. When Saul laid snares for David, and sought him daily, in person and through others, that he might be killed, David preserved his life by going abroad into foreign nations, and by hiding himself in mountains, woods and caves. Did he not also escape the fury of Absalom by flight? After the killing of Stephen, all the faithful, except the Apostles alone, were snatched away by flight.

units.la: Qui{k}Epistola ad Hebraeos, tantis laudibus, ac elogiis celebrantur: ut dicatur, mundum ipsorum consortio fuisse indignum: perhibentur tamen, in ouium & caprarum pellibus circumerrasse, & in eremis, in montibus, in speluncis, caeteisque terrae vixisse. Quod, quid aliud fuerat, quam noluisse istos, tyrannorum manibus, & malis deminantibus sese immiscere? Cum post ascensum Christi ferueret vndiquaque persecutio & fidelium grex misere discerperetur, & dilaniaretur: per annos trecentos, visq; ad Constantini tempora, è loco in locum migrare, & in tutiora se recipere, multoties fideles coacti sunt, vt Ecclesiastica Eusebii meminit historia: sicque & Diuinae gloriæ, & suæ incolumitati consultu censuerunt: cum nonnulli, qui sibi visi sunt robustiores: dum periculum operiendo, experiri voluissent vltima, sub onere defecerunt, & Idolis thura adolentes in altaribus, Ecclesiæ, {l}suisque conscientiis, scandalum dederunt, & ansam / Novato porrexerunt, schisma faciendi, ipsosque, ad Eucharistiam non esse amplius admittendos, d. sputandi. Quanto potius fuisset, si, cum suam ex se debilitatem considerassent paulisper diuertissent. Id, quod ex Nostratibus quam plurimi fecerunt, Marianis temporibus: & ex Gallis, Belgisque, plures nostro seculo, qui tempestatibus domi saeuientibus, magno numero, vt in reliquas orbis partes, sic in nostram Angliam, vt ad asylū aliquod confugerunt. Et pie sane. Non est etenim cuiusuis, eousq; Dominum (qui libertatem abeundi concessit) tentare, num mire velit in angustiis, auxilium subministrare, & e tricis expedire; aut constantiam patiendi, moriendique submittere, cum alia is obtulerit abeundi media, quae temere, & peruicaciter non sunt repudianda.
units.tr: The men of the Epistle to the Hebrews are celebrated with such great praises and eulogies that it is said the world was not worthy of their company; yet they are reported to have wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, and to have lived in deserts, on mountains, in caves and elsewhere on the earth. What else was this than being unwilling to mix themselves into the hands of tyrants and the threats of evil men? When persecution raged on every side after Christ's ascension, and the flock of the faithful was miserably torn apart and mangled, for three hundred years, down to the time of Constantine, the faithful were often compelled to migrate from place to place and to withdraw into safer places, as Eusebius's Ecclesiastical History records. Thus they judged that they consulted both the glory of God and their own safety. Some, who seemed to themselves stronger, wished by waiting for danger to test the extremes, and gave way under the burden, and burning incense to idols at the altars, they gave scandal to the Church and to their own consciences, and offered an occasion to Novatus to make a schism, and to cry out that they were no longer to be admitted to the Eucharist. How much better it would have been, if, having considered their own weakness, they had turned aside for a while! This is what very many of our own people did in Mary's times, and several of the French and Belgians in our age, who, when storms raged at home, fled in great numbers, as into the rest of the world, so into our England, as to some refuge. And certainly they did so piously. For it is not for anyone to tempt the Lord, who has granted the freedom to depart, to see whether He will wonderfully supply help in straits and free us from snares, or whether He will submit us to the constancy of suffering and dying, when He has offered other means of departing, which are not to be rashly and obstinately rejected.

units.la: 6. Tertulliani igitur, si non explodenda, propter tanti viri honorem, abiicienda tamen est sententia & repudian-da{m} qu libro suo, de Fuga in persecutione, standum esse so-lummodo, & confitendum docet, ac ad mortem usque, non vertendum tergum. Christiani, illo tempore graviter afflicti, se, periculis imminentibus, vertendo solum, aut clam se ad amicos recipiendo, subtraxerunt, & eorum ali-quot, pecunia sua, hoc est, Tributum & Vectigal locuple-tius, Imperatoris fisco, persoluendo, pacem redemerunt suam. Sic Praefectos & Proconsules placatos reddiderunt, nō tam donis secretis, & largitionib, quam aperto censu; co-freti Saluatoris testimonio,{n} facite vobis amicos e Mammona iniquitatis. Hoc, ut nulla faciendum ratione, improbat Ter-tullianus, & fugam nullo capessendam modo censet: id Christi,{o} Cum in una vos persecuti fuerint urbe, fugite in aliam, ut temporale praeceptum interpretans, Apostolis datum, non aliis: Apostolis inquam solis, ne ipsis occisis, Euangelium non praedicaretur, verum extinguueretur penitus. Sed infirmum est fundamentum, quo tota eius nititur structu-ra: quia etenim nihil contingit nobis, nisi disponente Deo, neque ulla est persecutio, nisi ex speciali Omnipotentis vo-luntate, neque eius beneplacito obstandum est, fugien-dum non esse concludit. Vere sane inquit nihil fieri, nisi volente Deo: At qui nosti, nunc accessisse tempus, quo vi-tam auferri voluit Deus? Et hosti permittit insequi, & tibi fugere. In utrisque, ipsius eminebit gloria. In tentationem idem ducit, & e tentatione expedit. Intendi malum pati-tur, & liberat a malo. Qui produci adhuc vult, & prolon-gari vitam tuam, medium etiam producendi suppeditat, idque per secessum. Male alias a Saulis conspectu se subtra-xisset Dauid, nisi euitandae essent insidiae: cum eae nonnisi volente Deo, poterant tendi. Eum igitur Tertulliani libri,{p} Hieronymus, speciali-ter contra Ecclesiam scriptu existi-mat, ut & illius etiam alios. Facessat igitur ea opinio. Licere
units.tr: Therefore the opinion of Tertullian, if it is not to be scorned out of respect for so great a man, is nevertheless to be rejected and repudiated, which in his book On Flight in Persecution teaches that one must only stand firm and confess, and not turn one's back even unto death. Christians, grievously afflicted at that time, when dangers threatened, withdrew by changing their place or by secretly retreating to friends, and some of them, paying their money, that is, the tribute and tax, more richly into the Emperor's treasury, bought their peace. Thus they made the prefects and proconsuls well disposed, not so much by secret gifts and bribes as by an open payment, relying on the Saviour's testimony, make for yourselves friends from the mammon of unrighteousness. This Tertullian disapproves as something not to be done on any ground, and he judges that flight is by no means to be undertaken; he interprets Christ's saying, When they persecute you in one city, flee into another, as a temporal precept given to the Apostles only and not to others: to the Apostles alone, I say, lest, if they were killed, the Gospel should not be preached but should be utterly extinguished. But his foundation is weak, on which his whole structure rests: for since nothing happens to us except by God's disposing, and there is no persecution except by the special will of the Almighty, and one must not resist His good pleasure, he concludes that one must not flee. Truly, he says, nothing happens unless God wills it. But do you know that the time has now come when God has willed that your life be taken away? He permits the enemy to pursue, and you to flee. In both, His own glory will stand out. He also leads into temptation and rescues from temptation. He allows evil to be inflicted, and frees from evil. He who still wills your life to be extended and prolonged supplies also the means of prolonging it, and that by withdrawal. Otherwise David would have withdrawn badly from Saul's sight, unless his snares were to be avoided, since these could be laid only with God's will. Therefore Jerome thinks that Tertullian's book was written especially against the Church, as also his other writings. Let that opinion, then, depart. It is not doubtful that it is lawful to withdraw from the layman, when one's own conscience suggests departure, not by rash impulse but by sober and prudent judgement; and conversely, if the Divine Spirit, who presides over the thoughts of His servants, shall suggest on due consideration that one should remain and meet death, and if circumstances and things allow it, one must wait with a confident mind.
Tertullian, On Flight in Persecution.
Luke 16. 9.
{o} Matth. 10. 23.

units.la: {p} Hier. de scriptoribus Ecclesiast. Laico se submouere, nõ dubitamus; cum propria conscien-tia, non motu temerario, sed sobrio, & prudenti, abeundum suggerit: cumque econtra, Diuinus spiritus, qui cogitatio-nibus famulorum suorum praeest, manendum esse, & morte oppetendum considerato submonebit, si res & circumstan-tiae ferant, confidenti animo operiendum est.
units.tr: {p} Hier. de scriptoribus Ecclesiast. We do not hesitate to withdraw from the laity; when one's own conscience suggests departure, it should be done not by rash impulse but soberly and prudently. And conversely, if the Divine Spirit, who presides over the thoughts of his servants, advises that one should remain and face death deliberately, and if circumstances and conditions allow it, one must wait with a confident spirit.

units.la: 7. Quae contra ducuntur argumenta, leuiora sunt, quam quae cursum progredientis ad difficiliora, remorentur. Qui legendi est cupidus, apud {q}Petrum Martyrem, &citata, quę in aduersum stant, & docte refutata comperiet. Ego inte-rim nihil addam, praeterquam purioris & antiquioris Eccle-siae in re hac iudicium. Audite Clementem Alexandrinum, {r}Si qui hominem Dei interimit, in Deum peccat, is quoque eius cædis reus tenetur, qui se offert iudicio. Is autem fuerit, qui non vitat perse-cutionem se capiendum praebens per audaciam. Audite Origenem super Iohannem: {s}Honestum quidem est, si inciderit certamen, pro confitendo Iesum, confessionem non differre, neque tardare mortem pro veritate oppetere. At non minus quam hoc honestum est, talitantaque tentationi occasionem non dare, sed omnimodo vitare eam: non solum, quia tanta rei exitus incertus fit nobis, verum etiam, ne nos occasio simus, ut magis peccatores, magisque impii euadant illi, qui nondum sanguinem nostrum quidem re ipsa effudisse reisunt facti, &c.
