Audite Cyprianum, {t}qui licet ipse Martyrii palmam postea tulerit, ita tamen populo fugam suasit, ut pro Christo Martyres existimaret, si inter discedendum, fame, bestiarum dentibus, & lanienis, aut huiusmodi euentibus interciperentur. Eius haec sunt verba: Solus non est, cui Christus in fuga comes est: solus non est, qui templum Dei seruans, vbicunque fuerit, sine Deo non est. Et si fugientem in solitudine, aut montibus, latro oppresserit, fera inuaserit, fames ac sitis, aut frigus afflixerit, vel per maria praeciputi nauigatione properantem, tempestas, aut procella submerserit, expectat militem suum Christus, vbicunq; pugnantem. Ita antiqui, & recentes, omnino & simpliciter, non interdictam Christiano fugam arbitrantur.
units.tr: 7. The arguments brought against this are lighter than those which would hold back one advancing to harder things. Whoever is eager to read should find them in Peter Martyr, where the opposing arguments are cited and learnedly refuted. For my part, I will add nothing except the judgment of the purer and more ancient Church on this matter. Hear Clement of Alexandria: If anyone kills the man of God, he sins against God; he too is held guilty of that murder who offers himself to judgment. Yet he is the one who does not avoid persecution, presenting himself to be seized through boldness. Hear Origen on John: It is indeed honourable, if a contest should come upon us, not to delay in confessing Jesus, nor to hesitate to meet death for the truth. But it is no less honourable not to give occasion to such a temptation, and to avoid it by every means: not only because the outcome of so great a matter is uncertain for us, but also lest we become the occasion for those who have not yet actually shed our blood, but have been made guilty, to become more sinful and more impious, etc. Hear Cyprian, who, although he himself later won the palm of martyrdom, nonetheless so counselled the people to flee that he judged them to be martyrs for Christ if, in the course of their departure, they were cut off by hunger, the teeth of wild beasts, butchers, or events of this kind. His words are these: He is not alone to whom Christ is a companion in flight; he is not alone who, keeping the temple of God, is wherever he may be, not without God. And if a robber should overtake one fleeing into solitude or the mountains, a wild beast should attack, hunger and thirst or cold should afflict him, or a tempest or storm should sink one hastening over the seas by a headlong voyage, Christ awaits his soldier, wherever he fights. Thus the ancients and the moderns alike, wholly and without qualification, judge that flight is not forbidden to a Christian.

units.la: §. Sed de Pastore gregis, & Praecone Euangelii, ex spe-ciali munere & vocatione, alia est determinatio. Siquidem ipsi, non sui corporis, sed alienarum animarum, cura agenda est. Ab eius ore pendet populus, ut è materna mamma infan-tulus. Eius & consilio & auxilio & exemplo standum est, & confessioni illius immorandum. Et ut dixit aliquando, Leo Romanus Episcopus. {u}Quis inter fluctus maris naues diriget, si gubernator abscedat? quis ab insidiis luporum oues custodiet, si Pastoris cura non vigilet? quis denique latronib. obsistet, & furibus, si speculatorem, in conspectu exploratonis locatum, ab intentione sollicitudinis, amor quietis abducat? Perpetuo necessaria est populo, docentis & consolantis persona: quanto magis, cum quouis die nova ingruant discrimina, neque ullus tranquillitati locus datus est? Perniciosum est, rectorem in malacia nauem deserere; quanto magis in fluctibus? Quam tremendum illud est, & formidandum, si tua culpa, sine Baptismo infantuli, sine sacramento Eucharistico languentes, sine venia Excommunicati, è vivis abscedant? quae quanta infirmis pariunt scandala? Imo quota pars tuae congregationis, de Euangelii veritate, doctrinaeque; quam docuisti certitudine, ambigere incipiet, si te fuga data, nolentem asseuerare, tuerique tua, conspexerit? Quod tibi, id & sibi licere arbitrabuntur. Tu pedibus & silentio, quodammodo Christum abnegasti; negabunt illi lingua & manu, revocando sententiam, & conceptis inimicorum verbis subscribendo. Cauendum igitur est, ne suo exemplo, in ruinam perpetuam, infirmorum animas Minister praecipitet; ne illorum sanguinem, severo cum examine, ab ipso, ἀρχιποίμην[?] ille Christus requirat. Confiten-do, & cōsidendo, aliorum segnities excutienda est; excitan-di sunt animi; erigendi spiritus, quo celebris Christi gloria elucescat amplius. Praeeunte duce, sequentur milites. Au-dente ariete, reliquus succedet grex. Non verebitur popu-lus, vel sanguine suo, Salvatoris veritatem obsignare, & pro-batiobationem igneam tolerare, cum Sacerdotem suum, in altari passionis immolatum intuebitur. Ei igitur ex peculiari munere id incumbit, quod non incumbit aliis.
units.tr: But concerning the shepherd of the flock and the herald of the Gospel, a different determination applies, from his special office and calling. For his care is to be exercised not for his own body but for other souls. The people hang upon his mouth, as a little infant upon its mother's breast. His counsel, his help and his example must be relied upon, and his confession must be persisted in. And as Leo, the Roman bishop, once said: Who will steer the ships amid the waves of the sea, if the helmsman withdraws? Who will guard the sheep from the snares of wolves, if the shepherd's care is not watchful? Who, finally, will resist robbers and thieves, if love of quiet draws away from the intent vigilance the watchman stationed in view of the enemy? The person of a teacher and comforter is always necessary to the people: how much more when new dangers press daily, and no place is given to tranquillity? It is destructive for a helmsman to abandon the ship in a calm; how much more in the waves? How fearful and dreadful it is, if through your fault infants depart from life without baptism, the sick without the Eucharistic sacrament, the excommunicated without pardon? What great scandals do these bring to the weak? Indeed, what a small part of your congregation will begin to doubt the truth of the Gospel and the doctrine which you taught with certainty, if, once you have given way in flight, they see you refusing to affirm and defend your own position? What you think is lawful, they will think is lawful for themselves as well. You have, as it were, denied Christ by your feet and your silence; they will deny Him with tongue and hand, by recalling their opinion and subscribing to the words of enemies. Care must therefore be taken lest the Minister, by his own example, plunge the souls of the weak into perpetual ruin; lest Christ, the chief Shepherd, require their blood from him at a severe examination. The sloth of others must be shaken off by confessing and by standing firm; souls must be roused, spirits raised up, so that the famous glory of Christ may shine forth more brightly. With the leader going before, the soldiers follow. With the ram leading, the rest of the flock will come after. The people will not hesitate to seal the Saviour's truth even with their own blood, and to endure the fiery trial, when they look upon their priest offered upon the altar of suffering. Therefore that falls to him by a peculiar duty which does not fall to others.

units.la: 9. Reperiri non potest, qui definiat terminetque hanc litem, sapientior, fidelior, verior, justiorque judex, quam Redemptor Christus: Qui, quid interfit inter bonum Pastorem, Mercenariumque demonstrans, ex suo id docet exemplo; boni {x}Pastoris esse, pro ouibus vitam impendere, se periculis aduentantibus medium interiicere, & interponere; suaque vita ipsorum incolumitatem redimere. Mercenarius autem, inquit, & qui non est Pastor, neque oues sua sunt, lupum videt venientem, & oues linquit, & fugit, & eas lupus rapit, & oues dispersit. Ecce non est alterius, quam hominis mercenarii, accurrente destructore, suum gregem deserere. Et in nomine Mercenarii, infidus dispensator, incuriosus proditor, indignus, cuius tanta sollicitudo concredatur, ibidem designatur. Quod, quantis quaesto gradib. aut parasangis potius, ab Oeconomo fideli, distare cogitabimus? Hinc, vitio aliquando {y}Nouato versum est, quod cum presbyter fuisset, (ut apud Eusebium; Cornelius Romanus Episcopus refert) procella persecutionis & furoris, in Ecclesia aduentante, non modo plebem, periculis iam obsitam reliquerit destitutam, sed & vocationem suam omnino deseruerit, Sacerdotio renunciando, Presbyterique officium abnegando. Fuit tunc temporis, Mercenarius, & defertor gregis, uti postea Haereticus. Debuisset potius eum exprimere amorem, & dilectionem in fideles, cuius meminit Johannes Apostolus, {z}Per hoc nouimus charitatem Dei, quod ille animam suam pro nobis posuit: nos igitur debemus pro fratribus animas ponere. Ubi, ne ad Christum solum ea moriendi praerogatiua, quae quae {a}Pastoris boni esse dicitur, spectare videretur, adiungit, nos etiam debemus pro fratrib. animas ponere. Quod ex aliis etiam Christi verbis colligere, non est difficile: Cum etenim dixisset, {b}Maiorem charita[?]tem nullus habet, quam istam, vt quispiam animam suam depo-nat, pro amicis suis: immediate subiungit, vos amici mei eritis, si secer-itis, quaecunq; ego mando vobis; ac si illis in memoriam reuocaret ipsum sanguinem, pro salute gregis, si necessitas ingrueret, effundendum esse.
units.tr: 9. There cannot be found anyone who could settle and end this dispute more wisely, faithfully, truly and justly than the Redeemer Christ. He, showing what difference there is between the good Shepherd and the hired man, teaches this from his own example: it belongs to the good Shepherd to lay down his life for the sheep, to place himself in the way of approaching dangers and to interpose himself, and to redeem the safety of the flock with his own life. "But the hired man," he says, "and he who is not the Shepherd, whose sheep are not his own, sees the wolf coming, and leaves the sheep and flees, and the wolf snatches them and scatters the sheep." Behold, it is characteristic of a hired man alone, when the destroyer comes running, to desert his flock. And in the name of the hired man, the faithless steward, the careless traitor, the one unworthy of so great a care entrusted to him, is marked out in the same place. How many steps, or rather how many miles, shall we reckon this lies from the faithful steward? Hence it was at one time turned into a fault by the Novatians, because when he had been a presbyter (as Cornelius, bishop of Rome, reports in Eusebius), a storm of persecution and fury arriving in the Church, he not only left the people, already beset by dangers, abandoned, but also utterly deserted his own calling, renouncing the priesthood and denying the office of presbyter. At that time he was a hired man and a deserter of the flock, and afterwards a heretic. He ought rather to have shown that love and affection towards the faithful of which the Apostle John speaks: "By this we have known the love of God, because he laid down his life for us; we therefore ought to lay down our lives for the brethren." Where, lest that prerogative of dying, which is said to belong to the good Shepherd, should seem to refer to Christ alone, he adds: "we also ought to lay down our lives for the brethren." It is not difficult to gather this also from other words of Christ: for when he had said, "No one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends," he immediately adds, "You are my friends, if you do whatever I command you"; as if he were reminding them that the very blood must be poured out for the salvation of the flock, should necessity press.

units.la: 10. Qui in Ecclesia primaeva viguerunt, sancti Sacerdotes & Episcopi, praeceptum istud, & memoriam retinuerunt, & passione praestiterunt. Hinc {c}Petrus, calcibus in caelum obuersus, cruci suffixus est. {d}Iacobus & Paulus, gladio sunt occisi. Neque fere quisquam fuerat Apostolorum, qui non morte violenta, & sanguinaria sublatus expiravit. Animam pro fratrib. cupidissime posuerunt; unde {e}magna Christianorum facta est sementis; nam, Sanguis martyrum, semen est Euangelii: Ita fecerat {f}Ignatius, qui, si quisquam alius, martyrii fuerat cupidissimus: & pro Christi amore, & confirmatione fratrum, crucem flammam, ferarum dentes, eculeum contempsit. Similibus iuit passibus piissimus {g}Polycarpus, qui veritati Euangelii, apud Tyrannum testimonium reddere; non erubuit. Sic Iustinus Martyr, sic elegans Cyprianus. Magis gregis, quam sui curam egerant, fidelissimi pastores. Nec nouissima nostra tempora, infecunda, aut sterilia, indigaque bonorum virorum fuerunt. Multi viri doctissimi, sanctissimi, constantissimi, sub Gardinero, & Bonnero, exhalarunt animam, nec congregationes suas dereliquerunt, vsque ad mortem. Imo Episcopi celeberrimi, Ridleius, Latimerus, Hooperus, Ferrarius, & Archiepiscopus Cranmerus, sua corpora flammis tradiderunt, vt ex animo suam patriam, & Christi fideles se diligere commonstrarent. Cum fugiendi multae viae offerrentur, cum, quae absconderent, latebrae non deessent, cum adhortationes ingeminarentur, vt vel tandem, post apprehensionem se subducerent, noluerunt vt Mercenarii suum populum deserere, sed pro lucro mortẽ existimantes, modo aliis infirmioribus, in via salutis praelucerent,
units.tr: 10. The holy priests and bishops who flourished in the primitive Church kept this precept and this example in memory, and performed it by suffering. Hence Peter, turned upside down with his feet towards heaven, was fastened to the cross. James and Paul were killed with the sword. Nor was there almost any of the Apostles who did not end his life by a violent and bloody death. They most eagerly laid down their lives for the brethren; whence a great harvest of Christians was made, for "the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the Gospel." So Ignatius did, who, if anyone, was most eager for martyrdom, and for love of Christ and the strengthening of the brethren despised the cross, the flame, the teeth of wild beasts and the rack. The most pious Polycarp went the same way, who did not blush to bear witness to the truth of the Gospel before a tyrant. So Justin Martyr, so the eloquent Cyprian. The most faithful pastors had cared more for their flock than for themselves. Nor have our most recent times been barren or unfruitful, or lacking in good men. Many most learned, most holy and most steadfast men, under Gardiner and Bonner, breathed out their lives, and did not forsake their congregations, even unto death. Indeed the most famous bishops, Ridley, Latimer, Hooper, Ferrar, and Archbishop Cranmer, gave up their bodies to the flames, that they might show from their heart that they loved their country and the faithful of Christ. When many ways of escape were offered, when hiding-places were not lacking in which they might conceal themselves, when exhortations were repeated that they should at least withdraw after their arrest, they would not, like hired men, desert their people, but, counting death gain, they only wished to shine as a light to others weaker on the way of salvation, and they endured the most bitter sufferings.
Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, book 3, chap. 1.
Acts 12. 2.
Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, 2. 24.
Book 2, chap. 1, sec. 8.
Book 3, chap. 30.

units.la: {g} Lib. 4. 14. [?] cerent, acerbissima perpessi sunt. Stulti sane hi omnes, & in-sipientes summo gradu, Apostoli, Patres, Episcopi, Ministri si cum obsequio ad Christum, & cura gregis debita, suam-posse stare fugam antumarent. Sed standi, manendique officium, suum esse cognouerunt. Dura si haec videatur sententia, Christi est: qui, ut omnibus {h}praecipit circumspicere & praeuidere, num amicos, patrem, matrem, uxorem, imo ipsam uitam velint pro Christo linquere, ita proculdubio, Ministris Euangelii, in memoriam reuocat, ut magno cum iudicio, & accurata consideratione, eam subeant prouinciam. Quis domum structurus, non sedet apud se, & rationem init, num habeat, ex quo, opus possit perficere? Et quae sequuntur.
units.tr: Book 4, chap. 14. Truly all these men, Apostles, Fathers, bishops, ministers, were foolish and most unwise, if they thought they could stand with obedience to Christ and due care of the flock by flight. But they recognised that it was their duty to stand and remain. If this judgement seems harsh, it is Christ's: who, as he commands everyone to look around and foresee whether they are willing to leave friends, father, mother, wife, indeed life itself for Christ, so without doubt he reminds the ministers of the Gospel that they should undertake that charge with great judgement and careful consideration. Who, wishing to build a house, does not sit down and reckon whether he has the means by which he can complete the work? And the rest that follows.

units.la: II. At non desunt, qui dum velum suae velint timiditati obducere, rationes, & exempla fidelium hominum, in aduersum adducunt. Carnis nostrae infirmitas ea est, ut vereri recte possimus, ne tormentis superati, in medio tentationum luc-cumbamus. Praestat igitur abesse, quam religioni infamiam, & Diuino nomini blasphemiam aduocare. At videte interea, ne qui alios docuisti, prae Christo, amicos, parentes, coniuges, possessiones, mundum, imo ipsum sanguinem despicere, & vilifacere, huius lucis usuram, & praesentis seculi delectationes, agnitioni Saluatoris praeferatis. Linquenda pro Christo esse omnia, probe nostis. Quamuis igitur impotens & imbellis videatur caro, si precibus, & inuocatione Domi-nus sollicitetur, ut iis benedicat, qui ex officio, ut adsint as-tringuntur, patientiam, & robur submi-nistrabit, quo quae grauia sunt, leuia videbuntur, & in mediis flammis, eum submittet rorem, quo refocillari possint, in augustiis, & tortura quae degunt corpora. Aut si tantam nolit adhuc donare constantiam, occasiones dabit consolationis alias, persecutorum corda molliendo, aut tempus differendo, donec ex ipsis faucibus eripiantur. Spospondit {i}[?]Deus se ultra uires non ten-tatutaturum, neque iniecturum unquam onus, cui ferendo, pa-res futuri non simus. Novit ille probe vires nostras, & quid sustinere valeamus, quid econtra. Pro singulari ergo sua & clementia, & prudentia, amice, placideque nobiscum aget, ut Patrem ipsum in intimis angustiis agnoscamus. Si secundo addatur, fugientem hodie, postea rediturum esse: Et cum magis opus fuerit, tunc rursum aderit: At caveat, ne Domino tempus constituat, in quo veritatem defendat sua. Nunc vocat Dominus, & parendum est. Non est faciendum malum, ut sequatur inde bonum. Nunc fremit, rugitque leo, nunc i-gitur oportet, ut adsit custos. Nunc oppugnat inimicus, bellator igitur seipsum opponat; tanquam murum pro domo Domini. Si deficiat, etiam hodie, quantum inter oues, vel hodie contingere potest excidium?
units.tr: II. Yet there are not wanting those who, wishing to draw a veil over their own timidity, bring forward reasons and examples of faithful men against us. The weakness of our flesh is such that we may rightly fear that, overcome by torments, we may succumb in the midst of temptations. It is better therefore to be absent than to bring infamy upon religion and blasphemy upon the divine name. But see meanwhile, you who have taught others to despise, for Christ's sake, friends, parents, spouses, possessions, the world, indeed blood itself, and to hold them cheap, that you do not prefer the use of this light and the pleasures of the present age to the knowledge of the Saviour. You well know that all things must be left for Christ. Although therefore the flesh may seem impotent and unwarlike, if the Lord is entreated with prayers and invocation, that he may bless those who are bound by their office to be present, he will supply patience and strength, so that what is grievous will seem light, and in the midst of the flames he will send down a dew by which the bodies that live in narrow straits and torture may be refreshed. Or if he is not yet willing to grant such great constancy, he will give other occasions of consolation, by softening the hearts of persecutors, or by delaying the time until they are snatched from the very jaws. God has promised that he will not tempt us beyond our strength, nor ever lay on us a burden to bear that we shall not be equal to. He knows well our strength, and what we are able to endure, and what not. Therefore, in his singular kindness, prudence and gentleness, he will deal with us as a friend and gently, so that we may recognise the Father himself in our deepest distress. If it is added in the second place that the one who flees today will return afterwards, and when there is more need he will then be present again: let him take care lest he appoint a time to the Lord in which he defends his own truth. Now the Lord calls, and we must obey. One must not do evil so that good may follow from it. Now the lion roars and growls; now therefore it is fitting that a guard should be present. Now the enemy attacks; let the fighter therefore place himself in the breach, like a wall for the house of the Lord. If he fails, even today, how great a slaughter among the sheep, which can happen even today?

units.la: 12. Verum nobis & id licet, quod licuit aliis. Sancti ho-mines in Scripturis (imo Saluator ipse) nonnunquam in fugam se proripuerunt, neque tamen, ut desertores gregis sui, taxantur. Moses{k} à Pharaone se subdicit; Elias{l} à Ieza-bele,{m} Vriah Propheta, à Rege Iehoiakin quaesitus, in Ægy-ptū se confert. Et Prophetæ isti fuerant; speculatores Israe-lis. Annon{n} Christus in Ægyptum; cum Iosepho & Maria, infantulus descendit; ut ab Herodis vesania incolumis de-geret? Annon postea, cum{o} procella imminere t maxima, ut lapidibus propediem obruendus esset; se mediae subtraxerat turbae, conspectumque furiosae multitudinis vitaverat? Et cuius potius vestigiis insistendum est, quam Christi, Ducis, Dominique nostri? Imo mandato{p} speciali Apostolis in-iunxit, ut cum illos in una civitate homines persequerentur, in aliam fugerent. Cuius praecepti, vel tolerationis beneficio, ii postea fruebantur saepissime. Sed num clarius, aut difertius quidquam haberi poterit, quam quod Paulus fecerat; qui eo ipso, de quo agitur loco,{q} in sporta per funem est di-missus, sicque fugiendo vitam est tutatus? Athanasius{r} etiam Alexandrinus Episcopus, cum Constantius Imperator ipsum quaeritaret, ut aut vinculis, aut morte plecteret, huc & illuc discurrendo, fugiendo, latitando, seamentiae[?], & tyrannidi insecutorum subtraxit. Et cum ipsi, ex hostibus quidam, sed praecipue Arrianis, contumeliae verterent, quod Diuinam voluntatem operiendo non expectaret, {ʃ}Apologiam, (seu defensionem, pro fuga sua conscripsit, qua copiose demonstrat, se eadem fuisse usum libertate, quam concedunt Scripturae, & Sanctorum facta confirmant. Ita grandi testiū corona videntur circundari, Prophetarum, Apostolorum, Episcopi Athanasii, Redemptoris Christi, qui Ministro, & Pastori, capessendam fugam existimarunt.
units.tr: 12. But we are allowed also what was allowed to others. Holy men in the Scriptures (indeed the Saviour himself) sometimes hurried away in flight, and yet they are not censured as deserters of their flock. Moses withdrew from Pharaoh; Elijah, sought by Jezebel, and the prophet Uriah, sought by King Jehoiakim, fled into Egypt. And those were prophets, the watchmen of Israel. Did not Christ, as an infant, go down into Egypt with Joseph and Mary, that he might live safe from the madness of Herod? Did he not afterwards, when a very great storm was about to break, so that he would soon be stoned, withdraw from the midst of the crowd and avoid the sight of the furious multitude? And whose footsteps ought we rather to follow than those of Christ, our Leader and Lord? Indeed by a special command he enjoined on the Apostles that when they were persecuted in one city they should flee into another. Of this precept, or of the benefit of toleration, they very often afterwards made use. But can anything clearer or more explicit be found than what Paul did, who in the very place under discussion was let down through the wall in a basket by a rope, and so by fleeing preserved his life? Athanasius also, bishop of Alexandria, when the Emperor Constantius sought him that he might punish him either with chains or with death, by running hither and thither, fleeing, and lying hidden, withdrew himself from the fury and tyranny of the persecutors. And when some of his enemies, but especially the Arians, turned it into an insult that he did not wait for the divine will but fled, he wrote an Apology (or defence) for his flight, in which he amply shows that he used the same liberty which the Scriptures grant and the deeds of the saints confirm. Thus the great crown of witnesses seems to surround us: the prophets, the Apostles, the bishop Athanasius, and Christ the Redeemer himself, who judged that flight was to be taken by a minister and pastor.

units.la: 13. Atistarum[?] actionum circumstantias si velimus accurate, ut decet, perpendere; nihil obstabit, quin, ut supra fugiendum non esse determinemus. Primum igitur, de Mosis discessu non est quod vereamur, dum Prophetico adhuc spiritu indutus non esset, cum a Pharaone primum discederet. Statuerat reuera Dominus per eius manum, postea miranda efficere, quibus cum usquedum par non esset, speciali instinctu edoctus est, (ut probabiliter coniiciatur) se submouere. Quod aperte in Elia contigit: diserto namque {†}Angeli edicto, iter quadraginta dierum capessere iussus est. Supererant alia, per ipsum facienda, quibus voluit Eliam reseruatum Dominus. Et Decretum erat Altissimi, morte ipsi non esse moriendum, sed igneo currui ad coelos transuehendum. Ita Christo, tunc infantulo, peragenda multa fuerant, docendo, sanando, miracula ostendendo priusquam tempus adueniret, quo, in altari crucis immolandus esset. Nondum venerat hora. Et ex vi Diuinitatis, cuius oculis patent omnia, praeterita, futura, hoc habuit cognitissimum. Isti autem omnes, cum standi, & permanendi, ingrueret occasio, validissime sua capita periculis obiectarunt. Ad {u}Pharaonem quoties intrepide accessit Moses, coram animi sententiam declaraturus? Annon {x}Elias, de fac e cognitus, praesensque, Ahabo idololatriam, & impie-tatem exprobrauit? Sic & Christus Pharisaeos, & Scribas, palam increpauit, in templo edocuit, Hierosolymis obuer-satus est; idque omni feredie; & tandem se capiendum, accusandum, flagellandum, crucifigendum ad tribunal stitit, acerrimum mortis iudicium subiturus. Cum igitur nostra tempora nihil habent horum simile, suffugium ex istis capiendum non est, sed constanter permanendum. Istos etenim non oppressit mortis metus, aut vultus inimicorum at sterruit, quibus vltro saepe iuerunt obuiam; sed & aliis maioribus experimentis, & exercitiis sunt reseruati, idque, ex certa per Deum praescientia, reuelatum fuerat; quo ū[?] nihil nobis est commune. Nos etenim, si languentes, & trepidantes, verta-mus terga, praelethi timore, hoc facimus; & qui nobis persuasum fuerit, maiora posthac nos manere? Non possumus celebrius Deo seruitium praestare, quam in persecutionum procellis, immobiles & immutabiles nos ostendere. Et qui semel nos in pedes coniecimus, & saepius, & semper fortassis coniiciemus. Et si contingat, ut supersint altiora, & magis ardua nobis toleranda, quo modo id cōstabit? num ex aliquo Oraculo, aut eloquio Diuino? Nihil minus. Carnalis igitur ista est imaginatio, nō Diuini spiritus suggestio, & consilium: Infirmitas humana, non prudentia Christiana.
units.tr: 13. If we want to weigh carefully, as is fitting, the circumstances of the actions of these men [Atistarum?], nothing will stand in the way of our deciding, as above, that flight is not to be counted as wrong. First, then, there is no need for us to worry about Moses' departure, since at the time when he first withdrew from Pharaoh he was not yet clothed with the prophetic spirit. The Lord had indeed determined to work wonderful things through his hand later on, and since it was not yet fitting, he was taught by a special prompting (as is probably to be conjectured) to withdraw himself. The same thing clearly happened with Elijah: by the plain command of an angel he was ordered to take a journey of forty days. Other things remained to be done through him, for which the Lord wished to keep Elijah in reserve. And it was the decree of the Most High that he should not die but be carried up to heaven in a fiery chariot. So too Christ, while still a little child, had many things to accomplish: teaching, healing, displaying miracles, before the time came when he would be offered on the altar of the cross. The hour had not yet come, and by the power of his divinity, to whose eyes all things past and future lie open, he knew this most certainly. But all those men, whenever the occasion arose for standing firm and remaining, most resolutely exposed their heads to dangers. How often did Moses approach Pharaoh fearlessly, to declare his mind to him face to face? Did not Elijah, known and present in person, rebuke Ahab for idolatry and impiety? So too Christ openly rebuked the Pharisees and the Scribes, taught in the temple, and dwelt in Jerusalem, and that every day; and at last he stood before the tribunal to be seized, accused, scourged and crucified, about to undergo the most bitter sentence of death. Since, then, our times have nothing like these, we must not take refuge in flight from them, but must remain steadfast. For the fear of death did not overwhelm those men, nor did the faces of their enemies terrify them, to whom they often went of their own accord to meet; but they were also reserved for other greater trials and exercises, and this had been revealed to them by God's certain foreknowledge; which is nothing in common with us. For if we, weak and trembling, turn our backs, fearing the ills that lie before us, we do this; and who has persuaded us that greater things await us hereafter? We cannot render God a more glorious service than by showing ourselves immovable and unchangeable amid the storms of persecutions. And whoever has once put us to flight will perhaps put us to flight again and again. And if it happens that higher and harder things remain for us to endure, how will this be established? By some oracle or divine utterance? Nothing of the kind. This, then, is a carnal imagining, not a suggestion and counsel of the divine Spirit: human weakness, not Christian prudence.

units.la: 14. Quod fugerint Apostoli, idq; praecipiente Saluatore: licet specie cum illis videatur consentire, reipsa non est assi-ne. Nam Apostoli tunc temporis nulli certae congregationi praeficiebantur; quin in Iudaea, vbicunque Euangelium praedicarent, ipsis succreuit seges. Non in vna magis vrbe, quam in alia expectandus erat verbi Dei proventus. Ita Christus, neque Hierosolymis, neque Nazareth, neq; Canae, neq; Ca-pernaum se astrinxit, sed in Iudaea quandoque, in Galilaeae aliis, interdum in Decapoli, vicatim, & oppidatim euns, semen regni disseminauit. Similis erat Apostolorum post Christi ascensionem prouincia, qui generaliter in Gentibus praeconizandum didicerunt, uti Paulo omnium {y}Ecclesiarum curam incubuit. Scopus igitur, & finis vocationis eorum, non erat irritus, aut inanis; cum a loco isto ad illum discederent, dum ubique fideles in unum congregare elaborarent. Imo credendum est, de industria nonnunquam, Dominum turbas, & tempestates excitasse, ut ab una regione digredientes Discipuli, in alia pietatem edocerent. Sed post sermonem Dei propagatum, Politia Ecclesiastica est aliter institu-ta. In qualibet congregatione, presbyteri per {z}Titum ordi-nandi erant: & certis caetibus, sui certi Pastores, in {a}Actis Apostolicis designabantur, id, quod hodie usu venit. Nunc ubi standum est, & qui nobis pascendi, & instituendi demandantur cognoscitur. Hoc tuae est ditionis, id illius, & quilibet in sua statione, & vigilia sit assiduus. Hinc Dioeceses, & Paroeciae, suis certis limitibus, & finibus distinguuntur, & in Rebuspublicis Christianis, quo cuique proficiscendum sit, in rebus sacris intelligitur. Et in istis, Episcopus in sua provincia, Minister in suo populo, officio per Christum commendato fungatur. Ex eius ore, ipsorum, post Deum, pendent animae: cibum ergo impertiat. Quis istorum subleuabit onera, si in maximo discrimine, patronus, & pater defe-rat? Paterfamilias summus Deus, illi suos liberos commisit educandos: ab ipso rursum exiget. Cum igitur lupus, aut tyrannus aduenerit, huic nullo fugiendum est modo. Qui liber est, arbitrio utatur suo. Qui non certis personis alligatur, discedat si volet; stationem non linquit. Ethoc ipsum, existimo in causa fuisse, cur flamma, ferroque apud Nostra-tes sequentibus, post beatissimae memoriae Edouardi Sexti felicia tempora, ex Episcopis, & Ministris nonnulli, ultima sint experti: erant scilicet certi gregis, pastores certi: Alii autem, praesertim ex Academiis, ista, & Cantabrigiensi, in partes transmarinas diuerterint. Nō præposuisset eos Deus, alicui populo, coram quo ingrediendum, aut egrediendum esset; sed tanquam filij Prophetarum, in scholis Prophetarum, libere sunt enutriti, ut, cum euocaret Deus, in promptu essent. Cum Socij igitur Collegiorum fuissent, neque cura Pastorali implicati, ingessit ipsis in mentem Dominus, ut aufugiendo, se, pro Seminario Ecclesiæ Anglicanæ, in sereniora usque tempora reservarent. Sed nihil hoc ad reliquos, qui astringuntur, ut nec aliud etiam Apostolorum & Christi, qui speciali alicui non præerant loco, ut Paulus itidem, cum è Damasco in sporta dimissus discederet.
units.tr: 14. As for the Apostles having fled, and that at the Saviour's command: although in appearance this seems to agree with them, in reality it is not the same. For the Apostles at that time were not placed over any particular congregation; rather, wherever they preached the Gospel in Judaea, the harvest sprang up for them. The fruit of the word of God was to be expected in one city no more than in another. So Christ bound himself neither to Jerusalem, nor to Nazareth, nor to Cana, nor to Capernaum, but going from village to village and from town to town, he scattered the seed of the kingdom sometimes in Judaea, at other times in other parts of Galilee, and at times in Decapolis. Similar was the task of the Apostles after Christ's ascension, who had been taught to proclaim the gospel in general among the Gentiles, just as the care of all the churches lay upon Paul. The aim and end of their calling, therefore, was not vain or empty, when they left one place for another, labouring everywhere to gather the faithful into one body. Indeed, it must be believed that the Lord sometimes deliberately stirred up crowds and tempests, so that the disciples, departing from one region, might teach piety in another. But after the word of God had been spread abroad, the ecclesiastical polity was instituted otherwise. In every congregation, elders were to be ordained by Titus; and for certain assemblies, their own particular ministers were appointed, as is recorded in the Acts of the Apostles, which is what happens today. Now it is known where we must stand, and who are entrusted to us to feed and instruct. This one belongs to your jurisdiction, that one to another's, and let each be constant in his own station and watch. Hence dioceses and parishes are distinguished by their fixed boundaries and limits, and in Christian commonwealths it is understood, in sacred matters, where each must go. And in these, let the bishop in his own province, and the minister in his own people, discharge the office committed to them by Christ. From their mouth, after God, the souls of those under them depend; let them therefore dispense food. Who among these will bear the burdens, if in the greatest danger the patron and father should desert? The Father of the household, God most high, has committed his children to them to be brought up; from them in turn he will require an account. Therefore, when a wolf or a tyrant comes, there is in no way to be flight for them. Whoever is free may use his own judgment. Whoever is not bound to certain persons may depart if he wishes; he does not abandon his station. And this very thing, I think, was the reason why, under the Nostrates [English?] who followed, after the happy times of Edward the Sixth of most blessed memory, some of the bishops and ministers experienced the final extremity by fire and sword: they were, to be sure, the pastors of a fixed flock. Others, however, especially from the universities, both Oxford and Cambridge, turned aside to lands beyond the sea. God had not set them over any people before whom they were to come in or go out; but, like the sons of the prophets, they were freely nurtured in the schools of the prophets, so that when God should call, they might be ready at hand. Since, then, they had been fellows of colleges and were not entangled in pastoral care, the Lord put it into their minds that by fleeing they should keep themselves, as a seminary of the English Church, for calmer times. But this does not apply to the rest, who are bound, just as neither did the other Apostles and Christ, who did not preside over any particular place, as Paul likewise did, when he was let down from Damascus in a basket and departed.

units.la: 15. Verum aliud etiam est, quod in Pauli persona excep-tionem patitur. Persecutio, quæ Damasci orta est, non adhuc aduersus omnes Christi-fideles, aut Pastores omnes est instituta, sed soli inuidebatur Paulo. In eum, eiusq; vnicum caput, ea erat cudenda faba, quippe qui ita vehementer Christum annunciasset. Fremebant igitur in ipsum crudeles homines; ipsiusq; vitæ insidias structas cupiebant. Tuti satis, & incolumes viuebant cæteri, & ipse Ananias Damasci substitit; qui, cum tanta præditus esset gratia, ut Saulum consolari, & sanare valeret; proculdubio, & reliquis Christū profitentibus opportune verbū subministrare poterat. Sed & alij etiam ex Discipulis adesse poterant, ita, ut per Pauli discessum, necessarium Ecclesiæ ministerium destituendum non esset. Non cum tanta fortassis copia, aut eloquentia, aut potentia, ut prius, docerentur, verum docerentur tamen. Specialis ergo ista cū esset persecutio, & Personalis alicuius poterat esse fuga. Hoc ipsum, de Vriah in Ægyptum recedente, ut furorem Regis Iehojakin euitaret, asseuerandum est. Tunc etenim, Hierosolymis mansit Jeremias Propheta, qui pro temporis necessitate, Diuinam voluntatem, Regi, populoque notam faceret. Neque alia erat Athanasij causa; cui tanta ab Arrianis apud Constantium inuidia conflata est, ut eius vitae insidiae struendae essent. Quemadmodum, cum reliqui Sacerdotum Constantinopoli manerent, Iohannes {b}Chrysostomus solus, unicusque in exilium pulsus est; & in ipsum omnis est deriuata rabies; ita solus Athanasius Imperatori stomachum moverat, cum reliqui e Clero Alexandriae permanerent. Id {c}quod ex eo constat, quod cum semel inter concionandum militibus templum ingeretur, qui Episcopum comprehenderent; accesserunt Diaconi, qui nolentem, & invitum recedere coegerunt; cum ipsi potius in animo fuisset, in templo expectare. Adfuerunt etiam ex Clero alij, qui ita exeuntem circundederunt, ut Deo quasi oculos inimicorum obcæcante, a militibus, inter alios non dignosceretur. Cum igitur per secessionem suam, Sacramentorum, sermonisque usum & pietatis seruitium cum persona sua non auferret; sic fugere licuerat Athanasio, quod & Pastoribus nostro etiam licet tempore, si non generalis, sed specialis sit persecutio, & supersint qui instituant.
units.tr: 15. Truly there is another thing, which in Paul's case suffers an exception. The persecution which arose at Damascus was not yet directed against all Christian believers, or against all ministers, but was aimed only at Paul. Against him, and against his one head, that was the bean to be hammered out, since he had preached Christ so vehemently. Cruel men therefore raged against him and were eager to lay plots against his life. The rest lived quite safely and unharmed, and Ananias himself remained at Damascus; who, since he was endowed with such grace that he could comfort and heal Saul, could undoubtedly also supply the word opportunely to the others who professed Christ. But other disciples also could be present, so that by Paul's departure the necessary ministry of the Church would not have to be abandoned. Perhaps not with as great a supply, or eloquence, or power as before, but they would nevertheless be taught. This persecution, then, was special, and the flight could be that of one particular person. The same must be asserted of Uriah, who withdrew into Egypt to escape the fury of King Jehoiakim. For at that time the prophet Jeremiah remained at Jerusalem, who, as the need of the time required, would make the divine will known to the king and the people. Nor was the cause of Athanasius any different; against him so great hatred was stirred up by the Arians with Constantius that plots against his life were laid. Just as, when the other priests remained at Constantinople, John Chrysostom alone and by himself was driven into exile, and all the madness was turned against him alone; so Athanasius alone had stirred the anger of the emperor, while the rest of the clergy in Alexandria remained. That this is evident from the fact that once, while he was preaching, soldiers were sent into the church to seize the bishop; the deacons came up and forced him, unwilling and unwilling, to withdraw, although he himself had rather intended to wait for them in the church. Other clergy also were present, who surrounded him as he went out, so that, as if God had blinded the eyes of the enemies, he was not recognised among the others by the soldiers. Therefore, since by his withdrawal he did not take away from his own person the use of the sacraments and of sermons, nor the service of piety, it was lawful for Athanasius to flee in this way; and this may be lawful for pastors in our own time too, if the persecution is not general but special, and if there remain others to carry on the work.

units.la: 17. Promiseram initio, me propter similitudinem Argumenti, de pestifera saeviente tempestate, adiecturu[?] aliquid; cuius rei materia, licet non ita directe, ex Paulino exemplo petiposs[?]it; ex sermone tamen Christi, apud {e}Ioannem, mul. to rectius; ubi sub lupi nomine periculosum, diuastansque omne intelligatur. Hic, uti dicam breuiter; quemadmodum fuerunt, qui nulli Christiano ineundam fugam in Persecutione disputarunt; in quibus, ut supra aliquet[?], fuerat Tertullianus: ita magna hominum pars, & in primaria Regni nostri vrbe, non pauci, praesertim autem, qui inferioris fortis sunt, à pestilentia ingruente, non esse secedendum, affirmabunt pertinaciter. Expertus loquor. Et assignant rationem, sibi fortassis speciosam, quod morbus iste & contagio, Diuina sit visitatio, cui se subducere, nulli licet hominum. Et quod cuilibet suum viuendi tempus assignetur, quod, vt nullo modo produci, aut protelari, sic nec contrahi, praeuerti aut anticipari potest. At quam ista sunt futilia, prudenter inspicienti? Nam si quidlibet mihi liceat pro arbitrio aggredi, quia certa mihi tempora moriendi sint praefixa, & periodus sit vitae; nec priusquam expirandi aduenerit hora, vllo pacto moriar; quid ni, & in mare me proiciam, aut à rupe mittam praecipitem, aut, vt {f}Satanas Christo suggesserat, me de templi pinnaculo deturbem? Ostendit Saluator, hoc esse, tentare Dominum, quod praecise {g}interdicitur. Summus Deus, vt fines nobis ordinauit, sic ordinauit media; & ea omni modo sunt nobis perquirenda. Conseruandae vitae medium, est edere, & dormire, & à malis me reuocare, & periculis ingruentibus: & oportet ista facere. Quod autem ad Diuinam visitationem attinet, esto sane virga Dei; & si ea te percusserit, patienter est ferenda, Sed cum non est opus, ne temere teipsum ingeras, ne tibi violentas videare ingessisse manus, sicque homicidij reus esse. {h}Pestilentiam, & morbos, in flagellorum suorum numero, & acerbissimorum, recenset Deus: Sed & gladium etiam, & famem, & noxiarum bestiarum dentes, & alia vt eiusdem plane generis. Cur igitur non in illis, Diuinam castigationem amplecteris, aeque ac in peste? Cum {i}Saul iaculo suo Dauidem confossum, parieti affigere cogitasset, cur aufugit Dauid? Cum fames magna Jacob, & Patriarchas premeret, quare frumenti causa, misit in Ægyptum Jacob, & non potius inedia periit, quia Divina esset castigatio? Magis pie & sapienter, tum Jacob, tum Dauid.
units.tr: 17. I promised at the outset that, because of the similarity of the subject, I would add something about the deadly raging storm of plague; the matter of this, though not so directly, could be sought from Paul's example, but much more rightly from Christ's saying in John, where danger and devastation are understood under the name of the wolf. Here, as I shall say briefly: just as there were those who argued that no Christian should take flight in persecution, among whom, as I noted above, Tertullian was one, so a great part of mankind, and not a few even in the chief city of our kingdom, especially those of lower rank, will stubbornly maintain that one should not withdraw from the approaching pestilence. I speak from experience. And they give a reason which perhaps seems plausible to themselves: that this disease and contagion is a divine visitation, from which no man may withdraw; and that to each person a time to live is appointed, which, as it cannot in any way be lengthened or prolonged, so it cannot be shortened, forestalled or anticipated. But how trifling are these things to one who looks at them prudently! For if I were free to undertake anything at my own discretion, because the times of my death are fixed for me and the course of my life is set, and I shall by no means die before the hour of expiring has come, why should I not also cast myself into the sea, or hurl myself headlong from a cliff, or, as Satan suggested to Christ, cast myself down from the pinnacle of the temple? The Saviour showed that this is to tempt the Lord, which is precisely what is forbidden. The highest God, as he has ordained the ends for us, so has he ordained the means; and these must be sought by us in every way. The means of preserving life is to eat and to sleep, and to keep myself from evils and from impending dangers; and these things one ought to do. As for divine visitation, let it indeed be the rod of God; and if it strikes you, it is to be borne patiently. But when there is no need, do not thrust yourself rashly into danger, lest you seem to have laid violent hands upon yourself and so be guilty of homicide. God counts pestilence and diseases among his scourges, and among the most bitter of them; but also the sword, and famine, and the teeth of harmful beasts, and others of the same plain kind. Why then do you not embrace divine chastisement in those as well as in the plague? When Saul, having tried to nail David, pierced by his javelin, to a wall, why did David flee away? When a great famine pressed Jacob and the patriarchs, why did Jacob send for grain into Egypt, and not rather perish by hunger, because it was divine chastisement? More godly and more wisely, both Jacob and David acted.

units.la: 18 Fugiendæ sunt cuilibet, sui perdendi occasiones. {k}& Speciale est præceptum, de vitanda cæde; si aliena, certe nostra: siquidem charitas incipit à seipsa: & diligendi sunt alij, non aliter, quàm /ut nos ipsi. Si nobis igitur non liceat,{l} mortem ullo modo conscisere, nec & viam ingredi, quæ ducit ad mortem; nec media aggredi, quæ iuxta sunt. Et ut in aliis istud, sic in peste; quæ, {m}occisor sane est, & millia multa quam cito dissipat. Iterum, proposuit Deus etiam plagas suas omnes, & terribiles, & metuendas; & animis igitur, & corporibus auertendas. In istis est Pestilentia. Præterea, cum incolumitatis sui populi rationem haberet Deus, de lepra copiose in lege disseruit; qui dignoscenda esset, quomodo discernenda; ad quem eius cura spectaret. Sed & leprosos, habitu distinctos esse voluit, & exclamare: {n}Ego im-mundus sum, ego immundus sum. Ita, extra castra, aut urbem degere seiunctim,{o} & separatim præcepit, ne contaminata fœditate sua alios inficerent. Si morbo leuiore, qui infestat profecto, sed non occidit ut Pestis, noluerit Deus suum populum inquinari, quanto magis à contagione plurimum formidabili, cito discedendum esse voluit? Turcæ igitur, id quod faciunt, in loca pestilentia, & contagiosa, sine discrimine irruant; Christiani autem, se contineant. Neq; importuni homines exclamando querelas faciant de fratribus suis; qui necessariis temporibus, se, & liberos, & familiam suam subducunt. Quibus Deus rei opportunitatem concessit, ij bono cum animo utantur. Sed absentes, languentibus suis fratribus, iam miseris, ne desint; verum consilio, auxilio, quibus poterint modis, iuuent, dirigant, consolentur. Ea Christianorum est sympathia, & compassio.
units.tr: 18. Every man must flee the occasions of his own destruction. And there is a special precept about avoiding slaughter; if of others, certainly of ourselves, since charity begins with itself, and others are to be loved only as we love ourselves. If therefore it is not lawful for us to bring about our own death in any way, nor to enter the path that leads to death, nor to approach the means that lie close to it, then so it is with others, and so it is with the plague, which is surely a killer and quickly scatters many thousands. Again, God has set forth all his plagues, both terrible and to be feared, and therefore they are to be averted from both souls and bodies. Pestilence is among these. Moreover, when God had regard for the safety of his people, he discoursed at length in the law about leprosy: how it was to be recognised, how to be distinguished, and to whom its care belonged. He also wished lepers to be marked by their dress and to cry out: "I am unclean, I am unclean." So he commanded them to dwell apart, outside the camp or the city, lest by their contaminating foulness they infect others. If God did not will his people to be defiled by a lighter disease, which indeed troubles but does not kill as the plague does, how much more did he will that one should quickly withdraw from a contagion that is most dreadful! Let the Turks therefore, as they do, rush without distinction into places stricken by plague and contagion; but let Christians restrain themselves. Nor should unreasonable men raise complaints with shouts against their brothers, who in necessary times withdraw themselves, their children, and their household. Let those to whom God has granted the opportunity use it with a good conscience. But let those who are absent not fail their brothers, who are now sick and wretched; rather, by counsel, by help, and by whatever means they can, let them assist, direct and console them. Such is the fellow-feeling and compassion of Christians.

units.la: 19. Sed de Ministro Euangelij, & Pastore gregis aliud sentio. Et quæ supra habentur rationes, de animabus hominum suæ curæ demandatis, unde in Persecutione non discedat, hic etiam locum habent. Si feruente Pestilentia in fugam se conuerterit, quis necessaria Ecclesiæ officia præstabit? quis sermonem sanioribus? quis ægrotantibus consolationem impertiet? infinita profecto sunt, quæ ipsum in usum quotidianum aduocant; neque recte possunt transi-gi, si Dux desit spiritualis, qui consilium adhibeat. Credo igitur Sacerdoti, hoc est, Pastori gregis, ne Mercenarius fiat, discedendum non esse ex peculiari sua vocatione, quæ libertatem, aliis impertitam & indultam, tollit. Quia tamen in priuata, secretaque morte, non eousque eminet Diuina gloria, ac in aperto martyrio, bonæ causa conscientiæ; & quoniam vniuersæ congregationi multa sunt præstanda munia, æque atque ægrotantibus; non existimo, ei necessitatem incumbere, vt thalamos, & cubicula ægrotantium ingrediatur, quod sine manifesto vitæ discrimine, fieri non potest. Media ergo aliqua sumenda est via, vt nec fugiat, nec contagioni, se confidenter nimis immisceat. Vbi aderit occasio, scribendo, nunciando, acclamando, à longe stando, & adhortando adsit; quibus, & aliorum consulat bono, & nimis etiam, in se non accersat mala. Quid si insignis a-liqua causa, ad Diuinam gloriam apertissime faciens, aut Ecclesiæ vtilitatem conspicuam, vehementer vrgeat, vt alicui adsit; modo post orationem seriam, & affectuosam, suæ conscientiæ instinctus, id prudenter, & sobrie, & summo cum iudicio submonuerit, (multum etenim tribuo, sobrio viri prudentis instinctui; & prudentissimus debebat esse, Minister Euangelij) potestatem ingrediendi, non audeo tollere. Sed vt Medici in talibus tempestatibus, se suffumigiis, & odoribus, & medicamentis, corroborant, ita corporis quam potest curam agat. Sed præsertim, orando humiliter, & præsumptuosam arrogantiam apud summum Numen diffiteatur, & animam in euentum omnem, Deo commendet. mendet. De populo, per Pastorem, in templa conuocan-do; cum ita grassabitur pestis, ut merito verendum sit, ne in arctum coeuntes, languorem inter se, & infectionem magis adaugeant, nihil præscribo; sed circumstantias, aut conueniendi, aut in domibus priuatis permanendi Magistratus, Ministri, piorumque, in congregatione iudicio vigilanti, & circumspecto relinquo; quibus curæ esse debet, ut sancte, amice, prudenter, & cum minimo, quantum fieri potest, incommodo, transigantur omnia. Neque hic quisquam, aut ultra sobrietatem sapiens, aut præter modestiam pertinax esse debet, sed in commune humiliter consulere.
units.tr: 19. But concerning the minister of the Gospel and the pastor of the flock I think otherwise. The reasons set out above, concerning the souls of men committed to his care, for which he should not depart in persecution, apply here too. If, while the pestilence rages, he turns to flight, who will perform the necessary duties of the Church? Who will preach sound doctrine to the people? Who will bring consolation to the sick? Indeed there are countless things that call for him in daily use, and these cannot rightly be carried out if the spiritual leader, who should give counsel, is absent. I believe therefore that the priest, that is, the pastor of the flock, lest he become a hireling, must not depart from his particular calling, which takes away the liberty granted and allowed to others. Yet because in a private and secret death the divine glory does not shine forth as clearly as in open martyrdom for the good cause of conscience; and because many duties are to be performed for the whole congregation, as well as for the sick, I do not think it lies upon him as a necessity to enter the bedchambers and rooms of the sick, which cannot be done without a manifest danger to life. Some middle way therefore must be taken, so that he neither flees nor exposes himself too confidently to contagion. Where there is occasion, let him be present by writing, by sending word, by calling out, by standing at a distance, and by exhorting; by these means he may both serve the good of others and not needlessly bring evils upon himself. But if some notable cause, clearly serving the divine glory or the conspicuous usefulness of the Church, urgently requires that he be present with someone, then, after serious and heartfelt prayer, and prompted by his conscience, if he has prudently, soberly and with the greatest judgment recognised this, (for I attribute great weight to the sober promptings of a prudent man, and a minister of the Gospel ought to be most prudent) I do not dare to take away his power of entering. But just as physicians in such stormy times fortify themselves with fumigations, scents and medicines, so let him take what care he can of his body. Above all, let him pray humbly, and confess before the supreme Deity his presumptuous arrogance, and commend his soul and all outcomes to God. Concerning the people, to be summoned to the churches through the pastor, when the plague rages so fiercely that it is rightly to be feared lest, gathering close together, they increase the sickness and infection among themselves, I prescribe nothing; but I leave the circumstances, whether of meeting or of remaining in private houses, to the watchful and circumspect judgment of the magistrates, the ministers and the godly within the congregation, to whom it should be a concern that everything be carried out holily, kindly, prudently, and with as little inconvenience as possible. Nor should anyone here be either wiser than sobriety allows or stubborn beyond moderation, but humbly consult together for the common good.

units.la: Sic habetis de Fuga, tum in Persecutione, tum in Peste, ani-mi mei iudicium. Auerte æterne Deus hæc mala à nobis, & à nostra Ecclesia; & concede propitius, ut per omnia secu-la, ad adventum usque tui filij, nostra Anglia pacate Euan-gelium amplectatur, ad filij tui gloriam, cui tecum, & cum Spiritu Sancto, sit honor, & immortalitas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Thus you have my judgement on flight, both in persecution and in plague. Eternal God, turn these evils away from us and from our Church; and graciously grant that, through all ages until the coming of your Son, our England may embrace the peaceful Gospel, to the glory of your Son, to whom, with you and with the Holy Spirit, be honour and immortality for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPUT SEXTUM. AN DEUS SIT AUTHOR peccati ?
units.tr: CHAPTER SIX. WHETHER GOD IS THE AUTHOR OF SIN?

units.la: Apocalyps. 17.17. Deus enim dedit in corda eorum, ut exequantur, quod ipsi visum est, & ut consentiant, dentque regnum suum Bestiæ, donec compleantur verba Dei.
units.tr: Revelation 17:17. For God has put it into their hearts to carry out his purpose, and to be of one mind, and to give their kingdom to the Beast, until the words of God are fulfilled.

units.la: 3. Pontificiorum calumnia contra Protestantes. 4. Ab homine, non à Deo peccatum ortum est: 5. Permissione Diuina contingit. 6. Et gratiam subducendo. 7. In actione operatur Deus, non in obliquitate. 10. Et offert ea quæ mali in peccatum conuertunt. 12. Explicatio testimoniorum Scripturæ, quæ ex adverso stare videntur.
units.tr: 3. The Papists' slander against the Protestants. 4. Sin arose from man, not from God. 5. It happens by divine permission. 6. And by withdrawing grace. 7. God works in the action, not in the wrongdoing. 10. And he offers those things which the wicked turn into sin. 12. Explanation of the testimonies of Scripture which seem to stand on the opposite side.

units.la: DE Antichristo, & Bestia, quorum gestus, sedes, potentia, totius fere mundi dementatio, si alicubi, praesenti isto capite ad viuum delineatur, non est instituti nostri hodie dicere. Eius etenim Controuersiae perplexi nodi, Joannisque Apocalyptici non rara Ae-nigmata, non vnam, quae nobis iam superest, horam, sed dies, mensesque multos desiderant, vt pro mysterij dignitate explicentur. Et si ea certe prouincia suscipienda esset, recenti, alacrique aggredienda esset militi; non fesso, vt nos sumus, & languenti. Sed Ducem illud requirit exercitatissimum, in omni militiae genere versatum; non hominem gregarium, cui bene est, si qualem, qualem operam, in praeliis Domini praestare possit. Quod istud igitur tetigerim (vt veritatem libere agnoscam) inuitus quasi, & renitens facio, Argumento iam tandem alio destitutus, quod Sexto repraesentari possit loco. Quae etenim praecesserunt Quaestio-nes quinque, aut ab animo obtrusae meo, aut ab aliis, quibus pauca negare possum, oblatae accesserunt: sed cum ad Sextum tandem lapidem peruenien-dum esset; & nostrum praesterilitate sua defecit ingenium, & hortatus defuit, copellatioque aliorum, quibus poteram, iam indigus subleuari. Tandem tamen, reuocato quasi spiritu me accinxi, non inutilem in praesenti (quod sperabam) negotio, operam positurus, si quo modo Deus hominibus malignis in animum suggerat, vt eas peragant actiones, quae malitiam in se continent, exposuero. Cui quidem ansam praebet, quod narrat Joannes, de Regibus, iugo Bestiae sua colla subdentibus.
units.tr: It is not my purpose today to describe in lively detail the Antichrist and the Beast, whose conduct, seat, power, and near-total derangement of the world, if anywhere, are depicted to the life in this present chapter. Their controversy has perplexing knots, and the riddles of John the Apocalyptist are not rare; they require not one hour, which is all that remains to us, but many days and months, if they are to be explained in a manner worthy of the mystery. And if indeed that province were to be undertaken, it ought to be entered by a fresh and eager soldier, not by one wearied and weak as we are. But it calls for a most experienced commander, versed in every kind of warfare, not a common soldier, who is content if he can render whatever small service he may in the battles of the Lord. Therefore, touching this matter (to acknowledge the truth freely), I do so somewhat unwillingly and reluctantly, being now at last without any other subject that could be presented in the sixth place. For the five questions which went before came either forced upon my mind or offered by others, to whom I can deny little; but when at last I had to reach the sixth milestone, my wit failed through its own barrenness, the impulse was lacking, and the encouragement of others, by whom I might have been supported, was now wanting. Yet at last, as if my spirit were recalled, I girded myself, intending to set forth, in the present business (which I hope will not be useless), a work by which, if in some way God should put into the minds of wicked men the will to carry out those actions which contain malice in themselves. The occasion for this is given by what John tells of the kings who bend their necks to the yoke of the Beast.

units.la: 2. Cum etenim de Principibus, & mundi Monarchis, Diuinus spiritus disseruisset, quos suis philtris, & medicamentis suarum fornicationum amatoriis inebriatos reddidit Babylonia Meretrix; Diuinam esse voluntatem contestatur, vt haec fiant; Dominum q; omnium, ipsis in cor indidisse, vt Dominia minia, Regnaq; sua Meretrici submittant. Cum vero {a}An-tichristus sit Aduersarius, & homo perditionis, sese Diuinis eloquiis opponens, & contramittens; & quantum in ipso est, è sede, throno que suo, Saluatorem mundi deturbans: cum religio,cultusque, quem sui sequacibus proponit, non nisi multis superstitionibus inuolutus, plurimisque fœdita-tibus contpurcatus esse poterit: cum eius milites & clientes, deuoti,iuratiq; Christi hostes censendi sint: cum, qui penes inimicum hunc, authoritatem, potestatemq; suam statuant, tenebrarum, & caliginis perpetuæ regnum promoueant, & adaugeant: quicq; istis faciendis, animum, aut operâ immit-tat,quæ mala sunt,& pessima,peccatoq; cõtaminata, sugge-rere, iuuare, efficere videatur, quid de Deo iudicabimus, aut de eius actionibus sentiemus? num mali, aut peccati au-thorem esse cogitabimus,quod non nisi blasphemum est,& à Maiestate tam sacrosancta alienum,aut leuiori interpreta-tione, dogma molliemus, & circumstantiis distinguendis, aut Scripturæ testimoniis reconciliandis, Deo suam inno-centiam,&integritatem,hominibus veropollutionem pro-priam, & multiplicem transgressionem asseremus? {b}Deus verax quidem sit, & omnis homo mendax.
units.tr: 2. For when the divine Spirit had spoken of princes and monarchs of the world, whom the Babylonian Harlot made drunk with her love-potions and drugs of her fornications, he testifies that it is the divine will that these things should happen, and that the Lord of all has put it into their hearts to surrender their lordships and kingdoms to the Harlot. But since the Antichrist is an adversary and a man of perdition, opposing himself to the divine oracles and setting himself against them, and, as far as in him lies, casting the Saviour of the world from his seat and throne; since the religion and worship which he proposes to his followers can be wrapped up only in many superstitions and defiled by very many foulnesses; since his soldiers and clients are to be counted as devoted and sworn enemies of Christ; since those who under this enemy establish and maintain their authority and power promote and increase the kingdom of perpetual darkness and gloom; and since whoever lends his mind or his work to doing these things, which are evil and most wicked and polluted with sin, appears to suggest, help, and bring them about, what shall we judge concerning God, or what shall we think of his actions? Shall we think him the author of evil or of sin? This is nothing but blasphemy, and alien to so sacrosanct a Majesty. Or shall we soften the doctrine by a milder interpretation, by distinguishing circumstances or by reconciling it with the testimonies of Scripture, and so assert God's innocence and integrity, but man's own pollution and manifold transgression? "Let God be true, but every man a liar."

units.la: 3. Edmundus Campianus, qui Romanæ synagogæ in Angliatum labentis ruinas suffulcire se posse iactitauerat, cum in Ecclesiæ contumeliam, & Protestantium omnium, vte Goliah quondam in exercitum Hebræorum, conuicia{c} quotquot poterat,voluisset congerere; Paradoxa,seu [illegible, ~3 letters]recenset, à nobis defensitata, in quibus illud primo occurritloco: {d}Deus est author, & causa peccati, volens, suggerens, efficiens, iubens, operans, & in hoc, impiorum scelerata consilia gubernans. Proprium Dei opus fuit, vt vocatio Pauli, sic adulterium Dauidis, Iudæque proditoris impietas. Etista implicare, & irretire sententia, Lutheranos, Zuinglianos, Caluinistas omnes, vt per contemptum ipsi nos appellant, parum curat, Sed & alij Pontificis assecla, multo maximæ Reformatorum caterua, ista solent obiicere; præcipue vero iis, qui modum, & ordinem Divinæ operationis, in reprobis, hominibusque impiis, penitius, & exactius discutierunt. Cuius quefelæ[?] amouendæ gratia, {e}nonnulli Apologias conscripserunt, suamque, & Ecclesiarum mentem explicatius tradiderunt. Quoniam tamen peruersa ipsorum malignitas non desistit obgannire; & quo plenius informentur, qui mehodie audiunt, neque magnam in Quæstione ista operam posuerunt; Operæ precium existimo, Ecclesiarum Reformatarum in præsenti causa doctrinam explicare & stabilire. Id igitur inconcussum, & firmissimum fundamentum apud nos permanet, Divinam Maiestatem, peccati, & vitii authorem non esse. Qui enim boni unicus est fons, cuius omnia {f}opera fuerant condita absolute bona; qui in Angelis immorigeris, in orbe antiquo per diluvium pereunte, in Sodomis sulphureo igne dissipatis, iniquitatem, & iniustitiam tam seuere vindicavit; qui in resurrectione iustorum, perpetuis cum tormentis, & gehennalibus, de transgressionibus impoenitentium, supplicium est sumptu-rus, suam gloriam immaculatam, eoque contaminari non vult, ut malitiæ, & ἀδικίας effector, opifexque existat. Hoc etenim illud esset, quod labe ineluibili[?] tam insignem innocentiam conspurcaret, & talibus innodaret laqueis, quibus est impossibile, ut supremum illud Numen distringeretur. Quoniam tamen nihil fit, quin Dei digitus quodammodo videatur in ipso se ostendere, ponemus Aphorismos quosdam, & conditiones; quibus Dei operatio ostendatur; & quæ putentur in aduersostare, Scripturæ testimonia secundum fidei Analogiam explicentur.
units.tr: 3. Edmund Campion, who had boasted that he could prop up the tottering ruins of the Roman synagogue in England, when he wished to heap up as many insults as he could against the Church and all Protestants, like Goliath once against the army of the Hebrews, recounted paradoxes, defended by us, of which the first that comes to mind is this: God is the author and cause of sin, willing, suggesting, effecting, commanding, working, and in this governing the wicked counsels of the impious. It was God's own work, as the calling of Paul, so the adultery of David and the impiety of Judas the traitor. He cares little to entangle and ensnare all Lutherans, Zwinglians, and Calvinists, whom they call by the contemptuous name of "us"; but other followers of the Pontiff, and a much greater host of the Reformed, are accustomed to bring these things forward, especially against those who have more deeply and exactly examined the manner and order of the divine operation in the reprobate and impious men. In order to remove this complaint, some have written Apologies and have more fully set forth their own mind and that of the Churches. Since, however, the perverse malignity of these men does not cease to snarl, and so that those who today hear me may be more fully informed, and since they have not taken much pains with this question, I think it worth the effort to explain and establish the doctrine of the Reformed Churches in the present case. That, then, remains among us an unshaken and most firm foundation: the divine Majesty is not the author of sin and vice. For he who is the sole fountain of good, by whose works all things were created absolutely good; who in the disobedient Angels, in the old world perishing by the flood, and in Sodom dissolved by sulphurous fire, avenged iniquity and injustice so severely; who in the resurrection of the just, with perpetual torments and in hell, is about to take punishment for the transgressions of the unrepentant, does not wish his glory, which is spotless, to be stained by this, so that he should exist as the author and workman of wickedness and unrighteousness. For this would be to defile so remarkable an innocence with an indelible stain and to bind it with such snares as would make it impossible for that supreme Deity to be unentangled. Yet since nothing happens without the finger of God in some way appearing to show itself in it, we will set down certain aphorisms and conditions by which the operation of God is shown, and the testimonies of Scripture which seem to stand on the opposite side will be explained according to the analogy of faith.

units.la: 4. Primo igitur in initio, cum à Divino præcepto facta esset per Adamum exorbitatio, non à pio conditore profecta est hæc transgressio, sed ab homine, & Diabolo. Fecit Deus impollutum hominem, & incontaminatum, arbitrio reuera fruentem libero, per quod stare potuisset, modo vo-luisset; & cuius etiam vi, penes ipsum esset, in perditionis foueam se immittere. Accessit Satanas (qui eadem libera voluntate cecidisset prius) & ex suo in Deum, eiusque crea-turam odio, suggessit, quod non oportuit. Ita loquitura-pud Iudaeos Christus: {g}Pater vester Diabolus, occisor fuit ab ini-tio, & in veritate non permansit, quia non est in ipso veritas. Cum mendacium loquitur, ex suo loquitur, mendax etenim ipse est, & eiusdem pater. Aduertite, quod ex proprio loquatur Sata-nas, non sic factus à Deo. Desciuit à primo gradu, in quo fuerat constitutus, Adamus etiam, per defectionem: Non aliter, quam vinum, quod per aeris circumambientis vi-tium, aut dolij, in quod funditur, corruptelam, austerum nimis, aut insipidum saporem contrahit, quo in naturam a-cerosam transmutatur. Qui carpendo vuas, vindemiauit, & qui calcauit torcular, culpandus non est, quod austerita-tem, postea contrahendo, è vino in acetum permutatur: generosum enim ille, salubreque reliquerat. Sed aliunde, & extrinsecus accessit defectio. Qui patre pio, bonoque natus est, neque vel vestigia audaciae, & impudentiae in pa-terna vita conspexit, sociorum foedis tamen moribus con-taminatus, in nequitiam prorumpit. Non est istud vitio ver-tendum Patri, quod labe filium infecerit, praesertim cum per aetatem, juiam[?] iuris factus sit filius, nec ulterius à paren-tis nutu pendeat; sed facilitate sua nimia, ab exemplo do-mestico honestatis, & virtutis, juvenis degeneravit. Mor-bos quoldam Medici appellant Haereditarios, per semen genitoris, in prolem propagatos. Non iniusta est querela nati; qui, se ex ipsis parentum lumbis, suum hausisse morbu[?] pr̄ nunciabit, cum putridum, malignumque intra se hu-morem senserit. Sin parentes sani, robustiq; sætum sui simi-lem procreauerint, ut valens, vigensq; corpus habeat, succi, sansanguinisque plenum; verum in rixas & pugnas, se ingeren-do, vulneratus fuerit; sicque languens ex vulnere decubue-rit; stultitiae iuuenili ascribendum hoc est, non parentum infectioni. Sic se habet tum Satanæ, tum Adami corruptio. Ingenerata non est, sed aliunde ascita. E vino, facti sunt ace-tum; e generosis, degeneres; e solidis, & sanis, vulnerati. Im-munis est Creator, vitiosa creatura. Egregie Basilius: {h}Non ingenitus est morbus, neque item Dei opus, sed bene creata sunt animalia, convenienti ei præparatione, secundum naturam, & memoribus distincta in vitam prodierunt, in morbos vero secundum naturam ceciderunt, à sanitate deficientes, vel ob malam diætam, seu aliam causam, quæ corporibus accidere solet: corpus itaque Deus fecit, morbum minime fecit. Et animam similiter Deus fecit, non autem peccatum. Ita Origenes: {1}Cum statuarius imaginem effictam, auroque exornatam tradiderit, post vero rubigo, tua negligentia qui possides, eam per sequidem splendescentem exedat, ac deformet, causa in statuarium transferenda est? Sic, num Deo hominis vitium imputabimus? Nullo modo. Hoc {2}ipsis Manichæis alioqui Hæreticis innotuit satis, qui, cum malum bono quoad tempus, adæquarent, & vtrumque à principio aliquo ortum crederent, duo rerum initia statuerunt, Deum à quo omne bonum, & Dæmonem à quo omne malum profectum est. Male sane, quod Dæmonem, actionum fontem esse, actionum, inquam, non vt malarum, posuerunt, sed recte, quod supremo Numini, nullam prauì, curuique suspicionem, affigere voluerunt. Sic nec in prima prævaricatione, nec in labe ea, quæ per traducem descendit; peruersi, & immutati humani animi, reus est iudicandus Creator omnium Deus.
units.tr: 4. First, therefore, at the beginning, when the transgression was made through Adam against the divine precept, this transgression did not proceed from the holy Creator but from man and the Devil. God made man undefiled and uncorrupted, truly enjoying a free will, through which he could have stood if he had wished; and by whose power it lay in his own hands to cast himself into the pit of destruction. Satan came (who had previously fallen by the same free will) and out of his hatred against God and his creature suggested what he ought not. Thus Christ speaks to the Jews: Your father is the Devil, who was a murderer from the beginning, and did not stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own resources, for he is a liar and the father of it. Notice that Satan speaks from his own resources, and was not made so by God. He fell from the first rank in which he had been placed, and Adam too fell away through defection, just as wine, through the force of the surrounding air or the spoiling of the cask into which it is poured, takes on a too harsh or insipid taste, by which it is changed into a sour nature. He who gathered the grapes and trod the winepress is not to be blamed because afterwards the wine, by acquiring its harshness, turns from wine into vinegar; for he had left it generous and wholesome. But the defection came from elsewhere, and from outside. A son who was born of a pious and good father, and who has never seen even traces of audacity and shamelessness in his father's life, yet, contaminated by the foul morals of companions, bursts out into wickedness. That fault is not to be laid against the father, because the son has been infected with the stain, especially since by age the son has come to his own right and no longer depends on the nod of his parent; but through his excessive easiness, the young man has degenerated from the domestic example of honesty and virtue. Physicians call certain diseases hereditary, propagated to the offspring through the seed of the begetter. The complaint of the child is not unjust, who will declare that he drew his disease from the very loins of his parents, when he has felt a putrid and malignant humour within himself. But if healthy and robust parents have produced an offspring like themselves, so that he has a strong, vigorous body, full of juice and blood, yet he, by throwing himself into quarrels and fights, is wounded and so, weakened by the wound, falls down, this must be ascribed to youthful folly, not to the infection of the parents. So stands the corruption both of Satan and of Adam. It was not engendered, but acquired from elsewhere. From wine they became vinegar; from generous things, degenerate; from solid and sound things, wounded. The Creator is blameless; the creature is vicious. Basil writes excellently: Disease is not innate, nor is it a work of God; but animals were well created, and, with a preparation suited to them according to their nature and distinguished by their proper memories, came forth into life; but they fell into diseases contrary to nature, failing from health, either because of a bad diet or some other cause which is wont to befall bodies. Thus God made the body, and in no way made the disease. And similarly God made the soul, but not sin. So Origen: When a sculptor has handed over a figure carved and adorned with gold, and afterwards rust, through your negligence who possess it, eats into and deforms it, which has shone through it, is the cause to be transferred to the sculptor? So shall we impute the fault of man to God? By no means. This has been sufficiently recognised even by the Manichaeans, otherwise heretics, who, since they held evil equal in time to good and believed both to have arisen from some beginning, posited two beginnings of things: God, from whom all good comes, and a Demon, from whom all evil proceeds. Badly indeed, because they posited the Demon as the source of actions, of actions, I say, not as evil ones, but rightly, and because they wished to attach to the supreme Deity no suspicion of depravity or crookedness. So neither in the first prevarication nor in that stain which descends through the transmission of the seed is the Creator, God of all, to be judged guilty of the perverted and changed human mind.

units.la: §. Secundo dicimus; quod peccata quælibet, in Principe vel in filiis tenebrarum, non nisi Diuina toleratione, & permissione committuntur. Cui etenim Omniscientiam, & Omniprævsentiam, & Omnipotentiam tribuimus, is nesci-re, &
units.tr: §. Secondly, we say that any sins whatever, committed by the Prince or by the children of darkness, are committed only by divine toleration and permission. For whoever we ascribe omniscience, omnipresence and omnipotence to, must not be believed to be ignorant of or unaware of the actions of mortals.

units.la: 2 Augustin. contra Faustum Manich. lib. 21. Et de Hæresib. ad Quodvultdeum Epi-pham. Hæref. 66. re, & ignorare actiones mortalium, non est credendus. Qui in {k}obbam lachrymas reponit; qui passerculos obseruat in terram descendentes, qui capillorum numerum inire cognoscitur, creaturarum facta omnia probe nouit. Nihil igitur, ipso insciente contingit nedum repugnante, & auertere laborante. Dissoluit ille ausus, & conatus potentissimorum, pro suo beneplacito, Ipsum Satanam ad obsequium, ut in catena habet, quanto magis ministros, cliētesq; suos? Non sæuitia maiore, aut ferociori rabie grassantur, quam ipsi omnium moderatori visum fuerit. {m}Iudæos Haman volebat radicitus extirpare; {n}Paulum tres & quadraginta coniurati occidere cupierunt, sed obstitit Deus. Neq; alia impiorum flagitia perpetrari valebunt, nisi Deo permittente. Sic, errata, & delicta renatorum, & electorum, eo patiente fiunt. Qui Dauidem à cæde {o}Nabalis iurata cohibuit: poterat etiam à cede Vriæ eundem reuocare, & à crimine adulterij. Qui 34 {p}magistri sui negationem prædixit Petro, poterat etiā prohibere, & omnino impedire, ne abnegaret. Sed homines in proposito suorum cordium perseuerare tolerat; partim, ut reproborum iustior fiat condemnatio; partim, ut electi humiliati ex consideratione suorum lapsuum, sese cautius in posterum gerant.
